items.question: The Spanish Heir (What If Carlos II had a son?)
human_answers: I'm very interested to see how the Habsburgs continue to manage their Mediterranean and American possessions. It might be too much to hope for, but perhaps if the final decades of his reign are less frantic, he might be a little more relaxed and not outlaw the use of Nahuatl and Quechua within the administration of the American colonies. Beyond that, continuing spanish rivalry with France will be interesting- I'd assume if Spain can get it's act together they'll be looking for a return of the franche comté. But as they're not as much of a land power as Austria, they might end up losing Belgium to France. Corsica and Tuscany are also up for grabs this century, which could confirm them as masters of all Italy. In the Mediterranean, Spanish support might lead to a longer lasting Catholic Morea, whether under the Venetians or under the Spanish themselves- and given how much the spanish the like Catholicism, it might scare the orthodox within the ottoman empire into closer association with the ottoman state. Austrian-ottoman wars in the beginning of the 18th century will be altered should the Spanish coordinate with their cousins by sea- Crete, Cyprus and even Rhodes could be targets here. The age of dynastic partitions is mainly over, but one more might just be on the cards- either Castile and the colonies Vs Aragon and the Mediterranean, or Spain and the colonies Vs Italy and the Mediterranean.

Interesting introduction and POD. I love the depiction of the Battle of Vienna that allows to put some background and context for the beginning of this thread, but also creates symbolism with a "Holy Day" for the Habsburg House. It will prevent the Spanish Sucession War (or at least, delaying it for many decades as I suspect a surviving heir and sucessor for Carlos II for this thread) and many of its aftermath (for example, the true thrive of Great Britain as it was during this war they acquired Gibraltar). Carlos II's heir would however have to face the quandary his kingdom is confronted to as it was during Carlos II's reign that the decline of Spain truly began. He would however rely on the old age of Louis XIV when he will be of age to rule, which could be helpful as France remains a powerful rival and neighbour (and I spoke of it as a Frenchman).

I: The Habsburg Miracles The Battle of Vienna (1683) ​ On September 8, 1683, the nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary arrived in Vienna. On this holy day, priests, citizens, and soldiers alike poured into the churches of Vienna or failing that, their steps, and prayed. For unlike any previous nativity, this one had been one that many expected to live to see. For two months, Vienna had been surrounded by more than 150,000 Turkish soldiers commanded by the Grand Vizier, Kara Mustafa, Pasha, himself. This mighty host had cut off Vienna entirely from the rest of the Christian world and bombarded it daily while the Ottoman trenches steadily advanced upon the city. The Austrian army and band of citizens that had been left behind by their frightened Emperor Leopold numbered less than 20,000. Their situation was desperate and even their stalwart garrison commander, Ernst Rudiger von Starhemberg, could sense that the city would not survive much longer, and once the Ottomans broke through its walls everyone knew that only a bloody execution awaited every one of them. In the grips of this terrible situation, Starhemberg and the defenders of Vienna could do nothing more than pray for deliverance from the Blessed Virgin Mary. That same Wednesday night those prayers were answered when the daily signal rockets of Vienna were answered by five rockets from Kahlenberg Hill in the west. Those five brilliant flashes signaled that the relief that Vienna had long-awaited and desperately needed was presently on its way. However, on Thursday, the only banners that waved in the fields around Vienna were the banners of the Ottomans and the soldiers beneath those banners remained in place, not diverted to fight some other foe. Of greatest concern, the cannonades against Vienna slackened, which only ever happened when the Ottomans were preparing a direct attack on the city. That afternoon, with the western horizon still devoid of signs of Christendom, an explosion rocked the western defenses of Vienna when a mine cratered part of Lobl Bastion. Soon after, hundreds of Ottoman soldiers charged up the slope toward Vienna's walls to wrench Lobl Bastion out of the defenders' hands. Starhemberg's expectation of this attack meant that the breach in Lobl's wall had been stuffed with Austrian soldiers. Even after close to sixty days of unending and horrific investment, the Austrians stood strong and drove back the Ottomans twice. The toll that the Austrians inflicted on their attacks was so severe that the Grand Vizier declined sending the third assault. Afterward, Starhemberg quickly organized the repairing and retrenchment of the outer defenses of Vienna. Additionally, Starhemberg backed up these fortifications with chains and barricades in the streets and homes behind the walls. Whether the signals of the day before were true precursors to a timely relief or not, Starhemberg had no intention of surrendering Austria's capital to the enemy. Death was a more palatable alternative. Those signals had not been for naught. A relief army had been formed and was in fact on its way. For the previous two months, just a mere 20,000 Imperial soldiers had remained within touching distance of Vienna to provide the vague suggestion of relief. But over the last weeks of August, that 20,000 men had been dramatically increased to create a real army. First, came 11,000 Bavarians under the personal command of the twenty-one-year-old Elector Maximilian II Emanuel. Unlike any other contingent, even the Emperor's own soldiers, Max Emanuel and his Bavarians had not demanded some incredible subsidy upfront or alternative reward to come to the aid of Vienna. The money could wait until Austria was not in the grips of catastrophe. For now, all Max Emanuel and the Bavarians required was an opportunity to demonstrate their bravery and prove their honor by saving the beleaguered city of Vienna. Shortly after the Bavarians arrived came an army of 6,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry from the Franconian and Swabian Circles. They had only come after weeks of careful negotiation between Emperor Leopold and the Circles, which ended with Emperor Leopold agreeing to pay them a large sum for their services. Next, came 7,000 foot and 2,000 horse of Saxony, who like the Bavarians were commanded by their ruler, Elector Johann Georg IV. While the Bavarians brought with them an impressive train of field artillery, the Saxons brought an essential set of light and mobile artillery pieces. Finally, some smaller units of Germans such as that of Julius Franz of Saxony-Lauenberg added to the army. The last piece of this army was 24,000 Polish footmen and hussars led by King Jan III Sobieski. This eastern army outdid the contribution of any single Imperial prince, even exceeding the army of Emperor Leopold himself. And this number was not even all of it. Some days behind the Poles lagged thousands of the Lithuanian subjects of King Jan III. Bringing this considerable army away from the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and then all the way to the Danube had left the Commonwealth itself practically defenseless. In fact, the only defense that King Jan III could offer was a stern warning and a threat of devastating retaliation against the Ottoman partisan Imre Thokoly if he attacked the Commonwealth in the King's absence. However, putting his home in danger was without a doubt necessary to give Christendom a chance to save Vienna. Without the Poles, the Imperial army counted only 50,000 men whereas, with them, the Christians numbered close to 75,000 soldiers. Although this final number was just half that of the Ottomans, it was far better than being only a third. With a King and two Imperial Electors holding commands within this great Christian army, the threat of splintered focus and disorganized tactics was high. Although Emperor Leopold was technically superior to each of them as the Holy Roman Emperor, his previous flight from Vienna had proven that the battlefield was not where his talents lay. Fortunately, the man who Emperor Leopold gave command of his soldiers to, Duke Charles V of Lorraine, proved to be the perfect individual to navigate this multinational army's complicated hierarchy. As the exiled ruler of an occupied duchy Charles of Lorraine's only vocation for the past decade had been being an Imperial general. Through this experience managing the Austrian army's diverse officer corps, Charles of Lorraine learned how to bring an army together around a singular goal through personally connecting with each and every commander of importance. Whereas others were brash and offensive or deferential and meek, Charles of Lorraine was straightforward and easy-going, which was a welcomed ideal among soldiers and commanders alike. Quickly, Charles of Lorraine gained the confidence of the Christian army's generals and bound them to the goal of rescuing Vienna above all else. Under Charles of Lorraine's guidance, Jan Sobieski, Max Emanuel, and Johann Georg all agreed to ignore Emperor Leopold's directive that the relief army should take a longer approach through the gentle grounds to the southwest of Vienna. Instead, in their eagerness to save Vienna, the relief army determined to reach the city as quickly as possible by taking the shortest path across the rocky outcrop of the Wienerwald. With all appropriate haste, the relief army soon cut its way through the forest to Vienna's northwest and then crossed the Danube dangerously close to the Ottoman outriders. By September 8, the army had made its way to Tulln, just 22 miles from Vienna, and was readying its final approach toward Vienna. That night they sent off the signal rockets to inform Vienna of their coming and inspire just a few more days of resistance from the city. When the relief army finally entered the Wienerwald on September 9, it was confronted by an unruly wilderness that had grown out of hand since the Habsburg Emperors had denied the forest to anyone but themselves. As a consequence, the relief army lost its cohesion as it filtered through the forest and up its steep slopes. No man found comfort as he marched or rode through the crowded woods and its sprawling undergrowth, all the while thoughts of a terrible battle hung over him. To make matters worse, a German scouting party spotted Ottomans holding part of the ridgeline in the way of the army's approach. The Ottomans, however, lacked the foresight to either fortify or sufficiently man that ridgeline. This allowed the Christians to pounce on the Ottoman position between dawn on September 11 and wrest control of the ridgeline before the Ottomans could realize their mistake. Yet this victory was not complete as several Ottomans managed to escape from the skirmish and flee back to the main camp where they made the Grand Vizier aware of the relief army's imminent approach. Ottoman scouts had already revealed the relief army to the Grand Vizier two days prior to this attack on the ridge. However, the survivors of the attack were able to confirm the whereabouts of the relief army and its size, which verified the Ottoman belief that the relief army intended to come straight at them from the west and that no attack should be expected from the south where the patrols had still not encountered any Christian soldiers. The narrow geography of the Wienerwald meant that the best avenue for an attack was straight at the center of the Ottoman position. This position could be defended by a series of mannered ridges, hills, and villages. Although the Grand Vizier decided against enhancing the natural defenses provided by the topography with either trenches or palisades, the series of obstacles still presented a formidable challenge. The Christians would have to funnel themselves into multiple zones of fire and if the Ottomans held their ground then it would be a slaughter. Another set of obstacles and an even greater challenge for the Christian army would have to be overcome before they could even reach the Ottoman defenses. After the morning's victory, the Christians were able to occupy the ridge of Kalhenburg and look down toward Vienna. The maps had led them to believe that between that ridge and Vienna lay gentle slopes and clear ploughed fields. Instead, the rocky and uneven ground that had begrudged them in the Wienerwald continued on all the way to the edge of Vienna. The lines that separated the fields were not low wooden fences but haphazard stone walls and thick hedgerows that could not easily be traversed. These demarcations enclosed not open fields of crops but thick and twisted vines of unharvested grapes. Further complicating this approach was a set of deep ravines, small streams, and some scattered villages. Any of these alone was an impediment, but all of them together formed a veritable wall against an assault. As the Christians piloted this difficult terrain they would be easy targets for the Ottoman cannons and muskets. The cavalrymen high up on their horses would be particularly exposed as they slowly negotiated the convoluted ground. All in all, the Christians would have no hope of sending in straight lines of pikemen and musketeers or charging forth coherent blocks of horsemen. Instead, the Christians would have to advance slowly and carefully across the difficult ground and under heavy fire before throwing themselves against prepared defenses and ready defenders. In the face of this adversity, the Christians did not cower. They had come all this way to save Vienna and they would do their damnedest to try, even with so much going against them. However, the Christians' willingness to push on was not the result of confidence or of faith. Many Christian soldiers spent that night sleepless and unable to stomach any food. Even Charles of Lorraine was nervous on the precipice of this battle. They all understood that the likelihood of their victory was low and believed that many of their souls would depart on the morrow. It would be a red day, all they could do was hope it would not be a black day too. On Sunday, September 12, 1683, the great battle for Vienna began when hundreds of Ottoman skirmishers began climbing up the slope toward Kalhenburg and opened fire on the Christian army at around 5 am. With men dropping left and right, the Christians could not hold still and simply return fire. Instead, the Saxon infantrymen abandoned their positions and drove down the hill toward the Ottomans. The whole left flank of the Christian army joined the Saxons in this counterattack that swept away the eastern skirmishers. Although the first Ottoman attack was thrown back, the left flank of the Christian army had placed itself well ahead of the rest of the army in doing so, which left it vulnerable to an Ottoman counterattack. Charles of Lorraine took quick notice of the danger and ordered the left to slow its advance while the rest of the Christian army was ordered to catch up. Although the Saxons had dragged the rest of the army out of its strong positions along the ridge, the earlier success had inspired the men with confidence and even Charles of Lorraine could feel something. The order for a general attack was given. As the Christians crowded around the Ottoman stronghold of Nussberg, they cried out "Ave Maria!" and the Ottomans threw back "Allah, Allah Akbar!" These screams and shouts were drowned out by the overwhelming sound of muskets firing, cannons blasting, and swords clattering. The fighting was vicious and uncertain. But at that particular spot, the Christians found themselves more numerous than the Ottomans and steadily overcame their Ottoman forest. Of great importance were the Saxon light cannons that had been successfully dragged down the slope to directly fire into the Ottoman formations. Within the Ottoman camp, the Grand Vizier was well-aware of the unfolding battle and committed his reserve to saving Nussberg and holding back the Christians. However, the Grand Vizier failed to organize a larger reinforcement from other parts of the army because he could not coordinate with the various pashas and Tatar chiefs. In contrast, even with the dreadful terrain and multinational nature of the army, Charles of Lorraine had maintained decent lines and formations. Close to noon, Johann Georg's cavalry was unleashed on the Ottoman sipahis, which allowed the Saxon infantrymen to wrest Nussberg away from the Ottomans. Still, the Saxons had to fight the Ottomans for each and every house in that village. the continuance of this attack faltered as the Saxons once more overextended themselves in the chase. But once the Christians regrouped they renewed their attack and took the next Ottoman stronghold in front of them. At this point, Charles of Lorraine called for the army to hold to avoid another overextension. He needed to ensure that the army did not lose its cohesion and under the hot summer sun, Charles of Lorraine was worried about his soldiers suffering from exhaustion and thirst. This pause allowed the thousands of Polish cavalry to make their way down the slopes from the Wienerwald and toward the southern edge of the Ottoman position. With the Christian army having successfully made it down the slopes and having already broken one Ottoman position, the Christians finally found themselves at the advantage. Even though the Ottoman army as a whole was larger than the Christian one, on those fields to the west of Vienna, the Christians were superior in number. And now that they had made it down the slope, those numbers could be fully deployed against the Ottomans. Both Charles of Lorraine and Jan Sobieski could feel this shift. To the northeast, Charles of Lorraine asked the German commanders if they wished to push on or whether they should delay the battle to the next day. To the south, Jan Sobieski asked his own commanders the same question. In both councils, the answer was the same: March on. With this order shouted out, the Christians moved forward once again and pushed up to the remaining positions. In the north, the Imperial soldiers led by the Bavarians and Saxons assaulted the Ottoman formations and after an hour and a half, conquered them. All the enemies within them were slaughtered. To the south, the Poles sent a forlorn hope forth to test the Ottoman positions. Although this lonesome company was mauled by the far more numerous Ottomans, their charge still shook the Ottomans just enough for Jan Sobieski to order the entirety of his hussars and the rest of the cavalry to charge the Ottomans. When the Poles bore down on them, the Ottomans did not present themselves as the vicious conquerors of Constantinople. Instead, demoralized by the morning and afternoon's travails, the Ottomans were a disorderly mess that lacked the spirit and discipline necessary to hold against a cavalry charge. The Poles punched through the Ottomans and began to cut them to pieces. Quickly, the Ottomans lost the last of their courage and began to flee. Meanwhile, the Germans to the north continued to stomp over the Ottomans in front of them. Within the hour, the Ottoman army was broken and sent into flight. The citizens of Vienna rejoiced when Charles of Lorraine's official messenger pronounced that "Vienna was relieved". Thousands exited their homes and cried out in jubilation in the streets while others exited the city to set their eyes on their glorious saviours. Everywhere music played and tears of joy and relief painted faces. Although the army remained on alert for the rest of the night in case the Ottomans came back, all knew that no such thing would happen. By some miracle of God, an army of fewer than 75,000 men had secured a true and complete victory over an army of more than 150,000. Vienna was saved and the Ottomans were shattered [1] . While this miracle on the Danube saved Emperor Leopold from suffering the same ignominy of losing Vienna as his ancestor Emperor Frederick III, it was not the only miracle to bless the House of Habsburg on that day. More than a thousand miles away in the heart of Spain at the Royal Alcazar of Madrid, another miracle was delivered to the Habsburgs. There, after twelve hours of screaming and crying, Queen Marie Louise of Spain gave birth to the long-awaited first child of King Carlos II of Spain [2] . Better yet, she gave birth to a son who could inherit the many crowns of Spain without any dispute. Thus, Marie Louise ended nearly two decades of uncertainty over who would next possess the crown of Spain. Just as the victory over the Ottomans was celebrated by all within Vienna, the birth of a son, a crown prince, was celebrated by all within Madrid. To them, there could be no greater miracle than that which saved them from a dozen European rulers laying claim to some piece of the Spanish empire once the sickly King Carlos II's heart finally gave out. Thus, both halves of the Habsburg dynasty were saved on the fateful day of September 12, 1683. [1] This is a retelling of the historical relief of Vienna. There is no alteration to make note of. [2] This is the Point of Divergence, Marie Louise produces an heir. There is at least one rumored pregnancy for Marie Louise during her marriage to Carlos II. Unlike the rumored pregnancies of her successor Maria Anna of Neuburg, this rumored pregnancy was taken seriously and not believed to be completely chimerical. One reason for that difference in reactions was that although Carlos II was never conventionally healthy, he was far more relatively healthy while married to Marie Louise. During this time, the only believed issue with conception was his premature ejaculation. Later, when married to Maria Anna, Carlos II was suffering from increasing health issues including atrophy. Here, the suggestion is that Carlos II and Marie Louise manage to get lucky and overcome his premature ejaculation to produce an heir. Alternatively, you are welcome to believe that Marie Louise found another partner. Or even that this is a legitimate miracle from God. Either way, she has produced a child whom Spain will accept as the heir.
items.model_answer:
If Carlos II of Spain had produced a legitimate surviving son, the most likely immediate result is that the War of the Spanish Succession would not have happened in the form it did, because the central problem of 1700—the extinction of the Spanish Habsburg male line—would have been solved.

Carlos II’s death created a terrifying diplomatic question: who would inherit Spain, its Italian possessions, the Spanish Netherlands, and its vast American empire? The two strongest claimants were the French Bourbons and the Austrian Habsburgs. If a son of Carlos II existed, that son would have been the natural and legally strongest heir to the Spanish Monarchy. France and Austria might still have tried to influence Spain, but they would have had far less justification for outright succession claims.

The new king would probably have been a child, since Carlos II died in 1700 at only thirty-eight. That means Spain would likely have been governed by a regency dominated by the queen mother, high nobles, churchmen, and foreign factions. If the child were born of Carlos’s second wife, Maria Anna of Neuburg, Austrian influence at Madrid would probably have been strong. France would have worked to counter it, but Louis XIV would have found it much harder to claim the throne for his grandson Philip of Anjou while a legitimate Spanish Habsburg heir was alive.

Spain itself would probably not have been dramatically revived simply because an heir existed. The Spanish Monarchy was suffering from deep structural problems: weak finances, regional privileges, military decline, dependence on silver revenues, and an overextended imperial system. A young Carlos III of the Spanish Habsburg line might have preserved continuity, but he would have inherited a weakened state. The absence of a succession war would have spared Spain devastation, especially in Catalonia, Aragon, Valencia, Italy, and the Low Countries, but it would not automatically have restored Spain to sixteenth-century greatness.

One major difference is that there would probably have been no Bourbon Spain, or at least not in 1700. That means no Philip V, no immediate Bourbon centralizing reforms, and probably no Nueva Planta decrees abolishing the traditional institutions of Aragon, Valencia, Catalonia, and Majorca. Spain might have remained a more composite monarchy, with Castile, Aragon, Catalonia, Naples, Sicily, Milan, the Netherlands, and the American kingdoms retaining more of their older legal identities. This could have made Spain less centralized and perhaps less administratively efficient, but also less internally embittered by conquest and repression.

Internationally, the consequences would have been enormous. Britain and the Dutch Republic entered the War of the Spanish Succession largely to prevent France from controlling Spain and its empire. With a Spanish Habsburg heir, that fear would have been reduced. There might have been diplomatic pressure to keep Spain independent of both France and Austria, but not necessarily a general European war. Britain might not have captured Gibraltar and Minorca, or at least not under the same circumstances. The Treaty of Utrecht would not have occurred in the same way, so Britain might not have received the asiento slave-trade contract or the same commercial privileges in Spanish America. Savoy, Prussia, and Austria would also have gained less from the redistribution of Spanish territories.

Austria would likely have remained closely involved, especially if the Spanish heir’s mother or regency leaned toward Vienna. But Austria would not have inherited Spain outright. The worst fear of the other powers was a union of Spain with either Bourbon France or Austrian Habsburg lands. A separate Spanish Habsburg child-king would have been an acceptable compromise for many European states because he preserved the balance of power.

The largest uncertainty is the child’s health and survival. If Carlos II’s son were sickly, died young, or produced no heir, Europe would simply face another succession crisis later. In that case, war might be delayed rather than avoided. But if the son survived into adulthood and had children of his own, the Spanish Habsburg line would continue, and eighteenth-century Europe would look very different: no Bourbon takeover of Spain, no War of the Spanish Succession as we know it, no Utrecht settlement in its historical form, and a Spain that remained more Habsburg, aristocratic, regional, and diplomatically tied to Austria.

So the short answer is: Carlos II having a surviving son would probably have prevented the great succession crisis of 1700, preserved the Spanish Habsburg dynasty, and avoided or greatly reduced the War of the Spanish Succession. But it would not by itself have made Spain strong again. It would have changed the diplomatic map of Europe more than it would have cured Spain’s internal decline.

human_answers: 1 0:10 PM- He vigorously pounded at the door. Perhaps a bit too vigorous. Powell stopped to calm himself before the door to the home slid open. A black man stared back at Powell. "Sir?" "Ah. Uh. Yes. Uhm," Powell grabbed a small vile out of his pocket. "Terribly sorry, Doctor Verdi requested that I deliver this medicinal product to the Secretary," the servant blankly stared back at Powell before responding. "The good doctor had requested that Mr. Seward remain undisturbed. Mister?-" "No, no I am the doctor's personal assistant he simply forgot to hand this vile to the secretaries' son." The servant looked back into the house and then back to Powell. "If you would excuse me for just a moment-" "No! No time. I insist!" Powell knew he had pushed his luck. He pushed past the black servant and rushed inside the home and started rushing up the stairs. "Excuse me sir!" Powell looked up to see the face of Fredrick Seward. The eldest son of the man he was rushing to visit. "Ah. Uhm Mr. Seward. I must see your father I have some- Uh." The next few seconds were a blur. He and Fredrick argued some it was really going nowhere. He had a mission. He pulled out his gun and fired at Fredrick. The gun misfired. Fuck. Powell slammed the gun against Seward's head, barged through the bedroom door, pulled out a knife slashed a guard against the arm and began giving his all, right at the bedridden Secretary of State's face and neck. Powell heard his knife clanking on some sort of metal. He saw the brace around Seward’s neck that was supporting his broken jaw. In a split second decision Powell removed the brace just enough to thrust his knife into Seward's neck. [1]. He knew then that his end of the plan was accomplished. 10:15 PM- Booth knew this play. He'd preformed it before. He bet he could recite every line of Our American Cousin by heart. The audience always laughed at one line. One line that blew the roof off. Wait... Wait... Wait... "Well, I guess I know you enough to turn you inside out old gal; you sockdologizing old man-trap!" The president laughed for the very final time. Booth squeezed his index finger and... BANG . The next moments were a blur. A man jumped towards him, Booth slashed him on the arm. Seeing few other options he jumped to the stage. He felt a sharp pain in his leg, he knew he had to say something to the audience who just witnessed John Wilkes Booth's magnum opus. So, Uh. "Sic Semper Tyrannus! The South is Avenged!" 10:17 PM- Oh god. Oh god. Come on George you have the courage. Oh lord almighty. I can do it I can! Atzerodt looked towards the stairs of the hotel. Then back to that sweet sweet bar. Then to the stairs. Then to-. [2] No. No not back to that damn bar. George Atzerodt will be a name feared by the north and honored by the south! He oughta slay the traitor from Tennessee! With all the courage he could muster he rushed up the stairs of the Kirkwood House. He walked down the hall, towards the Vice President's room for... admittedly the second time. He chickened out the first. NO MATTER! He walked right up to the right door and knocked! Oh shit. Oh fuck. What have I done by god! The palm grasping the revolver in his hand got very sweaty as he watched the door knob turn and then the door open and then- BANG. 10:22 PM- "BY GOD! HAVE YOU HEARD! THE PRESIDENT'S BEEN SHOT!" "Not just him sir! I heard from my dearest that the Secretary of State was stabbed just down the road!" "No! That simply cannot be! I heard that the Vice President was slain at the Kirkwood House!" TRIPLE CALAMITY! PRESIDENT LINCOLN DECLARED DEAD BY DOCTORS! SECRETARY OF STATE SEWARD DEAD MERE MINUTES AFTER STABBING! VICE PRESIDENT JOHNSON CLINGING TO LIFE IN HIS HOTEL ROOM SURROUNDED BY FAMILY! New York Herald April 15th with it's infamous Triple Headlines ​ "The death of Seward was found out relatively quickly. He died almost immediately following the stabbings at somewhere around 10:12 the night of April 14th. Over the next ten minutes, both the president and vice president would be mortally wounded. Most congressmen present in D.C. and cabinet members would be awoken around 11:00. The timeline gets confusing around here. We know that at 1:00 AM many members of Congress convened to figure out who would succeed Lincoln, should Johnson not survive. It is not known when a consensus was reached. What is known is that there was bitter debate between many figures over whether it was to be the Senate Pro Tempore Lafayette S. Foster or the Speaker of the House Schuyler Colfax. From a couple of memoirs, however, we can gather it was never a real debate; most people there thought the radical republicans were just complaining. To them, it was natural that the head of the Senate should assume the presidency; it's the 'upper house,' of course. That said, the radical view was that Colfax ought to be president because he was the Speaker of the People's House. Eventually bringing the 1792 Succession Act forth settled the discussion ; it became clear that the Foster faction won out. From what I was able to gather, this happened sometime between 3:00 and 6:00 AM. To appease the radicals, however, a special election would be held in November to ensure the people don't have a president no one voted for. At 7:22 in the morning, President Lincoln was pronounced dead. The next day, on the 17th, as Johnson's doctors made it clearer to Congress that he wouldn't make it, preparations were made to swear in Foster. The congressmen who weren't in the initial meeting were promptly informed of the line of succession around noon on the 17th. The next day's newspapers announced to the people that Foster would be sworn in should Johnson die. At 3:44 AM on April 19th, Vice President Johnson died. At 4:24 the same morning, Lafayette S. Foster became the 17th president of the United States. (Some circles like to say that he is actually the 18th president because Johnson was president for two days, yet that is false, as Johnson was never sworn in.) Instead, those two days simply had no president at all.)" [3] - From The President No One Voted For by Kieren Hutchinson, published 1982 [1]: The first POD, in our timeline the brace deflected the most damaging knife blows. (For those unaware Seward had been in a carriage accident a few days prior which is why he was in a brace.) [2]: The second POD, in our timeline George went to get a drink to bolster the nerves. He never went upstairs. [3]: Of course OTL this interpretation of the law is not the case. But here it is. The Presidency can be vacant. Butterfly effect. Treat this as a prologue. It'll be the shortest update by far. - ​
items.original_question: Triple Calamity: What if the Three Most Important Men in the Executive Branch Died in One Night? I have never written a timeline on this site. I've read a lot of other people's timelines and I have greatly enjoyed american political history, but I never thought my knowledge base was large enough or my writing skills good enough to try my hand at writing a timeline. That said on my own in a google document I wrote an alternate history timeline (or at least a basic outline of one) for my own enjoyment. I actually think it's pretty good and I'm willing to share it. Don't feel shy to tell me if something is unrealistic, chilched or doesn't make any sense I'd be more than happy to revise and or go more in depth. Triple Calamity has the POD of George Atzerodt not losing his nerve and Lewis Powell directing his stab just a bit better. Thus Lincoln, Johnson and Seward all die on the same day. I'm sure many of you american history nerds had guessed that by the title. It's a relatively popular hypothetical I gather, but I didn't know that when I started writing . Take this as my twist. Thank you to everyone who might take their time to read my senario! Hope I can pump updates out in a timely manner! (Note from Nov 6 2025): When ever you see a sentence or paragraph marked with two asterisks * ()()()() * it is a later addition or fix.

Assuming this refers to John Wilkes Booth’s full April 14, 1865 plot, in which Abraham Lincoln, Vice President Andrew Johnson, and Secretary of State William H. Seward were all to be killed, the United States would probably not have collapsed into constitutional chaos, but Reconstruction would have changed sharply.

Under the succession law in force in 1865, if both the president and vice president died, the next officer was the president pro tempore of the Senate, not the secretary of state. That man was Senator Lafayette S. Foster of Connecticut. So if Lincoln and Johnson had both died, Foster would likely have become acting president. Seward’s death would have been a major blow, but it would not have put the presidency into the Cabinet line as it would under modern succession law.

There would have been confusion because Congress was not in regular session and the House had no sitting Speaker at that exact moment, but the Senate did have a president pro tempore. Secretary of War Edwin Stanton would probably have managed the immediate emergency in Washington, as he largely did historically after Lincoln was shot, but legally the presidency would have passed to Foster. Congress would likely have been summoned quickly to ratify the succession, investigate the conspiracy, and organize a special presidential election under the 1792 Succession Act.

Booth’s larger hope—throwing the Union government into paralysis and reviving the Confederacy—would almost certainly have failed. By mid-April 1865 the Confederacy was militarily broken: Lee had surrendered at Appomattox, Johnston was near surrender, Richmond had fallen, and Union armies occupied the South. Killing Lincoln, Johnson, and Seward would have produced panic, rage, and perhaps harsher military measures, but it would not have restored Confederate military capacity.

The biggest difference would have been Reconstruction. Historically, Andrew Johnson became president and pursued a rapid, lenient restoration of the former Confederate states while opposing strong federal protection for freedpeople. His policies helped allow ex-Confederate elites back into power, encouraged the Black Codes, and led to a bitter conflict with the Republican Congress.

Without Johnson, Reconstruction would probably have been more firmly controlled by congressional Republicans from the beginning. Foster was not Lincoln, and he lacked Lincoln’s prestige, but he was a Republican from Connecticut, not a Southern Unionist Democrat with Johnson’s racial and constitutional views. He would likely have been more cooperative with Congress on the Freedmen’s Bureau, civil rights legislation, military occupation, and conditions for readmitting Southern states. There might have been no Johnson-style veto war and no Johnson impeachment crisis.

Lincoln’s absence would still matter. Lincoln might have combined firmness with political tact better than almost anyone else. His death removed the one figure who had enough authority to restrain both vindictiveness and white Southern defiance. If Seward also died, the administration would lose its most experienced diplomat and one of Lincoln’s closest political managers. The atmosphere after a triple assassination would likely have been more punitive toward Confederate leaders, and Jefferson Davis might have faced a greater chance of execution or long imprisonment.

A special election might have elevated a national Republican figure such as Ulysses S. Grant, Salmon P. Chase, Schuyler Colfax, or another Union leader. Whoever won, the new administration would probably have been more aligned with the Republican Congress than Johnson was. That could have meant an earlier and stronger version of Radical Reconstruction.

But it would not have guaranteed racial equality or a peaceful South. White Southern resistance, Northern racism, economic exhaustion, and eventual political fatigue would still have existed. The Ku Klux Klan or similar groups might still have arisen. Land redistribution for freedpeople would still have faced enormous opposition. The long-term retreat from Reconstruction might still have happened, though perhaps later or under different conditions.

So the most likely outcome is: a terrifying but survivable succession crisis; Lafayette S. Foster as acting president; no Confederate revival; a harsher reaction against the former Confederacy; and a Reconstruction policy more congressional, more Republican, and probably more protective of freedpeople than the one Andrew Johnson actually pursued.

items.original_question: What if Umar ibn Hafsun defeats the Umayyads - Mozarab/Muladí Al-Andalus One of my favorite historical subjects to research is Al-Andalus, the Muslim-ruled realms of the Iberian peninsula that existed between the 8th and 15th centuries. A land where East met West, Al-Andalus represented a rare example of Islamic Arab rule of Western European territory, resulting in the blending of cultures, religion, knowledge, and languages that proved to be massively influential on the development of European civilization and human history as a whole. Even though it was swept out of Iberia by the Reconquista, the influence of Al-Andalus can still be felt today, through Hispanic language, culture, art, and cuisine. For example, there are many Arabic loanwords in the Spanish language, tacos have middle eastern roots, and I remember a story my grandfather would tell me about when he met Bedouin tribesmen while deployed as a U.S. Marine during the Gulf War, and while they could not understand the English language, they could understand his Spanish. In the late 9th century, the once-Caliphs of the entire Muslim world, the Arab Umayyad dynasty, ruled over the vast majority of the Iberian peninsula from the prosperous city of Cordoba. Their rule would last for 300 years, but would not be without resistance. Although they comprised a small portion of the population, the ruling class of Al-Andalus was almost exclusively Arab. Mozarabs, local Iberians who remained Christian under Muslim rule, and Muladí, Iberians who had converted to Islam, resented the discriminatory racial and taxation policies of their Arab overlords, creating a degree of instability within Al-Andalus. Born around 850, Umar ibn Hafsun was a prominent leader of Iberian resistance to Umayyad rule. Simultaneously described as being of both North African and Visigothic descent, the rogue-ish and opportunistic ibn Hafsun attracted a following of disaffected Mozarab and Muladí alike, and alongside fellow rebels such as ibn Marwan and the Banu Qasi clan, would contest Umayyad rule from his fortress, Bobastro. While he would experience much success early on, several defeats against the Umayyads, such as at the Battle of Poley in 891, as well as his conversion to Christianity in 899, in what appeared to be a bid to attract the support of the Christian King of Asturias, would weaken his following. He would fight to the very end, dying in 917, and his sons would continue his fight until 928, when Bobastro fell to Emir Abd-ar-Rahman III. Umar ibn Hafsun remains somewhat of a tragic figure in Iberian history, but he also represents a glimpse into what could have been. Had he succeeded in supplanting the minority Arab ruling class with Mozarabs and Muladí, perhaps by winning battles such as the Battle of Poley, ibn Hafsun could have ensured the creation of a stronger, multicultural and multireligious Al-Andalus. This creates an interesting scenario for speculation. Could this alt-Andalus survive for longer, perhaps even to the present? What would the society of alt-Andalus look like? Would religious and ethnic differences eventually shatter this state, or would it strengthen it, combining the best of the Christian and Islamic worlds? Would alt-Andalus fall to neighboring Christian and Muslim invaders, or would it become one of the leading powers in Europe and the Mediterranean, an even greater conduit for the exchange of trade, knowledge, and culture than the Al-Andalus of OTL? And how would this alt-Andalus impact the development of Hispanic culture, and European and world history as a whole?

If Umar ibn Hafsun had decisively defeated the Umayyads of Córdoba, the most likely result would not have been a unified “Christian Spain” centuries early, but an earlier collapse of centralized Umayyad Al-Andalus into a mixed Mozarab–Muladí political order.

Umar ibn Hafsun’s rebellion was rooted in the grievances of Muladí converts to Islam, Mozarab Christians, Berber groups, and local Andalusi elites against the Arab-dominated Umayyad emirate. If he had taken Córdoba or permanently broken Umayyad power before Abd al-Rahman III restored authority, Al-Andalus would probably have fragmented much earlier than it did historically. Instead of the tenth-century Caliphate of Córdoba, there would likely have been a patchwork of regional lordships: some Muslim, some Christian-leaning, many culturally Arabic but politically anti-Umayyad.

Ibn Hafsun himself is the key complication. He was born into a Muladí family and later converted to Christianity, which would have made his regime unusual: not a northern Christian conquest state, but an Andalusi, Arabic-speaking, locally rooted power with Christian and Muslim constituencies. A victorious Hafsunid state would probably have relied on Mozarab clergy, Muladí landholders, mountain fortresses, and anti-Umayyad towns, while still using much of the Arabic administrative and cultural framework of Al-Andalus. It would have been Christian-influenced, but not simply “Latin” or “Frankish.” Arabic language, Andalusi urban culture, Islamic law in Muslim communities, and local autonomy would likely have remained important.

The biggest immediate effect would be the prevention of the Umayyad revival under Abd al-Rahman III. Historically, he crushed Ibn Hafsun’s heirs, reunited Al-Andalus, proclaimed the Caliphate of Córdoba, and made Córdoba one of the great powers of the Mediterranean. In this counterfactual, that caliphate probably never appears. Córdoba would lose its role as the dominant political and cultural center of Iberia, and the western Mediterranean balance of power would shift. The Fatimids in North Africa might become more influential, and Muslim cities such as Seville, Zaragoza, Toledo, or Mérida might seek outside allies or establish independent dynasties.

For the northern Christian kingdoms—León, Navarre, Castile, and the Catalan counties—the situation would be both an opportunity and a complication. They would face a weakened south, so their expansion might begin earlier. But the ideological frontier between Christian north and Muslim south would be less clear if a Christian or semi-Christian Andalusi ruler controlled parts of the south. León or Navarre might ally with Ibn Hafsun’s successors against Muslim rivals, or they might try to dominate them as client rulers. The “Reconquista” would likely become less a simple north-versus-south struggle and more a multipolar Iberian contest among Christian, Muslim, and hybrid Andalusi powers.

Religiously, a Hafsunid victory could have preserved a stronger public role for Mozarab Christianity in the south. Churches and bishops might have regained status in parts of Andalusia, especially around Málaga, Ronda, and Córdoba if he captured it. However, because much of the population was Muslim by this point, any durable regime would have needed religious compromise. Forced Christianization would probably have provoked rebellion and invited Muslim counterattacks. The more plausible outcome is a pragmatic mixed state: Christian rulers or patrons, Muslim-majority towns in some areas, Arabic administration, and negotiated communal autonomy.

Long term, the most plausible result is an earlier “Taifa age” beginning around 900 rather than after 1009. Iberia becomes politically fragmented sooner. The north advances earlier in some regions, but southern Andalusi culture remains powerful and hybrid. A Mozarab–Muladí kingdom might survive for a time in the mountains and cities of southern Iberia, but holding all Al-Andalus would be difficult. Arab elites, Muslim jurists, rival Muladí warlords, Berber groups, and outside Islamic powers would all resist a Hafsunid monopoly.

So the core answer is: Umar ibn Hafsun’s victory would likely have produced a less Arab-Umayyad, more locally Iberian Al-Andalus, with stronger Mozarab and Muladí influence, no golden-age Caliphate of Córdoba, earlier fragmentation, and a blurrier Christian-Muslim frontier. It would not necessarily mean the early end of Islam in Iberia, but it would create a very different Al-Andalus: decentralized, hybrid, and politically unstable.

Containing The Interval Of Three Years CHAPTER I How Herod Was Slain By Caesar's Command at Rhodes And How Agrippa Led An Expedition Against Alexander and Aristobolus Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa ​ After the defeat at Actium, when Antony’s fleet was scattered and his legions deserted him, Octavian stood as the undisputed master of the Roman world. He did not return immediately to Italy but remained at Rhodes, where he received embassies from kings who had formerly supported Antony and Cleopatra. The rulers of Cappadocia, Galatia, Paphlagonia, Media Atropatene, Armenia, Commagene, Pontus, and Comana sought pardon by offering gifts and tribute. Octavian’s health, which was often fragile, had been weakened by the campaign. He was prone to illness in times of strain, and the war had aggravated this condition. At the same time, Italy demanded attention. Heavy taxation to fund the fleet and legions had caused unrest in several towns, and soldiers were increasingly insistent that their long-promised rewards of land and pay be delivered. At this moment Herod, king of the Jews, came to Rhodes to seek an audience. He argued that Judea was a useful link between Syria and Egypt, that he alone could restrain his people, and that his rule preserved the appearance of independence while ensuring obedience. Octavian rejected these arguments. He replied that Judea could be reduced to a province and governed by a Roman official. When Herod pressed his case further, Octavian reminded him of his loyalty to Antony and declared such conduct unpardonable. Herod appealed to the memory of his father Antipater’s loyalty to Julius Caesar, but Octavian dismissed the plea, noting that Antony too had once been a friend of Caesar before turning against him. Herod, recognizing that his throne was lost, asked only for his life and that of his family, offering the treasury of Judea in return for estates in Italy. Octavian refused. Herod was executed, denied the honors of a king. His wives were taken captive. His eldest son, Antipater schemed a plan and took his two half brothers, Alexander and Aristobolus, sons of Herod's second wife Mariamne, with him. They fled towards Judea. Octavian ordered Marcus Agrippa to march against them, subdue the country, and decide its future. Opinion among his advisors was divided. Some argued Judea should be annexed and governed as a province, like Egypt after the fall of the Ptolemies. Others preferred that a native ruler be appointed under Roman authority, believing this better to restrain a turbulent people and prevent disorder in greater Syria. Agrippa first made his way through Asia Minor, where he gathered soldiers from the client kingdoms and strengthened the coastal garrisons. Amyntas of Galatia, eager to prove his loyalty after previously aligning himself with Antony, sent large numbers of Galatian infantry. These were hardy men, accustomed to mountain warfare, and fought with long shields and spears in the Celtic manner, often serving Rome as mercenaries. From Archelaus of Cappadocia came contingents of light cavalry, skilled at swift raids across the plains, together with slingers and javelin-men drawn from the hill tribes. Deiotarus of Paphlagonia furnished additional horsemen, small in number but valued for their endurance in rough country. Polemon of Pontus contributed archers from the Black Sea coast, as well as light-armed troops familiar with skirmishing in wooded terrain. The Lycian League, though reluctant, yielded auxiliaries and a few ships, for Agrippa made it clear that refusal would mean the loss of their cherished autonomy and absorption into direct Roman rule. By these means Agrippa’s force swelled to nearly twenty-five thousand men, drawn from diverse peoples but bound together under Roman discipline and command. Crossing the Taurus mountains into Cilicia, Agrippa met Quintus Didius, governor of Syria. Didius furnished five thousand men, many of them veterans who had fought in the eastern campaigns under both Antony and earlier commanders. Though their loyalties had been divided in the past, Agrippa secured their service with promises of land and pay in Octavian’s name. He reviewed them in the plain, commending their experience and reminding them that the struggle was not against the Jewish nation, but against two reckless youths who disturbed the peace. From Cilicia he advanced into Syria. The great cities sent delegations: Antioch contributed money and supplies from its considerable wealth; Apamea sent its cavalry, long trained in maneuvers and valuable for pursuit; Syllaeus, the Nabataean toparch governing Damascus provided infantry levies and stores of grain. Local dynasts added archers from the hill country and slingers from the towns, while Arab chiefs along the desert frontier furnished light cavalry skilled in raiding and ambush. Thus Agrippa found no shortage of auxiliaries. Fear that Judea’s unrest might disturb Syria moved each city to support Rome, for the Jews themselves were not in rebellion against Caesar, but were troubled by the ambition of Herod’s sons. When he had mustered them at the Roman colony of Berytus, Agrippa addressed the assembly. He reminded them of Rome’s victories, how Antony and Cleopatra had fallen, and how Octavian now ruled as master of land and sea. “We march not against the Jews,” he declared, “but against fugitives sons of a fallen house, who stir up the multitude. They are wolves in the fold, and it is our task to root them out before their madness spreads.” Thus encouraged, the army prepared to march south towards Galilee.

PREFACE​ Paul of Tarsus ​ I, Paul of Tarsus , though aged and near the end of life, have gathered from many sources the memory of my people, that it may not be lost in forgetfulness. The last hundred years have been the turning of an age. We might have suffered much more under Herod the Idumaean , a man cruel to the Jews and false to the Romans. His desire was always to please his Roman masters, yet he brought ruin by his tyranny. But Judea was spared the rule of his sons, who would have surpassed him in cruelty, and likewise spared the return of the Hasmoneans, who filled our past with strife and infighting. I dedicate this book to those without whom it could not be written. I give thanks to my companions Anacletus and Linus, who urged me to this task, and to Clement my disciple, whose pen surpasses mine in elegance and whose labors will endure when my own are ended. I remember Theocleia of Iconium, mother of my wife Thecla, whose piety strengthened her household. I thank Tiberius Julius Rhescuporis, king of the Bosphorans, who received me as a friend in my time of need. I give special thanks to the Emperor Gaius Caesar, princeps of Rome, protector and friend to the Jews. I also honor Agrippa, lord of Judea, though still young, from whom I received knowledge of his line and the claims of his house. Many have written of Moses our legislator, of the Judges, and of David and Solomon. Few have written of those nearer to us, though their deeds have shaped our present age. For in our own days a house has risen most unexpectedly, the Nazarenes, the family of Joseph Nazarene . After Joseph came Judas Nazarene , and from Judas came Jesus Nazarene . From them arose a dynasty unlike any before amongst the Jews, a carpenter declared King and whose descendants would be instructed in the learning of Greeks and Romans, yet holding in their breasts the hearts of Israel. They were heirs in spirit to David and Solomon, though distant in blood, and they joined the wisdom of foreigners with the faith of their fathers. I do not write to flatter Rome, for many Romans have done us wrong. Let Pompey be remembered, who defiled our Temple. Nor do I write to flatter the kings of Judea, for flattery fades and truth remains. I write that the truth may not be lost, for too many accounts are filled with falsehoods. Some magnify Rome beyond measure, others condemn our people without justice. Men have put speeches in our mouths that we never spoke, turned calamities into fables, raised up one king or cast down another according to their favor, not according to truth. Though my strength fails, I have undertaken this work, believing it useful not only to our own people but also to those among the Romans who seek the truth of their allies and their subjects. It is right that the affairs of Judea be known not by rumor or by prejudice, but as they were, in order, without addition or omission. I shall tell how a Nazarene carpenter was chosen by Rome to rule the Jews, how his sons after him bore rule, and how fortune, as with all men, preserved their line in one age and tested it in another. Let no one think that I write as an enemy of Rome, for Caesar’s authority is granted by God, nor as an enemy of our kings, for they too were appointed in their time. But I will not hide the miseries of our people, nor the errors of our rulers, nor the injustices endured, for history that flatters is not history. If at times I lament our calamities, let the reader forgive me, for I am a son of Israel, and what I write with my hand I feel also with my heart. This work I offer to Romans, to Greeks, and to barbarians alike, that all may know what came to pass. It will show how from humble beginnings a line of kings was established in Jerusalem, how a widowed carpenter was made king, how rulers were judged by their deeds, and how Rome and Judea remained joined together by providence. If Jesus of Nazareth, a village craftsman and preacher, had actually become “King of the Jews,” the most likely result would not have been a stable Jewish monarchy but a rapid collision with Rome.

In the first century, “King of the Jews” was a political title, not just a religious one. Judea was under Roman domination, and Rome tolerated local rulers only if they served imperial interests. For Jesus to become king, one of two things would have had to happen: either Rome would have to recognize him as a client king, which is very unlikely given his apocalyptic message and popularity among the poor, or a Jewish uprising would have to install him by force, which Rome would almost certainly crush.

If Jesus had taken or been given the throne in Jerusalem, his movement would have changed dramatically. Instead of becoming a crucified and risen savior at the center of Christianity, he would likely have been remembered as a messianic reformer-king, closer to a new Davidic ruler than to the divine Christ of later Christian theology. The “Nazarenes” might have remained a Jewish royal and religious party centered on Temple reform, purity, justice for the poor, and expectation of God’s kingdom on earth.

This would probably have made Christianity as we know it far less likely. Without the crucifixion and resurrection as the central drama, Paul’s Gentile mission may never have taken the same form. The movement might not have broken decisively from Judaism. Instead of a universal religion spreading through the Roman Empire, the Nazarene movement could have stayed a Jewish messianic sect tied to Jerusalem and the fate of Judea.

Politically, Jesus as king would have threatened several groups at once: the Roman governor, the Herodian elite, the Temple aristocracy, and rival Jewish factions. Even if he gained mass support, Rome had overwhelming military power. A Nazarene kingdom would probably have ended like other anti-Roman revolts: siege, massacre, exile, and destruction. The Roman response might even have brought the catastrophe of 70 CE earlier.

The only scenario in which Jesus could have survived as king would be as a Roman-approved client ruler. But that would require him to compromise with imperial power, taxation, and elite politics—almost the opposite of the gospel portrait of Jesus. Such a Jesus would be remembered less as a radical prophet and more as a reforming monarch, perhaps a holy king who tried to purify Judea while avoiding rebellion.

So the careful answer is: if a carpenter from Nazareth became King of the Jews, the Nazarene movement would likely have become a Jewish political-messianic kingdom rather than Christianity. But because Rome could not tolerate an independent messianic king in Judea, that kingdom would probably have been short-lived and violently suppressed. The world would then remember Jesus not as the founder of a global faith, but as a failed or martyred Jewish king who briefly challenged Rome.

If Princess Mary Tudor, the future Mary I of England, had married Philip of Bavaria in the late 1530s or early 1540s, the biggest effects would likely have been on the Tudor succession, England’s religious settlement, and Mary’s later decision to marry Philip II of Spain.

The most plausible immediate consequence is that Mary’s status would have been partly rehabilitated under Henry VIII. Since Henry had declared her illegitimate after annulling his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, any respectable foreign marriage would have required some clarification of her rank and inheritance rights. If Henry approved the match, it would have signaled that Mary still mattered dynastically, even if he did not fully restore her legitimacy.

Philip of Bavaria was far less powerful than the Habsburgs of Spain. So if Mary later became queen, a Bavarian marriage would not have produced the same English fear of Spanish domination that surrounded her real marriage to Philip II of Spain. The Wyatt Rebellion of 1554, which was largely provoked by opposition to the Spanish match, might not have happened, or would have been much weaker. Mary’s reign could therefore have begun with less domestic resistance.

The crucial question is whether Mary and Philip had children. If they had a surviving child, especially a son, the whole Tudor succession would have changed. Mary would not have needed to marry Philip II of Spain to try to secure a Catholic heir. When she became queen in 1553, her child would have stood next in line after her. That would have made Elizabeth’s eventual succession much less likely. In that scenario, England might have remained Catholic after Mary’s death in 1558, or at least the Protestant Elizabethan Settlement would probably never have happened in the form we know it.

That would have had enormous consequences. Without Elizabeth I’s accession, there may have been no long Elizabethan Protestant regime, no same pattern of conflict with Spain, no Elizabethan privateering against the Spanish empire, and a very different English role in the Dutch Revolt. The Church of England might have been reconciled more firmly with Rome, or England might have developed a more moderate Catholic settlement influenced by German politics rather than Spanish Counter-Reformation policy.

If Mary and Philip had no surviving children, the changes would be more limited. Philip of Bavaria died in 1548 historically, before Mary became queen. If that still happened, Mary would have been a widow by the time she inherited the throne in 1553. She might still have sought another marriage, possibly even with a Habsburg prince, but she would have entered her reign with different diplomatic connections and perhaps less pressure to choose Spain specifically. Elizabeth might still have succeeded in 1558 if Mary died childless, but the political atmosphere of Mary’s reign could have been less dominated by anti-Spanish feeling.

So the short answer is: if Mary Tudor married Philip of Bavaria and had children, Elizabeth I likely would not have become queen, and England might have remained Catholic much longer. If the marriage produced no heirs, Mary’s reign would still probably have been less tied to Spain, less unpopular in foreign-policy terms, and somewhat less explosive domestically, but the long-term outcome could still have ended with Elizabeth and a Protestant settlement.

If all of Anne Boleyn’s pregnancies had come to term, the biggest likely change is that Anne would not have been executed in 1536, especially if one of those children were a healthy son.

Historically, Anne’s position collapsed because she had produced only one surviving child, Elizabeth, and then miscarried in January 1536, reportedly a male fetus. Henry VIII had broken with Rome largely to secure a legitimate male Tudor heir. When Anne failed to provide one, her enemies at court moved against her, and Henry was willing to believe—or at least use—the charges of adultery and treason to remove her.

If that 1536 pregnancy had produced a living son, Anne’s position would have been transformed. As the mother of Henry’s legitimate male heir, she would have been much harder to destroy. Henry might still have grown tired of her, and court factions would still have hated the Boleyns, but executing the mother of the heir would have been politically dangerous and unnecessary. Jane Seymour probably would not have become queen, and Edward VI would likely never have been born.

The Tudor succession would also have changed dramatically. A son of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn would probably have succeeded Henry in 1547 instead of Edward VI. If that son were still a minor, England might still have had a regency government, but it would likely have been influenced by Anne, the Boleyn faction, Archbishop Cranmer, and other reform-minded figures rather than by the Seymour family. England’s Protestant Reformation might therefore have continued, possibly with a more openly evangelical tone, but under different political leadership.

Elizabeth’s life would also have been very different. She would not have been declared illegitimate after Anne’s fall, or at least not in the same way. But she also probably would not have become queen unless her brothers died without heirs. Instead of becoming Elizabeth I, she might have remained a prominent Tudor princess, perhaps married into a major European or English noble family.

Mary Tudor’s position would have been weaker. A healthy Boleyn son would have made it much harder for Mary, daughter of Catherine of Aragon, to claim the throne. The later Marian Catholic restoration of the 1550s might never have happened. That means no reign of Mary I, no marriage to Philip II of Spain, and possibly no major attempt to return England to Roman Catholicism.

The broader European consequences could have been significant. England may have become more steadily Protestant earlier, without the sharp swings from Henry’s religious conservatism to Edward’s Protestant reforms to Mary’s Catholic restoration and then Elizabeth’s settlement. The Elizabethan age as we know it—Elizabeth’s long unmarried reign, the defeat of the Spanish Armada under her, the particular form of the Elizabethan religious settlement—might never have occurred.

However, if Anne’s additional children had all been daughters, the result would be less certain. More daughters would have strengthened Anne somewhat, but Henry’s central obsession was a male heir. He might still have sought to replace her eventually, though perhaps not as quickly or as violently.

So the clearest answer is: if Anne Boleyn’s pregnancies had produced living children, especially a son, she probably would have survived as queen, the Tudor succession would have passed through the Boleyn line, Elizabeth likely would not have ruled, Mary’s Catholic restoration might never have occurred, and the English Reformation would probably have followed a more consistently Protestant path.

If Elizabeth Tudor had married Robert Dudley in 1550, the marriage would probably have damaged her chances of reaching the throne, and it might even have destroyed them.

In 1550 Elizabeth was about sixteen and Robert Dudley about seventeen. England was ruled by her half-brother Edward VI, and Robert’s father, John Dudley, Earl of Warwick and later Duke of Northumberland, was becoming the dominant figure in Edward’s government. So the marriage would not have been a romantic private matter. It would have looked like a political alliance between Elizabeth, the Protestant heir after Mary, and the Dudley faction.

That would have made Elizabeth much more vulnerable in 1553. When Edward VI died, Northumberland tried to exclude both Mary and Elizabeth from the succession and place Lady Jane Grey on the throne. Historically, Elizabeth stayed cautious and survived. But if she had been Robert Dudley’s wife, Mary Tudor would almost certainly have viewed her as part of the Dudley conspiracy. Robert himself was imprisoned after Jane Grey’s fall; as Elizabeth’s husband, he might have been executed, and Elizabeth might have been imprisoned more harshly, disinherited, or possibly tried for treason. Her survival would have depended on whether she could convincingly prove she had not supported Northumberland’s coup.

If Elizabeth survived Mary’s reign and still inherited in 1558, the consequences would be enormous. She would come to the throne already married, so the central diplomatic question of her reign—whom she might marry—would vanish. England would lose the possibility of using Elizabeth’s marriage as a bargaining tool with Spain, France, Austria, or other powers. Robert Dudley would become king consort or something close to it, which many nobles would resent. The old aristocracy distrusted the Dudleys as ambitious upstarts, and Catholics would see the marriage as confirmation that Elizabeth’s regime was aggressively Protestant and factional.

The biggest change would be succession. If Elizabeth and Dudley had children, the Tudor succession crisis would likely be solved. A Protestant Tudor-Dudley heir would make Mary Stuart’s claim far less important and could prevent much of the later anxiety over who would succeed Elizabeth. That might also reduce the political weight of plots centered on Mary Queen of Scots. On the other hand, if the couple remained childless, Elizabeth would be in a worse position than historically: she would have given up the diplomatic usefulness of remaining unmarried without gaining an heir.

So the most likely outcome is not simply “Elizabeth marries her favorite and everything continues.” A 1550 marriage to Robert Dudley would tie Elizabeth to the most dangerous political family in England just before the succession crisis of 1553. It would greatly increase the chance that Mary I would imprison, disinherit, or even execute her. If Elizabeth nevertheless survived and became queen, England would probably become more openly Dudley-influenced, more firmly Protestant earlier, and less diplomatically flexible, but potentially more stable if the marriage produced children.
