items.original_question: Administration of British colonies in North America if the USA would have never existed? I have seen several maps of North America in alternate history scenarios where the 13 colonies lost in 1775/1776. IF England would have won, how would they have administered their colonies in North America afterwards in the late 18th, the 19th, and the 20th century? Would they have administered their colonies separately (Pensilvania, Massachusetts, Newfoundland, Quebec, "Canada?", Florida, Louisiana, Oregon etc.) or would they have united them sooner or later in a big north american british dominion? Also, would they have eventually taken oregon/nootka? what about louisiana and alaska from france and russia respectively? PS: Yes I know there are a lot of "What if the US lost the war of 1776..." threads here but this is mostly about the administration of these colonies
items.model_answer:
If the USA had never existed because the Thirteen Colonies had remained within the British Empire, British North America would probably have been administered much like Canada eventually was: first as separate colonies under royal governors, and later as self-governing provinces or a federation within the empire.

In the short term, each colony—Virginia, Massachusetts, New York, Pennsylvania, Georgia, and so on—would likely have kept its own legislature, courts, governor, and local institutions. London would have retained authority over imperial trade, defense, diplomacy, and western expansion. The Crown and Parliament would probably have tried to tighten coordination after the Seven Years’ War, especially over taxation, Native American relations, and frontier settlement.

Over time, however, direct imperial control would have become difficult. The colonies were too large, populous, and politically developed to be ruled indefinitely from London without major concessions. Britain would likely have moved toward a model of “responsible government,” as it later did in Canada, Australia, and New Zealand. That means local elected assemblies would control domestic policy, while Britain would initially keep control of foreign affairs and defense.

A plausible outcome is that the British colonies in North America would have been reorganized into a larger federation, perhaps called British North America, with provincial governments for New England, the Middle Colonies, the South, Canada/Quebec, and the Maritimes. It might eventually have become a dominion similar to Canada: internally self-governing, loyal to the British Crown, and part of the British Empire/Commonwealth.

Slavery, westward expansion, and relations with Indigenous nations would have developed differently. Britain abolished slavery in its empire in 1833, so slavery in the southern mainland colonies might have ended earlier than it did historically in the United States, though probably with major resistance from plantation elites. Western settlement may also have been more tightly regulated by imperial authorities, at least for a time, because Britain had an interest in avoiding expensive frontier wars.

So the most likely answer is: there would not have been a single “American” national administration at first. The former American colonies would have remained separate British colonies, then gradually evolved into self-governing British provinces, and quite possibly into one or more Canadian-style dominions within the British Empire.

items.question: What If the Southern Ming had survived?
human_answers: I foresee a successful Chinese expedition to retake the North within a decade or two. Sichuan was perhaps ironically where the most effective anti-Qing forces were based in OTL. Remnants of Zhang Xianzhong and Li Zicheng’s forces continued fighting there for decades until well into Kangxi’s reign IOTL. The site saw repeated struggles between different forces for many decades. It’s actually the reason for the significant decline in the population of Sichuan IOTL, not Zhang Xianzhong’s Sichuan massacre. Population wise, the Qing Dynasty would have difficulty regrowing the population of the north due to lack of food. The North has always been a basket case since the end of the Northern Song Dynasty. During the Ming Dynasty, Southern China had at least two times the population of the North. And that is before the collapse of the Ming Dynasty Which saw massive fighting. You see plenty of areas throughout Northern China eating rice as staples today, but the truth was that this is evidence for how much northerners have come to rely on Southern grain. Rice does not grow in the North, and has to be imported from the South. Before the Sui-Tang Dynasties when the Grand Canal was not built, Northern diet was based on wheat. Still is to a lesser extent today. After this period, they became increasingly reliant on Southern crops until from the Ming Dynasty onwards, they became entirely reliant on it. Northern Qing can’t just regrow when they don’t even have the rice to feed the people. As time goes on, even by the 17th century, warfare is gonna increasingly dependant upon firearms, meaning population,technology and economy is gonna become decisive in eventual Southern victory. Individual prowess of the troops that the Manchus relied heavily on will become less relevant,especially as the Qing simply does not have Manchu population to supply large armies to both stamp out rebellions or to fight the Southern dynasty. The Manchus iotl exploited a critical window before that was gonna be a problem to conquer the South.

This is what I have in mind: 1. In OTL, as I understand it, by this point the Ming dynasty’s North China had been devastated, the population had grown unevenly, and the state had come to depend heavily on Jiangnan’s grain resources. In that situation, if the Qing were to occupy only North China while the Ming retained control of Jiangnan, the Qing would likely suffer from serious food shortages. Under such conditions, I think it is highly likely that the Qing would resort to massacres in North China similar to the Yangzhou massacre seen in OTL. However, in the end, the Qing might later face the problem of overpopulation once again. Personally, when it comes to the Malthusian trap, I think the Northern Qing would suffer from it more severely than the Southern Ming. What do you think? 2. In OTL, the Dzungars were destroyed by Qing expeditions. However, in this timeline, the Dzungars would likely expand their power significantly across Mongolia and Tibet. Unlike in OTL, the Qing would probably remain largely on the defensive. As a result, the Dzungars would not be destroyed and would likely enjoy a substantial imperial existence until they were eventually conquered by the Russian Empire. Russia, too, would likely push into Manchuria more frequently and more deeply than it did in OTL. The Qing would have a much harder time containing them and would probably have to request military assistance from Joseon more often than in OTL . It is even possible that, unlike the Treaty of Nerchinsk, Russia might succeed in extracting territorial gains much deeper inside the region. And here is the next question. In your view, assuming that the Southern Ming and the Northern Qing both survived until the mid-18th century, which state do you think would collapse first? And in what ways do you think each polity would face its respective crises? First of all, in OTL, the course of the Yellow River changed in the 1850s. This could also have significant effects on China.

Why do you say they will sinicise faster? By contrast, I think they’d sinicise even slower, as they can’t hope to match the southern Ming in chineseness and so would have to rely on other pillars of legitimacy to prop up their rule, perhaps leaning further into Tibetan Buddhism. Edit- looking more into how Tibetan Buddhism had spread so deeply into Mongol society in the late 16th century, people seem to say that the Qing need to appeal to Taoist and Confucian ideologies meant they could not be called a primarily Buddhist state. Ittl, I think the Qing would lean much more heavily into buddhist kingship, and this might also make their policy towards Han people less racist- there would be a way for Han people to politically abandon the Confucian-Taoist kingship embodied by the Ming, by adopting Tibetan Buddhism, which would make them part of the ruling group without becoming Manchu. Why do you say it didn’t happen in India? As an aside, there was a mid 17th century equivalent to the treaty of Westphalia in Central Asia, the Great Code of 1640, by which various Oirat and Mongol clans agreed to act as a collective body to uphold general peace and a universal legal code, while upholding the sovereignty of the individual tribes. Otl, it became irrelevant once the Qing got rid of any form of Mongol sovereignty by defeating the Dzunghars and winning the Khalkha Mongols to their cause, but in a world where the Qing aren’t so powerful, the “Holy Mongol Empire” likely maintains its constitutional structure for longer. Instead of a Dzunghar khanate, we’d therefore talk Ming China allying with the Western Yuan Dynasty to hold back the Qing, and perhaps the federal Yuan would be more successful than the Dzunghar were otl in their wars against the Kazakhs/the Khanates of Bukhara. Or perhaps, the Qing end up functioning as the Austria analogue- personally controlling by far the most land and people, but still unable to strip away the autonomy of the various Mongol and oirat ulus’, who regularly meet and would all revolt against imperial overreach.
items.original_question: If the Southern Ming had survived? Thread 'Perpetual Brightness: Surviving Southern Ming' Apr 12, 2006 Once, the Confucian school outside Quanzhou had bustled with students and scholars. Some of China’s greatest administrators had come from there, and in its day the school had been a center of learning. But since the famines, and the Manchu invasion, the school had grown quiet. The buildings were dilapidated, with peeling paint and rotten timber. There was only one man there, in the dark of night, standing by a fire. The man watched as the flames cast a red glow over the temple, as it consumed the robes of a scholar. An Empire was collapsing outside its walls, but inside the silence was... Faeelin Replies: 168 Forum: Alternate History Discussion: Before 1900 In OTL, after an empire collapsed in China, there were many cases where it was not completely destroyed and replaced by another empire, but instead split into northern and southern regimes. Even before the Qing dynasty, the Jurchen states themselves formed a northern empire, while the Southern Song continued to exist in the south. In the 17th century, the Ming dynasty, like the Song before it, also established the Southern Ming. However, it ultimately fell after only twenty years. Was there no way for the Southern Ming to survive? The problems of the Southern Ming, as I see them, are as follows. 1. In the case of the Southern Song, all other imperial claimants were captured by the Jurchens, and as a result, a person low in the line of succession became the only remaining claimant. This, paradoxically, allowed him to secure a certain degree of legitimacy and take power. By contrast, the Southern Ming began in a situation where the legitimate imperial princes had largely been captured from the outset, while there were still too many lower-ranking imperial relatives remaining. This excess of potential claimants triggered disputes over the imperial succession. 2. In the case of the Jin dynasty, it had not yet fully subdued the Western Xia or the Mongols. In particular, the Mongols were later unified by Genghis Khan, who went on to establish the most powerful nomadic empire in history. At the time, the Goryeo dynasty was nominally a tributary state of the Jin, but it had not been decisively subdued through war. The Jin lacked the capacity to invade Goryeo and had no choice but to settle for maintaining relatively moderate relations. In other words, the Jin dynasty could not devote all of its national strength to the conquest of the Southern Song. By contrast, the Qing dynasty had already conquered the Chahar Mongols and had invaded the capital of the Joseon dynasty, forcing it into clear submission. Although the Dzungars and Russia would later enter the Chinese arena, this occurred only after the game had effectively already been decided. 3. The Southern Song was able to survive thanks to outstanding generals such as Yue Fei and Han Shizhong, who successfully defeated the Jurchen armies. By contrast, on the eve of the Ming dynasty’s collapse, Wu Sangui’s forces—virtually the only remaining elite army—defected outright to the Qing side. As a result, the Southern Ming was forced to struggle on with inadequate military strength, trapped in a situation where incompetent warlords fought among themselves in constant internal conflict. Taking these factors into account, I think that for the Southern Ming to have survived for a long time, things would have had to be different from the very beginning. “Before the fall of Beijing, the Chongzhen Emperor decides to transfer the capital to Nanjing. Abandoning Beijing, he withdraws south, and Wu Sangui’s army joins the emperor’s entourage and moves to Nanjing as well.” In effect, this would mean that the Chongzhen Emperor is “ceding North China to the Jurchens,” but even so, the southern regions would be far more securely preserved. However, he did not do so. The reasons lie here. In short, he was an “indecisive and irresolute emperor,” and as a result, instead of taking responsibility for such a momentous decision, he merely kept postponing it. What I am curious about is this: 1. If the Chongzhen Emperor were to decide on relocating the capital, what kind of POD (point of divergence) would need to occur? 2. If the Southern Ming had survived at least until the 19th century, how would East Asian history from the 17th to the 19th centuries have changed? Assuming the Southern Ming succeeded in repelling the initial Qing offensives, who would be in the more advantageous position thereafter? If the Southern Ming were to endure, how would Western powers in the 19th century approach China?
items.model_answer:
If the Southern Ming had survived, the most likely outcome would not have been an immediate restoration of Ming rule over all China, but a long-term division between a Qing-dominated north and a Ming rump state in the south.

For that to happen, the Southern Ming would have needed to overcome its real historical weaknesses: court factionalism, rival claimants to the throne, weak finances, dependence on regional warlords, and poor coordination with maritime forces such as the Zheng family. Survival would probably require holding a defensible southern line—perhaps along the Yangzi or in the Fujian–Guangdong–Yunnan coastal and southwestern regions—while maintaining naval superiority and access to overseas trade.

The result might have resembled earlier periods of Chinese division, such as the Southern Song versus the Jin, or the Northern and Southern Dynasties. The Qing would likely control Beijing, the north China plain, Manchuria, and perhaps much of the interior, while the Southern Ming would claim legitimacy as the continuation of the Han Chinese imperial line. Both regimes would present themselves as the rightful rulers of “China,” creating a prolonged ideological and military rivalry.

A surviving Southern Ming would probably have become more maritime and commercially oriented than the old Ming state. Based in the southeast, it would depend heavily on coastal trade, overseas Chinese networks, silver flows, and naval power. The Zheng maritime organization, instead of retreating to Taiwan and being defeated later, might have become a central pillar of the state. Taiwan could have been integrated earlier and more permanently into a Ming-aligned maritime sphere. Fujian, Guangdong, and the South China Sea would likely become politically and economically more important.

The Qing, meanwhile, would face a much harder consolidation. Historically, Qing legitimacy was strengthened by unifying China and presenting itself as the successor to the Ming. If a Ming court survived in the south, many Han officials, literati, monks, merchants, and military families would have an alternative focus of loyalty. The queue order and other signs of submission to Manchu rule might provoke longer resistance. The Qing would also have to maintain larger armies in the south, delaying or weakening campaigns in Mongolia, Xinjiang, Tibet, or Taiwan.

Culturally, Chinese identity might develop differently. Instead of later imagining the Qing as simply another Chinese dynasty, many people might view China as divided between a Manchu-ruled northern empire and a Han Ming southern empire. The idea of Ming loyalism would remain a living political force rather than a defeated memory. Confucian scholars in the south might preserve a stronger anti-Qing tradition, while northern scholars would be drawn into Qing service. This could produce two competing centers of Chinese classical culture.

Foreign relations would also change. Korea, which had deep loyalty to the Ming after the Imjin War, might quietly favor the Southern Ming while formally dealing with the Qing. Japan might trade more openly with a maritime Ming south, especially through Nagasaki and Chinese merchant networks. European powers—the Dutch, Portuguese, Spanish, and later British—would find a divided China easier to negotiate with but harder to dominate outright. A commercially dependent Southern Ming might be more open to foreign trade than the historical Qing, though not necessarily more “Westernizing” in a modern sense.

The long-term balance could go in several directions. One possibility is that the Qing eventually conquers the south after decades of war, but at much greater cost, producing a more militarized and suspicious empire. Another is that the Southern Ming survives indefinitely as a separate Chinese state, leading to a north–south division comparable to Korea or Vietnam in later centuries, though rooted in dynastic legitimacy rather than modern ideology. A third possibility is that the Southern Ming, strengthened by trade and naval power, eventually reconquers parts of the north during a Qing succession crisis or frontier war, though this would be difficult unless the Qing state fractured.

The biggest historical consequence would be that China would not experience the same unified Qing imperial order that shaped the eighteenth century. There might be no single Qing “High Empire” under Kangxi, Yongzheng, and Qianlong ruling from Manchuria to Xinjiang and from Mongolia to the South China Sea. Instead, East Asia would likely be defined by a divided China: a continental Manchu-Qing empire in the north and west, and a maritime Han-Ming state in the south and southeast.

In short, if the Southern Ming had survived, China would probably have entered a prolonged period of dynastic and regional division. The south would become more commercially and maritime-oriented, the Qing would have a weaker claim to universal Chinese legitimacy, and East Asian politics would revolve around the rivalry between two competing Chinese states.

items.question: What If the British won the 1812 War?
human_answers: As far as the political landscape is concerned, I think the Federalists are routed as per OTL. They'll be blamed for losing the war, even if theyre ultimately vindicated over the long haul about being right about how the war would go. The whole post-war love affair that existed OTL is going to be gone, and I think the eight years following the war are going to be politically toxic. Depending on the border shuffling, the US might lose multiple free states which will affect the long term sectional rivalry already in development. Illinois might flip to a slave state due to butterflies if the slavers back a single candidate upon the state's formation. The Virginian dynasty probably crumbles and Monroe probably stays put as Secretary of State instead of seeking the presidency. If the Battle of New Orleans doeant take place Jackson's path to power is much longer and more arduous, if he even seeks the office at all. Theres a not unreasonable chance that the capital moves to Philadelphia and stays there. America may seek to purchase Texas around the time they signed the Adams-Onis Treaty of OTL, they could afford it, and if Monroe is still Secretary of State they're probably dabbling more in that area as it was already a pet project of his. If Texas isn't purchased, I think there's going to be a greater push against annexation by the Whigs given the greater disparity between free and slave states. A lot depends on the peace treaty, though.

I would consider OTL to be a tie, and I think spin city can depict it as such at the time. I've seen threads arguing it was a USAmerican victory because Britain wasn't able to conquer them. What does winning look like? Typically, it means taking something from the loser. Since USA never gained anything during the war, there's nothing they can be forced to give back. So, it would have to be something they held prior (or had claim to). Retaking control of any of the lost colonies is largely devoid of reality. Border adjustments in Maine/Vermont/New York are on the table. Making the old Northwest part of Canada, perhaps as a Native Reserve, is a possibility. Would Britain keep New Orleans if they had taken it prior to truce and/or the rest of Louisiana? Give it back to Spain? Trade it for full control of the NW, if they haven't secured control of that already? Realistically, how much could Britain gain? But, I think OP wants to discuss political ramifications if the war ends with there being zero doubt which side won. There could be a major territorial concession which is bound to completely change the USA even if it rebounds spectacularly (such as loss of New Orleans/Louisiana), in which case political ramifications are a secondary concern. Or, territorial concessions are more limited, leaving things a bit more recognizable. A lot of things left unsettled by the ARW, are going to be settled in Britain's favor. Trade agreements may emerge also favoring Britain. Depending on the severity of the peace, politics will also be severely affected far beyond a 'USA lost, unequivocally, but otherwise everything is the same' . So, yeah, we need to know the scope of the peace. The OP needs to be fleshed out more.
items.original_question: What if the British won the 1812 War? How would this influence the US political landscape? My opinion is: 1840 Democratic (Jacksonian, pro-States´ Rights) Whig (Anti-Jacksonian, pro-States´ Rights) Federalist (Anti-Jacksonian, anti-States´ Rights)
items.model_answer:
If Britain had clearly won the War of 1812, the most likely result would not have been the reconquest of the United States. Britain was still focused on Europe and had little desire to occupy and govern the former colonies again. A British “victory” would more likely have meant a peace settlement more favorable to Britain and Canada.

The biggest change would probably have been in the Great Lakes and Old Northwest. Britain might have forced the United States to accept a Native American buffer state between U.S. territory and British Canada, especially in areas around present-day Michigan, Wisconsin, Indiana, and Ohio. This had been one of Britain’s major negotiating aims because Native allies had helped defend Canada and because such a buffer would protect Canada from future American expansion.

The United States might also have lost some territory or rights along the northern frontier. Britain could have demanded control of parts of Maine, stronger rights to navigate the Mississippi or Great Lakes, limits on U.S. military presence near Canada, and possibly restrictions on American fishing rights in the North Atlantic. Canada would have emerged more secure, and British influence in North America would have remained stronger for longer.

Politically, a British victory would have badly damaged the American Republican leadership of James Madison and strengthened critics of the war, especially the Federalists in New England. The United States might have become more cautious internationally and less confident in westward expansion. The idea of “Manifest Destiny” would likely have developed more slowly, because a British-backed Native buffer state and a stronger Canada would have blocked U.S. movement into the Great Lakes region.

However, Britain probably still would not have destroyed the United States as an independent country. By 1815, Britain was exhausted from the Napoleonic Wars and wanted stability, trade, and secure borders more than a new imperial war in North America. So the most plausible outcome is a weaker, more constrained United States; a stronger Canada; greater protection for Native nations in the interior; and slower American expansion westward—not a return of America to British rule.

items.question: What If the English Armada of 1589 had succeeded in destroying Spain's remaining Atlantic fleet and triggering a Portuguese revolt?
human_answers: Actually, I think one could argue the opposite: that it's magically deterministic to assume that, in some unspecified way, this crisis will send the whole country into a downward spiral that will lead to its implosion. I mean, once you go over the list of changes, there isn't too much difference: yes, the Spanish Navy has been severely damaged; yes, Portugal has become independent; yes, Spain has lost all its possessions in Europe that are outside the Iberian Peninsula... but really the only significant difference from OTL is that Portugal became independent earlier, the burden that the Netherlands represented is now "someone else's problem," the remaining Spanish Navy is much smaller, and now Portugal has very serious reasons to hate England for keeping the Azores "because we can." The American Empire remains intact, it is doubtful that the English will be more successful in appropriating anything than in OTL, and they are possibly too busy antagonizing someone else once they see that the possibility of another Invincible Armada is not going to happen in the near future. OTL Spain recovered from that, even if 200 years later they declined for other reasons, but this alone should not condemn them to failure.

Spanish resilience at the time was incredible, considering how Philip II expended so many resources on fronts that ultimately yielded no tangible gains beyond preserving his honor (which was the sole reason he remained in the Flanders War). Even if England were to seize the Azores, I do not believe this would satisfy the Portuguese nobility and bourgeoisie—the main factions Antonio, Prior of Crato, would need in order to legitimize his rule. Furthermore, if Spain was able to rebuild a second fleet within two or three years—not as large as the first, but still significant—we must not forget that while the English might capture a treasure fleet, they could not always be expected to capture all of them. If there was one defining trait of Spanish admirals regarding their treasure fleets, it was their elusiveness. Even so, a Spain under Philip II, burdened by numerous problems, could compel Philip III to reconsider his policies and explore the possibility of a genuine peace with the Dutch Republic—something that could ultimately benefit Spain in the long run.

While I agree the OP is going way too far and too fast, I'd say 1589 had the potential to screw Spain over far worse than it did in OTL. I'd say your best POD is probably for Antonio to die on the way to the Iberian Peninsula, but too late for the fleet to turn back. To get out of that pickle, Drake and Norris opt to just try to do as much damage to Spain's fleet and resources as they can. In that they proved far more successful than in OTL, even temporarily occupying some of the Azores and capturing the treasure fleet. Spain has even more money problems than in OTL. The rebuilding of the Spanish fleet is an even bigger task than in OTL, and the Royal Navy does start to gain a reputation for invincibility. In France, Henri III's OTL assassin made his attempt when the Royalists celebrated the English successes, and the butterflies ensured Henri III survived ITTL. Henri III retakes Paris, and the wheel starts to come off the Catholic League significantly earlier than OTL, especially since the retaking of the capital is quickly followed by Henri of Navarre also winning the ITTL version of the battle of Arques. Spain is stuck providing far more resources to sustain the elements of the Catholic League than it had to in OTL until significantly later, when it has less resources available in the first place. And all over the Western World, the Habsburgs' enemies are taking heart... Colapse might be too strong a word but the ruin of Philip II's continental ambitions would probably come earlier, and cost more to Spain in the long run, than in OTL.
items.original_question: What if Spanish "collapse" in 1589 One of the most famous failures in modern European history, the 1588 Spanish Armada destroyed a big part of the Spanish naval forces, and was a major humiliation for Philip II. Yet England, one year later, completely blew its chance to fully wreck the Spanish by launching the ill-fated English Armada, which sought three main objectives: 1) Destroy the remaining Atlantic fleet of Spain 2) Incite a rebellion in Portugal against Philip II 3) Seize the Azores and turn it into a permanent English possession It failed in all of these objectives. Yet, the POD is not a minor or major decision, it is simple: somehow England succeeds. The remaining fleet of Spain that survived the 1588 Armada is destroyed in a series of naval battles, a landing is made in Portugal and António Prior of Crato is installed King of Portugal, starting a Portuguese Restoration War 50 years before OTL, and finally England manages to seize the Azores from Philip II's forces. Say that the Spanish naval forces are completely obliterated by the English; Portugal gains independence from Spain in 1590 with heavy English backing; the Azores (through negotiation with Portugal) become a English territory. What would happen with England, Spain, Portugal and the rest of Europe? How might the colonization of the New World be altered by a successful English Armada? Let's not get into details on **how** this happens, but assuming that it just does happen
items.model_answer:
If the English Armada of 1589 had destroyed Spain’s remaining Atlantic fleet and set off a serious Portuguese revolt, the most likely result would have been a major strategic defeat for Philip II and a much weaker Spanish position in the Atlantic, but not an immediate English “victory over Spain” or a sudden collapse of the Spanish Empire.

The immediate consequence would have been the loss of Spain’s ability to project naval power in the Atlantic for several years. After the 1588 Armada, Spain was damaged but not destroyed; historically it rebuilt quickly enough to continue the war. If Drake and Norris had instead wrecked the surviving Atlantic fleet and captured or neutralized key Portuguese ports, Spain would have faced a much deeper crisis. Its communications with the Americas, its treasure fleets, and its support for operations in the Netherlands would all have become more vulnerable. English and Dutch privateering would likely have intensified, and Spain would have had to divert money and manpower away from Flanders, France, and imperial defense to recover Portugal and rebuild its navy.

A Portuguese revolt would have been even more dangerous. Portugal had been united with Spain since 1580 under Philip II, but the union was resented by some Portuguese factions, especially those attached to the defeated claimant Dom António, Prior of Crato. If an English landing had helped spark a successful uprising in Lisbon or other major ports, Spain could have lost not only Portugal itself but also access to Portuguese naval infrastructure, pilots, Atlantic bases, and parts of the Portuguese overseas network. The Azores, Madeira, Brazil, West African forts, and Indian Ocean routes would suddenly become contested.

Still, the revolt’s success would depend on whether Portuguese elites joined it. Dom António had some support, but many nobles and merchants had accepted Habsburg rule because it offered stability and access to Spanish markets. An English-backed restoration might have seemed to some Portuguese Catholics like foreign Protestant intervention rather than national liberation. So the revolt could succeed militarily in the short term but remain politically fragile unless it quickly attracted broad Portuguese backing.

If Portugal did break away in 1589, England would probably gain a powerful diplomatic and naval advantage. It might secure Portuguese ports for resupply, trade, and privateering, especially Lisbon or the Azores. This would make Spanish treasure fleets harder to protect and give England a forward Atlantic position. The Dutch would also benefit, because Spanish pressure in the Low Countries would weaken. The Dutch Revolt might have stabilized earlier, and the eventual independence of the Dutch Republic would become more likely and perhaps faster.

Spain, however, would still not be finished. Castile remained wealthy by European standards, the American empire would still exist, and Philip II had large armies and administrative depth. Spain could rebuild ships, defend the Caribbean, and attempt to reconquer Portugal. The war might shift from a failed English raid into a long Iberian conflict, with England forced to finance troops, fleets, and subsidies to keep Portugal independent. That could become very expensive. Elizabethan England was not well equipped for sustained continental-style war, and its state finances were limited compared with Spain’s.

The biggest long-term change would likely be the earlier weakening of Spanish Atlantic hegemony. A successful 1589 campaign might prevent Spain from recovering the initiative after 1588. It could reduce Spanish ability to invade England or Ireland, lessen pressure on the Dutch, and open the Atlantic world sooner to English and Dutch expansion. Portuguese overseas possessions might remain under a restored Portuguese crown, but they would be more exposed to English and Dutch commercial penetration. Brazil, West Africa, and Asian trade routes could become arenas of earlier competition.

In European politics, Spain’s prestige would suffer badly. Philip II’s image as the great Catholic monarch would be damaged by losing Portugal only nine years after acquiring it. France’s Catholic League might receive less effective Spanish support, making Henry IV’s consolidation of power easier. The balance of power in western Europe would tilt away from Spain earlier than it did historically.

So the most plausible outcome is not an English conquest of Iberia or the destruction of the Spanish Empire, but a major acceleration of Spain’s relative decline. England and the Dutch Republic would gain strategic breathing room; Portugal might regain independence decades before 1640; Spanish naval recovery would be delayed; and the Atlantic would become a more open, contested space much earlier. The result would be a weakened Habsburg Spain, a stronger anti-Spanish coalition, and probably an earlier shift toward the English and Dutch maritime expansion that historically became clear in the seventeenth century.

items.original_question: What if Britain pursued a more hostile stance against the American Colonies following the Boston Tea Party, going on the offensive in 1774? As the title suggests, I've been trying to figure out what an earlier beginning to the American Revolutionary War might entail. As to how this happens specifically, military action was advocated as soon as news of the tea party reached London by some hard-line MPs such as Germain OTL. Some thoughts: - This happens before the Continental Congress even assembles, so everything might happen much more hastily. There probably is much less wrangling over things like sending an olive branch to the King and instead a more decisive stance taken on independence. - With the states forced to pick sides immediately, I think it's highly likely that Georgia remains decidedly loyalist, which has very interesting implications for the US post-independence Other than that, my knowledge on the American Revolutionary War is very much limited and it'd be great to have some input on this scenario. Cheers!
items.model_answer:
If Britain had responded to the Boston Tea Party by going openly on the offensive in 1774, the most likely result is that the American Revolution would have begun earlier, with a harder and broader colonial reaction, rather than Britain quickly restoring control.

In reality, Britain’s response was already severe: the Coercive or “Intolerable” Acts closed Boston’s port, altered Massachusetts’s charter, expanded royal authority, and allowed troops to be quartered more easily. But Britain still hoped that punishing Massachusetts would isolate radicals and frighten the other colonies back into obedience. If instead London had chosen a more aggressive policy—arresting colonial leaders, imposing martial law, seizing arms, dissolving assemblies, expanding military occupation, or launching punitive expeditions into the countryside—it would probably have destroyed the remaining space for compromise.

The immediate effect would have been to radicalize Massachusetts even faster. By 1774, local committees, militias, and provincial networks were already forming. A British offensive to disarm the countryside or arrest figures such as Samuel Adams and John Hancock would likely have produced armed resistance before Lexington and Concord occurred in April 1775. The first battles might have happened in late 1774 instead.

A harsher offensive would also have made it harder for moderate colonists elsewhere to argue that the dispute was only about taxation or constitutional rights within the empire. Many colonists outside Massachusetts were suspicious of Boston’s radicals, but they were even more suspicious of a British army being used to crush a colonial population. If Britain had used force in 1774, the First Continental Congress would probably have been more militant, colonial boycotts more intense, and preparations for war more urgent.

That said, an early British offensive might have had some short-term advantages. If Britain had moved quickly enough, it might have seized key powder stores, arrested some Patriot leaders, occupied Boston more tightly, and disrupted early resistance networks. The Patriot movement in 1774 was still not fully organized as a continental military effort. There was no Continental Army yet, no Declaration of Independence, and no French alliance. A decisive early strike might have delayed coordination among the colonies.

But Britain’s deeper problem would remain: it did not have enough troops in North America to occupy and pacify the countryside. British power was strongest in ports and along navigable waterways. Patriot strength lay in local institutions, militias, town meetings, committees of correspondence, and popular mobilization. Even if British forces won early tactical successes, harsh repression would likely have driven more colonists into resistance and made loyal neutrality harder to maintain.

A more hostile British policy would also have damaged loyalist prospects. Loyalists were important, but many depended on the perception that Britain represented law, order, and constitutional stability. If Britain appeared to be ruling by coercion and military force, some moderates who might otherwise have remained loyal would have shifted toward resistance or at least refused to support the Crown actively.

The timing of independence might have changed. The colonies might not have declared independence immediately in 1774, because many still hoped for reconciliation. But if British offensives produced bloodshed earlier, the psychological break with Britain would likely have come sooner. Instead of Lexington and Concord becoming the trigger in 1775, a 1774 crackdown could have served the same function.

Internationally, France probably would not have intervened right away. France waited until the rebellion proved durable and until American independence became a plausible anti-British opportunity. An earlier war in 1774 might initially have left the colonies more isolated. But if the conflict dragged on, French interest would still have grown, especially if Britain became bogged down militarily.

So the most plausible counterfactual is not a quick British victory, but an earlier and more bitter war. Britain might have gained some early advantages by striking before the colonies were fully organized, but a more hostile stance would likely have unified the colonies faster, strengthened radical arguments, weakened moderates, and made reconciliation far less likely. In the long run, offensive repression in 1774 would probably have accelerated the path toward full-scale revolution and independence rather than preventing it.

Leading up to WW1, moat of the communist parties of the great powers were following the line of the second international, and therefore we're unable to seize power, the exception being of course the Russians. I think the stickiest element here is the combo of ideology and great/superpower status necessary to mimic the Soviets. I do agree to some extent. Germany and France, though geopolitically disadvantaged, both demonstrated explosive potential for modernization. I think Tsarist Russia was the only country able to become a truly 'marxist' superpower. And even they immediately morphed into a 'Marxist-Leninist' and eventually 'Stalinist' one-party state. If for some reason the Russian Revolution never happened, failed, or never became 'Marxist', Marxism as we know it would remain a political philosophy rather than an ideology, although it would be embraced by various socialist or workers-right parties in the various European parliamentary systems. One-party state with the one party adhering to Chinese-style communism. Before that, any country where the Socialist/communist parties gain a majority in the democratic parliament would be the 'communist' world leader, be it Labour Britain, France, Weimar Germany or even a USA with a pro-labour pro-social(ist) president.
items.original_question: If not Russia, which country could have become the Soviet Union? In OTL, the Soviet Union was essentially the leader of communism, the state that embodied and exported the ideology. In France, after the birth of the “first republic in Europe,” the country faced massive wars against the old Western monarchies. As a result, although Napoleon, an extraordinary hero, almost succeeded in conquering Europe, France ultimately fell. Soviet Russia also faced a similar crisis. After the October Revolution, the first communist state was born, and the great powers, much like the monarchies a century before, sought to destroy Soviet Russia. However, unlike France, Soviet Russia survived the Russian Civil War. Afterward, the Soviet Union was no longer simply "Communist State A." They developed the potential of the land that was Russia. They transformed the underdeveloped economy of the Russian Empire into one of growth. Using that newfound capability, they exported revolution to various countries around the world. From Eastern Europe to Asia, the surrounding countries of Russia were all affected by communism. Furthermore, after 1945, they became a superpower alongside the United States, exporting revolution globally. Let’s consider a historical counterfactual. After Alexander II, the imperial succession changed. Unlike in OTL, Tsarevich Nicholas survived, and instead of the reactionary Alexander III, he ascended the throne. This alternate Nicholas II continued the reforms initiated by Alexander II, complementing, improving, and strengthening them. Unlike in OTL, Russia underwent a different trajectory. The Russian Empire was preserved, and Soviet Russia never came into being. In this scenario, which country could have replaced the Soviet Union? Which nation would need to become communist in order to "survive against surrounding capitalist powers" and "become a great power capable of exporting revolution?" Sometimes, in alternate history works (especially in game mods by Paradox Interactive), there are many timelines where a socialist revolution occurs in a country other than Russia. However, in my view, it’s questionable how many countries could do what the Soviet Union did. France? Germany? They have many geopolitical enemies. Even if they were to become communist after World War I, could they, like the Soviet Union, export revolution worldwide and become a superpower? It seems more likely that they would struggle just to survive. Britain, the United States? In OTL, Marx argued that a sufficiently developed capitalist system was necessary for a communist revolution to occur, with Britain being his example. Britain was also the world’s leading superpower at the time. However, a communist revolution did not occur in Britain. Because capitalism was so advanced, ironically, the entrenched privileges of the system were also too strong. British socialists who advocated for a revolutionary overthrow of the system did not have the power to challenge the entrenched elites, while others accepted the system and sought reforms within it. Ultimately, the conditions I believe are necessary for a "Soviet candidate" are as follows: 1. Geopolitically, it must be easy to defend. The country should be able to secure its borders and have a strategic position that allows for long-term survival and expansion. 2. It must have the potential to become a great power. The country needs the necessary resources, population, and industrial capacity to rise as a major global player. 3. Capitalism cannot be overly developed, and the elites must be driven toward 'system overthrow' rather than 'system compliance.' There must be enough dissatisfaction with the existing system to foster a desire for revolution, not merely reforms within the system. These are the core elements for a country to replicate the role of the Soviet Union. Where, besides Russia, could there be a land or country that fits these conditions? As a side note, it doesn’t necessarily have to be pure communism in this alternative Soviet ideology. It could be something like Maoism, syndicalism, or a unique form of socialism tailored to the needs of that country.
items.model_answer:
Strictly speaking, no other country could have “become the Soviet Union” in the same way, because the USSR was built out of the collapse of the Russian Empire and was dominated by the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic.

But if the question is asking which country was the most plausible alternative center of a Soviet-style communist state, the best answer is Germany.

After World War I, Germany had many conditions that Marxists thought made socialist revolution likely: a large industrial working class, severe wartime defeat, economic crisis, workers’ councils, and revolutionary uprisings such as the Spartacist revolt and the Bavarian Soviet Republic. Lenin and the Bolsheviks actually expected revolution in Germany to be crucial; they did not originally imagine isolated socialism in backward Russia as the ideal outcome.

If a communist revolution had succeeded in Germany around 1918–1923, Germany could have become the center of a powerful “Soviet” federation in Europe, possibly inspiring similar regimes in Austria, Hungary, Poland, or elsewhere. It would not have been the USSR as historically known, but it could have been the main communist superstate instead of Russia.

If the choice is limited to territories of the former Russian Empire, then Ukraine is the closest alternative, because it was populous, agriculturally rich, and industrially important. But Ukraine lacked Russia’s size, army, political center, and imperial administrative inheritance, so it was much less likely to replace Russia as the core of a Soviet Union.

items.question: What If the Alans had formed a lasting kingdom in Europe?
human_answers: Yeah, Medieval Europe in a lot of ways was already influenced by steppe culture like the Huns, Magyars, Avars. This is most obvious in the way these cultures introduced the stirrup and revolutionized cavalry warfare in the political and social structure. IMO knighthood would probably not have developed in its recognizable form without these cultures. I guess what I was thinking is that with the Alans, it wouldn’t just be inherited bits and pieces . A stable Alan kingdom could’ve institutionalized that heritage in law, military organization, and diplomacy in ways that a post-Hunnic and Avar kingdom probably wouldn’t. And yeah, I didn’t mean “Zoroastrian” in the sense of fire temples and Avesta orthodoxy. More like echoes of older Iranian cosmology or ritual that might’ve persisted under the surface alongside Christianity, at least in the early centuries. Basically, I think the difference is between having remnants of a steppe culture floating around versus having it as the living core of a political state right in the middle of medieval Western Europe. That alone could’ve made for a noticeably different flavor in the region’s history.

Looking at the map I wonder if we would see the Alans have their focus in what is Portugal especially when the Muslims go a-conquering. Also I wonder with this arrangement would we see a Alanic-Latinite language develop since it does seem that the elite would speak Alanic while the lower classes would speak some flavour of vulgar latin. A scenario where high register words that the ancestral Alans cared about, like rulership (leader, group meeting, horse, that kinda stuff) and normal stuff stays roughly Hispanic. items.original_question: What if the Alans had formed a lasting kingdom in Europe? Most people normally associate the Völkerwanderungen period with the mass migration of Germanic tribes into the Roman frontiers. But a large number of non-Germanic people also joined these groups. One of them were the Alans an Iranian people who crossed the Rhine in the winter of 406 along with the Vandals, Suebi, Goths Burgundians etc. and fanned out into Roman Gaul . They would eventually form a kingdom in North Africa alongside the Vandals. But what if Instead of getting absorbed by the Vandals and the Franks, and disappearing into history, they had actually carved out a stable kingdom, say in southwestern Gaul ? What would that look like? An equestrian -based kingdom with a mix of Iranian steppe traditions and local Roman and Germanic culture. Their language and customs might’ve stuck around longer, even mixing with early medieval Christianity or holding onto some older beliefs. I think that this Alan kingdom could’ve complicated Frankish expansion, maybe even keeping Charlemagne from totally dominating Western Europe or at least delaying it? Their military skills might have decided the outcome in battles and diplomacy, and their cultural blend could’ve made medieval Europe way more diverse , for example maybe in unique artistic terms, linguistic influence and traditions. They don't necessarily have to dominate Europe, but form a lasting kingdom long enough for their language, culture, military tradition, religion to make an impact. The whole medieval map could’ve looked very different, and who knows, maybe Zoroastrian-inspired beliefs and horse culture would still echo in some French villages today.
items.model_answer:
If the Alans had formed a lasting kingdom in Europe, the most likely result would have been the emergence of another post-Roman successor state, comparable to the Visigothic, Burgundian, Frankish, or Lombard kingdoms, but with a steppe-Iranian ruling tradition.

The Alans were an Iranian-speaking nomadic people related to the Sarmatians. In actual history, groups of Alans crossed into the Roman Empire in the early 5th century, moved through Gaul and Iberia, and were eventually absorbed by stronger peoples, especially the Vandals and Visigoths. A lasting Alan kingdom would therefore most plausibly have arisen in Gaul, northern Spain, or along the Danube frontier.

Politically, it would have changed the balance of power in western Europe. If an Alan kingdom had survived in Gaul or Iberia, the Visigoths might have been weaker or confined to a smaller territory, and the Franks might have faced a stronger rival during their expansion. A durable Alan state in Spain could have prevented or delayed Visigothic dominance there. A durable Alan state in Gaul could have complicated the rise of the Frankish kingdom and perhaps produced a more fragmented western Europe.

Culturally, the kingdom would probably have become Romanized and Christianized over time. Like the Franks or Visigoths, the Alans would have ruled over a largely Latin-speaking, Roman provincial population. Their own Iranian language and steppe customs might have survived among the warrior aristocracy for several centuries, but unless the Alan population was very large, Latin or later Romance languages would likely have prevailed. The result might have resembled Hungary in a broad sense: a state founded by steppe-origin warriors that eventually became part of Latin Christendom while preserving a distinct origin myth and aristocratic identity.

Militarily, an Alan kingdom could have strengthened the role of heavy cavalry in western Europe earlier and more visibly. The Alans were famous horsemen, and their traditions might have influenced aristocratic warfare, cavalry tactics, and possibly the later culture of mounted nobility. Medieval chivalry would not have been “Alan” in any simple sense, but an enduring Alan elite could have added a stronger Iranian-steppe element to western military culture.

One major consequence might involve North Africa. In real history, the Alans were tied to the Vandals, who crossed into North Africa and captured Carthage in 439. That was disastrous for the Western Roman Empire because Africa was a major source of grain and tax revenue. If a strong Alan kingdom had remained in Europe and weakened or diverted the Vandals, the Vandal conquest of North Africa might not have happened, or might have been delayed. In that case the Western Roman Empire could have survived longer, or at least collapsed differently. The Byzantine reconquest under Justinian might also never have taken the same form.

Religiously, the Alans would probably have adopted Christianity for legitimacy. If they became Arian Christians like many Germanic successor kingdoms, they might have faced tension with the Catholic Roman population. If they adopted Nicene Catholicism early, as the Franks eventually did, they could have integrated more smoothly and become a powerful long-term kingdom.

In the long run, a lasting Alan kingdom would probably not have made Europe predominantly Iranian-speaking or radically non-Roman. The deeper structures of post-Roman Europe—Christianity, Roman law, Latin literacy, landed aristocracy, and local agrarian society—would still have shaped it. But Europe’s ethnic and political map would have been noticeably different. Instead of the Alans surviving mainly in the Caucasus as ancestors of the Ossetians, there might have been a medieval “Alania” in western or central Europe, remembered alongside Francia, Gothia, Burgundy, and Lombardy as one of the major successor kingdoms of Rome.

items.original_question: What if Partition of the Austrian Netherlands in the 18th Century? Hi, everyone. This is my second post sharing some lesser-known yet fascinating PoDs in European history. I stumbled upon a historical academic journal written by Frederik Dhondt, a history professor from the Ghent University in Belgium titled " So Great a Revolution’: Charles Townshend and the Partition of the Austrian Netherlands, September 1725 " (2012, Journal of Low Countries Studies). According to the article, Charles Townshend, the British Northern Secretary (equivalent to the Foreign Minister) and his predecessor James Stanhope (†. 1721) had proposed a partition of the Austrian Netherlands. The plan would see Austria surrendering its holdings in the Low Countries. The article summarised three possibilities. Some background before moving on. In the Nine Years' Year and the War of the Spanish Succession, Austria had allied with the Dutch Republic and Great Britain (or England-Scotland before 1707) to counter French ambitions in the Low Countries and the Rhineland. Towards the end of the Spanish Succession War, Britain became weary of increasing Austrian power. In 1716, it allied with France. The Austro-Spanish alliance confirmed by the Treaty of Vienna rang alarm bells in London. Not only did it reconcile the enmity between Emperor Charles XI and King Philip V, the combined power of Spain and Austria threatened the established balance of power. There were even talks to marry Maria Theresa to Don Carlos (future Charles III). Prime Minister Walpole and Townshend, therefore, desired to weaken the power of Austria. These plans were never made public, Townshend only discussed them with the ambassador in Paris, Horace Walpole. On page 56, Townshend suggested the partition plan could be implemented if the marriage between Maria Theresa and Don Carlos took place. James Stanhope first suggested that the Duke of Lorraine could receive Austria Netherlands. Alternatively, Stanhope suggested awarding it either to the Elector of Cologne or the Elector of Trier. The Electorate would be secularised. Townshend outright dismissed these ridiculous ideas, and offered his own solution. The Dutch will annex some territories including Antwerp. Ypres, Bruges, and Ostend would fall under joint Dutch-British control while the inland and southern portions of the Austrian Netherlands will go to France. What will be the geopolitical and diplomatic consequences of one of these plans was realised? Although I personally doubt the likelihood of this happening, nevertheless the ramifications will be interesting. You can access the article here through your university: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1179/0309656411Z.0000000002 .

If the Austrian Netherlands had been partitioned in the 18th century, the most important consequence would likely have been the disappearance of the later “Belgian” political space before it could become a modern nation-state. The region that became Belgium in 1830 existed partly because the southern Low Countries remained administratively connected under Habsburg rule, then under France, then under the United Kingdom of the Netherlands. A partition would have broken that continuity.

The most plausible moment would have been the 1780s, when Emperor Joseph II considered exchanging the Austrian Netherlands for Bavaria. If the great powers had accepted some partition or exchange, Austria would have withdrawn from the Low Countries and concentrated more on Central Europe. That would have made the Habsburg monarchy more German and Danubian in orientation, and less involved in western European buffer politics.

For France, a partition would have been tempting but dangerous. If France received Flanders, Hainaut, Namur, or Brabant, it would have pushed the French frontier north and east, possibly to the Scheldt or Meuse. That would have given France richer cities, ports, and industrial districts, but it would also have alarmed Britain, the Dutch Republic, and Prussia. Since the Austrian Netherlands were meant to serve as a barrier against French expansion, any French acquisition there could have triggered an earlier anti-French coalition, even before the French Revolution.

For the Dutch Republic, gaining parts of the Austrian Netherlands would have looked strategically useful but politically difficult. The southern provinces were largely Catholic, more populous than some northern provinces, and economically distinct. Incorporating them into the Protestant-dominated Dutch Republic might have produced severe internal tension. In effect, the problem that later weakened the United Kingdom of the Netherlands after 1815 could have appeared decades earlier.

For Prussia, a share of the region would have been less geographically natural unless connected through the Rhineland or Liège area. But Prussian involvement would have strengthened its position in western Germany and accelerated the rivalry between Prussia and Austria. A partition that compensated Austria elsewhere, especially in Bavaria, would also have intensified the Austro-Prussian struggle over leadership in the German world.

The French Revolution and Revolutionary Wars would also have unfolded differently. Historically, revolutionary France invaded and annexed the Austrian Netherlands in the 1790s. If the region had already been divided, France might have had less of a single obvious target, but any French-held portion would have become a forward base, while any Dutch or Prussian-held portion would have become a battlefield. The wars might still have reached the Low Countries, but the diplomatic justification and military geography would have changed.

The long-term result would probably have been no independent Belgium in 1830, or at least a very different one. Flemish areas might have been absorbed into France or the Netherlands; Walloon industrial districts might have been French, Prussian, or attached to a smaller buffer state; Luxembourg might have remained tied more closely to German politics. Brussels might not have emerged as the capital of a unified Belgian state.

So, in broad terms, a partition of the Austrian Netherlands would have weakened Austria’s western role, strengthened whichever powers received territory, made the balance of power in northwest Europe more fragile, and likely prevented the later creation of Belgium in its familiar form. It could have brought short-term diplomatic convenience, especially for Austria, but at the cost of making the Low Countries an even sharper point of rivalry among France, Britain, the Dutch, Prussia, and Austria.

EPISODE THREE​ German Pact ​ ​ A sudden storm breaking out across Europe had created a massive shockwave. Austria, still struggling to recover from the economic and military wounds of the War of the Second Coalition, was deeply displeased by France’s abrupt rekindling of hostilities. Emperor Francis II had been expecting a long period of peace, one he intended to devote to revitalizing Germany. Unfortunately, history had once again disappointed him. His federalist ambitions had not yet completely faded, but this meant confronting French republicanism earlier than anticipated. Moreover, following the referendum held on 18 February 1803 and the subsequent election, the country transitioned into what was called a presidential system. As a result, Fourier—who came to power and was a prominent representative of socialist thought—began spreading his ideas more widely across Europe. This signified a gradual shift of the German peoples toward republicanism. Although the Kingdom of Prussia and the Habsburg Monarchy did not hold each other in high regard, they shared a common enemy: France and republicanism. Approximately one week had passed since the outbreak of the Franco-Spanish War. French armies advanced rapidly, exploiting the dire condition of the Spanish forces to seize Catalonia and push toward Eastern Aragon. The Basque region had also fallen. Emperor Francis convened his cabinet, and they debated at length what course of action should be taken. Johann Amadeus Franz, the Minister of Finance of the era, was firmly opposed to breaking the peace with France, as any potential war would further devastate Austria’s already fragile economy. József Alvinczi, the Chief of the General Staff, argued that this war represented an opportunity to eliminate both France and the spread of republican ideas on the European continent. He maintained that, as demonstrated in the previous conflict, the Austrian army was not in as poor a condition as believed and demanded that an open ultimatum be issued to France. However, the Emperor had a different plan in mind. Although there was no certainty it would succeed, he deemed it worth attempting. For this reason, he decided to send a delegate to the Kingdom of Prussia, carrying a note requesting a private meeting with the King. The delegation set out on 15 March 1803. Meanwhile, across Europe, no clear decision had yet emerged from the British Isles. Prime Minister Henry Addington had no desire to see Spain under French control, but he also believed that the British Army was not yet prepared. After lengthy discussions with other statesmen, he sent an envoy to the Kingdom of Portugal to further expand the Anglo-Portuguese Alliance and present several proposals. In the meantime, the delegation sent by Austria to Prussia returned two weeks later. The Emperor’s proposal to the King of Prussia was to intervene in the Franco-Spanish War by forming a German coalition. The Prussian King, eager to enhance his prestige among the German states, responded favorably and announced his acceptance. Thus, the German Pact was formed. Both sides began final preparations for their already mobilized armies, and within approximately two weeks, everything was ready. A note bearing the personal signatures of both the Emperor and the King was delivered to the French delegates by a joint Austro-Prussian mission. The note demanded that France sever its alliance with the United States, withdraw from Spain, and agree to certain trade arrangements. French President Charles Fourier tore the original document to pieces in parliament. This act provided the Habsburg Monarchy and the Kingdom of Prussia with sufficient legitimacy to launch a military intervention against France. Emperor Francis II was deeply uneasy about Russia’s ambiguous stance. He neither wanted Russia to emerge excessively strong nor excessively weak. Poland could be the first step, and the Russian flag might one day fly over Hungary or the borders of the Holy Roman Empire. Taking such a risk seemed irrational. Therefore, depending on the course of the war, he considered enticing Russia into joining their side by offering the Balkan territories of the already weakened Ottoman Empire—despite his preference for preserving the balance of power in the Balkans and Eastern Europe. The French threat, however, took precedence. Although the United States did not yet pose a direct threat to Europe, it continued to threaten the colonial powers in the Americas. While it had not yet entered the conflict, such an involvement was not impossible. On the other hand, the Emperor foresaw that the French government’s aggressive and overly idealistic actions would ultimately lead to its downfall. By initiating this war, France had effectively shot itself in the foot, and these events would pave the way for a rise in anti-French sentiment throughout Europe.

If Napoleon could not return to France in 1799, the most likely result is that the coup of 18 Brumaire either fails or happens under a different general, producing a weaker military regime rather than the Napoleonic Consulate.

In real history, France in 1799 was politically unstable. The Directory was unpopular, the economy was strained, and France was still at war with the Second Coalition. Emmanuel-Joseph Sieyès and other political figures wanted to replace the Directory with a stronger executive government, but they needed a famous and reliable general to give the coup legitimacy and force. Napoleon was ideal because he was young, victorious, popular, and politically flexible.

Without Napoleon, Sieyès would probably have looked to another general, especially Jean Victor Moreau. Moreau was respected and competent, but he lacked Napoleon’s ambition, charisma, and political boldness. So a coup might still occur, but it would likely create a more parliamentary or oligarchic military republic, not a personal dictatorship like Napoleon’s Consulate. France might get a stronger constitution, but not a Napoleon-style regime centered on one man.

Militarily, France would not automatically collapse. By late 1799, the situation was already improving. Masséna’s victory at Zurich had weakened the Coalition, and Russia was becoming disillusioned with the war. France still had capable commanders such as Moreau, Masséna, Brune, and Soult. However, without Napoleon, France probably would not win the dramatic Italian campaign of 1800 or the Battle of Marengo. Austria might hold northern Italy longer, and peace with Austria could be delayed or reached on less favorable terms.

The Egyptian expedition would likely end even worse for France. If Napoleon were trapped in Egypt, captured by the British, or killed, the French army there would lose its most famous figure much earlier. The expedition was already strategically isolated, so Egypt would probably still be surrendered eventually, as it was historically in 1801.

The biggest long-term change is that there may be no Napoleonic Empire. Without Napoleon personally taking power, France is less likely to launch the massive campaigns that reshaped Europe between 1805 and 1812. There might be no Austerlitz, no Confederation of the Rhine, no dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806, no Peninsular War in the same form, and no disastrous invasion of Russia. Europe would still be unstable, but the huge “Napoleonic Wars” as we know them would probably not happen.

France would still remain a major revolutionary power, and European monarchies would still fear it. But instead of one dominant emperor conquering much of Europe, France might evolve into a military republic or authoritarian constitutional regime led by generals and politicians. A Bourbon restoration would be possible later, but probably not immediately in 1799, because the French army and much of the political class still opposed returning to the old monarchy.

Several major historical consequences would follow. The Napoleonic Code might not be created in the same form, though some legal reforms from the Revolution would likely remain. German and Italian nationalism might develop more slowly without Napoleon’s reorganization of Europe. Britain would still be France’s enemy, but without Napoleon’s empire, Britain might face less pressure on the continent. The Louisiana Purchase might also not happen in 1803, because that sale depended heavily on Napoleon’s strategic decisions.

So, in short: if Napoleon could not reach France in 1799, France probably avoids becoming the Napoleonic Empire. The Directory may still fall, but the replacement government would likely be weaker, more collective, and less expansionist. Europe would still experience war and instability, but probably not the same continent-wide Napoleonic transformation.

items.question: What If the Greek 'Great Plan' had succeeded and the Greek War of Independence had triggered an early collapse of the Ottoman Empire?
human_answers: A more decisive Ottoman defeat against Greece can give birth to the "Megali Idea" before 1844. In such a scenario, a larger independent Greek state can invited Louis-Philippe d’Orléans to become its king, before 1830 of course. This arrangement can be supported by both France and its Bourbon king, who might want to sideline a troublesome cousin, and by the United Kingdom. For the British, the presence of a Great European power south of the Straits, one aligned with neither Austria nor Russia can further divide the continental great powers and serve British strategic interests. With France satisfied in Greece and Austria compensated with territories along the Adriatic coast, Britain can focus on securing Egypt for itself. Even if the Suez Canal is not even a dream, control of Egypt is already strategically valuable for strengthening connections with India. By 1829, railway projects are already under consideration, making overland transit increasingly plausible and reinforcing Egypt’s geopolitical importance. And if its happen after 1830, Louis-Philippe has enough sons (6 minus one who died in 1828) to send one to Greece.

Considering their interest is not even religious (GB: Protestant, France: Catholic, Russia: Orthodox) and that really none of these Great Powers saw the Greek War of Independence with positive eyes (to them it was no different than the revolutions in Spain, Portugal and Naples; which, btw, they sent huge armies to crush). There was later a British change, but even the Metternich, Alexander and so on weren't super happy about it. Remember: at this point, the memory of Napoleon is far fresher than that of the Ottoman invasions into the Balkans, so the concern, far above Islam, is revolutionary sentiment. What I do see happening is them deliberating and taking too long to make a decision that the situation ends up devolving on its own (it took them like 3 years to agree to send an invasion to Spain). Then again, the French were sympathetic to Muhammad Ali while the British aided Ali Pasha plenty of times (through Maitland, specifically). They will always prefer a rotting corpse of the Ottoman empire maintaining power over the ambitious and reformist Albanian Pashas in power, this is why they went out of their way to put them out IRL, but when shit hits the fan, they have to re-examine their approach of course.

Agreed that the Great Powers, including even Russia under Alexander, don't want a full Ottoman collapse. That's not the same as saying they would intervene to stop it. It's hard to conceive of a situation in which Great Britain, France, or Russia would go to war to suppress Christian rebels fighting against the Sultan, particularly after the various atrocities committed at Chios and other places. There were also similar atrocities committed by the Greeks against Muslims, but this did not register in the European consciousness of the time and would not be a factor. It's also not a given that any intervention would be successful at stopping chaos and preserving the Empire, even if it did somehow occur. This would be a formidable job if the situation became so extreme that the Ottomans asked for such support. More likely the intervention would be directed towards managing the collapse and achieving a partition either formally or in terms of spheres of influence.

If the Greek “Great Plan” had succeeded in the 1820s and the Greek War of Independence had helped bring down the Ottoman Empire, the most likely result would not have been a stable revived Byzantine-style Greek empire. It would have been an early and chaotic version of the “Eastern Question”: the sudden partition of Ottoman lands among new Balkan states, local rulers, and the great powers.

A larger Greece would probably have emerged, perhaps including the Peloponnese, central Greece, the Aegean islands, Crete, parts of Epirus and Macedonia, and possibly Constantinople or western Anatolian coastal zones if Britain, France, and Russia allowed it. But Greek military and administrative capacity in the 1820s was limited. Greeks were commercially influential and widely dispersed, but they were not a majority in many of the territories claimed by later Greek nationalism. Macedonia, Thrace, Anatolia, Epirus, and Constantinople were ethnically and religiously mixed. A “Greater Greece” would therefore have faced immediate problems governing large Muslim, Slavic, Albanian, Armenian, Jewish, and Turkish populations.

Constantinople would have been the central issue. Russia would have wanted influence over the Straits and Orthodox Christians; Britain would have wanted to prevent Russia from controlling the route to the Mediterranean; Austria would have feared revolutionary nationalism spreading through the Balkans; France would have sought prestige and influence. For that reason, Constantinople might not have become a straightforward Greek capital. It might instead have become an internationalized city, a Russian-backed Greek possession, or the trigger for a major European war decades before the Crimean War.

The Balkans would likely have fragmented earlier. Serbia would probably have gained full independence sooner. Bulgaria might have emerged under Russian patronage, though Bulgarian nationalism was less developed in the 1820s than it became later. Wallachia and Moldavia could have moved earlier toward autonomy or union, eventually producing a Romanian state sooner. Albania, Bosnia, and Macedonia would have become contested zones among Greeks, Serbs, Bulgarians, local Muslim elites, and the great powers. Instead of one Ottoman imperial framework containing these rivalries, the region would have faced nationalist border conflicts much earlier.

In the Arab provinces, Ottoman collapse would likely have empowered Muhammad Ali’s Egypt. Egypt might have taken Syria, Palestine, parts of Arabia, and perhaps become the dominant post-Ottoman power in the eastern Mediterranean. Britain and France would have intervened to prevent any single regional state from becoming too strong. British involvement in Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean might have begun earlier, especially because of the route to India, even before the Suez Canal made Egypt still more strategic.

For Greece itself, success would have been dangerous as well as glorious. A small revolutionary state suddenly inheriting imperial ambitions would have depended heavily on foreign loans, foreign fleets, and great-power protection. It would have had to choose between a relatively liberal multinational kingdom and a centralizing nationalist state trying to Hellenize non-Greek populations. The latter would likely have produced expulsions, massacres, reprisals, and refugee crises much earlier than those that occurred in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

The broader European consequences could have been enormous. Without the Ottoman Empire as a buffer, Russia might have expanded more rapidly toward the Straits and the eastern Mediterranean. Britain would almost certainly have resisted. Austria would have feared both Russian influence and Balkan nationalism. A great-power conflict over the Ottoman inheritance might have happened in the 1830s or 1840s rather than in the Crimean War of the 1850s. The Concert of Europe, already strained by revolution and nationalism, might have broken down earlier.

Some later events would be transformed or avoided. There would be no Tanzimat reform era in the same form, no late Ottoman constitutionalism, and probably no Ottoman survival into the First World War. The Armenian, Balkan, and Anatolian crises of the late Ottoman period would not occur in the same way, but ethnic violence and population transfers might happen earlier under different successor states. A Turkish national movement might still arise, but as a post-imperial Anatolian reaction against Greek, Russian, Egyptian, or European encroachment rather than out of the collapse after World War I.

So the most plausible outcome is an earlier Ottoman disintegration followed by an unstable settlement, not a clean Greek triumph. Greece would be larger and more prestigious, but also overextended and dependent on the great powers. The Balkans and eastern Mediterranean would become the arena of nationalist competition and imperial intervention a century earlier, making the nineteenth century far more volatile and possibly bringing a major European war well before 1914.
