If *Star Trek* had survived for five seasons and the Enterprise had actually completed its “five-year mission,” the most likely result is a stronger original series in the short term but a somewhat different path for the later franchise.

The original show would probably have ended around 1971 with roughly 130 episodes instead of 79. That larger library would have made it even more valuable in syndication, which is where *Star Trek* actually became a cultural phenomenon. More episodes would also have given Kirk, Spock, McCoy, Uhura, Scotty, Sulu, and Chekov more development and possibly a real finale about returning to Earth or handing the Enterprise to a new crew. The Klingons, Romulans, Vulcans, Starfleet, and Federation politics would likely have been fleshed out earlier, giving the franchise a deeper canon before the films.

But the extra seasons would not necessarily have been better. By season 3 the show was already suffering from budget cuts, weak scheduling, and uneven scripts. If NBC had kept it alive reluctantly, seasons 4 and 5 might have included some excellent episodes but also more cheap bottle shows, recycled plots, and network-driven compromises. A five-season *Star Trek* might have felt more complete, but also more exhausted.

The fan movement would have changed too. In real history, cancellation helped create the sense that *Star Trek* was an underappreciated masterpiece rescued by fans. If the show had run its full five years, there would be less of a “tragic cancellation” legend. Fandom would still grow through conventions, reruns, and college audiences, but the emotional mythology around saving the show might be weaker.

The animated series might not have happened, or it would have been different. Many ideas that appeared in *The Animated Series* could instead have been used in seasons 4 and 5. Likewise, some concepts later developed for *Star Trek: Phase II*, the films, or even *The Next Generation* might have appeared earlier in live action.

The movies would probably still happen, because the major cause was not only fan demand but also the post-*Star Wars* boom in science fiction. Paramount would still look at *Star Trek* as a recognizable property. However, the first film might have been framed more explicitly as a reunion after a completed mission rather than a revival of a prematurely canceled show. The cast would be slightly older, but not dramatically so, and the nostalgia factor would still be strong.

The biggest long-term difference is that the original series would cast an even larger shadow. With five full seasons, later *Star Trek* would have more canon to honor and more audience attachment to Kirk’s crew. *The Next Generation* might still exist, but it might arrive later or work harder to distinguish itself from an even more dominant original. On the other hand, a longer original run could have normalized serious televised science fiction earlier, making networks more willing to take chances on space-based dramas in the 1970s and 1980s.

So the likely counterfactual is this: *Star Trek* becomes a somewhat bigger television success in its own time, gains a richer original canon, and still becomes a major franchise, but its later revival story is less dramatic. The franchise probably survives either way, but instead of being remembered as “the canceled show fans brought back from the dead,” it is remembered as a landmark 1960s–70s science-fiction series that completed its mission and then returned through films and spin-offs.

items.question: I Hear a New World: What If Nixon Was Killed in Venezuela
human_answers: Prelude: Adios a Ocumare Vice Presidents are, traditionally, nothing more than the answers to questions that you, and only you, can answer on trivia night at the bar. Richard Milhouse Nixon was no exception. As most Vice Presidents of his time were, he was not elected separately or of his own merit, rather he was a sap to the losers of his party’s nomination stapled onto a winner. And there really was no bigger winner than Dwight David Eisenhower, the man he served under. Eisenhower, it should be noted, did not choose Nixon when he won the 1952 nomination (a nomination that, by the way, Nixon played a major part in giving him), he wanted the convention to pick him a running mate. Nor did Eisenhower particularly like him. Eisenhower (or more accurately Eisenhower's aides) chose Nixon to handle the politics while the architect of Allied victory in Europe stayed above the fray. Nixon was to whip the various used car salesmen that had backed Eisenhower's convention opponent into supporting him and handle the conservative leadership he did not particularly like. When Nixon got caught up in scandal during the 1952 campaign, Eisenhower tried to use the opportunity to kick him off the ticket, calling William Knowland, another California conservative and noted rival of Nixon's in California, home from vacation in Hawaii in anticipation of Nixon's resignation from the ticket[1], only reconsidering when Nixon jerked enough tears out of his famed "Checkers" speech. Eisenhower won easily, and likely would have with or without Nixon. In 1955, when Eisenhower suffered a heart attack in Colorado, Nixon handled much of the administrative affairs, but was still told by Eisenhower to stand down and accept a cabinet position. Once again, Nixon waited out the General, and was renominated despite the opposition of many in the liberal wing. Nixon, it should be noted, was distrusted and often disliked by Eisenhower, but Eisenhower's need for a handle on domestic and foreign politics led to Nixon being given a much larger role than other Vice Presidents, often being described as the "first modern Vice President". This led to Nixon often going on foreign trips at the behest of the president and meeting with congress. His 1958 visit to Venezuela was expected to be no different, yet another goodwill trip to the countries in the Western Hemisphere to demonstrate America's "commitment" to the region and its governments. Early in the trip, Nixon had suffered indignities, most notably in Peru, where he was hit with rocks and stones while addressing student protestors, an incident which led Eisenhower to personally cable Nixon and send his love and support. In Columbia he was heckled by students. But in Venezuela, a nation which had seen a left-wing backed coup that very year, things turned for the worse. The Communist Party of Venezuela, which had backed the coup, began to agitate at the Vice-President's appearance, tearing up a wreath he was supposed to place on Simon Bolivar's grave, which led to the Americans deciding to go straight to the American embassy. However, on the way to the embassy, the Vice President's car, stuck in heavy traffic, was met by hundreds of protestors, who, while bombarding the car and eventually tipping it over. The "shatter-proof" glass of Nixon's limousine, of course, shattered, which led to glass slicing his radial artery. In the attempt to defend themselves from the crowd, Nixon, the Vice President of what was then the most powerful nation on earth, bled out on the streets of Caracas. The response from Eisenhower was instant. While not a fan of Nixon's politically or personally, he was a man with pride in the United States, and the killing of one of its most important officials needed a response. Venezuelan president Wolfgang Larrazabal, who had worked with the Communist party, refused to denounce the attacks publicly, and was largely standoffish with the United States. Questions emerged about the Venezuelan police's lack of interference with the riots, and with United States Marines mobilised just miles away, Larrazabal was removed from power via coup, before elections were expected to occur, and killed. Jesús María Castro, an army general and former Minister of Defense, led the coup, with heavy backing from United States Marines and the CIA. Elections were cancelled for 1958, and would not occur until the mid 1960s. Nixon's wife Pat sustained serious injuries from the incident, and returned home to a "hero's welcome". Pat, who detested politics, would spend the rest of her life in quiet retirement in California, occasionally making speeches at the prodding of Republican candidates but largely staying out of the limelight. As for the domestic implications, the incident led to a vast majority of Americans supporting an overthrow of the Larrazabal regime, but shocked a country that had, for much of the 1950s, believed themselves invincible from anything other than nuclear war. The vice president bleeding out on the street was a grim reminder of the humanity of the country, and is often remembered as the "end to the 1950s" as a golden decade in the popular consciousness. Congress would investigate the Secret Service in the aftermath, but much of the blame was largely put on the Venezuelan Communist Party. In electoral politics, the Republican party, which had been staring down the barrel of a midterm landslide, performed better than expected, leading to many Republicans to darkly point at the "Nixon bump". Not only that, but Nixon had been seen as Eisenhower's heir apparent since at least 1955, and now the party scrambled to find its great unifier for 1960. [1] Knowland would, ironically, issue the oath to Nixon during both of his Vice-Presidential inaugurations.
items.model_answer:
If Richard Nixon had been killed during the 1958 anti-American riots in Caracas, the immediate result would have been a major U.S.–Venezuelan crisis, but probably not a full American invasion. Nixon was vice president, not president, so Eisenhower would have remained in office. Because the 25th Amendment did not yet exist, there would have been no appointed replacement vice president; the office would simply have stayed vacant until 1961. That would have made Eisenhower’s health a much more serious constitutional issue, since if he had died, the presidency would have passed to the Democratic Speaker of the House, Sam Rayburn.

In Venezuela, the killing of an American vice president would likely have forced the provisional government to crack down hard on communist and nationalist street groups. Washington would have demanded arrests, compensation, and security guarantees, and it might have landed Marines briefly to secure U.S. personnel or the embassy if the situation collapsed. But because Venezuela was an important oil supplier and was in the middle of a fragile democratic transition after the fall of Pérez Jiménez, a long occupation would have been politically costly and strategically foolish. More likely, the United States would have used diplomatic pressure, naval deployments, intelligence operations, and aid leverage to stabilize a friendly government.

The assassination would have hardened U.S. attitudes toward Latin American radicalism before Castro even took power in Cuba. American conservatives would have treated Nixon as a Cold War martyr killed by mobs encouraged by anti-American leftism. That could have made Washington even less patient with neutralism, populism, and revolutionary movements in the hemisphere. The later Cuban Revolution, when it came in 1959, would have been interpreted through the memory of Caracas, possibly making U.S.–Cuban relations deteriorate even faster.

The biggest long-term effect is that there is no Nixon presidency. In 1960, the Republican Party would have lacked its obvious heir to Eisenhower. The likely contenders would have been Nelson Rockefeller, Henry Cabot Lodge Jr., or another Eisenhower Republican. Rockefeller is the most plausible major beneficiary: he was ambitious, wealthy, moderate, and had just become governor of New York. A Kennedy–Rockefeller race in 1960 could have been extremely close. Rockefeller might have done better than Nixon in the Northeast, especially New York, but worse among conservative Republicans. Kennedy could still win, but Nixon’s absence makes 1960 much less predictable.

If Kennedy still became president, many early-1960s events might remain broadly similar: Cuba, Berlin, civil rights pressure, and Vietnam would still dominate. But the politics of the late 1960s would change sharply. There would be no Nixon comeback in 1968, no Nixon “law and order” campaign, no Nixon Southern Strategy in its familiar form, no Watergate, no President Ford, and probably no Carter victory as a post-Watergate reaction. The Republican Party might instead split earlier between Rockefeller moderates and Reagan conservatives.

Foreign policy would also look different. The opening to China might still happen eventually because the Sino-Soviet split gave the United States strong strategic reasons to engage Beijing, but Nixon’s anti-communist reputation made the real-world opening easier. Without him, it might be delayed, handled more cautiously, or carried out by a different president under different political cover. Vietnam policy would also depend heavily on who won in 1968; a Rockefeller, Romney, Reagan, or Humphrey administration would each have taken a different route.

So the most direct answer is: Nixon’s death in Venezuela would probably not have caused a U.S. conquest of Venezuela or an immediate world war, but it would have intensified Cold War hostility in Latin America, left Eisenhower without a vice president, reshaped the 1960 election, and almost certainly erased the Nixon presidency. The largest consequences would come not in 1958 itself, but in the missing political chain from 1960 through Watergate, China, Vietnam, and the transformation of the Republican Party.

items.original_question: The Long Jump - What if the Big Three were killed at Teheran? July 7, 1943 began as usual. Speer, Gobbels and Goering were summoned to the Chancellery to communicate information about the war and listen to the Führer's reactions. I am still not sure what Morell injected him with that day, but it must have been something stronger than usual. He kept fidgeting in his chair, barely listening to reports and reassurances from his staff. At one point, he pounded his fists on his desk, interrupting Speer's analysis of the industries affected by the latest aerial bombings. As was routine, he stood up and began ranting about whatever was on his mind at the time. “Who are our enemies? The American mongrels, the Untermenschen of the East, and the decadent British.” The Furher continued to walk in circles as he ranted his latest plan. “All of them were created by the Jews to destroy the Aryan race!” The rest of the circle continued to smile and nod vigorously, but Hitler did not seem to care. He continued to complain about the Judeo-Bolsheviks, the losses at Stalingrad and in North Africa, and how utterly useless the German generals and Mussolini were. At one point, he even complained that the Allied leaders had faced less adversity despite their racial inferiority. Then, suddenly, the Fuher stopped and his eyes took on a manic gleam. For the first time since the defeat of Stalingrand, he smiled again. “Traudl,” he seemed to have finally realized that I was in the room with him, ”could you phone Canaris and Himmler for me? I need a list of the best agents at our disposal.” Excerpt from “In the devil's den: my life from 1942 to 1945” by Gertraud Junge. …… The first thing you notice about Otto Skorzeny is the smile. It is small, almost imperceptible, as if he has just heard the funniest joke in the world but is trying to hide it. I know he could give me a friendly hug or slowly slit my throat while maintaining the same damn expression. I suppose that's why he hasn't had a visitor in almost 15 years. The guards lead him to the other end of the table, ignoring his attempts at conversation. Only after securing him to the chair are his chains removed and he can turn his attention to me. The smile becomes bigger. “John,” the tone is that of an old friend rather than someone I am meeting for the first time, ‘I admit I am a big fan of your writings....’. His attempts to syncopate me are not worth transcribing. After a couple of minutes, his one-sided conversation finally ends and he expects the usual question. “Tehran.” I finally say. “Why did you do that?” He looks annoyed. He probably has other stories to tell, but in the end he cannot escape his greatest success. “Because the Führer told me to. Please tell me you're not going to scream the usual nonsense.” “I just want to know the story behind it.” He shrugs. “There is not much to tell. In early August 1943, Himmler called me back urgently to Berlin. There, I and seven other agents met with the Führer to discuss our new mission.” "None of you had any doubt about the mission?" “Of course, we had. Still, criticing the Furher's soundity of mind was an unwise decision at the time." He pauses and tilts his head to the right, waiting for a reason to continue his story. I pull out of my pocket the only thing that can catch his interest. His eyes light up seeing the American cigarettes in my hand. I hand him one and he finally restarts to talk. “I won't give you any names.” He says, savoring the taste of the smoke. “Not of my colleagues or those who helped us in Turkey and Iran. I'm just telling you how we killed those three assholes.” This time his smile seems a little more sincere. “The Soviets were still killing our soldiers all around Kiev, so reaching Bulgaria and then Turkey was the easy part. We had some trouble finding a good landing spot in Iran, but your and Moscow's invasion pissed off some locals enough that they were willing to cooperate with us." The smile disappears for a second, replaced by a bored grimace . “One of us even suggested breaking into the conference with guns blazing. The idiot wanted a glorious but useless death to please the party leadership in Berlin. Fortunately, common sense prevailed and we decided that a bomb was a better idea.” He stops briefly and looks around wearily. “Of course, it didn't work out as we had hoped. Still Landsberg is better than some shitty camp in Siberia.” “You practically killed Germany.” I say before I can restrain myself. His smile is back, but it doesn't reach his eyes. “Oh, I played almost no part in the subsequent madness. If the “Big Three” had been killed at Teheran in late 1943, the result would have been a huge political shock but probably not a German victory or a fundamentally different military outcome in World War II. By that point Germany had already lost the strategic initiative: Stalingrad and Kursk were over, Italy had surrendered, the U-boat campaign was failing, and American industrial power was fully mobilized. The Allied war machines were too large and institutionalized to collapse because three leaders died.

In the United States, Vice President Henry Wallace would have become president. He would almost certainly have continued the war against Germany and Japan, kept the Manhattan Project going, and supported the planned invasion of France. The main difference would have been political: Wallace was more sympathetic to cooperation with the Soviet Union than Truman later was. If he remained president after 1944, the early Cold War might have been less confrontational, at least at first. But he also might have faced strong domestic opposition, and the Democrats might still have tried to replace him on the 1944 ticket.

In Britain, there was no automatic equivalent to the American succession. Clement Attlee, as deputy prime minister, might have acted as caretaker, but a Conservative such as Anthony Eden could plausibly have become prime minister to preserve the wartime coalition. Either way, Britain would have continued the war. Churchill’s death might have reduced British pressure for Mediterranean and Balkan strategies, making the cross-Channel invasion even more clearly dominant.

The most uncertain case is the Soviet Union. Stalin’s death could have produced a dangerous power struggle among Molotov, Beria, Malenkov, and the military leadership. But the USSR was in a war of survival, and the Red Army had already recovered its momentum. A separate peace with Hitler is unlikely: Nazi occupation had been too brutal, Soviet losses too immense, and German aims too uncompromising. More likely, a collective leadership would have continued the war, perhaps with Marshal Zhukov and the Stavka gaining even more practical influence.

The invasion of France might have been delayed by confusion, mourning, and security fears, but probably not cancelled. The Combined Chiefs of Staff, Eisenhower, Marshall, Brooke, and other commanders already had the machinery in place. The Soviet summer offensives of 1944 would also likely have proceeded. Germany might gain a few months, but not a reversal of fortune.

The largest long-term change would probably come after Germany’s defeat. Without Stalin personally directing Soviet policy, Eastern Europe might still fall under Soviet domination because the Red Army would be physically occupying it, but the shape of that domination could be less rigid or less terror-driven. Poland, the Balkans, and Germany would remain major sources of conflict. A Wallace-led United States might accept a Soviet sphere of influence more readily than Truman did, possibly producing a softer, slower-starting Cold War. But structural rivalry between the capitalist West and a Soviet-controlled Eastern Europe would still exist.

So the careful answer is: the assassination of Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin at Teheran would have been one of the most dramatic terrorist successes in history and might have delayed Allied operations, changed the personalities of postwar diplomacy, and softened or reshaped the early Cold War. But it probably would not have saved Nazi Germany. By late 1943, the material balance of the war had already turned decisively against Hitler.

items.model_answer:
If the Netherlands had been invaded in World War I—most plausibly by Germany in 1914—the war would probably have become harder for Germany, not easier.

Germany avoided invading the Netherlands historically because Dutch neutrality was useful. Neutral Dutch ports and trade routes gave Germany indirect access to goods, finance, and information despite the British blockade. If Germany had invaded, that advantage would disappear. Britain would tighten the blockade further, and the invasion would add another neutral country to the list of victims alongside Belgium, strengthening Allied propaganda and likely hardening opinion in Britain, France, and eventually the United States.

Militarily, Germany might have gained some short-term advantages. An invasion through the Netherlands could have widened the German right wing and allowed German armies to move through Dutch territory toward Belgium and northern France. It might also have helped Germany threaten Antwerp and the Scheldt region from more directions. However, the Netherlands was not an empty corridor. The Dutch army had mobilized, and the country’s geography favored defense: rivers, canals, flooded polders, and the “Water Line” defenses around the core western provinces could slow an invader. Germany would have had to commit troops to occupation and coastal defense, stretching forces that were already needed in Belgium, France, and later the Eastern Front.

The British reaction would have been severe. Britain would not want German control of the Dutch coast, especially ports near the North Sea and the approaches to the Channel. The Royal Navy would blockade Dutch ports under German occupation, mine coastal waters, and possibly support Dutch resistance or Allied landings if feasible. German possession of Rotterdam or Amsterdam would not automatically give Germany useful naval bases, because the Royal Navy’s superiority would make them difficult to use.

For the Netherlands, the consequences would have been disastrous. Much of the country could have been occupied, especially the east and south. The government might have retreated into “Fortress Holland” around Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague, and Utrecht, or possibly fled abroad if resistance collapsed. Flooding defenses could protect some areas but would also damage farmland and civilian life. Food shortages, repression, refugees, and economic breakdown would likely follow.

The Dutch colonial empire would also matter. The Dutch East Indies, with oil, rubber, and other resources, would likely come under Allied protection or influence if the Netherlands joined the Allied side. Germany had little ability to reach or defend against Allied naval power in that region. Dutch colonial resources could therefore become more available to Britain and its allies rather than indirectly useful to Germany.

The overall effect would probably be a wider Western Front and an even more isolated Germany. Unless the invasion somehow produced a much faster German victory in 1914—which is possible but not very likely—the strategic result would be negative for Germany: more enemies, more coastline to defend, more occupation duties, loss of neutral trade, and stronger Allied moral and diplomatic arguments.

So the most likely outcome is that the Netherlands would join the Allies or become an occupied Allied-aligned state, Germany would gain some territory but lose the benefits of Dutch neutrality, and the war would become more costly and diplomatically damaging for Germany.

items.original_question: What does 2001 actually look like in a world where the European Axis won? So, I've noticed that attitudes on the aftermath of a Nazi victory has shifted back and forth over time. Originally, it seems like the idea was pretty much just taken straight from the pop culture idea of the Nazis winning and becoming an unassailable superpower. Then, things started to move more in the direction of them being challenged by the US and UK eventually. Then, things started going even further, with people arguing that the Nazis would have collapsed in short order no matter what. Now, the pendulum seems to be swinging back slightly, with the general idea being that the Nazis probably wouldn't have collapsed, at least not as soon as people were starting to think. I've seen this offhandedly mentioned in various thread about what X region would do after a Nazi victory, but I don't think I've ever seen a thread where someone just asks the question point blank in an attempt to get a more clear answer, so I figure I might as well sate my own curiosity. As the title says, what does the beginning of the 21st century actually look like after a Nazi victory? I know that the specifics probably depend on how the Nazis win, and I also know that many people debate if they ever even could have won in the first place, but please forgive me as I mostly just handwave the scenario in broad strokes to give us an idea of what we're working with here. Basically, by 1950: 1. The Germans and Italians are completely victorious in Europe. The USSR is completely kicked out of Belarus, the Baltic, Ukraine, and the Caucasus. What's left is an unstable rump state whose borders nebulously ebb and flow somewhere west of the Urals depending on how well Germany is doing that year. 2. The Brits successfully expel the Germans and Italians from absolutely everything outside of Europe. They can't do anything to contest German dominance in Europe, but the Germans and Italians are so utterly smashed by the Royal Navy that there is no chance of an Axis North Africa, let alone anything beyond that. Likewise, the Middle East is Axis-free 3. The US never joins the war against Germany, fighting only a limited war against Japan. Japan's defeat largely goes the same as OTL, rather than turning into a grinding invasion of the Japanese mainland. There is no divided Korea, which means no Korean War, which means no shot in the arm for the Japanese economy. Still, Japan's overall economic future looks quite bright nonetheless. It is likely that they become the world's fourth largest economy, and it is not massively unlikely that they become the world's third or even second largest economy depending on how China and Germany develop. 4. Again, Korea is united under a single capitalist state. It's corrupt and authoritarian, but generally not so much so as KMT China. The lack of devastation from the Korean War helps immensely. Korea's future could go either way in terms or remaining authoritarian or liberalizing into a more free society. 5. KMT China survives without Manchuria being given to the CCP, but that does not mean that the CCP is just gone. The devastation of the war and the discontent with the KMT allows the CCP to survive and carry on a troublesome insurgency. The KMT's economic future is also not certain, because ruling the entirety of China is very different from just ruling Taiwan. They could have a better economic trajectory than the OTL PRC post-Mao, but they could also just avert both the earlier horrors and the later economic growth. 6. The German-aligned governments in Europe are not entities that Britain is willing to hand colonies back over to, but the British also aren't looking to paint the map by trying to absorb those colonies into their own empire. Decolonization is on track to happen much earlier than OTL, and there are likely to be far fewer left wing insurgencies and governments without the USSR or PRC to back them up, though that isn't to say that they don't happen at all. 7. The US absolutely does not want global German dominance. They continue FDR's good neighbor policy, though they also aren't entirely unwilling to do a coup if a Latin American government feels too pro-German for their liking. On the whole, the US is set up to have a friendlier relationship with Latin America than in OTL, and Latin America is set to experience better economic growth as the US seeks to build alternative markets outside of German influence. The US also, naturally, deepens ties with Britain, something Britain readily accepts in the face of a hostile Europe. 8. Turkey is vaguely pro-German, if only out of pragmatism. Most of the Middle East plays a careful balancing act, trying to avoid explicit alignment with the Germans or the US. Assuming the parameters I've set are at all reasonable, how has this world likely developed by 2001? Is Germany still around as a pariah? Has Germany surpassed the US and become the foremost global power? Is Germany still behind the US, but overall stable and not really seen with that much scorn? Has Germany collapsed already? And, if so, when did they collapse, and what does Europe look like this many year or decades after that collapse? Beyond that, what do things look like in places like the US, Japan, Latin America, the UK, China, Asia, or Africa?
items.model_answer:
In a plausible 2001 where the European Axis won World War II, the world would not look like a stable Nazi utopia or a technologically frozen 1940s dictatorship. It would more likely look like a grim, militarized, racially stratified Cold War world dominated by a German imperial bloc in Europe, facing rival powers abroad and permanent insurgency inside its own empire.

The center of that world would be a “Greater German Reich” stretching across or dominating most of continental Europe. Germany would have annexed Austria, much of Poland, Alsace-Lorraine, parts of the Czech lands, and large zones in the east. France, the Low Countries, Denmark, Norway, Hungary, Romania, Croatia, Slovakia, and others would likely exist as client states or tightly controlled satellites. Italy might retain prestige in the Mediterranean, but by 2001 it would probably be the junior partner, not Germany’s equal.

Eastern Europe would be the darkest part of the map. Nazi plans for the east were not just military occupation but settler colonialism and racial reordering. By 2001, much of Poland, Ukraine, Belarus, and western Russia might contain German settler enclaves, militarized agricultural estates, rail corridors, and fortified cities, surrounded by impoverished Slavic labor populations with few rights. Some areas would have been depopulated by famine, deportation, execution, or long-term forced labor. There would likely be continuing guerrilla resistance, especially in forests, mountains, and ruined former Soviet regions.

The Holocaust would not be remembered as a moral catastrophe in the dominant European order, because the victorious regime would suppress or invert the truth. Europe’s Jewish population would be almost entirely gone. Roma communities, disabled people, political dissidents, gay people, and others targeted by Nazi policy would also have suffered destruction or severe repression. In public culture, their disappearance would be explained through lies, euphemisms, or silence.

Politically, Germany in 2001 would probably no longer look exactly like Hitler’s 1930s movement. Hitler would be long dead. The regime might have evolved into a bureaucratic, security-state dictatorship led by party officials, military men, technocrats, and SS-derived institutions. It could be less theatrically revolutionary than early Nazism, but not necessarily less brutal. Think less endless mass rallies and more ministries, police files, internal passports, controlled media, racial law, surveillance, informant networks, and periodic purges.

There would likely be no liberal European Union. Instead there might be a German-led continental economic bloc: efficient in some sectors, deeply exploitative in others. Western Europe could have modern roads, airports, industry, television, consumer goods, and advanced medicine for privileged populations. But the prosperity would be hierarchical. Germans would sit at the top; “acceptable” western Europeans beneath them; eastern Europeans, colonial subjects, and racialized groups at the bottom.

Technology would probably be advanced, but distorted by the priorities of empire. Aerospace, rocketry, nuclear weapons, chemical industry, surveillance systems, railways, military logistics, and propaganda media would be highly developed. Computing would exist by 2001, but the open internet as we know it might not. A German bloc might have restricted state networks, censored communications, monitored universities, and controlled scientific exchange. Consumer electronics could be less dynamic than in our timeline if intellectual freedom, migration, and open markets were restricted.

The United States would probably remain the major counterweight unless it had also been defeated or forced into isolation. A very plausible 2001 is a nuclear Cold War between a German-dominated Europe and the United States, possibly with Japan, China, or a surviving Russian/Siberian state as additional powers depending on how the wider war ended. The U.S. might be more militarized, more paranoid, and more nationalist than in our world, but still the main refuge for anti-Nazi exiles and democratic opposition.

The Soviet Union would not exist. If Germany truly won in Europe, the USSR would have been destroyed, partitioned, or driven eastward beyond the Urals. Russia might survive as a rump state in Siberia or Central Asia, bitter, militarized, and perhaps backed by the United States. Alternatively, former Soviet territories could be a patchwork of German colonies, puppet regimes, warlord zones, and resistance movements.

The Middle East would look very different. Israel would almost certainly not exist in its familiar form, because its creation depended heavily on the postwar collapse of European imperial legitimacy and the aftermath of the Holocaust becoming globally known. Oil would make the region strategically vital, with German, Italian, British, American, and perhaps Japanese influence competing there. Arab nationalism, Islamist movements, and anti-imperial struggles would still exist, but in different forms and against different patrons.

Africa and Asia would also be changed. A victorious Axis Europe would strengthen the idea that racial empire could survive. Decolonization might be delayed, bloodier, or redirected into proxy wars. Britain and France, if reduced to client or semi-client states, might lose colonies differently. Germany and Italy might seek African spheres of influence. Anti-colonial movements would still arise, but they would face a harsher and more openly racist world order.

Daily life would depend entirely on who and where you were. A German professional in Munich, Hamburg, or a rebuilt Berlin might experience order, modern housing, state holidays, television, cars, vacations in controlled European resorts, and pride in imperial power. A Polish laborer near Warsaw, a Ukrainian villager under German settlement policy, or a dissident in Paris would experience censorship, police intimidation, legal inequality, and fear. For the groups marked as racial enemies, the world would already have been catastrophic.

Berlin itself might be physically transformed. Nazi planners imagined rebuilding it as “Germania,” a monumental imperial capital of giant avenues, domes, ministries, parade grounds, and neoclassical stone architecture. By 2001, some version of that might exist: impressive, sterile, oversized, and symbolic of power rather than civic freedom. Much of Europe would carry visible marks of conquest: renamed cities, German military cemeteries, occupation monuments, racial zoning, and memorials celebrating Axis victory rather than mourning its crimes.

There probably would not be a 9/11 as we know it, because the political chain leading to it would be different: no same Cold War alignment, no same Afghan jihad, no same U.S.-Middle East relationship, and perhaps no same World Trade Center symbolism. But political violence would not be absent. Terrorism, assassinations, sabotage, colonial wars, and state massacres would be common features of this world.

So, in 2001, an Axis-victory world would likely be modern but morally devastated: nuclear-armed, industrial, bureaucratic, censored, and divided into hostile blocs. It would have highways, jets, computers, satellites, and television, but also legalized racial hierarchy, erased peoples, imperial forced labor, and permanent police rule. The most important difference is not that the world would look old-fashioned. It is that much of what our 2001 took for granted—human rights language, Holocaust memory, decolonization, democratic Europe, and the idea that Nazi racial empire had been decisively discredited—would either not exist or would survive only in exile, resistance, and underground memory.

items.question: What If Israel existed during the Holocaust?
human_answers: Chapter 1: Independence In Geneva, the League of Nations debated the partition of Palestine for three days. While the world deliberated on whether there would be a Jewish state, the Jewish leaders engaged in a battle over whether to accept one, should it be offered. Dan, who had accompanied Ben-Gurion to Geneva, found it unconscionable that some of his people’s leaders could be against partition when the Jews in Germany were suffering such persecution. The Old Man faced constant anger from those who believed the Zionist Movement should refuse any deal that gave the Jews less than the entirety of the Land of Israel. These were the same people who had opposed Ben Gurion’s transfer agreement with the Nazis in 1933, even though it had allowed Dan to bring new emigrants to Palestine. Rabbi Stephen Wise, a leader of the American Reform Movement, had been pushing for a boycott of Nazi Germany for years and continued to decry the ongoing dealings with Berlin. He buttonholed Ben-Gurion in the lobby of their hotel as Dan accompanied his boss to the Palais des Nations for the final vote on statehood. “I can only express revulsion at your attitude,” the rabbi said. Fifty thousand people—fifty thousand—packed Madison Square Garden at a rally in support of a total boycott of German goods not long ago. Macy’s, Gimbel’s, Sears & Roebuck, Woolworths, and a good many other major American stores have removed German goods from their shelves and ended all commercial transactions with Germany. How can our people in Palestine, to whom we all turn for moral leadership, do anything less?Dealings with the Nazis of any sort are abhorrent, but your signed agreement is despicable. Now you would do a similar deal with the entire world, in which you will agree to sign away our Jewish birthright in favor of a mini-state just so you can have control over it.” Ben-Gurion rubbed his belly as though Wise’s attack disturbed his digestion. “The calamity that has befallen the Jews of Germany casts a shadow over all else. Trading with Hitler is acutely distasteful, but if that’s what is necessary to save Jews and bring them to Palestine, I will deal with the Nazis—even if it brings benefit to them. It is a true Zionist answer to Nazism. ”To Dan’s eye, Wise looked remarkably like the White Anglo-Saxon Protestants who ran Harvard. The rabbi was tall, with a thin mustache and a long, aristocratic face set in a combative frown even when he wasn’t angry. But now he was angry. “You’re dealing with the devil.” “How else are we going to save Jews? How do you get an agreement unless the other side—in this case, the Nazis—sees something to its advantage in it?” “It pains me to say this, but your whole attitude is dishonorable. You are behaving like a Levantine merchant at the expense of the honor of the Jewish people.” Dan caught his breath. “Levantine” was, after all, a euphemism for the grasping, untrustworthy Jew of anti-Semitic prejudice. But the Old Man was a master of the unfair rhetorical advantage, easily able to shame a critic for his anger and shut him down.“ Rabbi Wise, we are old colleagues, so I shall ignore your impetuous comments. Just let me say that the difference between us is that I have to deal with harsh Jewish realities, not virtuous American liberalities. While you, American Zionists, are mounting your boycott campaigns, we Jews in Palestine are struggling to provide a safe haven for German Jewish refugees—refugees to whom your president is denying entry to the United States. We have to find a practical Zionist response. Speeches in Madison Square Garden do nothing.” The rabbi took a step back, as though Ben-Gurion had jabbed his chin. He turned and went quickly from the hotel. Ben-Gurion twitched his head to the side. “You think I made a mistake, Dan?” “He’s quite an influential man.” “American Jews will support us once we have a state. So will Rabbi Wise.” “If we lose the vote today, there’ll be nothing for them to support.” “If we lose today, there’ll be nowhere for Germany’s Jews to go. That’s what I care about. Come on.” They walked to the Palais, where Ben Gurion tapped every last influential contact he could find outside the hall. At the end of another day of arduous debate, amid a hush blotted by nervous coughs, the representative of each state responded to the question of partition in Palestine with “Yes,” “No,” or “ Abstention.” When the last country’s vote was heard, the Assembly Hall erupted. The Resolution was accepted. Palestine was divided. The Jews had a state. Ben-Gurion fought his way out of the chamber through a scrum of exhilarated well-wishers, shepherded by Dan Lavi. Neither spoke as they crossed the Avenue de la Paix to their hotel. Ben-Gurion stomped along with his eyes to the ground, as though he were making his way through a repulsive slum in the dead of night, but Dan took in everything around him with the kind of joy that comes to a man who has just seen the luminous face of his child for the first time. The Alps shone in the spring sunshine, and the breeze off Lake Geneva seemed to carry him with it like a dancing partner. The phone rang as they entered their suite. Dan ran to pick it up. Through earsplitting static as raucous as the atmosphere in the Assembly Hall had been, the international exchange connected him to Jerusalem.“ Can you hear me?” Shmulik shouted. “Is the Old Man with you?” “Yes. I’ll give you to him now. Isn’t it a miracle, Shmulik? A state for us. For the Jews.” “We’ll need another miracle to keep it. Give me the Old Man now.” Ben-Gurion grabbed the phone, growling impatiently. He listened as his intelligence adviser spoke. Finally, he demanded to know, “What’s that din I hear in the background? Celebrations? Are they meshuga?” He hammered the phone down. Dan caught the heaviness in his boss’s demeanor. The struggle wasn’t finished. It was barely beginning.“Shmulik reports that the Arab armies are already on the move.” Ben Gurion slumped into a wing chair, but was uncomfortable in its stiff leather and upright back. He stood and punched a hand down on the side of the chair. “We have the independence we wanted. Now we are to have our war to keep it." (This is an excerpt from the book "The Ambassador" by Yehuda Avner. I wanted to see what you guys think of this type of narrative style-presentation. The rest will be from me after this.)

items.original_question: What if Israel existed during the Holocaust? This idea, inspired by the book "The Ambassador", will focus on an alternate reality where the Peel Commission is accepted by the British in 1937, in the same way as the UN partition plan was received in 1947. "You will sup with the Devil. You will do everything the Devil requires. Whatever it takes, you will maintain the transfer of Jews from Germany to Israel. Remember not to fear him. After all, he thinks it is you who the Devil is." -David Ben Gurion, to the future Ambassador to Nazi Germany, 1938.
items.model_answer:
If a sovereign Israel had existed during the Holocaust, it likely would have changed the fate of some Jews, but it probably would not have prevented the Holocaust itself.

The most important difference would have been immigration. In actual history, many Jews trying to flee Nazi Europe were blocked by restrictive immigration policies in the United States, Britain, and elsewhere, and by British limits on Jewish immigration to Mandatory Palestine. If Israel had existed as an internationally recognized Jewish state willing and able to receive refugees, it could have provided a destination for many more Jews before the war and perhaps in its early years. That might have saved significant numbers, especially from Germany, Austria, Czechoslovakia, Poland, and other countries before escape became impossible.

Israel also might have used diplomacy, intelligence, and military organization to help Jews escape, pressure Allied governments, or publicize Nazi crimes earlier and more forcefully. A Jewish state could have had embassies, passports, rescue networks, and perhaps armed forces or special operations focused on evacuation and resistance. It might also have strengthened Jewish morale and organization in Europe.

But there are major limits. Once Nazi Germany occupied much of Europe, emigration became extremely difficult or impossible. The Nazis did not murder Jews because Jews lacked a state; they murdered them because of genocidal antisemitic ideology, wartime radicalization, and state power. A small Israel in the Middle East would not have been able to militarily defeat Nazi Germany. It also might have faced invasion or pressure from Axis forces, especially if Rommel’s forces in North Africa had reached Palestine. Its survival would likely have depended heavily on British or Allied support.

There would also have been regional consequences. An Israel existing before or during World War II would have changed Arab-Jewish relations, British imperial policy, and Middle Eastern politics. Depending on its borders, population, and international recognition, it might have faced conflict with neighboring Arab communities or states even before 1948.

So the careful answer is: an existing Israel could have saved many Jews by offering refuge and organized rescue, especially before the “Final Solution” reached its full scale. But it is unlikely to have stopped the Holocaust as a whole, because Nazi Germany’s control over Europe, Allied wartime priorities, and the machinery of genocide would still have been decisive.

items.original_question: What If Sega Saturn Adopts SGI Technology: Brainstorming thread. Hi everyone, I'm new to this website, and I wanted to try my hand at making my own alternate timeline. While this one is going to be mainly a video game based timeline, It'll also look at pop culture as a whole, if I can come up with any good ideas. So, here's my pitch. Sega. One of the most well known gaming companies in the world, creators of franchises such as Golden Axe, Virtua Fighter, Phantasy Star, and of course, Sonic The Hedgehog. A big player in the console wars, and the biggest rival to Nintendo. Despite all that, Sega went from making consoles, to being relegated to a third party manufacturer. A series of missteps and poor decisions led to the company struggling in the 5th generation, and not long after, they ended up ceasing console production after the release of the dreamcast. But there was one way they could have managed to keep making consoles. And not just stay in the console market, but change gaming history as we know it... That's right! SGI, the company that helped Nintendo develop the n64, were at one point going to work with Sega instead! Tom Kalinske, Ceo of Sega of America (SoA) at the time, was Approached by SGI who had told him about a chip that they thought would work great for a video game console. Kalinske was impressed by their work and wanted to get approval by Sega of Japan's (SoJ) hardware team to move forward with this deal. SoJ rejected the SGI chip, even after the team had managed to fix the "problems" that Japanese hardware team pointed out, a meeting with SoJ CEO Hayao Nakayama who rejected the chip, killed any chance of SGI working on a Sega Console. SGI would then go on to pitch their technology to Nintendo, who approved of their design, and the rest is history. So with all that out of the way, here's the basic premise for this timeline. What if SGI was not only allowed to work with Sega, but their technology was integrated into the Saturn? I'll be the first to admit, that i'm not the first one to come up with this question. But from what I can tell, no one else has tried to make a full timeline for this concept. So that's where I decided to step in. While I have a general idea of how I want this timeline to pan out, there's still some details I need help with. Which is why I'm making a brainstorming thread. As for what I need help with? Anything to do with console specs would be a major help. As well as trying to figure out who the heck Nintendo would work with for the N64, or whatever they'd call it in this timeline. So to anyone that's reading this, be sure to give me some ideas, I'm all ears.
items.model_answer:
If Sega had adopted SGI technology for the Saturn and produced a cleaner, more powerful 3D-focused console, the fifth-generation market would probably have been much more competitive, but Sega still would not have been guaranteed victory over Sony.

The biggest change would have been technical. The real Saturn was excellent at 2D but awkward for 3D because of its complex dual-CPU architecture and unconventional graphics hardware. Developers often struggled to get strong polygonal performance out of it, especially compared with the PlayStation, which was cheaper to develop for and clearly marketed around 3D gaming. An SGI-based Saturn, likely closer in spirit to what became the Nintendo 64’s technology, would have given Sega a much stronger answer to the industry’s shift toward texture-mapped 3D graphics.

That would have helped Sega enormously. Games like Virtua Fighter, Daytona USA, Sega Rally, Panzer Dragoon, and later Sonic projects could have looked and run better. More importantly, third-party developers would have had an easier time producing competitive 3D games. If Sega combined SGI hardware with a CD-ROM format rather than cartridges, it could have offered both strong 3D capability and cheap, high-capacity media. That combination might have been more attractive than either the real Saturn’s difficult architecture or the Nintendo 64’s cartridge limitations.

In this scenario, Sony’s PlayStation would face a much harder fight. Sony succeeded not only because of hardware, but because it courted third parties aggressively, offered favorable licensing, used CDs, marketed to older players, and positioned PlayStation as the home of the new 3D era. A strong SGI-powered Saturn could have blunted that advantage. Sega might have kept more Western and Japanese third-party support, reduced the perception that Saturn was outdated, and avoided the early narrative that PlayStation was simply the better machine for the future.

Nintendo would also be affected. If Sega had accepted SGI, Nintendo would either need a different technology partner or would have had to redesign what became the Nintendo 64. That could delay Nintendo’s entry further or produce a less distinctive machine. Since the real N64 already suffered from late release and cartridges, a strong Sega SGI-CD console could have taken some of the market space Nintendo occupied, especially among players who wanted advanced 3D games but also wanted affordable CD-based software.

However, Sega’s deeper problems would still matter. The company was hurt by internal conflict between Sega of Japan and Sega of America, the mishandling of the Sega CD and 32X, a damaged relationship with retailers, and confusing launch decisions. Better hardware alone would not fix all of that. If Sega still launched abruptly, priced the console too high, alienated developers, or failed to provide a strong Sonic game, it could still lose momentum.

The most plausible result is that Sega survives the generation in a much stronger position. Instead of the Saturn being a distant third-place system outside Japan, it might become a serious rival to the PlayStation, perhaps competing for second place globally or even leading in some regions. Sega’s arcade conversions and first-party brands would have had more impact, and third-party support would likely have been healthier. The Dreamcast might either arrive later, be more powerful, or not be needed as an emergency reset.

Sony would probably still remain a major force because its business strategy was excellent, but its dominance would be reduced. The fifth generation might become a three-way contest rather than a PlayStation-led generation with Saturn struggling and Nintendo isolated. In the long run, a successful SGI-based Saturn could plausibly keep Sega in the console hardware business beyond the Dreamcast era, though only if Sega also improved its management, pricing, marketing, and developer relations. Better technology would have given Sega the opportunity; it would not by itself have guaranteed that Sega used it well.

items.question: What If Tom Daschle wins re-election in 2004
human_answers: Another Daschle term would have been a real step down for Democrats in terms of leadership. Reid and Pelosi were the best Democratic floor leaders in generations and having them commanding the two chambers at the same time is a very big part of why Obama's first two years were so damn productive. Daschle rose through the ranks because he was really good on TV. Reid was terrible on camera, so Daschle is a plus for Democrats here, but I'm not sure it really matters. W was so badly screwing up his second term that Dems didn't really need to convince anyone that things were on the wrong track. The really interesting Qs are what Dems would do with an extra vote's breathing room in the Senate -- is it enough for Daschle to actually get things done even if he's less of a vote-counter than Reid? -- and what impact Daschle's somewhat more expansionist personal opinion on healthcare reform does to Obamacare. Daschle's tax fraud stemmed from income he earned from 2005-2007 -- i.e, after he lost re-election. He won't have that job or that income in ATL, so the whole scandal is butterflied away.

I don't see anyone mentioning the biggest butterfly: Ted Kennedy. Ted Kennedy died in August (I think?) taking Dems down to 59 seats. That's not going to happen if there's an extra seat. They're not going to have to bargain with Ben Nelson to get anything through. Dems are going to be at 60 seats through 2010. Also consequential, they're going to beat 60 seats before March of 2009 because of Al Franken. They had to do a run-off election which meant the Obama administration had to wait an extra 2-3 months to get their super majority. Daschle-Reid were effective. They got Jim Jeffords to switch. They'll be able to get something passed. Daschle wrote a book about how how single-payer is the ideal system but it's problematic in the states. I expect him to push for some Federal Health Board which will only increase death panel comparisons. I'd be interested in what others thing they can get passed through 2009-2010. More stimulus. More infrastructure. I'd love to hear thoughts. There's a small miracle that Daschle can survive in 2010 especially if he's up against a Tea Party lunatic. It's forgotten now but there was some talk after 2012 post-Sandy Hook that Obama might be the rare President who makes gains in the sixth year midterms. I think that's a stretch but it's not inconceivable. If Daschle can convince the retiring Senate Democrats to stay they certainly don't need to lose 9 seats.

Daschle loosing was a real bit of mud in the eye for Democrats in 2004. Him squeaking through would have been a help for sure; anything that gives Democrats an extra vote in the Senate in 2008-2010 will be a big help for Obama's agenda and the ACA. I don't remember how effective he was as a senate leader, Reid wasn't exactly a slouch though. He also had a corruption scandal in 2009 which might become a bigger deal if he's Senate majority leader. Big picture wise, the question is does the extra vote in the Senate and easier passage of a stronger ACA snowball into a more successful presidency for Obama? There's still going to be backlash in 2010, but if more gets done in 2008-2010 thanks to a less intransigent senate, then that momentum could carry forwards. Do they try to do immigration reform, or a stronger recovery package if less of the oxygen is sucked up by healthcare? Big picture the country would have all the same fundamental issues it currently does, but if the vibes are shifted enough in 2016 things could get very different, especially if a certain Orange man decides to stay out of the race.
items.original_question: What if Tom Daschle wins re-election in 2004 Tom Daschle was a Democratic senator from South Dakota who served as the Senate Democratic Caucus leader from 1995 to 2005. In 2004, Daschle was defeated by Republican John Thune by a narrow margin of only 4,508 votes. Daschle would be succeeded as the Senate Democratic leader by Harry Reid of Nevada, who would go on to serve as Senate Majority Leader during the last two years of George W. Bush’s second term and the first two years of Barack Obama’s first term. Democrats would achieve a supermajority during Obama’s first term, enabling the passage of the Affordable Care Act. However, the presence of Senator Joe Lieberman in the Democratic caucus would frustrate Obama’s agenda, axing the public option from the ACA. However, had Tom Daschle won re-election in 2004, perhaps Daschle would have been the 60th vote instead of Joe Lieberman. And unlike Lieberman, Daschle would very likely be for the public option. What would be the impact of a public option being passed as part of ObamaCare? What might change in the 2006, 2008, and 2010 elections if Daschle continued to lead the Democrats rather than Harry Reid? Would Democrats still win all of the seats they would win IOTL?
items.model_answer:
If Tom Daschle had won re-election in South Dakota in 2004, the immediate national effect would have been limited but the medium-term effect on Democratic Senate leadership could have been substantial.

Republicans would still have controlled the Senate after the 2004 election, but by a smaller margin: roughly 54–46 instead of 55–45, counting independent Jim Jeffords with the Democrats. George W. Bush would still have had a Republican Congress, so Daschle’s victory probably would not have stopped major second-term fights over judges, taxes, Iraq, or Social Security by itself. Bush’s Social Security privatization push likely still fails, as it did historically, because it lacked broad public and congressional support. Supreme Court nominees John Roberts and Samuel Alito probably still get confirmed, though Daschle may have managed the Democratic opposition differently than Harry Reid did.

The bigger change is that Daschle likely remains Senate Democratic leader. In real history, his 2004 defeat allowed Harry Reid to become minority leader and then majority leader after Democrats won the Senate in 2006. If Daschle survives, he probably stays on as minority leader and becomes majority leader in 2007 when Democrats take the Senate. That would give Democrats a somewhat different leadership style: Daschle was more policy-oriented, Midwestern, and institutional, while Reid was famously tactical and procedural. The overall Democratic agenda—opposition to Bush on Iraq, ethics reform, minimum wage increases, and preparation for the 2008 election—would probably look similar, but the internal Senate strategy might be less Reid-centered.

In 2006, Democrats would likely take control of the Senate with a slightly larger cushion than they had historically. Instead of a razor-thin 51-seat caucus, they might have had about 52 seats, assuming the same Democratic gains elsewhere. That extra seat could matter on close votes and committee margins, though it would not eliminate the filibuster problem.

The 2008 presidential race could also be affected. In real life, after losing his Senate seat, Daschle became an early and important Barack Obama supporter, and several people from Daschle’s network helped Obama’s rise. If Daschle were still Senate Democratic leader, he might have stayed neutral longer rather than openly backing Obama against Hillary Clinton. That could modestly weaken Obama’s establishment support, though it probably would not by itself prevent Obama from winning if the broader forces—his Iowa victory, anti-Iraq War appeal, fundraising, and campaign organization—remained the same.

The largest policy ripple would likely come during the Obama years. Daschle was deeply interested in health care reform; in real history Obama nominated him for Health and Human Services secretary, but Daschle withdrew over tax problems. If Daschle were Senate majority leader instead, he might have played a central role in shaping and passing health reform from inside the Senate. The Affordable Care Act probably still passes if Democrats have the same 2008 wave, possibly with a slightly larger Senate cushion. But it is unlikely to become dramatically more liberal, because the same moderate senators—Ben Nelson, Joe Lieberman, Blanche Lincoln, Mary Landrieu and others—would still constrain what could get 60 votes. A public option might still fail.

For South Dakota and Republican politics, the biggest consequence is that John Thune does not enter the Senate in 2005. That changes the future Republican leadership pipeline: Thune later became a major Senate Republican figure and eventually Senate GOP leader. Without that seat, he might run again later, seek statewide office, or fade from national prominence. South Dakota remains more politically contested for a time, but given its Republican trend, Daschle would be highly vulnerable in 2010, especially if he had become the face of Senate Democrats and voted for Obama’s stimulus and health care law. A 2010 Daschle defeat in the Republican wave would be very plausible.

So the most likely counterfactual is not a dramatically different Bush second term, but a different Democratic Senate leadership path. Daschle’s survival probably means no Harry Reid-led Senate, a somewhat stronger Democratic position after 2006, a different Obama-era health care process, and no John Thune rise through the Senate—at least not on the same timeline.

items.question: Beauty of a Red Star: What If the Soviets Landed on the Moon
human_answers: 13/12/2025 Lyamtsino, Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic, U.S.S.R. School was something I never really struggled at. I knew many kids, many soon-to-be model citizens, and those delinquents who would always ask for the homework assignment they missed because of some laundry list of excuses. I didn’t mind though, as long as they were happy, got what they wanted, and they left me alone, it was just the way things worked and I didn’t feel the need to come in like an American and tear the whole structure down! As long as the people were happy, I could just enjoy the little free time the school provided. This particular day, I was sitting in the little library my school had. It had many works, most of them related to the great soviets achievements and literature of our time, though that was mostly taught in our labour class. It was an easy thing to memorize, the men seemed to really only focus on the hard physical theory while the girls on the more intellectual ones… what was I saying? Oh! The library! I remember browsing the selection of books they had. One caught my eyes, I don’t remember the exact title but it was something like ‘The Cosmos’. Now the thing about this book was that it was entirely in English. Which was strange, it shouldnt've been at the time, we had many books in many languages! My school growing up was one of the more diverse ones in Russia, we had a Kazakh teacher, I remember one of my friends was Armenian, I even met a few Ukrainians and Poles. Oh sorry, right the book! I looked at the pages, I didn’t understand most of it, English wasn’t really taught at my younger age… At least I don’t think so. I brought the book up to the first teacher I saw. “Maria Ivanovna!” I asked, I remember her old boney face, She must’ve been teaching there since Stalin was around. She adjusted her glasses, those beady brown eyes bearing down on me. “Irina Serebryákova, what is it?” I am not sure if she was disinterested or merely tired, I would be tired too if I had to teach the same group of students for years and years. Holding up the book, I flipped through the pages showing the text inside, and looking at her confused old face I remember saying, “What is this about! Why is it in English?” “It is about space.” She snatched the book, adjusting her glasses as she skimmed the pages, “The cosmos... in the eyes of the west.” “The west?" I asked, she could probably have seen my innocent gaze, that look of confusion as I followed it up, "I didn’t know they thought differently about that.” The old woman scoffed a bit, setting the book down, “In every aspect they do, it’s not an ideological thing, it’s the very core of their beliefs. The societies that make up the west only understand science as a means of capital.” At the time I wasn’t sure what she entirely meant. America and her friends were the enemy, ideologically we oppose each other at every turn, but science? Wasn’t that something every nation agrees on? “Remember, Irina Serebryákova, there is a reason we landed on the moon .” There is a reason. There’s always a reason for something. After that I don’t remember much, I think I thanked her and went on my way, I had stayed a little later and began walking home. We landed on the moon, yes, and what I was told the world celebrated. But was that not really the case? My younger self was struggling with these odd ideas… and I know it should’ve been more obvious, but I am older, and you think about things differently. Like how when I was younger I had a crush on… Oh, I am sorry, I’m rambling again. Can we take a short break?

items.model_answer:
If the Soviets had landed on the Moon before the United States, the immediate effect would have been a major political and psychological victory for the USSR, but it probably would not have changed the long-term outcome of the Cold War by itself.

A Soviet first landing would have overturned the central American goal of the Apollo program: proving that the United States could beat the USSR in a spectacular technological contest. Since the Soviets had already achieved Sputnik, the first human in space, the first spacewalk, and several other early milestones, a lunar landing would have made the Soviet space program appear decisively superior in the eyes of much of the world. It would have strengthened Soviet prestige, especially among non-aligned and developing countries, and would have been used heavily in communist propaganda as proof that socialism could outproduce capitalism in science and engineering.

The United States would almost certainly still have landed on the Moon. Apollo was too far advanced by 1968–69 to abandon simply because the Soviets got there first. But the American landing would have felt different: less like a triumphant “giant leap for mankind” and more like catching up after a humiliating defeat. NASA might even have received stronger short-term funding, because Washington would have wanted to restore American prestige. Instead of Apollo winding down so quickly after Apollo 11, the U.S. might have pushed harder for longer lunar stays, a lunar base, or a more ambitious post-Apollo program.

For the Soviet Union, the victory would have been real but fragile. The actual Soviet lunar program was technically troubled, especially the N1 rocket, which repeatedly failed. Their planned lunar landing system was also more limited than Apollo’s: it would likely have placed only one cosmonaut on the surface, for a shorter and riskier mission, with less scientific equipment and less public spectacle. Because the Soviet program was secretive, the event might not have had the same global emotional force as Apollo 11’s live television broadcast unless Moscow deliberately opened the mission to the world.

The cultural symbolism would have been enormous: a red flag or red star on the Moon before the Stars and Stripes. It would have deepened the sense that space was the ultimate ideological battlefield. In the short run, this could have intensified the space race rather than ended it. The U.S. might have pursued more aggressive space goals, while the USSR would have tried to convert the landing into a sustained program. There may also have been more pressure to discuss demilitarization and rules for lunar activity, although the 1967 Outer Space Treaty had already banned national sovereignty claims and weapons of mass destruction in space.

Still, a Soviet Moon landing would not have fixed the deeper weaknesses of the Soviet system: economic inefficiency, political rigidity, technological bottlenecks, and the burdens of military competition. It would have improved Soviet prestige, perhaps delayed some perceptions of decline, and changed the mythology of the Space Age. But it probably would not have prevented the eventual stagnation of the USSR or its collapse decades later.

So the most likely outcome is this: a Soviet first landing would have been one of the greatest propaganda victories in modern history, would have humiliated the United States temporarily, and might have produced a more intense and prolonged lunar competition. But it would not, by itself, have made the Soviet Union the permanent winner of the Cold War.
