items.model_answer:
If Germany had secured a reliable wartime supply of food, oil, and rubber despite the Allied blockade, World War II would probably have lasted longer and become more costly, but Germany would still not automatically have won.

The biggest effect would have been oil. Germany’s war machine was chronically fuel-constrained. Shortages limited tank operations, aircraft training, naval activity, mechanized logistics, and later even the ability to move reserves. With abundant oil, the Luftwaffe could have trained more pilots, flown more defensive sorties, and kept pressure on Allied bombers. Panzer divisions would have been less often immobilized for lack of fuel. The German army could have mounted more flexible counterattacks in the East and West. The desperate 1944 Ardennes offensive, for example, was partly shaped by fuel scarcity; with adequate oil, Germany’s late-war defensive capacity would have been much stronger.

Rubber would also have mattered. Modern armies depended on tires, seals, hoses, vehicle parts, and aircraft components. Germany’s lack of natural rubber forced reliance on synthetic substitutes and rationing. A sustainable rubber supply would have improved mobility, vehicle maintenance, aircraft reliability, and logistics. It would not have transformed Germany into an American-style motorized army, but it would have reduced one of the persistent weaknesses of German operations.

Food security would have affected the home front and occupied Europe. Germany could have maintained civilian morale more easily and avoided some of the internal pressure created by rationing. It might also have reduced the economic need to extract food brutally from occupied territories, though Nazi racial policy and occupation ideology would still have produced mass violence, starvation policies, and genocide. A better-fed German population would have been more resilient, but food alone would not solve Germany’s military overextension.

Strategically, secure resources would have changed German decision-making. Hitler’s drive toward the Caucasus in 1942 was heavily influenced by oil needs. If Germany already had secure oil, it might have concentrated more coherently on defeating Soviet armies, taking Moscow, consolidating Ukraine, or forcing Leningrad’s collapse. That could have made the Eastern Front far more dangerous for the Soviet Union. German offensives might have lasted longer, retreats might have been better organized, and Soviet victories might have come later and at higher cost.

However, resource abundance would not eliminate Germany’s deeper problems. Germany was fighting a coalition with vastly greater manpower, industrial capacity, shipping, financial resources, and strategic depth. The United States and Soviet Union together could produce more aircraft, tanks, trucks, artillery, ammunition, and merchant shipping than Germany could match. The Soviet Union also demonstrated an extraordinary ability to absorb losses, relocate industry, and rebuild armies. Even with more German fuel and rubber, the Wehrmacht still faced huge distances, poor infrastructure in the East, partisan warfare, manpower attrition, and Hitler’s often disastrous command decisions.

The Allied bombing campaign would also adapt. If oil targets were less decisive, the Allies would put even more emphasis on transport networks, power systems, aircraft production, ball-bearing plants, rail hubs, and cities. Germany’s air defense would be stronger with more fuel, but the Allies’ numerical and technological advantages would still grow. By 1944–45, the Allies could bring overwhelming air power, radar, long-range fighters, and massive production to bear.

The Western Allies’ invasion of France would likely have been harder. A Germany not crippled by fuel shortages could move reserves faster, contest Allied air superiority more effectively, and counterattack more forcefully after D-Day. Normandy might still succeed because of Allied naval power, air power, deception, logistics, and material superiority, but the campaign could be slower and bloodier. Alternatively, the Allies might delay the invasion or choose a different strategy while the Soviet Union continued to bear the main land burden.

The most plausible outcome is therefore not a German victory, but a prolonged war. Germany might avoid the rapid collapse of 1944–45, hold parts of Europe longer, and impose far greater casualties on the Allies and Soviets. The war might extend into 1946 or beyond. If Germany remained in the war long enough, it could even face atomic bombing, since the Manhattan Project was originally motivated in part by fear of Nazi Germany.

A German victory becomes plausible only if the resource solution is combined with other major counterfactuals: better strategic leadership, no declaration of war on the United States, a more limited war against the Soviet Union, successful exploitation of anti-Soviet sentiment in occupied territories, or an early negotiated peace. But if the political and military structure of Nazi Germany remains otherwise unchanged, secure supplies of food, oil, and rubber would make Germany more dangerous and more durable, not necessarily victorious.

items.question: What If nuclear fission had been discovered early enough for a practical reactor to be built around the 1900s?
human_answers: Well, according to Google "Canada's first CANDU prototype, the Nuclear Power Demonstration (NPD) reactor, required a significant amount of heavy water (D2O) for its moderator and coolant, generally around 1 tonne of heavy water per megawatt (MW) of capacity, translating to roughly 20-25 tonnes for its small 20 MWe output..." and "In the 1930's Norwegian company Norsk Hydro began industrial-scale extraction of heavy water (deuterium oxide) at its Vemork plant in Rjukan, using electrolysis as a byproduct of fertilizer production, " Finally from Wikipedia (yes, I know this may well be nonsense) "It was the world's first site to mass-produce heavy water (as a byproduct of nitrogen fixing), with a capacity of 1.2 tonnes per year. " So, by the late 1930's / early 1940's it might well be possible to build a 1 or 2MW CANDU stream generator using just one or two years production from the single Norsk Hydro plant. I assume Canadian hydro plants were built with higher capacity since they (the Canadians) managed to build commercial output (GW) plants requiring 200-300 tones of heavy water in a 'reasonable' timescale (ie. less than 200 years )

Believe it or not, my first engineering degree was in Nuclear Engineering (it was a dead field when I graduated 30 plus years ago, and still is, so I got another degree in Manufacturing Engineering). Yes, you can run reactors with natural enrichment, and the right neutron moderator - heavy water (as in the water molecules have Deuterium instead of your usual one proton no neutrons hydrogen) or graphite come to mind. Both would avoid the need to enrich the fuel (which is a major hassle to do). BUT, that's only part of the story - you need the instrumentation for monitoring the nuclear reactions (to make sure they're occurring, and not getting out of control) which is basically electronic in nature (sorry mechanical won't cut it). In the early 1900s, the field of electronics was embryonic at best. Then there's the material science aspect - you need materials seriously capable of dealing with the high reactor temperatures, and radiation effects (oh yeah, and the material can't interfere excessively with the neutron flux, which would disrupt the reaction) - sorry not happening, material science was in its infancy IMO. There is also the safety aspect - you need shielding for any radiation emitted from the reactor. The health aspects of radiation exposure were basically unknown, resulting in many people getting exposed to and dying of cancer (Marie Curie, early X-Ray technicians, the so called "Radium Girls" who painted the glowing dots on watch faces). In certain cases of extreme exposure (due to reactor surges, etc.), you can die from the radiation days after the exposure. In short, IMO, having a viable nuclear reactor in the early 1900s is a non-starter.

To your first part: Fair enough. It seems like this might require ASB, like just magically gifting people the entire lexicon of nuclear understanding and teaching them how to make purer graphite. I'm not sure I entirely agree with the second part. Were the engineers that built the Chicago Pile doing sophisticated core analysis? Did they know the neutron flux? I feel like you could "fly blind" and just go by heat/steam output, especially since "won't immediately melt down and ruin my investment" is probably considered sufficient by 1900s standards of safety (especially if the health effects of radiation are not yet understood). Granted, it seems very, very likely that the long term effects of this mentality would make for a much more radioactively contaminated world... Ah, but I didn't say for generating electricity, per se. A nuclear boiler just for steam would be useful. And I doubt they'd come up with a design that requires steam generators or controlling boron concentration in the coolant: I wouldn't expect anything like a PWR with its separation between a primary and secondary loop. More like a BWR or RBMK, where the radioactive steam is directly used. If the objective is electricity, it may require a bit longer than early 1900s. But by the time you have coal plants coming online, you have everything you need for the conventional thermal plant.

To elaborate on some things: as far as I can tell, there are possibly 3 historical reactor designs that used unenriched/natural uranium: heavy-water moderated CANDU reactors, graphite-moderated gas-cooled reactors (Magnox and UNGG), and possibly the graphite-moderated Soviet RBMK reactors (although RBMK reactors typically used low-enriched uranium). Heavy water's out of the question; it was only discovered in the 1930s, and even WW2-era methods for extracting heavy water were massively energy-intensive. NPD, the first CANDU reactor producing some 20 MW of electricity, required 28,660kg of heavy water. Using pure electrolysis to extract the heavy water - the initial method used to extract heavy water at Vemork - required about 58,000 kilowatt hours per pound of heavy water, or 3.6 billion kilowatt-hours to produce all the necessary heavy water. As a quick comparison, the US' entire monthly electricity generation in April 1922 was about 3.6 billion kilowatt hours. That means the NPD reactor, if it obtained heavy water using pre-WW2 methods, could run for 20 years straight and not break even on the power needed to create the heavy water necessary to run the plant (not to mention some heavy water will be lost in operation) before the development of postwar heavy water production methods. UNGG and RBMK definitely used zirconium cladding for their fuel elements (necessary because zirconium has a smaller neutron absorption cross-section and is resistant to corrosion); the issue is that metal zirconium wasn't commercially synthesized until 1925, and it wasn't commercially synthesized cheaply until after WW2. The specific zirconium alloys used in the fuel claddings weren't developed until the postwar either. RBMK reactors operate with water at pressures of about 1,000 psi; that wasn't achieved by land-based power generation systems until 1925. Uranium metal used in the gas-cooled reactors is difficult to work with considering it corrodes a lot of metals when molten, thus requiring graphite molds of decently high purity (maybe not as pure as nuclear graphite, but boron has to be minimized). Also the furnaces used to cast the uranium were vacuum induction furnaces, a technology not invented until the 1920s. Turning the uranium metal into fuel rods that can be inserted also required a ton of research and development to the point where it was once considered the most critical job at Hanford for the Manhattan Project.
items.original_question: What if A nuclear reactor, four decades early? I posit that with the technology of the early 1900s, a nuclear reactor could've been theoretically possible had the theory been understood. Uranium enrichment is entirely out of the question, but not all reactor designs require it. The industrialists of the 1900s had access to graphite, yellowcake, and boron, which would allow the creation and control of a graphite-moderated natural uranium reactor, so long as the graphite was pure enough (I am admittedly unsure if that level of purity would be possible, but I am presuming so given what little I know of the process). Is there any plausible scenario where the discovery of nuclear fission is pushed back far enough for our enterprising titans of industry to begin harnessing nuclear steam, short of dropping off a modern nuclear physics textbook in their engineers' laps? If so, what effects would this have on the world?
items.model_answer:
If nuclear fission had been understood early enough for a working reactor to be built around 1900, the biggest consequence would probably not have been immediate cheap electricity, but an earlier arrival of nuclear science, nuclear state secrecy, and eventually nuclear weapons.

A practical reactor in 1900 would have transformed physics. Radioactivity had only just been discovered in the 1890s, and atomic structure was still poorly understood. A reactor would have revealed that the atom contained enormous usable energy decades before quantum mechanics and nuclear physics matured. Chemistry, medicine, and materials science would also have advanced faster because reactors produce radioisotopes and new elements. Radiotherapy, tracers in biology, and industrial radiography might have appeared much earlier.

But nuclear power would not instantly have displaced coal. Around 1900, electrical grids were small, turbines were still developing, and coal was cheap and abundant. Early reactors would likely have been experimental heat sources and isotope factories rather than mass commercial power plants. Nuclear electricity might have become important in the 1920s or 1930s instead of the 1950s, especially in countries with strong engineering capacity such as Britain, Germany, France, and the United States.

The military implications would have been profound. A reactor by itself is not a bomb, and building a bomb requires isotope separation or plutonium production, critical-mass calculations, precision engineering, and large industrial facilities. Those would have been hard in 1900, but not impossible given enough time and state funding. If the existence of fission energy were known before World War I, the war might have accelerated nuclear research dramatically. Nuclear weapons probably would not have appeared in 1914, but they might plausibly have appeared in the 1920s or 1930s rather than 1945.

That could have changed the entire course of the twentieth century. If nuclear weapons existed before or during the interwar period, the balance of power between empires would have been altered. Britain, Germany, France, Russia, and the United States would all have tried to control uranium supplies and reactor technology. Colonial territories with uranium deposits—such as parts of Africa and Central Asia—would have gained new strategic importance. Nuclear secrecy and espionage would likely have emerged much earlier.

World War I itself might still have happened, because its causes were diplomatic, imperial, and nationalist rather than technological. However, if nuclear research were already underway, the war could have become a race to turn reactors into weapons. If one side obtained even a small number of atomic bombs by the late stages of the war, the psychological and political shock would have been enormous. Cities, ports, and troop concentrations could have become targets. The moral horror associated with chemical weapons might instead have been attached to nuclear weapons much earlier.

If nuclear weapons emerged in the 1920s or 1930s, World War II might have been prevented, shortened, or made far worse. A nuclear-armed Germany, Britain, United States, or Soviet Union would have changed calculations of aggression. Deterrence might have appeared earlier, but so might preventive-war thinking: states might have attacked rivals before they could build nuclear arsenals. The Nazi regime with access to mature nuclear technology would have been an especially dangerous possibility.

Environmentally, earlier nuclear power could have reduced some coal use and urban air pollution, but only gradually. It might also have produced an earlier history of radiation accidents, waste problems, and occupational exposure, especially because early understanding of radiation safety was poor. The first generation of nuclear workers would likely have suffered badly from cancers and contamination before protective standards developed.

So the most likely outcome is not a peaceful Edwardian nuclear age with abundant clean energy. It is an earlier nuclear-industrial age: faster physics, earlier medical isotopes, some earlier nuclear electricity, intensified great-power competition, and a serious chance that atomic weapons would enter world politics one or two decades before they actually did. The twentieth century would probably have become nuclear sooner, with all the benefits and dangers arriving before the political institutions needed to manage them.

items.question: Skywalker Ranch Foundation: What If Lucasfilm Was Never Sold to Disney
human_answers: Lucas didn’t expend much effort in assembling the rest of the Creative Council. It was mostly a collection of people who had defined Lucasfilm properties for a generation. The first member was Kiri Hart, Lucasfilm’s resident surveyor of canon. Doug Chiang was the second to agree. He had created the stunning visual spectacles that were Naboo and Coruscant in The Phantom Menace. He had made the prequels more mythic in appearance than the originals and that was someone Filoni felt this new Foundation needed. Kathleen Kennedy was the last member. She had overseen the creation of many classics, mostly outside of Lucasfilm. Even if that wasn’t the case, Filoni could not pretend there wasn’t a corporate aspect to the Foundation. The corporation was what would keep the Foundation propped up. Filoni felt both eager to get underway and terrified about what would happen in this meeting. Lucas had essentially anointed him his successor. There was a lot to live up to, but Filoni trusted Lucas’ judgement and that was the only consolation he could come up with. Filoni walked into the boardroom and he clapped his hands. “Hey, everyone. Thank you for coming”, he said. The creators nodded in Filoni’s direction as he sat down. Doug pushed his notepad to the centre of the desk as Kiri closed her binder full of canon notes. “I know what you’re thinking. This is new territory for me too. But, let’s see how this pans out”, Filoni replied. The creators didn’t respond. “Our mandate is clear. We have the responsibility to protect what Lucasfilm stands for. We need to tell new stories while protecting what the old ones stand for”, As some of the creators shifted position in their seats, Dave continued. “This is about the generations of people who see Lucasfilm as the pillar of mythic entertainment”, he said. “What do we do first?” Kennedy asked. “The Foundation goes public in October. Before then, I want a clear statement of what the Foundation will stand for. We don’t want our fans to have any doubt about our integrity”, Kiri nodded, but asked. “What is our integrity? What do we stand for?” Dave looked around the table. “We stand for storytelling and for what it can bring to the world”, he said. “That is a noble goal, Dave. But we can’t forget that part of this Foundation is a business. We need to operate within current and upcoming industries. We need to form connections”, Kennedy replied. Doug then replied. “I don’t think Dave is forgetting that, but we need to tell the industry that we decide what stories are told. Too many stories are being decided in high rise boardrooms”, Filoni nodded. “Exactly. There is a balance we need to respect”, he said. “Creative sovereignty will be our first pillar then. We will work with the industry, but we won’t let them rewrite our stories to fit social media trends”, Kiri replied. Dave nodded in her direction. “We also need to figure out a commercially viable way to support new creators. Are we going to let everyone with a camera and dream camp outside of Skywalker Ranch and hope for their shot?” Kennedy asked. “Once we work out that process, how do we protect their work?” she continued. “Okay, so we’ve decided on our values. Creative sovereignty, visual and emotional integrity and creator support”, Dave said as he counted the values on his fingers. “Who wants to work on the statement?” he called out. Kiri and Doug stood up. “We’ll get it started”, Dave nodded as he looked at Kennedy. “I’ll get the production framework going”, she said. Filoni laid back in his seat. This first meeting was remarkably painless, but he suspected this was where the ease of the job ended. Comments We are a long way off from dealing with the sequels, but they will be addressed eventually. I will be preserving the Mandalorian, since that was Filoni's pet project for a while. And yes, Lucasfilm will be retaining their relationship with Disney. If there is something like Galaxy's Edge, it won't be entirely based around the sequels.
items.original_question: Skywalker Ranch Foundation: What if Lucasfilm Was Never Sold to Disney (I originally intended for this to be a timeline which would've covered the production of a Clone Wars-style animated series set in a different version of the sequel trilogy, but when I determined that Disney was too business oriented to create something like what I was making, I went back to the drawing board and I came up with this instead. This will be my first production timeline so I may or may not update this on the regular, but I wanted to do something to mark the 10th anniversary of The Force Awakens) Anyway, sound off on what you think. # June 2012 “Well done, everybody!” Dave Filoni shouted when he saw the final animation of The Wrong Jedi, the last episode of The Clone Wars Season 5. There was loud applause from across the room. Filoni looked back towards George Lucas. He could’ve sworn he saw a tear in the old man’s eye. The Clone Wars was out for another season. The final step was to send the seasons to Cartoon Network to show the fans. Filoni thought this was probably the best season yet. He wasn’t surprised since he knew he had the best team in the business working alongside him. But, the celebration couldn’t last forever. He had to work with his team on the next season. Lucas had been a felt absence through the production of Season 5, but he had his input on scripts he thought were special. Filoni smiled as he wondered how long he could keep luring Lucas back to Skywalker Ranch. Before the team could leave, Lucas called out. “Before you leave, I have an announcement to make”, he said. The team turned to face Lucas, but Lucas raised his hand. “Not here. Let’s go somewhere less shadowy”, he said. Lucas led his team out of the Ranch proper and towards the artificially created lake that sat in the middle of the Skywalker Ranch complex. Filoni was never tired of the verdant paradise that Skywalker Ranch was. “Alright, George. What’s up?” Filoni asked with a brief smile. Lucas looked to his fellow creators and took a deep breath. “I don’t know what to say, so I am just going to come right out and say it. I will be stepping down from Lucasfilm at the end of the year”, The creators looked at each other. Lucas’s felt absence suddenly made sense. There was no shock or gasp of surprise. Instead, there was a quiet acknowledgement. “Are you sure you want that?” Filoni asked. “Yes. I’ve been thinking about it for about a year. I’ve told my stories and I want to spend the rest of my life with my family”, “Who’s going to take over?” Kliner asked. “Kathleen Kennedy is going to be handling the corporate side of things, but that’s not why I called you here”, Lucas continued. The shock of the news that one of Spielberg’s top collaborators was going to run Lucasfilm briefly subsided as they waited for Lucas. “I’ve been considering what to do with this alliance that I’ve spent the better part of my life putting together. When I first built this place, I had just dodged a bullet when A New Hope smashed the box office. I’ve put my life and my psyche on the line to not only make art for people to enjoy, but to make an environment where filmmakers can tell their stories”, Lucas said as he stretched out his arms to take in the entirety of the Ranch. “You’ve certainly accomplished that”, Athena Portillo said to everyone’s agreement. “I’ve considered selling all of this to Disney. They have reach that I can only dream of, but I’ve had my doubts”, he said as he turned around from the lake. “When I first became a filmmaker, I hated the studio system. They were all hacks who made films based on what was popular at the time. I’m not saying Disney is a company full of hacks, but I don’t want their corporate attitudes diluting what I, Gary, Ralph, Ben and Maria created thirty years ago. I want this place to remain pure”, Lucas continued. “I’m sorry, George, but what are you trying to say?” Kliner asked. Lucas exhaled. “I’ve talked with Kathy and Brennan. They were reluctant at first, but they’ve agreed to keep Lucasfilm as an independent entity. Not only that, but they’ve agreed to begin laying the groundwork for the Skywalker Ranch Foundation”, “And what is that?” Filoni asked. “It is what is going to keep Lucasfilm in the public consciousness for the next decade or so. It is going to protect the integrity of everything we’ve made here. Not just Star Wars, but Indiana Jones, Willow and everything else that has this place’s name on it. Nobody will be able to touch the properties inside this building until they can prove they can do the work necessary to preserve it”, Before the creators could ask further questions, Lucas continued. “But the Foundation will also produce new content that fits what this place stands for. We’re still putting the infrastructure together, but it will produce new content outside of the studio system, just like back when the original trilogy was being produced”, “Who’s going to lead this Foundation?” Filoni asked. “Like I said, Kathy is going to lead the corporate side of it, but she won’t be the voice of the Foundation. The Foundation will be led by creators”, Lucas replied. He then looked towards Dave and walked towards him. “When you first joined Lucasfilm in 2008, I was surprised by how connected you were to what this company stood for. You weren’t just a director, you were a storyteller through and through. That’s the kind of person I need keeping the Ranch intact. I want you to be the first leader of the Creative Council”, Dave felt his cheeks turning red. He suddenly felt like he had been pulled back in time to when he first joined Lucasfilm. He thought that had been a joke at first. This didn’t feel like a joke. This was something Dave couldn’t put into words. “You want me to be in charge of your legacy? George, I’m flattered, but that’s a whole different thing from making a TV show”, Dave pointed out. “Just keep the story straight. That will be your job. You will have other creators working alongside you on the Council and these people will stay on to help you in the trenches”, Lucas reassured him as he pointed to the creators, some of whom Filoni had known since he first joined the company. The creators watched as Dave looked out across the water. He could’ve sworn Binary Sunset was playing in the back of his head. This was his threshold. He thought he had crossed that line in 2008, but he had been wrong. Lucas wasn’t just trusting him with his story, he was trusting him with what Lucasfilm was going to stand for after he was gone. Dave separated himself from the real world for a moment. He saw X Wings and TIE Fighters flying over the Ranch, he could hear the ethereal hum of lightsabers and finally, he heard Yoda’s famous phrase. “Do or do not. There is no try”, Filoni turned around. “I’ll do it”, he said which led to applause from his fellow creators and Lucas shaking his hand. “Lucasfilm couldn’t be in better hands”, Lucas simply said.
items.model_answer:
If Lucasfilm had never been sold to Disney, the most plausible “Skywalker Ranch Foundation” scenario is that George Lucas would have kept Lucasfilm private for longer and gradually shifted its value toward philanthropy, education, film preservation, and the arts rather than turning *Star Wars* into the large-scale Disney franchise machine it became.

In reality, Lucas sold Lucasfilm to Disney in 2012 for about $4 billion and said much of the proceeds would go to philanthropy, especially education. Without that sale, he still likely would have wanted a succession plan, because by then he was already trying to step back from day-to-day control. Kathleen Kennedy may still have taken over operational leadership, but Lucas would probably have retained stronger creative veto power.

A “Skywalker Ranch Foundation” could have functioned as a charitable or cultural institution built around Lucas’s assets: Skywalker Ranch, the Lucasfilm archives, film and sound technology, education programs, and possibly profits from *Star Wars* licensing. It might have supported filmmaking fellowships, digital arts training, narrative art, film restoration, and educational media. In that world, Lucasfilm could have become less like Marvel under Disney and more like a private creative empire whose earnings funded Lucas’s philanthropic goals.

The biggest difference would be the pace and style of *Star Wars*. Disney produced the sequel trilogy, standalone films, animated projects, theme-park lands, and streaming series at a scale Lucasfilm alone probably would not have matched. Without Disney, there may still have been Episodes VII–IX, but they likely would have followed Lucas’s own story treatments more closely, released more slowly, and carried a stronger Lucas/Kennedy authorship rather than Disney’s corporate franchise strategy. Projects like *The Mandalorian* might still have happened in some form, but Disney+ was crucial to making that kind of streaming expansion central.

Financially, Lucasfilm would have remained extremely valuable, but it would have faced harder limits. Disney provided distribution power, marketing scale, theme-park integration, consumer-products infrastructure, and streaming platforms. An independent Lucasfilm or foundation-linked Lucasfilm would have needed partnerships with studios, networks, or tech companies. It could earn billions from licensing, but probably not with the same global saturation.

So the likely outcome is: *Star Wars* becomes smaller, slower, and more Lucas-shaped; Skywalker Ranch becomes a more prominent cultural and educational center; Lucas’s philanthropy grows through ongoing Lucasfilm revenues rather than a single Disney-sale windfall; and the modern Disney-era version of *Star Wars*—the sequel trilogy as made, Galaxy’s Edge, Disney+ series, and constant franchise expansion—does not exist in the same form.

items.question: What If SpaceX had continued developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon for crewed lunar missions?
human_answers: I don't think you understand SpaceX very well. The Starship "failures" are the result of rapid design-test-redesign, pushing the hardware to its limits to find out just what those limits actually are. items.model_answer:
If SpaceX had continued developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon for crewed lunar missions instead of shifting its lunar ambitions mainly toward Starship, the most likely result would have been an earlier but much more limited commercial lunar capability: crewed circumlunar flights, not a full lunar landing system.

A Falcon Heavy-launched Crew Dragon could plausibly have been developed for a lunar flyby mission. SpaceX actually announced such a plan in 2017, intending to send private passengers around the Moon before later canceling that path. With continued investment, SpaceX might have modified Dragon for longer-duration life support, deep-space communications, radiation monitoring, navigation beyond Earth orbit, and high-speed lunar-return reentry. Since Falcon Heavy flew successfully in 2018 and Crew Dragon carried astronauts in 2020, a crewed lunar flyby in the early-to-mid 2020s would have been plausible, though not guaranteed.

But the architecture would have had serious limits. Dragon is a compact Earth-orbit capsule. It lacks the large service module, propulsion capacity, consumables margin, and mission volume needed for robust lunar orbital operations. A free-return lunar flyby—looping around the Moon and returning to Earth—would be far easier than entering lunar orbit. Landing on the Moon would require additional hardware: a lunar lander, propulsion stages, orbital rendezvous systems, and probably multiple launches. Falcon Heavy and Dragon could support pieces of that, but they would not by themselves create an Apollo-like landing architecture.

The biggest impact would have been political and commercial. A successful private lunar flyby on Falcon Heavy/Dragon would have put enormous pressure on NASA’s Space Launch System and Orion program. It would have shown that at least some human lunar missions could be done with commercial hardware at far lower cost. Congress probably would still have protected SLS and Orion, because those programs had strong institutional and regional support, but the public comparison would have been awkward: SpaceX might have appeared able to send people around the Moon faster and cheaper than NASA’s government-owned rocket.

NASA’s Artemis program might have changed around the edges. NASA could have considered buying commercial circumlunar transport services, using Falcon Heavy/Dragon for demonstration missions, or relying more heavily on commercial launchers for cargo and support. However, Dragon would not have been a clean substitute for Orion on Artemis missions involving lunar orbit, Gateway operations, or long-duration crew support. Orion was designed for deep-space mission endurance in a way Dragon was not. So Falcon Heavy/Dragon might have supplemented Artemis, but probably would not have fully replaced SLS/Orion without major redesigns.

Commercially, it could have created a small market for lunar tourism earlier than Starship. Wealthy private customers might have paid for circumlunar Dragon flights, especially if SpaceX could offer them before any government lunar landing. Such missions would have been spectacular and historically important, but rare. The cost, risk, and training requirements would still have limited the customer base.

The tradeoff is that continued focus on Falcon Heavy and Dragon may have slowed Starship. If SpaceX had devoted more engineering resources to making Dragon a deep-space vehicle, it might have delayed the fully reusable heavy-lift system that later became central to SpaceX’s Mars and Artemis lunar-lander plans. In that scenario, SpaceX might have achieved an earlier “tourist loop around the Moon,” but at the cost of a less ambitious long-term architecture.

So the counterfactual outcome is probably this: SpaceX could have made crewed lunar flybys happen sooner and cheaper than traditional government systems, strengthening the case for commercial deep-space flight. But Falcon Heavy and Dragon would not have been enough for sustained lunar exploration or landings without major extra infrastructure. It would have been an impressive intermediate path—more capable than low Earth orbit, less transformative than Starship.

items.model_answer:
If by “a second attack at Taranto” you mean a follow-up raid on the next night after the successful 11–12 November 1940 strike, the most likely result is that the British would have inflicted some additional damage on the Italian fleet or port facilities, but probably not enough to knock Italy out of the naval war altogether.

The first attack achieved surprise. That was its great advantage. Twenty-one Swordfish aircraft from HMS Illustrious damaged three Italian battleships: Conte di Cavour, Littorio, and Caio Duilio. Cavour never returned to effective service, while Littorio and Duilio were out for months. A second raid, however, would have faced an alerted Taranto. Italian anti-aircraft guns, searchlights, smoke screens, and emergency defenses would have been ready. The harbor would also have been more chaotic, with damaged ships, rescue work, and defensive measures underway. The British Swordfish were slow and vulnerable; without surprise, losses could have been much higher.

Still, a second attack might have mattered. If the British had hit Vittorio Veneto, further damaged Littorio, or struck dockyard and fuel facilities, the Regia Marina’s battlefleet could have been crippled for longer. That would have given the Royal Navy a freer hand in the central Mediterranean during late 1940 and early 1941. British convoys to Malta, Greece, and Egypt might have been safer. Italian supply lines to Libya could have come under heavier pressure earlier, possibly worsening the Axis position in North Africa before Rommel’s Afrika Korps became established.

But it would not necessarily have been decisive. The Italian navy was not just battleships; it still had cruisers, destroyers, submarines, mines, and, crucially, support from land-based aircraft. The central Mediterranean was dominated as much by air power from Sicily, Sardinia, and mainland Italy as by surface fleets. In early 1941 the German Luftwaffe entered the Mediterranean in strength and badly damaged HMS Illustrious, which changed the balance again. A second Taranto attack could not have prevented that by itself.

So the most plausible counterfactual is this: a successful second British strike would have deepened the Italian naval setback, perhaps delayed Italian fleet recovery, and improved Britain’s short-term position in the Mediterranean. It might have made Axis logistics to North Africa more difficult and reduced the chance of major Italian fleet operations. But it probably would not have ended the Mediterranean naval campaign or by itself changed the outcome in North Africa. The first Taranto raid was already a major strategic success; a second one could have amplified it, but not transformed the war on its own.

items.model_answer:
If Vichy France had somehow sent 100,000 French troops to help Germany defend the Atlantic Wall in 1944, it would probably have made the Normandy landings costlier and politically uglier, but it is unlikely to have stopped the Allied liberation of France.

The first problem is plausibility. By 1944, Vichy France was no longer a truly independent military actor. After the Allied landings in North Africa in November 1942, Germany occupied the formerly unoccupied zone of France and largely disarmed the Vichy army. Vichy still had police, militia, colonial connections, and collaborationist volunteers, but fielding 100,000 reliable, equipped troops for coastal defense would have required German approval, German arms, and German confidence in their loyalty. That confidence would have been limited. Many French soldiers might have been reluctant to fight Americans, British, Canadians, and Free French forces on French soil.

If the 100,000 troops were poorly equipped, scattered along the coast, and used as static garrison forces, their effect would have been modest. The Atlantic Wall was enormous, stretching from Norway to the Franco-Spanish border. An extra 100,000 men spread across that front would have thickened defenses but not transformed them. Allied deception operations such as Operation Fortitude were designed precisely to keep German forces dispersed and uncertain about the landing site. If Vichy troops were spread widely, many would have been nowhere near Normandy on D-Day.

If, however, a large portion of them had been concentrated in Normandy and used effectively, they could have made the initial landings more difficult. They might have increased Allied casualties, reinforced strongpoints, slowed the capture of beach exits, and made places like Omaha Beach even more dangerous. They could also have freed some German units for mobile reserve duties. In that case, the Allies might still have secured a beachhead, but the first days could have been bloodier and the breakout from Normandy might have been delayed.

Even then, the basic strategic balance would not change much. The Allies had overwhelming naval gunfire, air superiority, logistical depth, and the ability to reinforce the beachhead faster than Germany could move reserves under Allied air attack. German armored counterattacks were already hampered by fuel shortages, command confusion, Allied bombing, and Hitler’s rigid control. Additional Vichy infantry would not solve those problems. Unless these French troops were highly motivated, well-armed, and backed by more German armor and air power, they would not likely throw the Allies back into the sea.

Their morale and reliability would be the central issue. Many might surrender quickly, avoid combat, desert, or even pass information to the Resistance. Some collaborationist units would fight hard, especially ideologically committed militia or volunteers, but ordinary French conscripts ordered to defend Nazi positions against the liberation of France would be politically and psychologically unstable. The Germans would probably mistrust them and assign them to secondary sectors, reducing their military value.

The political consequences would be severe. A Vichy decision to put 100,000 Frenchmen into German coastal defenses would make the regime appear far more openly treasonous in the eyes of many French people. It would strengthen the legitimacy of de Gaulle, the Free French, and the Resistance. After liberation, the purge of collaborators would likely be harsher, and France’s postwar memory of occupation would be even more bitter. Instead of Vichy being able to claim that it had shielded France from worse outcomes, it would be remembered more plainly as having sent French soldiers to fight for Germany against France’s liberators.

So the most likely result is this: D-Day becomes somewhat harder and perhaps bloodier; the Normandy campaign may be delayed; but the Allies still win in France. The largest long-term effect would probably be political and social rather than military: deeper French internal division, a more discredited Vichy regime, and a harsher reckoning after liberation.

items.model_answer:
If World War I had occurred 9 years earlier, in 1905 rather than 1914, it would probably have been a major European war, but not the same kind of war and not necessarily with the same outcome.

The most important difference is that the balance of power in 1905 was less favorable to the Entente than it was in 1914. Russia had just been badly weakened by the Russo-Japanese War and was facing the Revolution of 1905. Its army, finances, railways, and political stability were in poor condition. If Germany and Austria-Hungary had gone to war against Russia and France at that moment, Russia would likely have performed worse than it did in 1914. Germany might therefore have had a better chance of defeating France quickly or forcing a favorable settlement before Russia could fully mobilize.

France would still have been Germany’s main western opponent, but Britain’s role would have been less certain. In 1914, Britain entered the war largely because Germany violated Belgian neutrality and because German naval power had become a more urgent threat. In 1905, Britain was already suspicious of Germany, but the Anglo-French Entente was still new and less militarily binding. Britain might still have joined if Belgium were invaded, but its intervention may have been slower, smaller, or politically more contested.

The war would also likely have been somewhat less mechanized and less destructive than the actual First World War, though still extremely bloody. Machine guns, heavy artillery, rail mobilization, and modern rifles already existed, so trench warfare was still possible. But aircraft, tanks, motor transport, wireless communications, poison gas, and some forms of industrialized warfare were less developed. The conflict might have looked more like a transitional war: modern enough to be devastating, but perhaps less technologically total than 1914–1918.

The Balkans and the Ottoman Empire would have been different as well. In 1914, Balkan tensions had been intensified by the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913 and by Serbia’s expansion. In 1905, Serbia was still important, but the regional crisis had not reached the same level. A 1905 war might have been triggered more by a Moroccan-style crisis, a Russian collapse, or a confrontation among the great powers than by an assassination in Sarajevo. The Ottoman Empire might have had a different role, possibly remaining neutral longer or entering under different conditions.

Politically, an earlier war could have changed the fate of several empires. Russia, already unstable in 1905, might have suffered revolution or collapse much earlier if it were defeated in a European war. Austria-Hungary might have survived longer if Germany won, but it could also have been shaken by nationalist pressures. Germany, if victorious, might have become the dominant power on the continent before Britain, France, and Russia were fully prepared to contain it.

The United States would probably have played a much smaller role. In 1905, the U.S. was rising as a world power but was less militarily prepared and less likely to intervene in a European conflict. Without the same submarine warfare crisis and without years of global financial entanglement, American entry would have been less likely.

Overall, a World War I beginning in 1905 would probably have favored Germany more than the real war did, mainly because Russia was much weaker and Britain’s commitment was less firm. It might have ended sooner and with a German-dominated Europe, or it might have produced an earlier Russian revolution and a different pattern of imperial collapse. But it would still have been a dangerous industrial war, and even if shorter, it could have radically reshaped the twentieth century.

human_answers: Think about it--when Truman lost, it wasn't *just* because Democrats had been in power a long time. It was *also* because Harry Truman never saw a hornet's nest he didn't want to kick, a temperamental flaw that contributed to a sense of chaos in all walks of life. items.original_question: What if A clash between Rockefeller/Cisneros vs Quayle/Alexander in the US 1996 elections I'm trying to create a 1996 US election scenario where the Democrats have the Jay Rockefeller/Henry Cisneros ticket, while the Republicans have the Dan Quayle/Lamar Alexander ticket. I have a test map showing which states are likely to be won by each party, but there are some states where I'm not sure who would win. That's why I'm asking for help figuring out how many states the Democrats and Republicans would win. I appreciate any suggestions P.S. I forgot to add Indiana as a Republican.
items.model_answer:
If the 1996 U.S. presidential election had been Rockefeller/Cisneros versus Quayle/Alexander, the likeliest outcome would be a Democratic victory, probably by a comfortable but not Clinton-sized margin.

Assuming this means Senator Jay Rockefeller of West Virginia heading the Democratic ticket with Henry Cisneros as his running mate, against former Vice President Dan Quayle with Lamar Alexander as the Republican vice-presidential nominee, the basic 1996 conditions would still strongly favor the Democrats: the economy was growing, crime was falling, the deficit was shrinking, and the Republican Congress elected in 1994 had become politically polarizing after the government shutdowns. Any competent Democratic nominee would have benefited from that environment.

Rockefeller would have run as a wealthy, establishment, center-left Democrat with strong appeal on health care, poverty, education, and social policy. He would probably have been less personally charismatic than Bill Clinton, but also less scandal-plagued in the public mind. His Appalachian background and West Virginia base could help him with working-class white voters in parts of the border South and industrial Midwest. Henry Cisneros would add symbolic and practical appeal among Latino voters, especially in Texas, California, New Mexico, Arizona, and Colorado, though his personal legal troubles would be a vulnerability.

The Republican ticket would have major problems. Dan Quayle had national name recognition and conservative credentials, but by 1996 he was still widely perceived as lightweight because of his vice-presidency under George H. W. Bush and repeated media ridicule. Lamar Alexander would add executive experience, moderation, and Southern respectability, but he would not fully erase doubts about Quayle at the top of the ticket. Compared with Bob Dole, Quayle would probably be easier for Democrats to attack as unprepared for the presidency.

The campaign would likely revolve around competence, economic stewardship, welfare reform, crime, taxes, and the legacy of the Gingrich Republican Congress. Rockefeller would try to portray himself as a serious, compassionate, pragmatic Democrat defending Medicare, education, and working families. Quayle would attack him as a liberal heir to privilege and try to unite social conservatives, tax-cutters, and anti-Clinton-style voters. But without Clinton’s personal scandals as a central issue, Republicans would have less to exploit, unless Cisneros’ controversies became a major campaign story.

Electorally, Rockefeller/Cisneros would probably hold the Democratic base: the Northeast, the Pacific Coast, Illinois, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and most of the upper Midwest. Rockefeller might perform especially well in West Virginia, Kentucky-adjacent areas, Ohio, and Pennsylvania. Cisneros could help improve Democratic margins among Hispanic voters, though probably not enough to flip Texas in 1996. Quayle/Alexander would likely carry much of the Deep South, Great Plains, Mountain West, and Indiana, but would struggle in the decisive industrial states.

A plausible result would be something like Rockefeller/Cisneros winning around 50–52% of the popular vote, Quayle/Alexander around 42–45%, with a third-party or independent vote taking the rest. In the Electoral College, Rockefeller would likely win somewhere in the range of 300 to 360 electoral votes, depending on how badly Quayle underperformed and how damaging the Cisneros issue became.

The biggest difference from the real 1996 election is tone and personality. It would be less about Clinton’s triangulation and personal controversies, and more about whether voters trusted a patrician liberal Democrat over a socially conservative Republican former vice president with a weak public image. Under the political and economic conditions of 1996, Rockefeller/Cisneros would probably defeat Quayle/Alexander, though not necessarily with the same political skill or broad appeal that Clinton/Gore achieved against Dole/Kemp.

items.question: What If Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest
human_answers: I would think that you would see a Nelsonian style of celebration and loss. Assuming that the weather was clear enough to allow for Odell, who was alone, to witness their summit and subsequent descent and deadly fall, the MAJOR issue is that Odell does not have a camera on him. The one thing that would irrefutably prove that Mallory and Irvine summited the mountain and then died on their decent would be a photograph, even a distant one, of them on or practically at the summit. Now, Irvine or Mallory did have a camera on them, the near legendary Kodak that is still missing to this day and may hold the truth of whether or not they made it. Assuming that Odell witnessed the summit and the subsequent fall, AND he could record where their bodies fell or near where they fell, then it becomes an issue of finding their bodies and the Kodak. Odell was a respected and trusted witness so i do not think that many would dispute his claim, but finding their remains and the camera would be a major point of corroborating his account. If their bodies and the camera were found, with photographic proof that they did make the summit found in it, it would be both widely celebrated and mourned. Mallory and Irvine would be national heroes in Britain and probably recognized across the world for their achievement. They were historically given a memorial service at St Paul's in London, which was widely attended by many people up to an including the then Prince of Wales, the future Edward VIII. Unlike Franklin or Scott, who were either not found or left where they died, Mallory's body at the least was in a location that its recovery was certainly possible, an Irvine's body may have ended up in a similar location if their death was witnessed. If their bodies were recovered, probably with a sponsored expedition, i could easily see a joint funeral for both in St. Paul's, potentially even reaching a State Funeral with full Royal attendance. Then you have the lasting impact that this would have on the psyche of Britain and the world. After the 1924 Expedition there was a major underswell in mountaineering circles, especially British ones, and to a lesser extent in the greater British populace, that Everest was "unfinished business." While there was a drop off in attempts after the 1924 failure, there was a massive resurgence in the 1930s, a pause during the war for obvious reasons, and then a similar surge in the 1950s culminating in the 1953 success. If Mallory and Irvine reached the top in 1924, that would greatly decrease the interest in Everest. Ironically, Mallory's and Irvine's death, and the debate that raged and still rages over whether they made the summit or not, drove the popularity and allure of the mountain far beyond what it would be if they succeeded but died on the way down. There probably would be several more attempts in the aftermath, at least one of which would probably be sponsored by groups like the British Alpine Club or the Royal Geographic Society as a symbolic summit and successful decent in tribute to Mallory and Irvine. I wouldn't be surprised if they hauled a plaque all the way up there to set up a memorial for them. But Everest probably wouldn't have the same level of mystique is has today. By provably succeeding and dying in the aftermath, Mallory and Irvine would probably completely reshape how we see Everest. Edit: Having gone over this again, the nerd in me now wants the Kodak to be a legendary item in a video game OR an SCP entry. would be a fun nod to an event few people would ever know about.

Yes ! I didn't knew they had had found Irvine (well, his foot at last). https://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/article/sandy-irvine-body-found-everest Unbelievable. And then there is this Holly cow they were so close - less than 400 meters to 8848 ! I understand better why so many people are confident they made it to the summit. Also the missing photography of Mallory wife. Unfortunately poor Irvine was found much lower and inside a melting glacier. Hopefully they will found more remains within the next few years. And that infamous camera. What we know for sure: the cylinder, the ice axe and Mallory's body tells us they were roped together at a minimum of 8475 metres, before they fell. Bummers, that's 2133 meters below. Talk about a fall, even if the glacier probably lowered the body on the moutain, along the years. The remaining question is: did the fall happened while climbing, less than 400 m from glory - or descending, having done it ? And there, is the missing photography of Mallory wife. AAAAARGH we are so close from knowing the truth.

So I can tell you that summit fever is very real. I have never climbed anything like Everest obviously but I have scaled (as in hiked) a few 14,000 footers in Colorado and even with that I can state with authority that due to the combination of being tired and euphoric on the way down along with the general feeling that the mission has been accomplished, the brain is not working quite right. That's just reality. Plus, you now have gravity pulling you along. Given that I agree that it is far more likely Mallory and Irvine fell on the descent, either after making the summit or deciding to turn back for whatever reason. While it is unlikely they would have turned back that close to the summit we can't dismiss it either. 400 meters from the summit may not sound like much but at that altitude is actually a very long distance and maybe the combination of bad weather, declining oxygen supplies, or overall uncertainty caused them to turn around. My personal opinion - they made it to the top (it part because I want it to be true) and fell badly on the way down but until we can get actual physical evidence that clearly shows they made the summit that's all it is, an opinion.

Interestingly a lot of practical research has gone into trying to answer the question of whether or not the clothing worn by Mallory and Irvine would have been sufficient to enable them to survive the extreme environment. This has included tests in weather chambers and even a 2006 Everest expedition with climbers wearing exact replicas of Mallory's clothing. The overall conclusion of these tests in generally that the clothing itself was actually quite comfortable and well insulated and that provided Mallory and Irvine kept moving and didn't stop for any length of time or encounter any serious deterioration in weather conditions they could have continued to "operate effectively". Weather chamber tests showed that with the clothing they had Mallory and Irvine could have survived temperatures of −30 °C. Although it was also found that if wind speed picked up the insulation of the clothing would only just be sufficient to −10 °C. While a lot of luck would have been required its not beyond the realms of possibility that Mallory and Irvine could have succeeded in the right conditions. A bigger factor would have probably been whether or not they were carrying sufficient oxygen and if their relatively primitive breathing apparatus could be relied on not to fail (One of the reasons why Mallory chose the relatively inexperienced Irvine to accompany him on his summit attempt was due to the latter's expertise with the breathing apparatus).

They never intended to climb the second step. In fact, no one knew the second step existed in 1924. And Mallory wrote that he considered the NE ridge route impossible. Odell's sighting put them at the base of the summit pyramid, above the third step, anyway. Mallory very clearly explained his intended route in his letters, which was to bypass the steps and either take the zig-zag or the couloir. Anker is ... a controversial source on anything 1924. He has a habit of disregarding any evidence that contradicts his theories on Mallory/Irvine. It's more likely than not that they summited and died on the way down, by virtue of the fact that they died . The vast majority of climbers who've died on Everest got summit fever and died on the descent because they pushed themselves way too hard to reach the peak. Michael Tracy is a grump, but he's done more to shed light on the truth of 1924 Mallory/Irvine than basically anyone else. This video is one of his that cover's their intended routes. We'll never know what actually happened of course – the '99 team utterly botched their investigation upon finding Mallory, and given Irvine's foot was found in the Rongbuk Glacier, his body probably fell clean off the mountain below Mallory in '24 so we're unlikely ever find it. But barring new evidence, the most plausible theory is that they made the summit and died on the descent that evening/night.
items.original_question: What if Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest In 1953 the New Zealand Mountaineer Edmund Hillary and Nepalese Sherpa Tenzing Norgay became the first people to reach the summit of Mount Everest (8.849m). However there remains to this day an enduring question about whether or not Hillary and Norgay actually were the first people to reach the summit of Everest or simply the first to do so and survive the experience. In 1924 during the second British expedition to attempt to conquer Everest British climbers George Mallory and Sandy Irvine set off on the expeditions third attempt to reach the summit. An attempt from which neither man would return. On the morning of the 6th of June Mallory and Irvine had set off for the summit from their final camp (8,138 m on the North Ridge). Their progress was tracked and filmed by expedition leader Noel Oddell who had positioned himself on a ridge further down the mountain to observe and record the expected first summit of the mountain. Mallory and Irvine were last spotted through a gap in the clouds approximately 240 metres from the summit still proceeding onwards. After this the pair simply disappeared. Despite many searches in the days and years following their disappearance the pair would not be seen again for another 75 years when Mallory's remarkably well preserved body would be discovered at an altitude of 8,156m. In the 1933 expedition an ice axe that could only have belonged to Mallory or Irvine was discovered at an altitude of 8,380m proving that the pair had reached at least this altitude. The location and state of Mallory's body (Irvine's partial remains in the form of a detached foot would later emerge from a glacier at a much lower altitude) indicated that he had suffered a fall which had resulted in his death either as a direct result or by later exposure likely during a decent of the mountain. The body revealed circumstantial evidence that suggests Mallory might have successfully reached the summit. Mallory carried a photo of his wife with the intention of leaving it on the summit. No such photo was found on the body. Given the excellent preservation of the body and personal possessions, the absence of the photo suggests he may have reached the summit and deposited it there. Mallory's snow goggles were in his pocket, indicating he may have died at night; that he and Irvine had made a push for the summit and were descending very late in the day. Given their known departure time and movements, had they not made the summit, it is unlikely they would have still been out by nightfall. Perhaps the one artefact that may put the mystery to bed is the Kodak pocket camera that Irvine was known to be carrying and which he presumably would have used to take a photo of the first successful ascent had such a thing occurred and may still contain useable photographs of the attempt. Assuming that Mallory had been successful in reaching the summit and managed to avoid whatever calamity befell on their decent and are able to survive the whole ordeal what would the the effects have been of Mount Everest having been summited for the first time by George Mallory in 1924? How would this have affected the history of Everest and expeditions to climb the mountain after 1924? How would Mallory and Irvine's achievement have been received and remembered?
items.model_answer:
If George Mallory and Andrew Irvine had reached Everest’s summit in 1924 and survived the descent, the main consequence would be that Everest history would become a story of late-imperial British triumph rather than a postwar Commonwealth/Himalayan achievement.

Mallory and Irvine would almost certainly have been celebrated as the first people to climb Everest, nearly three decades before Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay in 1953. The famous question “Did Mallory summit?” would never become one of mountaineering’s great mysteries. Mallory, already well known and eloquent, would likely have become a national hero in Britain. Irvine, younger and less famous, would have been remembered as the brilliant technical partner whose work with oxygen equipment helped make the climb possible.

The symbolic meaning of Everest would also change. In 1953, Hillary and Tenzing’s ascent came just after World War II and shortly before Queen Elizabeth II’s coronation. It was framed as a morale-boosting Commonwealth achievement, with New Zealand, Nepal, India, and Britain all tied into the story. A successful 1924 ascent would instead have belonged to the age of the British Empire. It would have been celebrated as proof of British endurance, exploration, and imperial prestige after the trauma of World War I. The language around it would probably have been more imperial and less international.

Mountaineering itself might have changed, though not instantly. A successful 1924 ascent would have demonstrated that Everest could be climbed with relatively primitive equipment, wool clothing, hobnailed boots, and early oxygen apparatus. That could have encouraged more ambitious Himalayan climbing earlier than in our timeline. However, access to Everest was limited: expeditions depended on Tibetan permission from the north side, and later politics in Tibet, Nepal, China, and India would still have shaped what was possible. The mountain would not necessarily have become crowded in the 1930s or 1940s, but the psychological barrier would have been broken.

The reputation of supplemental oxygen would have been very different. In the 1920s, oxygen use was controversial, with some climbers seeing it as artificial or unsporting. If Mallory and Irvine had succeeded using oxygen, it would have gained legitimacy much earlier. Future high-altitude expeditions might have adopted it more confidently instead of debating its value for decades.

Hillary and Tenzing would still have been important mountaineers, but they would not be remembered as the first Everest summiteers. The 1953 British expedition, if it happened at all, would have been an attempt to repeat, improve, or perhaps make the first ascent from the Nepalese south side. Tenzing’s symbolic role would be especially affected. In real history, his ascent made him an international icon and a source of pride for Sherpas, Nepalis, Indians, and many formerly colonized peoples. If the first ascent had belonged to two British climbers in 1924, Sherpa recognition might have been delayed or reduced, even though Sherpas were already essential to Himalayan expeditions.

Mallory himself would likely have shaped the public philosophy of climbing. His famous phrase, “Because it’s there,” already defined the romantic ideal of mountaineering. Had he survived after summiting, he might have become the living spokesman for that ideal rather than a tragic symbol of it. The culture of Everest might have leaned even more heavily into heroic exploration and personal courage.

But some things would not change. Everest would still be dangerous. Later climbers would still seek new routes, faster ascents, oxygenless ascents, winter ascents, and national “firsts.” The mountain’s political geography would still matter. Nepal’s later opening to foreigners, China’s control of Tibet, and the commercialization of Everest in the late twentieth century would still be major turning points.

So the biggest change is not that Everest would become easy or that Himalayan history would be transformed overnight. The biggest change is symbolic: the “conquest of Everest” would move from 1953 to 1924, from Hillary and Tenzing to Mallory and Irvine, from a postwar Commonwealth moment to a dramatic imperial-era British success. Everest’s mythology would be less about a long-unsolved mystery and more about a daring early triumph that proved, astonishingly, that the mountain could be climbed with 1920s equipment and determination.

items.original_question: What if Pop Culture gets 1st Amendment and Union Protections for Production and Distribution Early From 1930 to 1968, the Motion Picture Production Code ("Hays Code") governed the production and distribution of motion picture content in the United States of America - a self-imposed by movie studios and exhibitors set of guidelines about what could and could not be shown/mentioned/referred to in film (be it a feature whether live-action or animated, a short whether live-action or animated, a serial chapter, or a documentary newsreel). Similar sets of guidelines governed graphic novels, comic books and newspaper comic strips (the Comics Code from 1954 to 2011), the National Association of Broadcasters' Code of Practices for Television Broadcasters (the so-called Television Code from 1952 to 1983) with a similar set of guidelines for radio, and the near-censorship of video games by the North American nations' governments before the Entertainment Software Association came up with the voluntary, self-regulating Entertainment Software Rating Board to inform consumers about content. There were various religious and secular moralistic censorship groups across the United States at the time dedicating themselves to preserving morality and good taste in American culture of the time through literature, music, sports, comic strips, motion pictures and radio. Various Tinseltown scandals led up to the 1915 U.S. Supreme Court case Mutual Film Corp. v. Industrial Commission of Ohio which unanimously held that free speech protections of the U.S. Constitution's 1st Amendment did not extend to motion pictures. But for our purposes, let's examine what if instead the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that radio, literature, comic strips, music and motion pictures were in fact protected by the 1st Amendment. If the Supreme Court were to decide that no local, state, or federal political body had the right to regulate or censor the production and distribution of any work of radio, film, literature, music within reason and neither did any religious or business organization within reason, then what? If the National/Catholic Legion of Decency, the National Board of Review and the Motion Picture Association (then the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America) were ordered by the Supreme Court to within reason allow for almost any type of motion pictures to be created so long as no people (especially children) and or animals were harmed by the making of a film, where should they go from here? I would suggest that instead of restrictive production/distribution codes, film distributors would possibly make an early version of the Film Rating System which would check film patrons' identifications at the box office against a film's rating. This would give many makers and distributors of motion pictures more creative freedom to explore the kinds of topics and subject matter they want to explore as well as spur various technological developments of all sorts. If film, comics, and broadcasting had received strong First Amendment protection and effective union protection much earlier in the twentieth century, American mass culture would probably have become more politically open, more adult in subject matter, and somewhat less dominated by studios, publishers, advertisers, and moral-pressure groups.

For film, the biggest change would have been the weakening or avoidance of the censorship system that grew after the Supreme Court’s 1915 decision in *Mutual Film*, which denied movies full First Amendment status. If films had been protected like newspapers or books from the 1910s or 1920s, local censorship boards and the later Production Code would have had much less power. Hollywood would still have worried about audiences, church groups, advertisers, and boycotts, but it would have been harder to impose a national regime of self-censorship over sex, race, labor conflict, drugs, homosexuality, interracial relationships, and political radicalism. The “Pre-Code” atmosphere of the early 1930s might have continued rather than being shut down. American cinema could have developed sooner into something closer to postwar European art cinema: more explicit, more politically varied, and less constrained by rules requiring criminals to be punished, marriages to be upheld, and social authority to be respected.

For comics, earlier First Amendment recognition would likely have prevented or softened the 1950s moral panic that produced the Comics Code Authority. Horror, crime, romance, satire, and politically critical comics would have had a better chance of surviving alongside superheroes. Publishers such as EC Comics might not have been crippled, and the medium might have matured earlier as a form for adults as well as children. The later emergence of underground comix, graphic novels, and alternative comics might have happened decades sooner, or at least would not have needed to define itself so sharply against a juvenile, Code-approved mainstream.

For broadcasting, the counterfactual is more complicated because radio and television used scarce spectrum, which gave the federal government a stronger regulatory claim than it had over print. But if broadcasters had gained stronger speech protections earlier, the Federal Radio Commission and later FCC might have focused more narrowly on technical allocation and less on content, “public interest” standards, political balance, indecency, and licensing pressure. That could have produced livelier and more ideological radio and television earlier, with more radical labor programming, anti-racist programming, religious controversy, sexual discussion, and partisan argument. On the other hand, it might also have allowed more demagoguery and extremist broadcasting, because fewer content-based controls would have existed.

Earlier union protections would have changed the economics as much as the content. Stronger unions for screenwriters, actors, directors, animators, radio performers, technicians, and comic-book creators would have reduced the power of studios, networks, and publishers. Creators might have won better wages, credits, residuals, health benefits, and perhaps more control over characters and scripts. In comics especially, early collective bargaining could have altered the history of superhero ownership: figures like Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster might not have lost control of Superman so completely, and the “work-for-hire” model might have been challenged much earlier. In animation and film, stronger unions might have limited brutal working hours and made strikes less desperate and more institutionalized.

Politically, earlier First Amendment and union protection would also have made blacklisting harder. The anti-communist purges of Hollywood, radio, and television depended not only on government pressure but also on employers’ willingness to fire or exclude politically suspect workers. Strong unions and clearer speech rights would not have eliminated Cold War repression, but they would have raised its legal and economic cost. Some left-wing writers, actors, directors, and broadcasters might have continued working openly, which would have left American popular culture with a more visible socialist, labor, and anti-racist strand.

The effects would not all have been liberating. Strong unions can become exclusionary, especially in a racially segregated and sexist society; they might have protected established white male workers while keeping women and minorities out unless civil-rights enforcement developed alongside them. Stronger speech rights would not have eliminated commercial pressure: advertisers, theater owners, distributors, and network sponsors would still have shaped content. Nor would censorship disappear entirely; private censorship by studios, publishers, and retailers could remain powerful. There might also have been a stronger conservative backlash, possibly producing new federal legislation or organized boycotts.

Overall, the United States would likely have had a less sanitized and more openly contested mass culture by mid-century. Film noir, social-problem films, adult comics, political radio, and controversial television would have developed earlier and with fewer interruptions. Creators would have had more bargaining power and possibly more ownership of their work. The broad direction would have been toward a more pluralistic and mature media environment, though still constrained by markets, racism, sexism, anticommunism, and corporate concentration.

Luigi Casale develops the Casale process after WWI. Italy had a deficit of fertilizers pre-war; it didn't have the trade networks or finances of other nations to purchase Chilean saltpeter in large amounts, and they invested heavily in nitrogen fixation as a result. WWI worsened that deficit, compounded by the loss of wheat imports from Russia, so Casale started work in 1917 on a more efficient method of nitrogen fixation. Said research continued in the postwar, because BASF refused to license the Haber-Bosch process elsewhere, and the Haber-Bosch process would have required modification anyways because Italy didn't have sufficient coal to use it to produce hydrogen gas in the original Haber-Bosch process. So Italy has the incentive to develop efficient nitrogen fixation processes for strategic autonomy, and Casale has the means to do so. Casale did postgraduate research in Berlin under Walter Nernst, whose research into physical chemistry mirrored that of Haber's, before returning to Italy. Casale then works near the Terni steelworks, which provided the steel to build pressure reactors able to stand pressures more than 3 times that of the Haber-Bosch process (notably by providing an unused battleship gun barrel). Even if we assume some sort of inexplicable theft or espionage on the part of Casale not mentioned in these histories and somehow nobody else thinks to apply Le Chatelier's Principle or try different catalysts, that just means the Frank-Caro process dominates. Sure, the 3x difference in energy usage is going to be difficult to bear, but between that and losing a total war/starving, people will just build more power plants and mine more fossil fuels or mineral nitrates/phosphates.
