If the Haber process were never invented, the modern world would be poorer, less populous, more agrarian, and more dependent on natural sources of nitrogen.

The central consequence would be agricultural. The Haber-Bosch process made it possible to synthesize ammonia from atmospheric nitrogen on an industrial scale, creating cheap nitrogen fertilizer. Without it, farmers would have to rely much more on manure, compost, crop rotation with legumes, guano, Chilean nitrate, and less efficient industrial nitrogen-fixation methods such as electric arc or calcium cyanamide processes. These alternatives could help, but they would be more limited, more expensive, and often tied to geography or abundant cheap electricity.

As a result, crop yields would be much lower, especially for cereals such as wheat, rice, and maize. Food would be more expensive, diets would be less meat-heavy, and more land would be needed to feed fewer people. The twentieth-century population boom would likely be much smaller. Instead of a world of over 8 billion people, global population might be billions lower, not because everyone would simply starve, but because higher food prices, slower economic growth, higher infant mortality, and different fertility patterns would constrain population growth over generations.

The political geography of nitrogen would also matter much more. Before synthetic ammonia, natural nitrate deposits—especially in Chile—were strategically vital. Without Haber-Bosch, nitrate-rich regions would become far more important to global trade and imperial competition. States with access to natural nitrates, large livestock populations, or strong legume-based farming systems would have advantages over those without them.

War would also be affected. Ammonia is not only used for fertilizer; it is a key feedstock for explosives. In World War I, the Haber-Bosch process allowed Germany to keep producing explosives despite the Allied blockade cutting it off from Chilean nitrates. Without it, Germany’s war effort would likely have been constrained much earlier. The war might have been shorter, or Germany might have had to fight very differently. More broadly, twentieth-century warfare would face tighter limits on munitions unless alternative nitrate supplies were secured.

Industrialization and urbanization would probably slow. Cheap fertilizer allowed fewer farmers to feed more city dwellers, supporting mass urban societies, large industrial labor forces, and globalized food systems. Without it, a larger share of the population would remain tied to agriculture, and economic growth in many regions would be slower. The Green Revolution in Asia and Latin America would be much weaker or would take a different form, relying more heavily on irrigation, crop breeding, legumes, and organic nutrient cycling.

There would be environmental benefits, but not simple ones. The world would have far less nitrogen runoff, fewer algal blooms and coastal dead zones, less nitrate contamination of groundwater, and lower nitrous oxide emissions from fertilizer use. On the other hand, lower yields would put pressure on forests, grasslands, and wetlands because more land would be needed for farming. So the planet might have less chemical nitrogen pollution but more habitat conversion.

In short, without the Haber process, humanity would not lose agriculture, but it would lose the cheap synthetic nitrogen that made modern high-yield farming possible. The likely world would have fewer people, more expensive food, greater geopolitical competition over natural nitrates, slower urban-industrial growth, and a less nitrogen-polluted but more land-hungry agricultural system.

Part I: Secret Dealings ​ December 1932 Reichskanzlei, Wilhelmstraße no. 77, Berlin The night was deep and dark, and a chill was in the air in Berlin. Wilhelmstraße, the street where many of the official German government offices, including the Reichspräsidentenpalais, are located, was especially quiet as the day's normal government activity had concluded. Away from the eye of any onlookers, in a tucked-away office in the Reichskanzlei, the second-most important man in Germany sat. Reichskanzler Kurt von Schleicher smoked a cigar at his desk. His guest was one of the leading figures within the NSDAP, Gregor Strasser, who had only recently arrived to the office. von Schleicher took out his cigar and began talking to Strasser. "Now, you may be wondering why I have called you here," von Schleicher declared. "I would like to offer you a position in my cabinet. Vice-Chancellor, in fact." "What would you like in return, Herr Reichskanzler?" Strasser asked. The general stood up. "Now, you know that my cabinet is only being held up by presidential power. I would like to find a Reichstag majority to support my cabinet, and the support of you and the like-minded Reichstag deputies would be instrumental in providing this. I am prepared to fill the vacancy in the position with you, if you agree to my proposal, however." "I feel accepting this proposal would create the highest ire in Herr Hitler." "Well, you have a large following in the party, correct?" von Schleicher did not wait for Strasser to respond before continuing, "I believe that you could simply split from the party—of course, this new party would join a coalition with some other prospective parties." Strasser quietly asked, "How do you think this would go through easily? The Sturmabteilung is everywhere. How are we supposed to keep it secret during the planning stages?" Now, von Schleicher paused to take a puff of his cigar before continuing, growing more animated as he detailed his plan. "You must keep this very secret, do not share it with anybody! Only you and I must know about this until it is time for the plan to be executed." "And if Hitler finds out?" Schleicher turned to look at Strasser, 10 years his junior, and stared intently into his eyes. "I am sure you would be removed from all political power within the NSDAP. I'm sure you don't want that." Strasser shuddered, perhaps from the cold or the thought of his removal. "I shall consider your offer, Herr Reichskanzler." As Strasser turned to leave, von Schleicher interrupted with one last remark. "Make sure to watch out for anyone who has contacts to Herr Hitler, even indirectly. Do not act suspicious, for they might track you. I shall see you tomorrow." Strasser closed the door, exited the building, and entered the cold winter night.

If Gregor Strasser had actually split the NSDAP in late 1932, the most likely result is not a successful “Querfront” regime, but a serious weakening of Hitler at exactly the moment when his route to power depended on appearing indispensable.

By late 1932 the Nazi Party was vulnerable. It had lost votes in the November Reichstag election, its finances were strained, the SA was restless, and Hitler had repeatedly failed to obtain the chancellorship on his own terms. Strasser, as the party’s national organizer and its leading “social-revolutionary” figure, had real influence, especially among some northern and western party functionaries. General Kurt von Schleicher hoped to exploit this by drawing Strasser, parts of the unions, and other nationalist-social forces into a “Querfront” — a cross-front coalition meant to split the Nazis and stabilize a presidential government without Hitler.

If Strasser had broken away decisively, he probably could have taken some deputies, organizers, and local activists with him. But he almost certainly would not have taken anything like half the party. The NSDAP was already intensely Hitler-centered. Most Gauleiters owed their positions to Hitler, the propaganda machine was loyal to Hitler, and the party’s emotional appeal was bound to the Führer myth rather than to Strasser’s program. Goebbels, Göring, Himmler, and the core leadership would have attacked Strasser as a traitor. Many wavering Nazis would likely have stayed with Hitler out of ideological loyalty, fear, opportunism, or because they believed only Hitler could win power.

Still, even a partial split could have mattered enormously. Hitler’s bargaining power in January 1933 rested on the claim that he commanded Germany’s largest mass party and that conservatives had to deal with him or face continuing paralysis. A Strasser breakaway would have punctured that claim. It would have made Hitler look less inevitable, less able to control his own movement, and less useful to conservative elites such as Papen, Hindenburg, and industrial-nationalist circles. In that case, the Papen-Hitler deal that produced Hitler’s appointment as chancellor on 30 January 1933 becomes much less likely, or at least harder to justify.

The most plausible short-term outcome would be that Schleicher survives longer as chancellor. He might try to govern through emergency decrees while using the Strasser split to neutralize the Nazis and tempt parts of the labor movement or Catholic Centre into toleration. But a durable Querfront government would still be unlikely. The Social Democrats and trade unions distrusted Schleicher; the Communists would oppose any such arrangement; conservatives disliked Strasser’s anti-capitalist rhetoric; and Strasser himself lacked a coherent mass base independent of Hitler. So the result would probably be a prolonged presidential-authoritarian crisis rather than a stable new coalition.

If the split were large enough — for example, if Strasser took dozens of Reichstag deputies and a meaningful part of the party apparatus — it might have prevented Hitler from becoming chancellor in January 1933. Germany could then have moved toward one of several alternatives: a continued Schleicher dictatorship-by-decree, new elections in which the divided Nazi vote declined further, or a more openly military-presidential regime under Hindenburg. None of these would have guaranteed the survival of Weimar democracy, but they would likely have reduced the chance of a rapid Nazi seizure of total power in 1933.

If the split were small, however, Hitler might have survived it. He would have purged Strasserites, denounced the “betrayal,” tightened control over the party, and still presented himself as the only leader capable of mobilizing the nationalist right. In that case Hitler might still have become chancellor, though perhaps later and in a somewhat weakened position.

So the careful answer is: a Strasser split in 1932 could plausibly have blocked or delayed Hitler’s appointment, especially if it visibly fractured the Nazi Reichstag bloc and party machine. But Strasser was unlikely to build a successful Querfront alternative. His split would most likely have deepened the crisis of the Weimar state and weakened Nazism’s momentum, not produced a stable “left-national” government. The biggest historical consequence would have been negative rather than constructive: it might have deprived Hitler of the aura of unity and inevitability that helped carry him into power in January 1933.

If the Montreal Expos had remained a Canadian Major League Baseball team, the biggest difference is that MLB would likely have had a much stronger and more continuous presence in Canada, while Washington, D.C. might not have regained a team in 2005—at least not through the Expos’ relocation.

For the Expos to survive in Montreal, several things probably would have needed to change: a better stadium situation than Olympic Stadium, stronger local ownership, and a recovery from the damage caused by the 1994 strike. The strike was especially devastating because the 1994 Expos had the best record in baseball and looked like a serious World Series contender. When the season was canceled, Montreal lost its best chance to turn competitive success into long-term fan and corporate support.

Had they stayed and received a new downtown ballpark, the Expos might have become a viable small-to-mid-market franchise similar to the Minnesota Twins, Cleveland Guardians, or Milwaukee Brewers: not always wealthy, but capable of competing in cycles through scouting, player development, and smart roster management. Montreal had a history of producing or developing stars, including Gary Carter, Andre Dawson, Tim Raines, Larry Walker, Pedro Martínez, Vladimir Guerrero, and others. With modern revenue sharing and a better stadium, the club could plausibly have survived as a respected, occasionally competitive franchise.

Canadian baseball culture would also look different. The Toronto Blue Jays would not have been Canada’s only MLB team for two decades. A continuing Expos franchise would have preserved a natural national rivalry: French Canada versus English Canada, Montreal versus Toronto, National League versus American League. Interleague games between the Expos and Blue Jays could have become a major annual event, similar to regional rivalries like Cubs–White Sox or Yankees–Mets. Baseball’s footprint in Quebec likely would be much larger today, with more youth participation, media attention, and local identification with the sport.

The Washington Nationals, as we know them, probably would not exist. Washington might eventually have received an expansion team or another relocated club, but the Nationals’ specific history—including their 2019 World Series title—would be different or might belong to another franchise identity. Players associated with the Nationals’ rise, such as Ryan Zimmerman, Stephen Strasburg, Bryce Harper, Max Scherzer, and Juan Soto, might have played for a Montreal franchise if the Expos had remained and followed a similar draft-and-development path.

The National League East would also have retained a different character. The Expos would have continued rivalries with the Mets, Phillies, Braves, and Marlins. Montreal’s presence would have kept MLB more visibly international, with two Canadian clubs and a stronger bilingual identity. It might also have encouraged MLB to take expansion or relocation to nontraditional markets more seriously, because a successful Montreal team would have shown that baseball could still work outside the largest U.S. media centers.

Still, survival would not have guaranteed greatness. Montreal would likely have faced the same challenges as other smaller-revenue teams: retaining stars, competing with richer clubs, and depending heavily on attendance and player development. Without a new stadium and serious ownership, merely keeping the team in Montreal would not have solved the underlying problems.

In short, if the Expos had remained in Canada under healthier financial and stadium conditions, MLB would likely have had a stronger Canadian identity, Montreal would have remained one of baseball’s distinctive markets, the Blue Jays would have had a true domestic rival, and the Washington Nationals’ modern history might never have happened. The Expos probably would not have become a financial powerhouse, but they could have become a stable, culturally important franchise with periodic chances to contend.

items.original_question: What if Both Germany and Italy don't join PANAVIA Tornado program? What if both Germany and Italy for some reason both bail or don't join the PANAVIA Tornado program at it's inception? What are the options regarding this? What does Germany, Italy and the UK do? Could the UK carry on alone? What aircraft could replace the Tornado and fill in this role? Could a two seat, big wing SEPECAT Jaguar work? Would an advanced Buccaneer work with a modern avionics upgrade? Regards
items.model_answer:
If West Germany and Italy had withdrawn from the PANAVIA Tornado program at the outset, the most likely result is that the Tornado as historically built would never have existed. The aircraft depended on shared costs, shared production, and a large combined order. Britain alone probably could not have justified developing such an expensive variable-geometry strike aircraft so soon after the cancellation of TSR-2 and the abandoned F-111K purchase.

Britain would probably have faced a difficult choice: either buy an American aircraft or stretch the life of existing types. In the short term the RAF might have relied longer on Buccaneers, Phantoms and Jaguars for strike and reconnaissance roles. For deep interdiction and nuclear strike, Britain might have reconsidered a version of the F-111 or later moved toward American fighters such as the F-15 or F-16, though these would not have matched the Tornado’s exact low-level penetration concept without modification. The Tornado ADV interceptor variant would also not have appeared, meaning Britain would likely have replaced Lightnings and Phantoms with a foreign air-defense fighter or extended them longer at considerable cost.

West Germany and Italy would probably have turned toward American or French alternatives. West Germany needed replacements for the F-104 Starfighter and for NATO nuclear-strike, reconnaissance and maritime roles. Without Tornado, it might have bought more F-4 Phantoms initially and then joined the wider European F-16 movement, as Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and Norway did. Italy might likewise have prolonged the F-104S, bought F-16s or Mirages, and later relied more heavily on indigenous or joint light-attack projects such as the AMX.

The broader effect would have been a major setback for European military aerospace cooperation. PANAVIA and the RB199 engine consortium helped bind together British, German and Italian industry and created a model for later collaboration. Without Tornado, British Aerospace, MBB and Aeritalia would have had less experience working together on a complex combat aircraft. That could have weakened or delayed the later Eurofighter Typhoon program, or changed its membership and design path. France, meanwhile, might have gained more influence through Mirage exports, while the United States would likely have sold many more fighters to NATO Europe.

Militarily, NATO would still have found ways to cover the central-front strike mission, but with a different balance. The United States would have carried a larger share through F-111s, F-4s and later F-16s, while European air forces would have been less independent in deep-strike and specialized low-level interdiction. In the 1991 Gulf War, there would have been no RAF and Italian Tornado force performing the famous low-level runway-attack missions; those tasks would likely have been handled by U.S. or French aircraft, or by a different British aircraft if Britain had bought one.

So the main consequence would not simply have been “no Tornado.” It would have meant a more American-dominated NATO fighter market, weaker European defense-industrial integration, a different RAF force structure, and possibly a delayed or altered path toward later European combat aircraft cooperation.

items.question: What If No nuclear weapons?
human_answers: As has been noted it is pretty much impossible to avoid having nuclear weapons ever being created. The science is pretty obvious. What CAN be altered, to a degree, is the "when". The U.S. threw a dramatic amount of funding at the effort, along with huge amounts of resources (Manhattan literally built the entire city of Oak Ridge TN to house the workers on the project. It was farmland, with about 3,000 people living in the area then in less than 2 years, it was a city with a population of 75,000. Government just walked in and "acquired" 59,000 acres, evicted everyone in the local farms and villages, and started building a fence (BIG ASS fence). The same thing happened in Washington with Hanford, except it was 500,000 acres and 39,000 people, Just a little less funding, or a project manager less driven than General Groves and the Bomb isn't ready.

Based on the described scenario, the USSR becomes the first country to test a nuclear weapon in the early 1950s, whereupon the US and UK governments demand an explanation for who filed the relevant reports in the wrong section back in 1940. In the case of the US, it's probably Lyman Briggs, who in OTL actually did lock away a key report in his safe without showing it to anyone else, which may have delayed the start of the Manhattan Project by several months. But even then, uranium fission was discovered in France in December 1938. The Einsten-Szilard letter warned the US government of the possibilities in August 1939. The Frisch-Peierls memorandum, the first description of a nuclear weapon, was written in March 1940 for the British government. By Frisch's own description, the work he and Peierls did was straightforward for any competent nuclear physicist. There might be a PoD wherein Frisch and Peierls are interned as enemy aliens and not allowed to work as physicists. Oliphant is focussed on the higher priority radar work, so Thomson's conclusion that it was not worth pursuing a chain reaction in uranium is accepted by the British government. There is therefore no MAUD committee, no report for Briggs to ignore, and no reason for Oliphant to kick things into gear. Instead, what is likely to happen is that eventually someone in the US does ask the questions that Frisch and Peierls asked, and they reach similar answers. Given OTL's trajectory, it's hard to see why that would happen any earlier than August 1941, given that US research was initially largely concerned with power plants rather than weapons. If we say it does, it might take the best part of a year for a US equivalent of the MAUD report to be carried out and an atomic weapons programme started. That puts a US weapons programme without the MAUD input as starting in mid-1942 - so about a six month delay. An arbitrarily longer delay is entirely plausible, but eventually - and probably sooner rather than later - someone is going to ask the right questions, and then things will start moving very quickly.

items.original_question: What if No nuclear weapons? No Tubes Alloy or Los Alamos, and no German atomic research. Sadly, Japan is invaded - high causalities on both sides especially Japanese civilians much of it from starvation. No organised surrender, just quiet acceptance from district, to town, then the next. Japanese Americans were 'encouraged' to return to the homeland and rebuild - from the stone age! But what happens - with no nuclear umbrella - no ballistic missiles. WMD were confined to the Grandslams & Tallboys, with fuel air explosives via aircraft bombs or short range (V2) missiles. Research was more focused on better guidance for V1 type cruise missiles, and other ASM. Would the Berlin Blockade still happen, would it get hot? How would this affect Defence spending? Where would the focus on the difference between here and OTL?
items.model_answer:
If nuclear weapons had never existed, the 20th and 21st centuries would likely have been less dominated by fear of instant global annihilation, but not necessarily more peaceful.

The most immediate difference would be World War II’s ending. Without atomic bombs, Japan might still have surrendered because of Soviet entry into the war, naval blockade, firebombing, and exhaustion, but surrender may have taken longer. A U.S. invasion or prolonged siege could have caused enormous casualties among Japanese civilians, Japanese soldiers, American forces, and possibly Soviet forces in East Asia. Hiroshima and Nagasaki would not have become symbols of nuclear devastation, but Japan’s defeat would still likely have occurred.

The Cold War would have looked very different. Nuclear deterrence made direct war between the United States and the Soviet Union terrifyingly risky. Without nuclear weapons, the superpowers might have been more willing to fight each other directly, especially in Europe, Korea, or the Middle East. NATO and the Warsaw Pact would probably have invested even more heavily in conventional armies, air forces, chemical weapons, biological weapons, missiles, and possibly space-based military systems. The absence of nuclear weapons might have reduced the risk of human extinction, but it could have increased the likelihood of large conventional great-power wars.

International politics would also be different. Nuclear weapons gave a small number of states extraordinary strategic status: the United States, Soviet Union/Russia, Britain, France, China, India, Pakistan, Israel, and North Korea. Without them, global power would depend more on population, industrial capacity, geography, alliances, technology, and conventional military strength. Countries such as Japan, Germany, and India might have had even greater strategic weight because advanced industry and conventional military capability would matter more.

Arms control and nonproliferation institutions would be far less central. There would be no Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, no nuclear deterrence doctrines, no nuclear umbrella, and no crises like the Cuban Missile Crisis in the same form. But other weapons of mass destruction might have received more attention. Chemical and biological weapons could have become more important as “ultimate” deterrents, unless they too were strongly stigmatized and controlled.

Decolonization and regional wars might also have changed. Nuclear-armed powers sometimes avoided escalation because of nuclear risk, but they still fought proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan, Africa, and Latin America. Without nuclear weapons, some of those conflicts might have escalated into direct clashes between major powers. On the other hand, smaller states would not be able to use nuclear programs as tools of regime survival or diplomatic leverage, as North Korea has done.

Overall, a world without nuclear weapons would be safer in one crucial sense: humanity would not live under the threat of sudden nuclear catastrophe. There would be no risk of accidental launch, nuclear terrorism, radioactive fallout from nuclear war, or civilization-ending nuclear winter. But it would not automatically be a peaceful world. Nuclear weapons may have prevented some great-power wars by making them too dangerous to fight, while also creating an unprecedented existential threat. Without them, the world might have had fewer apocalyptic risks but more frequent large-scale conventional wars.

items.question: What If the USSR was leaked information about OB just before it happened and were thus better prepared and more competent in 1941? (No strike though)
human_answers: A couple days or weeks isn’t really enough if you’re going with the “Stalin finally makes a good decision” scenario. You need at least a couple months to have the Soviets dug in and prepared at more defensible spots further east than iotl, and considering the German initial manpower advantage (to say nothing of the purges creating widespread incompetence in the red army and said incompetence making their logistics horrible), they still probably lose pretty hard, although not quite as much as iotl. I think at least 6 or so (probably a bit more) months is needed to help close the manpower gap and create a Minsk-Kiev line that the Germans can’t penetrate if you don’t want Soviet losses to be seen as proportionally a lot bigger (though there’s a strong chance they still are in this scenario, just not enough to give the impression that all you need to do is kick in the rotten door enough and it’ll fall).

The Soviet Union possessed highly precise intelligence indicating that the German military's logistics were insufficient to sustain a protracted war and that its armaments factories had not yet shifted to a wartime footing. (This intelligence was derived from the infiltration of German industry by communist sympathizers.) Hitler also couldn't been so foolish as to believe that the mighty Soviet Union could be conquered within three months—at least, no analyst would have dared to venture such an insulting conjecture. Consequently, the less reliable intelligence from military and western country must have been false, and war is in next year. This chain of logic is remarkably robust; You cannot convince the Soviets that Germany is about to attack without introducing collateral changes—and different changes would inevitably lead to different outcomes in the war. Would they perceive their own military as weaker? Would they place their trust in Anglo-American intelligence while disregarding the Comintern’s own network? Or would they have managed to plant exceptionally reliable spies deep within the German military itself? Each of these scenarios would necessitate a distinct defensive strategy, thereby altering the very trajectory of the conflict. One thing, however, remains certain: if the Soviet Union were to lose the war while the United States remained an active belligerent, the Americans would undoubtedly drop the nuclear bomb.

Again, as usual these scenarios entirely depend on one or both sides failing to react to changing circumstances. Firstly, USSR had information about possibility of German attack and was reacting. 'Stalin refused to believe the intelligence' is basically a myth. Soviet problem was not lack of the information or anyone's willingness or unwillingness 'to believe'. And Germans were positioned to attack better than Soviets were positioned to defend. Let's say USSR starts mobilizing mid-April. And yes, it could screw Mussolini by preventing Germany from bailing him out, but it was simple question of Germany already having mobilized army and having a better logistical infrastructure on their side of the border, so whatever obvious thing Soviets would do, Germans will have an opportunity to react. What I wanted to ask is this What if the USSR was leaked information about OB just before it happened and were thus better prepared and more competent in 1941? (But they don't do a preemptive strike though. This question is not about that. Thats a whole different story) 1)Would this lead to an earlier Soviet victory in WW2? If yes then, 1.1)How much more of Europe could Stalin get if his pushing force from the east is sooner and stronger. If yes then 2.1)Would this be enough to win the war for Germany? 2.2)Would the US use nukes to deter Germany from winning if they reach close enough to Moscow and assuming Hitler has still declared war on the USA?
items.model_answer:
If the USSR received a credible leak about Operation Barbarossa shortly before 22 June 1941 and actually acted on it competently, but did not launch a preemptive strike, the main effect would be to reduce the catastrophic scale of the initial Soviet collapse. It would not likely stop the German invasion at the border, but it would probably make Barbarossa slower, bloodier, and less strategically successful.

Historically, the USSR already had many warnings, but Stalin distrusted them and feared provoking Germany. So the key counterfactual is not merely “the Soviets know,” but “Stalin and the high command believe it and prepare rationally.” Even a few days of serious preparation would matter. Soviet aircraft could be dispersed from exposed forward airfields, ammunition and fuel could be issued, units could be brought to alert, communications could be checked, border troops could occupy defensive positions, bridges and depots could be prepared for demolition, and commanders could be given permission to retreat rather than wait for impossible orders from Moscow.

That would significantly blunt the German opening blow. The Luftwaffe would destroy fewer Soviet aircraft on the ground. Forward Soviet armies would still be under pressure, but fewer would be immobilized by confusion and contradictory orders. The great encirclements at Bialystok-Minsk, Smolensk, Uman, and Kiev might still occur in some form, but they would likely be smaller, slower, and more costly for Germany. The Soviets would lose territory, but not quite so many men and weapons in the first months.

The Germans would still have major advantages in 1941: better operational coordination, more experienced officers, superior tactical air-ground cooperation, and a mature doctrine for mobile warfare. The Red Army was still recovering from purges, rapid expansion, poor training, weak communications, and half-formed mechanized corps. So a prepared USSR does not mean the Wehrmacht is thrown back immediately. Army Group Centre probably still advances deep into Belarus and toward Smolensk; Army Group North probably still threatens Leningrad; Army Group South still pushes into Ukraine. But the tempo is slower.

The biggest difference could be around Moscow and Ukraine. If Soviet leadership is not only warned but more competent, it might avoid the disastrous decision to hold Kiev too long. A timely withdrawal from Ukraine could save hundreds of thousands of troops. That alone would make the 1941 campaign far harder for Germany. Likewise, if Army Group Centre takes heavier losses earlier and loses more time, the final drive on Moscow may begin later, with fewer fresh units and worse logistics. In that case, Germany probably does not get as close to Moscow as it did historically, or its offensive stalls earlier.

The strategic result is that the USSR survives more comfortably. Germany’s chance of winning a quick campaign, already doubtful, becomes even worse. Barbarossa depended on destroying the Red Army near the frontier and collapsing Soviet command before the USSR could mobilize its depth. Better Soviet readiness would undercut that premise. Germany would still occupy large areas, but it would fail sooner as a war of annihilation and become trapped earlier in a long attritional war it was poorly positioned to win.

By 1942, the consequences could be large. If the Red Army preserves more manpower and equipment in 1941, Germany enters 1942 weaker relative to the USSR. Case Blue, the drive toward the Caucasus and Stalingrad, might be less ambitious or less successful. Stalingrad as we know it might not happen, or Germany might suffer a major defeat earlier and farther west. The Eastern Front would still be brutal, but the Soviet recovery would begin from a stronger position.

So the most likely outcome is not “Germany is stopped at the border,” but “Germany still invades successfully at first, yet loses the campaign’s decisive momentum much earlier.” The USSR avoids some of the worst disasters of 1941, Moscow is less endangered, German losses rise, and the war in the East probably turns against Germany sooner. The overall war may end somewhat earlier, or at least with the Red Army reaching Central Europe from a stronger position than it did historically.

I’m not saying that nothing would change. There absolutely would be changes from neither artist existing. It’s just that fundamentally: You still have popular music derived from Black American musical traditions. You still have a push away from large swing-style bands and towards smaller guitar-based bands - especially since before the digital era the guitar is the most accessible music instrument for young people wanting to make music. You still have the Baby Boom yielding a much larger youth cohort than before - thus yielding a significant generational divide by the early to mid 1960s as they’ve grown up having not known the struggles of their parents or older siblings - and have more room tackling lifestyle changes without worry for economic precarity. You still have big labels and radio stations wanting to play “different music” for “different races” so to speak. You still have the post-WWII dominance and saturation of American pop culture - including music - in Europe and across the globe. And since the UK and the Commonwealth have virtually zero language barrier with the US - music that imitates American musical traditions (twice removed from Black American roots) has the potential to take off. You still have the advancements in recording technology that gave artists room to make more experimental and groundbreaking music than before. Plus the steady rise of FM radio later in the 1960s to provide a market for more ambitious music. You still have the Sexual Revolution to loosen norms around sex. On top of the various other drivers of the counterculture. You still have the payola scandal and the burnout of 1950s rock stars causing the 1959-64 dearth in the quality of pop music. But that’s just structurally speaking. Aesthetically speaking, things could be shifted around - with some new genre inspired by surf rock and garage rock (though realistically not actually either one of them) blowing up out of nowhere by 1964-65 - and Pat Boone is the King of Rock ‘n’ Roll all the artists of the 1960s are inspired by in terms of singing style and aura. While British rock bands are basically seen as a store brand that only gains later appreciation in the social media era decades later a la Japanese city pop. But it would still fundamentally fit the bigger variables that had been brewing years or even decades before the mid 1960s.

While the absence of the Beatles (and particularly Lennon and McCartney) would deprive us of some very good songs, there were vast numbers of competent bands in Britain that could have filled the niche if given the opportunity- whether together or singly. The bigger impact would probably have been on the penetration of British artists into the USA [1], but that's quite likely to happen eventually because there's money to be made from big crowds of relatively wealthy teenagers who happen to hit on a good enough band. The other impact might have been on the pressure to become singer-songwriters, rather than just singers/performers. Again, money is a big driver so it's likely to happen sooner or later. Otherwise, US innovation is likely to remain largely unchanged (Iggy and the Stooges will still form, and the drivers for hippy culture and rock bands is still there). Meanwhile, the Rolling Stones would still be experimenting with blues and quality musicians like Buddy Holly, Carl Perkins will be filling the niche that Elvis is no longer dominating. In short, different but still broadly recognisable. [1] The Monkees are unlikely to be formed, but songs like Day Dream Believer are too good not to end up being a success, even if it takes a few cover versions to become a real hit.

No Beatles or Elvis? Hmmm the amateur musicologist in me (that's what happens when you're a musician, who has also played in rock bands) says that rock 'n roll would still exist. The chances are also good that you would still have its superstar in the 50s - I read years ago that there were plans to push Carl Perkins (he of "Blue Suede Shoes" fame) towards superstardom by Sun Records. He might have actually become one if he hadn't suffered a major injury (he was in a car crash that kept him out of commission for a long time). Sam Phillips and even Elvis stated that Carl was doing rockabilly before Elvis, and unlike Elvis, Carl was also a songwriter. Most musicians will tell you that having that skill gives you much more staying power - you're not just a performer, you can make money off or songwriting royalties. By the time Carl recovered from the car crash it was too late, Elvis had overshadowed him. Jerry Lee Lewis, courtesy of his flamboyant personality might have become the 50s rock 'n roll superstar (how long he would have lasted would have depended upon whether or not he was still foolish enough to marry his underage cousin). The 60s? Hmmm that's not so certain - in the early 60s, rock 'n roll seemed to be on it's way out (or at least heading towards just being a niche genre of music). What rock 'n roll there was on Top 40 radio was mostly bland, and barely even qualified as rock 'n roll (Frankie Avalon anybody?). The Beach Boys were making songs with lame-o lyrics ("Be True to Your School", etc.). Even in Europe it was only doing so-so - I remember reading an interview of Jimmy Page (who along with playing guitar in Led Zeppelin, and the Yardbirds, was an in-demand session guitarist in the early and mid 60s), where he stated that in the early 60s, it was hard to even find rock 'n roll recording sessions to play on. Without the Beatles, rock'n roll might have just kept on being 50s-style teen hearthrob music performed by Cliff Richard, instrumental music played by bands like The Shadows (who also happened to be Cliff Richard's backing band), and possibly music played by 50s American rock 'n roll musicians, who were going nowhere in the USA with their careers (Bo Diddly, Eddie Cochran, etc. performed extensively in Europe in the early 60s when their careers fizzled out in the US). One of the big elements of the Beatles that helped to propel them to stardom IMO, was that for its time (the early 60s), the Beatles' music was considered HARD ROCK. As a result, it had more energy to it than your typical music of the period, and people liked it. The Stones? They were in their infancy, playing what is to me, watered down blues, that sounded nowhere near as intense. That hard rock edge the Beatles had is what kick started rock 'n roll again, and resulted in a million bands wanting to sound like them (even in the US, after they were on the Ed Sullivan Show). No Beatles and IMO, rock 'n roll continues its decline into a niche music genre, with the occasional Top 40 hit by bland groups like Gary Pucket and The Union Gap, Gary Lewis and The Playboys, etc. Not much in the way of edgy, interesting music. In the US, Link Wray never charts as high as he did with "Rumble" (which was actually banned by radio stations because it was "too threatening - it'll incite people to riot"), and Lonnie Mack at most has a few very modest hits like he had with "Wham".

Oh, for the love of Pete, not THIS again.... I just don't understand how some on this board can analyze military events down to the level of minutiae where they can argue that if a particular German general farted at a given moment in 1940, the entirety of World War II would come out differently, and yet at the same time assume that popular culture would remain essentially unaltered without the presence of two of its most important figures. Just as one example: before the Beatles, there was no such thing as a "British rock and roll group" in the eyes of Americans, and particularly American record companies, radio programmers, and concert promoters. Cliff Richard, who was Britain's biggest rock and roll superstar prior to the Beatles, went absolutely nowhere in America. Americans knew that rock and roll had originated in the U.S., and they were very parochial about it - the assumption, and it was not often wrong, before the Beatles was that anything coming from Britain would be a poor copy of records American teenagers already owned. (And it WAS teenagers almost exclusively who listened to rock and roll in 1963; projecting one's own current cultural dynamics into the past is part of the reason one gets lost). No British rock group - not one - had broken in the U.S. before 1964. The Beatles themselves at first were turned down by Capitol, the American division of EMI, who held their recording contract in the UK; Capitol refused to issue their first four singles in the U.S. It took the "Beatlemania" phenomenon to convince Capitol that it was worth giving the Beatles a shot, which enabled Beatlemania to cross the Atlantic. I'm sorry, but it's not as if "Holliemania" or "Dave Clark Fivemania" simply takes the place of that. There's a whole set of intangibles here. You can't just assume that you like the Rolling Stones better, so they automatically take the place of the Beatles. It would never have worked like that. What happens to the Rolling Stones becomes essentially undefinable. And that's just one example. I didn't even address the fact of no Elvis - which probably would have meant no Beatles AND virtually none of the other British Invasion acts either. Removing Elvis from the picture (which automatically would remove the Beatles as we know them) changes the ENTIRE trajectory of popular music from that day to this, in well-nigh unpredictable ways. Period.
items.original_question: What if Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley. American Singer and Actor Elvis Presley and British Rock Band The Beatles are the most Influential musicians in existence. With the former codifying Rockabilly and is credited for advancing the Feminist movement in America, and the Latter spearheaded the British Invasion, increased public interest in Psychedelic Drugs, Asian Spirituality and heralded the Album Era. Let's say both the musician and the Band never had any interest in music, preventing the codifying of Rockabilly and The British Invasion. How would this influence modern music?
items.model_answer:
If modern music had developed without The Beatles and Elvis Presley, it would still exist in recognizable forms, but its timeline, symbols, and cultural center of gravity would likely be very different.

Elvis Presley did not invent rock and roll, but he became the figure who brought Black rhythm and blues, country, gospel, and pop into a hugely visible mainstream package for white American audiences in the 1950s. Without Elvis, rock and roll would probably still have broken through through artists such as Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Fats Domino, Buddy Holly, Jerry Lee Lewis, Bo Diddley, and others. However, the mainstream acceptance of rock might have been slower, less centered on a single superstar, and perhaps more openly associated with its Black musical origins. The image of the rebellious male rock star—sexual, youthful, dangerous but marketable—would have emerged differently, possibly through several artists rather than one dominant icon.

Without The Beatles, the effect on the 1960s and later popular music would be even broader. They helped turn the pop group into an artistic unit, made self-written songs the norm for rock bands, expanded the possibilities of studio recording, and gave albums greater status as coherent artistic statements rather than collections of singles. If they had never existed, other acts—The Beach Boys, Bob Dylan, The Rolling Stones, The Kinks, The Who, Motown writers and producers, Phil Spector, and later psychedelic and progressive bands—would still have pushed popular music forward. But the specific fusion of melody, experimentation, mass popularity, and cultural influence that The Beatles represented would be missing.

The “British Invasion” might also have been smaller or delayed. British rock bands would still have appeared, but without The Beatles as the breakthrough model, American popular music might have remained more dominated by Motown, soul, folk, surf rock, girl groups, and domestic rock and roll for longer. The Rolling Stones or another British group might have become the leading export, but the tone of the movement could have been bluesier, harder-edged, and less pop-melodic.

Modern genres would still have developed: rock, pop, soul, funk, disco, hip-hop, electronic music, punk, metal, and R&B all had multiple roots. But their evolution would likely sound different. Rock might have leaned more heavily toward blues, garage rock, folk, and soul rather than the Beatles-style mixture of tight songwriting, harmony, experimentation, and studio craft. Pop songwriting might have remained more producer- and songwriter-driven for longer, rather than shifting so strongly toward bands and artists writing their own material.

Culturally, youth music would still have become powerful because the postwar teenage market, radio, television, civil rights struggles, urbanization, and new recording technology were already transforming society. But Elvis and The Beatles gave those transformations iconic faces. Without them, modern music would probably be less centered on the mythology of the rock star and the self-contained band. Other figures would have filled parts of the gap, but no replacement would necessarily have had the same combination of timing, charisma, controversy, innovation, and global reach.

So the best answer is: modern music would not disappear, but it would be less Beatles-shaped and less Elvis-shaped. Rock and pop would still rise, but probably more slowly, with different heroes, a different balance between Black and white musical influence in the mainstream, a weaker or altered British Invasion, and a different idea of what a pop artist or rock band could be.

items.question: What If the Royal Navy had deployed carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward?
human_answers: Far too big Even with folding wings I don't think they would fit on the elevators and would take up too much room in the hanger even of they fit which again I suspect not Its landing on performance of he Beaufighter is about the same as an avenger (60 knots?) but its much heavier than the TBF so I am not sure the arrestor cables of the day could handle such a plane. Its a nice idea but its too much of a plane for the carriers of the day - might work on an Audacious class but not the carriers built in the late 30s. The Whispering Death is already doing sterling work as a land based anti shipping aircraft during the war and it has great range - not quite 'Rikko' (G3m and G4m Japanese bombers) range, but close too it, but still a scourge where ever it operated.

In the last thread on the subject I mentioned, given any wing-break would have to be somewhat outboard the engines*, that you could probably take one up and down on Implacable's forward lift but the hangar height would preclude you rolling it off. You could store one in Illustrious's hangar, if you made it from a kit of parts, as the lift is too narrow. So deck parks only. You could use some form of depressing oleos to lower the Beaufighter's resting angle. You might just scrape it into Implacable's hangar but clearances would be marginal. Any kind of seaway would make deck handling tricky to impossible. You could also only load a torpedo on the flight deck with the aircraft back up to full height. I also suggested an increased-chord rudder and handed props because the Beaufighter could be a handful with all the room in the world. Operating a Beau on/off of a carrier is an expensive way to give a pilot a coronary... ETA: The wing-breaks are going to be in the order of 25ft apart and Illustrious's elevators are only 22ft across. Folding the wings is also going to involve re-siting the cooling ducts from the outboard leading edge.
items.original_question: What if Sea Beaufort and Sea Beaufighters used on Royal Navy aircraft carriers? What if the Royal Navy used a possible Bristol Sea variant of both Beauforts and Beaufighters on their carriers starting in 1940 replacing Fairy Swordfish aircraft in the torpedo attack role for example? Would this be possible design wise? Would they be better than the bomb and torpedo attack aircraft available at the time? Would the aircraft actually be able to be used like this or would they be too large? How effective would they be if used on aircraft carriers? Regards
items.model_answer:
If the Royal Navy had had genuinely carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward, the Fleet Air Arm would have been much more dangerous earlier in the war, especially in the Mediterranean and in long-range fleet defence. But it probably would not have transformed the course of the war by itself, because British carriers, doctrine, production capacity, and deck-handling limits would still have constrained their use.

The biggest change would have been that the Royal Navy would have escaped some of the weakness caused by relying on slow biplane torpedo bombers and mediocre early-war fighters. The Swordfish was extraordinarily useful, but it was slow and vulnerable in daylight against modern fighters. The Fulmar had range and reliability but was not a first-rate interceptor. Carrier Beauforts would have given the Fleet Air Arm a faster, heavier torpedo and strike aircraft earlier than the Albacore and before the arrival of American Avengers. Carrier Beaufighters would have provided a powerful long-range fighter, strike fighter, anti-shipping aircraft, and later a good radar night fighter.

In the Mediterranean this could have mattered a lot. British carriers operating from Gibraltar, Alexandria, and around Malta were repeatedly exposed to Italian and German bombers. Sea Beaufighters would have been much better at intercepting Ju 88s, He 111s, Cant Z.1007s, and reconnaissance aircraft than Fulmars or Sea Hurricanes in many situations, particularly at longer range. They would also have been deadly against Italian shipping, destroyers, tankers, and coastal targets. A carrier group with Beaufighters could project a much more dangerous anti-shipping umbrella into the central Mediterranean, making Axis supply runs to North Africa more costly.

Sea Beauforts might also have improved torpedo attacks against Italian fleet units and convoys. They were faster than Swordfish and could carry a proper torpedo load, so daylight attacks would be less suicidal than with biplanes. British operations against Italian convoys to Libya, against Taranto follow-up opportunities, and against heavy units such as Vittorio Veneto or Littorio-class battleships might have been more effective. Malta convoys might have benefited from stronger carrier fighter cover and from more effective pre-emptive strikes against Axis airfields and naval forces.

Against the German surface fleet, the effect is more mixed. In the Bismarck chase, faster carrier torpedo aircraft could have been useful, but the historical Swordfish succeeded partly because they could fly slowly and attack in terrible weather from a pitching carrier deck. A Sea Beaufort would have had more speed and range, but it would also have been harder to operate from a carrier in foul Atlantic conditions. The famous disabling hit on Bismarck’s rudder might or might not still happen. The counterfactual aircraft improve British chances, but they do not guarantee a better result than the historically lucky Swordfish attack.

For fleet air defence, Sea Beaufighters would have been a major improvement but not a complete solution. The Beaufighter was fast, heavily armed, rugged, and long-ranged, but it was not a nimble dogfighter. It would have been excellent against bombers, maritime patrol aircraft, and transport aircraft, and useful as a night fighter with radar. Against Bf 109s or later Japanese Zeros, it would have been at a disadvantage in close combat. The Royal Navy would still have needed small, agile single-seat fighters such as Martlets/Wildcats, Sea Hurricanes, Seafires, Hellcats, and Corsairs.

There would also have been serious practical penalties. Beauforts and Beaufighters were large twin-engine aircraft. To operate them from British carriers in 1940, they would need folding wings, arrestor hooks, strengthened undercarriages, catapult fittings, naval radios, corrosion protection, and careful low-speed deck-handling characteristics. These modifications would add weight and reduce performance. More importantly, they would take up much more hangar and deck space than Swordfish, Fulmars, or Martlets. British armoured carriers already had limited aircraft capacity. A carrier air group built around twin-engine Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters would probably carry fewer aircraft overall.

That matters because carrier warfare is not just about individual aircraft quality. It is also about sortie rate, deck cycle, maintenance, spare parts, pilot training, and numbers. A carrier with twelve powerful twin-engine strike aircraft might not always be more useful than one with twenty-four simpler aircraft. Twin-engine machines would impose heavier maintenance demands and would be harder to move around cramped hangars and lifts. Smaller escort carriers could probably not use them efficiently at all. Their main value would be aboard fleet carriers such as Ark Royal, Illustrious, Formidable, Victorious, Indomitable, and later Implacable-class ships.

There is also a production issue. Beauforts and Beaufighters were already needed by RAF Coastal Command and other theatres. Diverting enough of them to the Fleet Air Arm might improve naval strike power but weaken land-based anti-shipping, anti-submarine, and night-fighter operations. Britain in 1940–42 had too many requirements and not enough modern aircraft. A successful “Sea Beaufighter” program would probably require pre-war planning, not an emergency improvisation after France fell.

In the Far East and Indian Ocean, the effect would depend on timing. If the Royal Navy had deployed these aircraft before Japan entered the war, British carriers might have been better prepared for long-range reconnaissance, anti-shipping strikes, and bomber interception. But Beaufighters would still not have been ideal against the Zero, and Sea Beauforts would still be vulnerable without fighter escort. They would be useful in the Indian Ocean and later in strikes against Japanese shipping, but they would not make British carriers equivalent to the large American Essex-class carrier groups.

Overall, the main consequences would likely be:

The Royal Navy’s early-war carrier air arm would look less obsolete. It would have a credible fast torpedo bomber and a powerful long-range fighter/strike aircraft before American types arrived in quantity.

Mediterranean operations would become more dangerous for Axis convoys and bombers. Axis supply to North Africa might suffer more heavily, possibly worsening Rommel’s logistical problems earlier.

British carriers might suffer fewer losses from air attack, especially if Sea Beaufighters were available with radar for night and bad-weather interception.

The Fleet Air Arm would still need conventional single-engine fighters and simpler torpedo aircraft. Twin-engine carrier aircraft would be powerful but space-consuming and maintenance-heavy.

The war’s broad outcome probably would not change. Britain was already going to remain in the war, the Axis already faced severe logistical limits, and later Allied industrial superiority would still dominate. But several campaigns, especially in the Mediterranean, could become easier and less costly for the British.

So the best answer is: carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 would have given the Royal Navy a real tactical and operational edge, particularly in anti-shipping strike and long-range fleet defence. They might have accelerated the strangling of Axis supply lines to North Africa and reduced British carrier vulnerability. But they would not be a magic weapon. Their size, maintenance burden, limited carrier capacity, and imperfect fighter performance would prevent them from revolutionizing naval warfare or replacing the need for later American carrier aircraft.

items.question: What If : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944
human_answers: The only Southerner who got any serious support at the DNC in 1944 was Alabama Senator John H. Bankhead II, who came in a distant third with 98 votes (8.33%) on the first ballot. The only other (non Alben W. Barkley) Southerners who got even one vote were: J. Melville Broughton (Governor of North Carolina), Prentice Cooper (Governor of Tennessee), Robert S. Kerr (Senator from Oklahoma), Herbert O'Conor (Governor of Maryland), Claude Pepper (Senator from Florida), Sam Rayburn (Speaker of the House), and Bascom N. Timmons (D.C. based newspaperman who grew up in Texas). Of these, only Bankhead II, Barkley, Broughton, Cooper, Kerr, and O’Conor got double digits. So your best case scenario is Roosevelt and/or the convention see a need to nominate a Southerner, and go with Bankhead II who IOTL died on June 12, 1946 following a stroke on May 24, 1946, which means you end up with three Presidents in little over a year. Based on the 1886 Succession Act, Bankhead II’s successor would be none other than… James F. Byrnes. IOTL, Truman appointed him in July of 1945, and it’s pretty likely Bankhead II does similarly, wanting to support a follow Southerner. (Prior to the Succession Act of 1947, neither the Speaker of the House nor the President pro tempore of the Senate were in the line of succession.) So in a roundabout way, you do end up with Byrnes as President…

Right. Byrnes thought he was Roosevelt's choice. Truman went to the DNC planning to make a nominating speech for Byrnes. If Byrnes does get the nod... FDR wins in 1944 anyway. But things diverge after that. IMO the Republicans sweep in 1946 as OTL. Byrnes was a very capable man and won't make any big missteps, so IMO he will be renominated in 1948. There may be a feeling that the 1948 nomination is a poisoned chalice, what with the 1946 GOP sweep and general public fatigue with 16 years of Democrat Presidents. The "Humphreyite" liberals may still try to push a civil rights plank at the DNC, but against Byrnes' at least tacit opposition will fail. They won't bolt to support Wallace overtly. Instead they may sit back to watch Byrnes crash and burn in November, while they regroup for 1952. Byrnes will lose a fair number of voters to Wallace outside the South. Also, AIUI, Dewey chose to soft-pedal civil rights OTL in the vain hope of winning some Upper South states with the Democrats divided. TTL that ignis fatuus isn't around, so Dewey probably emphasizes civil rights to draw the increasingly important black vote in the North and also some white liberals. This should be enough for Dewey to win. The next question is whether he has enough "coat tails" for Republicans to hold Congress. Another question is how the civil rights issue shapes across the next decade. OTL, leadership on the issue was taken by liberal non-Southern Democrats, with the low-key support of Republicans. The first cracks in the "Solid South" came in the 1950s, as a few white Southerners who could no longer rely on the national Democratic party to protect Jim Crow found they could vote Republican. If under Dewey, Republicans claim the leading role, that's not going to happen. The "Humphreyites" will gain control of the Democrats by 1952; there may be a Dixiecrat ticket that year. Dewey will be re-elected, barring some debacle in Korea or whatever. Warren won't be Chief Justice, but the Court will still be making rulings like Brown .
items.original_question: What if : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944 In 1944, after intense pressure, President Franklin Delano Roosevelt would drop Vice President Henry Asgard Wallace from the ticket but due to his initial choice of James F. Byrnes being rejected due to his conversion from Catholicism, he would ultimately be convinced to go with Missouri Senator Harry S. Truman. Truman, as President, proved to be a liberal on racial issues and on labor rights, seeing as his SCOTUS Appointments sealed the deal on Brown v Board of Education being unanimous. However, what if ultimately, FDR went with a strict segregationist who was in favor of the New Deal at least early in their career? What happens when he becomes President and any ideas who this could be (one idea is Russell and another is Connally but both might say no to the offer)? Who do they appoint to SCOTUS instead of Burton and Vinson in 1945 and 1946 and Clark and Minton if they won a full term in 1948? What would 1948 look like in this TL? I suspect the southern president would probably appoint segregationist justices or lawyers to the court who make it through thanks to the Conservative Coalition being aligned on this one issue, though I admit I am unsure how they would handle the post war time frame, especially with 1945-1949. Furthermore, I could see a case for Dewey not being nominated ittl as in 1948 iotl, his nomination wasn't guaranteed but his wing of the party was able to get things to align with him by the convention. Here, with a more conservative leaning court and administration, the Republicans may pick a Conservative who can bring stability to both the party and the nation as long as it isn't Taft Sr. Also, I imagine the effects this has on American politics, specifically the civil rights movement, especially if Brown v Board goes the other way, if this has happened with perhaps more radical actions being taken and maybe an earlier Black Panther Party if things get really bad, but that's up in the air for the first decade of this period in time.
items.model_answer:
If FDR had chosen an open segregationist as his running mate in 1944, the biggest change would have come after April 1945, when that vice president would have become president instead of Harry Truman. The war’s military outcome probably would not change much: Germany was already near defeat, Japan was being pushed back, and the atomic bomb program was already far advanced. A segregationist president would likely still have used the atomic bomb, accepted Germany’s surrender, helped found the United Nations, and moved into a Cold War posture against the Soviet Union.

The largest difference would be domestic, especially on civil rights. Truman was personally a man of his time, but as president he took historically important steps: he created the President’s Committee on Civil Rights, backed a civil rights plank in 1948, and desegregated the armed forces by executive order. A genuinely segregationist president would almost certainly not have done those things. Federal civil rights policy would have stalled. The armed forces might have remained segregated into the 1950s. Anti-lynching, anti-poll-tax, and fair employment measures would have received little or no White House support. Black voters in northern cities would have become more alienated from the Democratic Party, and liberal Democrats would have been furious.

The party politics of 1948 would also change sharply. In real history, Truman’s civil rights moves triggered the Dixiecrat revolt led by Strom Thurmond. If the president himself were a segregationist, that revolt probably would not happen, because southern white Democrats would feel protected. But the opposite problem would emerge: northern liberals, labor groups, Black voters, and progressive Democrats might abandon the ticket or support a third-party candidate. The Democratic coalition would fracture from the left rather than from the segregationist South.

That means the Democrats would probably be weaker in 1948 than they were under Truman. Thomas Dewey or another Republican would have had a better chance of winning the presidency. Truman’s surprise victory depended on holding enough of the old New Deal coalition while surviving the Dixiecrat and Wallace challenges. A segregationist Democrat might hold the Deep South more easily, but lose crucial northern industrial states where Black voters, unions, and urban liberals mattered.

On economic policy, a segregationist Democratic president—especially someone like James F. Byrnes of South Carolina—would probably have governed more conservatively than Truman. He might have been less supportive of organized labor, less committed to expanding New Deal programs, and more willing to compromise with congressional conservatives. The Taft-Hartley Act, which Truman vetoed in real life, might have been signed or opposed less forcefully. The Fair Deal likely would never have emerged in the same form.

The Cold War might look broadly similar but with some differences in tone. Many southern conservative Democrats were strongly anti-communist, so containment of the Soviet Union would probably still develop. The Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, NATO, and early Cold War institutions might still appear, though perhaps under different names and with different political coalitions. A President Byrnes, for example, would likely have been tough toward Moscow; he was already influential in early Cold War diplomacy.

The long-term civil rights timeline would likely be delayed, but not erased. The Great Migration, Black voting power in northern states, Cold War pressure over American racism, court challenges by the NAACP, and grassroots activism would still push the issue forward. Brown v. Board of Education might still happen because it depended heavily on the Supreme Court and NAACP litigation, though presidential appointments could affect the Court’s direction. But without Truman’s executive actions and symbolic shift, the federal government would enter the 1950s more openly aligned with segregation or at least more passive toward it.

So the most likely outcome is this: World War II ends much the same way, the Cold War still begins, but civil rights progress at the federal level is delayed, the Democratic Party’s northern liberal wing becomes much more disillusioned, and the Republicans have a much better chance of winning in 1948. The choice of a segregationist vice president in 1944 would not have changed the war’s outcome as much as it would have changed the moral and political direction of postwar America.

items.question: What If the Allies lose on the Salonica front?
human_answers: Alan Wakefield (IWM expert on Salonika, among other subjects) commented that most of the Bulgarian forces in September 1918 facing the British were well motivated, apart from the 1st Macedonian Bde that consisted of many men of Serbian origin. It was the collapse further west when the French & Serbian forces broke through three lines of defence, followed by the Greek breakthrough at Petit Couronne and Doiran Hill to the Bulgarian second line that unhinged the Bulgarian defences. Bulgarian C-in-C Todorov met with the German commanders von Steuben (German 11th Army) and von Reuter (Division Reuter) on 18 September, and agreed that Bulgarian 1st Army would be pulled back from positions east of the Vadar River, while the German 11th Army and Bulgarian 3rd Division would maintain contact. However the orders to 1st Army came as a severe blow to morale as the men were celebrating their stalling the British attacks, They started marching to Kosturino Pass but there was a serious shortage of draught animals, and of the survivors: " The majority of horses & oxen were absolutely unfit for work and they had need of at least six months rest in the interior, where they could be well nourished, Others had need of at least 45 days rest" - Major Nedeff, 9th Division, quoted in Under the Devil's Eye (Alan Wakefield & Simon Moody) from which much of the first three paragraphs are sourced. This was when the RAF caught the Bulgarian withdrawal through the passes, causing serious casualties & further delays. With foreign troops now on Bulgarian soil, political opposition to the war in the Sobranie was widespread. The PM, Malinov, was pro-western and had been appointed that June by Tsar Ferdinand with the purpose of proposing an armistice to the Allies, and on 26 September emissaries were sent through the lines to start discussions, although Franchet d'Esperey would only accept an unilateral unconditional armistice, which the Bugarian government then agreed to give, So it looks like the Bulgarian army was in generally good morale status until the final victories sparked by the French, Serbian & Greek forces, when the order of and losses taken on the retreat caused a final decline. But it looks like the home front collapsed first, if the Tsar was considering an armistice in June, so not sure what caused the domestic problems that drove the government to seek peace (I understand that a military rebelliion / mutiny at Radomir formulated by Bulgarian Agrarian National Union attempted to overthrow the government and establish a republic). Wiki suggests the following reasons: - Extreme war weariness, given Bulgaria had been at war since 1912 (short break 1914-15). Exhausted manpower (see #1 above) - I would add this resulted in dissatisfied minority groups supplying more troops, such as Macedonian Serbs & Greeks, diluting the Bulgar core. Both military & civilians suffering extreme food shortages (result of your point regarding harvests?). Troops poorly supplied - not only food but ammunition, clothing, boots, etc. Troops believing profiteers making hay at home at their expense. Feeling of betrayal by their allies, principally Germany, especialy regarding promised levels of supplies not being met, and lack of support for Bulgarian territorial ambitions at expense of Romania. Not sure how far the German troop levels had been reduced as you comment. The impact of the Russian Revolution. The impact of Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points (maybe a surrender would't be as bad as keep fighting) Recommended is 'The Enemy is Behind Us': The Morale Crisis in the Bulgarian Army during the Summer of 1918 - Richard C Hall, War in History Vol. 11 No. 4 which again refers to the collapse in morale starting by June 1918. Bulgarian C-in-C Nikola Zhekov reported to Tsar Ferdinand on 121 June that: "Today it is impossible ton have any illusions that the spirit of the soldiers is the same as at the beginning of the war, or even last year." I can't access as I don't have a school account! It does look like some units, such as the 9th (Pleven) Division, kept their high morale almost to the end. My main comment on demoralised forces would apply further north and primarily to the Austro-Hungarian troops who fell apart in October 1918, when I daresay no one suggests they were of high morale status. When you mentioned the Allies, I almost thought it was World War II. It's my impression that it's something of a convention on this post 1900 forum to use "Entente" instead of "Allies", presumably to avoid confusion with the Allies of WW2. The allies couldn't overcome a German ally with more than 50 divisions and more than a million men on the field you mean, which in 1915 were about as well armed as their own troops. No. You essentially suggest Berlin says "to hell with the shenanigans to keep the Greeks neutral, let's invade them too. " So you just about gave numerical parity to the defenders... who don't have to move everything but food and fodder for the Macedonian and Turkish fronts though a single track railway going all the way back to Vienna. Before Dobro Polie and Desperate Frankie advancing all the way to Hungary and Austria putting the final nail in the Austro-Hungarian empire's coffin the actual front looked a pretty good deal to Berlin. Biggest POW camp in the world jokes and all that.

Well, Alternate History Challenge: An equivalent of Dobro Polie and subsequent desperate Frankie advances happen six months to a year earlier than OTL, *before* the Germans start getting pushed back on the western front, not after, and perhaps as a consequence, we get to see see the desperate Frankie international force *keep advancing* through the territory of capitulated Austria-Hungary, and over onto German territory from its southern and eastern borders (to Munich, Passau, Dresden, Gorlitz, Liegnitz or further to Cottbus or Berlin) before the Germans actually capitulate.
