Could an earlier resolution of the Greek political divide in favor of the Venizelist side, committing the full Greek Army to the Entente side earlier, have helped with this? What might it take, faster French seduction? Or, going the opposite direction, more in line with what the OP wants, is there any way the Venizelist side could have been so marginalized that the Royalist side in Greece became willing to openly side with the Central Powers and openly welcomed/sought CP support in expelling Allied forces from Salonica and any other parts of Greece at any point during the war?
items.original_question: What if the Allies lose on the Salonica front? As I loosely understand it, the Salonica front was established after the Serbian army was routed. What if the Central Powers were able to continue advancing into Greece and expelled the Allies from the mainland Balkans? The Salonica front in some ways seems to resemble Gallipoli (an Allied lodgment supplied by sea) and the Central powers were able to prevail at Gallipoli, so it seems possible. The Allies also had to deal with the fact that the Greek government was divided - if the Central powers were more successful it seems possible Greece would have “switched sides”, or at least had a compliant government installed.
items.model_answer:
If the Allies lose on the Salonica front, the First World War probably lasts longer and ends less cleanly in the Balkans, but it does not automatically become a Central Powers victory.

The key historical importance of Salonica was that the Allied breakthrough in September 1918 knocked Bulgaria out of the war. Once Bulgaria asked for an armistice, the Central Powers’ Balkan system collapsed: Serbia was liberated, Austria-Hungary’s southern flank was exposed, and the Ottoman Empire became increasingly isolated. This helped accelerate the general collapse of the Central Powers in autumn 1918.

If instead the Allies are defeated there, Bulgaria remains in the war, at least for a time. The land connection between Germany, Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria, and the Ottoman Empire stays open. Serbia is not liberated from the south, and the Allies lose their best route into the Balkans. Greece might become politically unstable again, especially if the defeat discredits the pro-Allied government. A serious Allied defeat could also free Bulgarian and perhaps German or Austro-Hungarian units for use elsewhere, though by 1918 the Central Powers were already short of food, transport, morale, and reserves.

The biggest effect would be delay. Bulgaria’s collapse would likely be postponed, the Ottoman Empire might hold out somewhat longer, and Austria-Hungary would face less immediate pressure from the south. The armistices of autumn 1918 might come weeks or months later, and the postwar settlement in the Balkans could look different: Bulgaria might bargain from a slightly less disastrous position, Serbia’s recovery would be delayed, and the creation of Yugoslavia might be messier or less favorable to Serbian ambitions.

But unless the Allied defeat at Salonica is so catastrophic that it changes the wider war, Germany still probably loses. By late 1918 the decisive front was the Western Front, where the German army was being pushed back by the British, French, Americans, and others during the Hundred Days Offensive. Germany’s economy was exhausted, its population was hungry, and its allies were collapsing from internal strain. Austria-Hungary was also breaking apart from nationalist pressures and military failure, especially after defeats against Italy.

So the most likely counterfactual is not “Central Powers win World War I.” It is “World War I ends later, with a more prolonged and chaotic collapse in southeastern Europe.” The Allied victory would be slower and costlier, the Balkans would be less decisively settled by the Salonica breakthrough, and Bulgaria and the Ottoman Empire might survive in the war longer—but the overall strategic balance would still favor the Allies.

items.question: What If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin engine?
human_answers: 1 - as noted by the fellow member, the P-40F and L used the Merlin 2 - it was a pretty simple upgrade 3 - engine itself does not require a laminar flow wing; a laminar flow wing will cut some drag, however, and thus allow for some speed increase 4 - historically, it offered some 30 mph over the P-40E at 18000 ft and above, IOW it was an improvement the P-40 badly needed 5 - P-51s used the better Merlins, these with 2-stage supercharger; a P-40 with such an engine would've probably be as fast as the Spitfire IX, but not as fast as the Merlin Mustang, nor as rangy - and thus the answer is 'no' 6 - as-is, the performance was better on the P-40F than on the ubiquitous P-40E; with 2-stage Merlin, it would've probably been good for 400+ mph, and much better rate of climb (the XP-40Q did 420+ mph with a 2-stage supercharged V-1710)

I'll have to take your word for it as I'm forbidden from your links but that sounds about right. A more advanced Merlin won't really help the P-40 though. There are availability issues with the Merlin, as ever, which historically forced Curtiss to revert to the V-1710-81 for the P-40M, despite more than half the production run going to the RAF. Not even every P-40F/L received a Merlin as some were completed as V-1710-81 engined P-40Rs. More though, there is the tale of the XP-60, which was a P-40D fuselage with a new laminar-flow wing. It was an improvement, with 387mph at 22,000ft. Modified as the XP-60D with an enlarged tail, it may or may not have received the V-1650-3 slated for it by the time of it's destruction in a crash on 6th May 1943. It certainly didn't perform any substantive testing with it. By that time the Merlin Mustang was established as superior in performance and was already entering production. The XP-60A with 1425hp V-1710-75, good for 420mph at 29,000ft, was part-cancelled in January 1942 (with the remainder following in June 1943) in favour of P-40Ks, Ls and P-47Gs. I think that is going to be the fate of any advanced or improved P-40 variant. Cancelled in favour of sustained production of known quantities.
items.original_question: What if Curtiss P-40 used Merlins? What instead of using Allison V-12's the Curtiss P-40 used the Merlin V-12 instead ? Would this be possible or would it need major airframe development? Would it need a redesigned laminar flow wing to really utilise the engine? How successful would this instillation be? Would it allow the P-40 to be more successful than the later P-51? What boost in combat performance would this instillation allow? Regards
items.model_answer:
If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed from the start around the Rolls-Royce Merlin, it would probably have been a noticeably better medium-altitude fighter, but it still would not have become a P-51 Mustang or a Spitfire-equivalent.

The main gain would have been altitude performance. The historical P-40 used the Allison V-1710, which was strong and reliable at low and medium altitude but suffered because most P-40s lacked an efficient two-stage supercharger. That made the aircraft increasingly uncompetitive above roughly 15,000–20,000 feet. A Merlin-powered P-40, especially one designed around the Merlin rather than adapted later, would have climbed better, held power higher up, and been more useful in the European air war than the early Allison P-40s.

There is a real-world clue: the P-40F and P-40L were fitted with Packard-built Merlins. They did improve high-altitude performance and were generally more competitive above medium altitude, but they did not transform the P-40. The airframe still had limitations: relatively high drag, a thick wing compared with newer designs, and less aerodynamic refinement than the later P-51. A clean-sheet Merlin P-40 could have had better cowling, radiator placement, balance, and cooling arrangements, so it might have gained more than the actual P-40F did. But the P-40’s basic structure and wing would still have limited its top speed, climb, and ceiling.

A Merlin-designed P-40 might have been especially valuable in 1940–42. It could have given the RAF and USAAF a tougher, longer-ranged fighter than the Hurricane with better high-altitude performance than the Allison P-40. In North Africa and the Mediterranean it might have been a very useful fighter-bomber and escort aircraft. In the Pacific and China-Burma-India theaters, however, the improvement would have mattered less, because much combat occurred at lower and medium altitudes where the Allison P-40 was already effective.

The biggest obstacle would have been engine supply. In 1940–41 Britain needed Merlins for Spitfires, Hurricanes, Lancasters, Mosquitos, and other aircraft. The United States did not have large-scale Packard Merlin production immediately available. So an early Merlin P-40 might have competed with more important British programs unless American Merlin production began earlier and in greater volume.

Strategically, the result would likely have been a better P-40, not a war-changing aircraft. It might have prolonged the P-40’s usefulness in front-line fighter roles and reduced the performance gap against the Bf 109 and later Japanese fighters. But once the P-51, P-47, F6F, and F4U matured, a Merlin P-40 would still have been overtaken. Its best counterfactual role would have been as an earlier, more capable stopgap fighter—stronger above medium altitude, still rugged and useful as a fighter-bomber, but not a substitute for the Mustang.

items.question: PT-109: What If JFK Died on 7/2/43?
human_answers: It seems plausible to me that if Jack were to die in the Pacific, Sr would use connections to ensure that Jr would come home in one piece so that grooming for public office could begin. That said, I've read several accounts that suggest/indicate Jr was not as approachable/astute/able to think on his feet as well as Jack. That might make a political career more challenging: still feasible, but more challenging and quite possibly more costly (Sr might have had to write more and/or larger checks to make things happen?). I could see Jr with a House, and later a Senate seat. Then the question becomes: could he work his way into such a position that Adlai Stevenson might consider him as a running mate in 1956? Arguably, that propelled Jack into the limelight enough to become a presidential contender in 1960. My sense is that Jr would not get the same consideration ITTL that Jack did IOTL. Rather, he would plausibly have tried a presidential run having something like 8-10 years of Senate experience under his belt in 1960. We're talking a crowded field for the Dems in 1960: Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Jr, and the usual cast of favorite sons. Johnson might be the favorite, but not a prohibitive favorite: coming from Texas would assure that. Too manybut Lodge won northerners would be skeptical. On the other hand, Humphrey would definitely not play well in the south. Could Jr emerge as a compromise candidate? Maybe, but he'd be a tough sell in the south given his Catholic faith. My sense is that a protracted, multiple ballot convention would ultimately result in a Johnson nomination, with a middle of the road midwesterner (I'll yield to someone else here) as a VP candidate. Nixon will still be the GOP nominee, but Lodge won't be his running mate: don't need to counter a Kennedy. I suggest it would be MD governor Theodore McKeldin, a man who knew how to work with both sides (he was the last GOP mayor of Baltimore). McKeldin would bring a great deal more to the ticket than Lodge, but that's a pretty low bar. While we're at it, look for the 1960 campaign to be nasty. Lyndon Johnson had few scruples if any as far as that went, so I wouldn't be surprised if he started it. Then all Nixon has to do is take the high road and point out how well things have gone during Ike's tenure, and pump up his role (maybe this time Ike wouldn't make his famous "...if you give me a week..." remark?). And I don't see Richard Daley doing much to help Lyndon Johnson in Chicago, so IL might well flip to the GOP. Long story short: Nixon wins in '60. That leaves 1968 as Jr's next shot at the White House: he wouldn't try to unseat Nixon unless something totally unforeseen happened.

I once posted on another thread about a different pathway that Joe Jr's career would look like. IOTL JFK had the choice of running for Congress or for Lt. Governor of Massachusetts, and he chose to run for Congress in 1946. My alternate path for Joe Jr. had him running for Lt. Governor in 1946 and getting Statewide exposure, IOTL the Democratic ticket lost, but with Joe Sr's money the Democrats win. Joe Jr. runs for US Senate against Republican incumbent Leverett Saltonstall in 1948 and wins in a Democratic year. The main character flaw of Joe Jr. was his fierce loyalty to his father. There is a story about how Joe Sr. was on the Harvard baseball team and by playing on the Harvard-Yale game he would get a letter, but due to anti-Catholic bigotry, he was left on the bench and didn't get a letter. When Joe Jr. as a senior on the team, he was the first baseman and made the final put out of the Harvard-Yale game, and by tradition the ball is given to the team captain and Joe Jr. kept it himself and gave the ball to his father. How this would play out is uncertain, how far would he go in defending Joe Sr.'s isolation? JFK was able use his service to separate himself against any criticism against his father, but could Joe Jr. do that?

Both are possible, but I do think that Jor Sr trying to pull some strings would be more plausible (at least to me). But if Joe Jr still does his mission (maybe the dates between Jack's death and Joe's mission are too close), it could be that Robert gets chosen as the next. That being said... This was something I didn't think about, but from what I read it would make sense. Robert was always known as the black sheep of the family. If Ted was chosen by Joe Sr, he may very well have been thrown into Korea. The only question would be where Ted's future would go: He would have been far too young to run for President in 1960, but he could have won a seat as Senator in Massachusetts (although it would have been difficult). Maybe eight years later (say 1968), Ted might try to make his move, although 1972 might be more plausible.
items.original_question: PT-109: What if JFK Died on 7/2/43? In 1943, John F Kennedy's patrol boat PT-109 was rammed by the battleship Amagiri. After PT-109 exploded, JFK was able to survive, swimming from the wreck to a nearby island to stay alive while also saving his fellow soldiers. The moment cemented Jack as a war hero, and after his brother Joe died in a special mission, Jack was seen as next in line to join the Senate, before finally becoming President (which we all know how it ended). But what if things went slightly differently? Maybe Jack is closer to the blast and dies in the initial explosion. What next? What would happen to Joe Jr, and by extension, the Kennedy family? In our timeline, Joe Jr was killed in a special mission, but could the death of JFK stopped Joe Jr from going on the mission, and continue to stay alive to be the frontrunner of the family? Joe Jr had approved of Hitler, but his ideals could have easily morphed over time. Could Joe have done what Jack did and become President, and how would his presidency have looked? And if Joe Jr did in fact die anyway, who would replace him? Robert would have been far too young, along with Ted. Would the Kennedy family fade out of the limelight? What would become of the 1960 elections? The more obvious question, with Jack dead, who would be the man to lead the Democrats against Nixon? The most likely options are Hubert Humphrey, Lyndon Baines Johnson, and (although less likely), Adali Stevenson. Who would have been able to win the primaries, and could they have dealt with Nixon? With whoever becomes President, how would their Presidency look, and what could happen to them if they were also assassinated? For me personally, the most likely ticket would have been Johnson, causing him to be President.
items.model_answer:
Assuming you mean the PT-109 sinking in the Solomon Islands, which occurred on the night of August 1–2, 1943, the biggest consequence of JFK dying there is simple: there is almost certainly no President John F. Kennedy, and the entire political chain from 1960 through the mid-1960s changes.

In the short term, Kennedy would likely have been remembered as a brave young naval officer killed in action. His family’s political ambitions would not have disappeared, but they would have been badly disrupted. Joseph P. Kennedy Sr. originally expected his eldest son, Joe Jr., to be the family’s political star; Joe Jr. was killed in 1944. If both Joe Jr. and Jack were dead by war’s end, the burden would probably shift later to Robert Kennedy or perhaps Ted Kennedy, but neither was positioned in the 1940s and 1950s to reproduce Jack’s exact path. The “Kennedy dynasty” might still emerge, but probably later, weaker, and without the same national romance.

The most immediate political change is in Massachusetts. JFK would not run for Congress in 1946, would not become senator in 1952, and would not narrowly defeat Henry Cabot Lodge Jr. That matters because JFK’s Senate career and national visibility were the foundation of his 1960 presidential campaign. Without him, the 1960 Democratic nomination likely goes to Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Stuart Symington, or possibly Adlai Stevenson. Johnson is the strongest alternate candidate, but he was less attractive to northern liberals and television-age swing voters than Kennedy. Against Richard Nixon in 1960, a non-Kennedy Democrat might still have won, but Nixon’s chances improve substantially. Since Kennedy’s actual victory was extremely narrow, the likeliest single alternate outcome is Nixon becoming president in 1961.

That would reshape the Cold War. The Bay of Pigs operation was already being prepared under Eisenhower, and Nixon had supported aggressive anti-Castro policy, so some version of the invasion might still occur. Nixon might have given it stronger air support, potentially making it more successful, or he might have produced an even larger U.S. entanglement in Cuba. The Cuban Missile Crisis as we know it might not happen, because Soviet decisions in 1962 were partly based on Khrushchev’s reading of Kennedy after Vienna and the Bay of Pigs. If a missile crisis did occur under Nixon, it might be handled more aggressively, though Nixon was also capable of strategic caution. The risk of a more dangerous U.S.-Soviet confrontation would be real.

Civil rights would probably move more slowly. The civil rights movement itself would still exist, because it was driven by Black activists, court decisions, demographic change, television, and Cold War pressures, not just by Kennedy. But the exact legislative breakthrough of 1964–65 depended heavily on Kennedy’s assassination placing Lyndon Johnson in the presidency with a moral mandate and exceptional congressional skill. Without JFK’s death in Dallas, and especially without Johnson succeeding him in 1963, the Civil Rights Act and Voting Rights Act might be delayed, weakened, or passed under very different political circumstances.

Vietnam is the hardest case. Kennedy had increased U.S. involvement but had not yet committed major ground forces. If Nixon were president from 1961, he might be hawkish, but he also came from the Eisenhower school that was wary of open-ended land wars in Asia. If Johnson somehow became president in 1961 instead, escalation might still occur, perhaps even earlier. The safest conclusion is that JFK’s death in 1943 removes the exact path to the Johnson escalation after 1963, but it does not guarantee that the U.S. avoids Vietnam. Anti-communist pressures were strong enough that another president might still deepen involvement.

Domestically, there would be no “New Frontier” in the same form, no JFK tax-cut program as framed, no Kennedy charisma in television politics, and no Camelot myth. The space race would also look different. Kennedy’s 1961 commitment to landing a man on the Moon before the decade’s end was decisive. Without him, Apollo might proceed more slowly, receive less funding, or lack the 1969 deadline. The United States might still reach the Moon eventually, but not necessarily when it did.

So the concise answer is: if JFK died with PT-109, the United States probably avoids the Kennedy presidency entirely. Nixon likely has a better chance of winning in 1960; Johnson probably does not become president through the shock of assassination; civil rights legislation is likely delayed or altered; the Cuban and Vietnam crises unfold differently; and the Kennedy family becomes a tragic wartime family rather than the central American political dynasty of the 1960s. The broad Cold War, civil rights struggle, and postwar liberal-conservative conflict would continue, but without JFK they would follow a noticeably different and probably less symbolically powerful path.

items.question: What If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981?
human_answers: The core problem with these discussions is that you wind up with a lot of people who had personal experience with home computers imagining their home computer was a long-term viable platform particularly killed by the IBM PC. The inherent market dynamic was, instead, that all the home computers were doomed to extinction at the hands of the standard business personal computer platform. It is businesses that care about backward compatibility with their internal installed base, while the home computer user market has an observable willingness to abandon old platforms and adopt new ones. This means home-targeted versions of the business platform can easily be adopted by the home market, while business-targeted versions of home platforms can only get adopted by businesses if they have a specific compelling business advantage. And then, as soon as the business platform clones the advantage, the home platform is again on the defensive. Home platforms are thus in an inherently weak position, and will be smashed flat by the standard business platform. And, well, there was already a standard business personal computer platform in 1980-1981 -- the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. You could buy that platform as an Osborne 1, or as a Xerox 820, or from any of dozens of other of other makers. You even had the Microsoft Softcard (originally, "Z-80 Softcard", but Zilog complained) which used an Apple II as a host for a 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The major problem that the CP/M-80 platform had going forward was that it had run up against the 64k RAM addressing limit of the 8080/8085/Z80, at a time when RAM prices had dropped enough that it was entirely practical to buy more. And since none of the chipmakers had had the sense to make a 8080-compatible processor with wider addressing, the only real way forward was the 8086/8088, since 8080 assembly code could be easily machine-translated into 8086 code. Everybody was just waiting on Digital Research to get CP/M-86 out. The IBM PC then arrived, with an OS that was arguably even more compatible in its system calls with CP/M-80, and the ability to use all the RAM anybody could practically afford. (Even if Gates never said 640K was enough for anybody, in 1981 that was true. Indeed, the first version of the PC's BIOS had a 544K limit.) It was the perfectly natural successor to the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The IBM endorsement made the transition smoother, and did have some secondary consequences (killing the S-100 bus, for example), but the true key to the IBM PC's success is that it was the natural successor-host for a software ecosystem that had grown up on top of the Altair 8800. What happens in the absence of the IBM PC is simple enough. Digital Research will release CP/M-86. At which point the CP/M-86 systems take over the business market, and eventually all the home computer platforms are killed by the multi-manufacturer business standard, just as in the original timeline.

As I understand it, the IBM machine was intended as an 'intelligent terminal' for their mainframes .. Businesses already had mainframes & dumb terminals but because the terminals were dumb the mainframe had to do everything - which led to limits on the numbers - and whilst IBM would be happy to sell (rent) you another mainframe they then run into the problem of getting the mainframes to talk 'seamlessly' to each other ... so IBM work on evermore powerful / more expensive mainframes as the number of users go up .. If, however, you can off-load some of the 'housekeeping' (things like deciding how to repaint the screen as the user edits a file, without the entire screen contents having to be resent from the mainframe, for example) onto the terminal, you can roll out cheap low end mainframes (at the same cost as the high end ones, naturally) able to cope with 100's more users .. Other companies wanted to 'get in on' IBM's business but had difficulties building mainframes as powerful as the IBM ones = thus, sooner or later, some-one else is going to come up with the concept of 'intelligent terminals' .. after which the PC becomes more or less inevitable ..
items.original_question: What if no IBM PC (2026 ed.) In short - the IBM PC (model 5150) was not an inevitable thing, the IBM leadership was highly skeptical of the project and it would not have seen the light of the day had things gone just slightly differently. So, what if that computer had never been created? My take - the personal computer market would look a lot like mobile or console market - a walled garden of 2-3 incompatible standards, probably Apple and Commodore (which, would do better financially without the competition from PC clones). It's interesting what would happen in Japan and (later) China.
items.model_answer:
If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981, personal computers would still have spread, but the industry would likely have developed more slowly, less uniformly, and with a different set of dominant companies.

The IBM PC’s importance was not that it was technically revolutionary. Apple, Commodore, Tandy, Atari, and many CP/M-based machines already existed. Its importance was that IBM made the microcomputer respectable for business. Large companies that distrusted hobbyist machines were willing to buy “a PC” because IBM sold it. Without that endorsement, corporate adoption of personal computers would probably have been delayed and more fragmented, with firms continuing longer to rely on terminals connected to minicomputers and mainframes.

The biggest difference would be the absence, or delay, of the IBM-compatible standard. IBM’s relatively open design allowed other companies to clone the machine, which created a huge ecosystem around Intel processors, Microsoft DOS, and standardized expansion hardware. Without the IBM PC, there may have been no rapid rise of “PC compatibles,” or at least not in the same form. The market might have remained divided among Apple machines, CP/M systems, Commodore-style low-cost home computers, UNIX workstations, and proprietary business machines.

Microsoft’s rise would probably have been much less explosive. MS-DOS became dominant because IBM chose it and because clones copied the IBM PC architecture. Without that choice, Microsoft might still have become a major software company, but it would not necessarily have become the operating-system gatekeeper of the 1980s and 1990s. Intel’s dominance would also have been less certain; Motorola 68000-based systems, Zilog machines, or other architectures might have had more room to grow.

Apple might have benefited, especially in education, publishing, and perhaps parts of business. The Macintosh could have faced a less entrenched DOS-compatible world in the mid-1980s. On the other hand, Apple’s high prices and closed hardware strategy might still have limited its market share. A different open standard could have emerged from another company or consortium, possibly based on CP/M, UNIX, or a non-Intel processor.

The clone manufacturers that shaped the modern PC industry—Compaq, Dell, Gateway, and many Asian motherboard and component suppliers—would either have emerged later or around a different standard. Software markets would have been messier because developers would have had to support more incompatible platforms. That fragmentation could have slowed the spread of business applications like spreadsheets, word processors, and databases.

In the long run, personal computing almost certainly would still have become central to work and home life. The economic and technological pressures were already strong: microprocessors were getting cheaper, memory was improving, and demand for desktop computing was growing. But without the IBM PC, the path would likely have been less standardized, Microsoft and Intel might not have become as dominant, and the familiar “Windows on x86 PC” world might never have become the default computing platform.

items.question: What If No P51 Bomber Escort?

items.model_answer:
If the Allies had not had the P-51 Mustang as a long-range bomber escort, the air war over Germany would likely have been much costlier and slower, but it probably would not have changed the final outcome of World War II.

The P-51’s importance was that it could escort American B-17 and B-24 bombers deep into Germany and fight effectively against German interceptors. Before long-range escorts were available, unescorted daylight bombing raids suffered severe losses, such as the 1943 raids on Schweinfurt and Regensburg. Without the P-51, the U.S. daylight bombing campaign would probably have had to be reduced, delayed, or shifted more toward night bombing and shorter-range targets.

The biggest consequence would have been that the Luftwaffe might have survived as a stronger force for longer. Historically, the P-51 did not just protect bombers; it helped destroy the German fighter arm by forcing the Luftwaffe into battle and then shooting down its experienced pilots. This contributed directly to Allied air superiority before and after D-Day. Without that escort, Germany would have had more fighters available to attack bombers, resist the Normandy invasion, and defend its cities and industry.

However, Germany was already under enormous pressure from multiple directions: the Soviet advance in the east, the British blockade, fuel shortages, Allied production superiority, and eventually the Normandy landings. Other aircraft, especially improved P-47s and P-38s with drop tanks, might have filled part of the escort role, though probably less efficiently than the P-51. The Allies could also have changed tactics, relying more on tactical air power, night bombing, and attacks on nearer targets.

So the likely result is not a German victory, but a more difficult Allied victory. The strategic bombing campaign would have been less effective in 1944, bomber losses would have been higher, German fighter strength might have lasted longer, and the invasion of Western Europe could have been riskier or possibly delayed. The P-51 was not the sole reason the Allies won, but it was one of the key tools that made Allied air superiority over Germany achievable when it was.

items.original_question: How would the population of the Falklands have been treated if Argentina had won in 1982? Let’s suppose that HMS Hermes and HMS Invincible had been sunk, forcing the British to make peace and accept the loss of the Falklands. Let’s also suppose that this victory gave the Argentine junta a reprieve of 2-3 additional years, but that it still eventually collapsed so that Argentina followed a political path similar as IOTL. What would the Falklands population have faced? It's almost certain that Buenos Aires would have sent thousands of Argentine settlers to Puerto Argentino/Port Stanley in order to, at least, make the Anglo population a numerical minority and to extinguish any secessionist aspirations. But would this Anglo population have been allowed to remain and then obtain full Argentine citizenship, perhaps even some degree of cultural autonomy, or would it have faced a complete ethnic cleansing in order to permanently erase the Anglo identity of the Falklands? There are fewer than 2,000 people, so if Argentina decided to do it, it wouldn’t have any problem doing so.
items.model_answer:
If Argentina had won the 1982 Falklands War, the islanders would probably not have been massacred or forcibly removed en masse, but they would almost certainly have lost their British political status and been subjected to strong “Argentinization.”

Argentina’s government regarded the Falklands/Malvinas as Argentine territory occupied by Britain, and it did not accept the islanders’ claim to self-determination as decisive. So the local population, overwhelmingly English-speaking and pro-British, would likely have been treated as residents of recovered Argentine territory rather than as a people entitled to choose sovereignty.

In the short term, they would probably have lived under military administration, with restrictions on movement, communication, political expression, and contact with Britain. During the actual Argentine occupation in 1982, Argentine forces generally tried to avoid large-scale abuse of civilians, partly for propaganda and diplomatic reasons, though there were detentions, intimidation, censorship, and some mistreatment. That pattern suggests a victorious Argentina would likely have been repressive but not exterminatory.

In the longer term, Argentina would likely have imposed Argentine law, Spanish-language administration, Argentine schooling, new place names, and possibly Argentine citizenship requirements. Islanders who accepted Argentine sovereignty might have been allowed to remain, keep property, and continue local life in a limited form. Those who resisted, refused allegiance, or openly campaigned for British rule could have faced surveillance, dismissal from public roles, detention, deportation, or pressure to emigrate. Argentina might also have encouraged settlement from the mainland, gradually reducing the islanders’ political and cultural dominance.

The harshness would have depended on whether the military junta survived after victory. Given Argentina’s dictatorship and its human-rights record, the risk of coercion was real. But because the islanders were a small, visible civilian population under international scrutiny, Argentina would probably have avoided mass violence and instead pursued controlled integration, political suppression, and cultural assimilation.

items.original_question: If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank? If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank in the twentieth century? In other words, it takes all the modernization and technological upgrade steps it can to protect its sovereignty in the late 19th century world, but either is deterred or self-deters from annexing Chinese or Russian territory, or territory possibly in their sphere, like Korea, or if attempting to do so, because such attempts were rather fashionable among *many* (but not all) modern industrial states, they fail, would the same things constraining Japanese aggression or success *also* doom Japan's ability to increase its economic productive capacity and standard of living over most of the decades of the 20th century? Or not? Could Japan do as well, or better, in absolute GDP growth, per capital GDP growth, PPP measured GDP growth, and GDP global rank, by, for instance, 1920, 1940, or 1960 or 1980, without having any expansionary success beyond consolidating control over the Ryukyu Kingdom and diplomatically clarifying its ownership of the Kurile and Bonin Islands and never having won a territory in a foreign war? I think I can illustrate it best using this graphic. This helpfully long term chart of real GDP growth of Japan, Britain and the US shows Japan's growth curve in * red *. Would Japan's line be higher, lower, or about the same, without Japan's early successful wars with China and Russia, annexation of Korea, WWI absorption of Micronesia, 1930s exploitation of Manchuria and then occupied China, followed by the ultimately futile and highly destructive Pacific War, and the Cold War alliance arrangement the US and Japan set up to deal with the Soviet Union and avoid the recurrence of mutual war? Maybe the red line in the alternate history of an alternate Japan would have lower at some points and higher at others, but if so, please specify roughly when, and where do you think things would be stabilizing by the 1960 through present-day era. It may be tempting to call a Meiji (and beyond) Japan, with this type of foreign policy record that lacks success at military-naval territorial expansion as a Japan "pulling a Thailand" or analogous to a Thailand. But I would urge caution in making such an analogy. Sure, Thailand protected its sovereignty uniquely within its Southeast Asian neighborhood, while not being able to clash with colonial powers head on. But that's as far as the analogy would apply. Thailand's technological advancement and industrialization was for long, until the 1960s, pretty weak, and a Japan on Thailand's *economic* trajectory would be *categorically* poorer and less technologically, industrially, scientifically, and financially sophisticated than OTL's Japan. Thailand also only *began* experiments with constitutional government about fifty years later than Japan, even though Japan in the mid-20th century had some spectacular democratic and especially liberal failures and has some democratic deficits to this day. But their internal political cultures and societies are quite different.
items.model_answer:
Yes. A Meiji Japan that modernized but did not successfully expand into Korea, Taiwan, Manchuria, China, or against Russia could still plausibly have become a G7-level economy, though not necessarily a pre-1945 “great power” in the same military-diplomatic sense.

The strongest evidence is that postwar Japan actually did become a G7 member after losing the entire empire. Its rise after 1945 rested mainly on the home islands: a large population, high literacy, strong state capacity, disciplined firms and banks, technical education, export competitiveness, and access to world markets. Those factors were already being built in the Meiji period and did not inherently require colonial conquest.

Empire helped Japan in some ways: Taiwan, Korea, and later Manchuria provided markets, food, minerals, strategic depth, prestige, and outlets for investment. Victory over China and Russia also gave Japan diplomatic status and domestic confidence. But these were not the core source of Japan’s eventual economic strength. Japan’s home-island population was already large by European standards, and industrial powers such as Britain, Germany, Italy, and later South Korea showed that resource-poor states could become wealthy through trade, manufacturing, and human capital rather than territorial self-sufficiency.

In fact, a non-expansionist Japan might have done better in the long run if avoiding imperial war also meant avoiding militarism, sanctions, the Pacific War, bombing, defeat, and occupation. Lower military spending and fewer colonial commitments could have left more resources for civilian industry and infrastructure. A Japan that stayed constitutional, commercial, and export-oriented might have resembled a larger version of the Netherlands, Sweden, or later South Korea: less feared militarily, but potentially very rich.

The caveat is timing and politics. Without victories over China and Russia, Japan might have been treated less as an equal by the Western powers. If “fails to expand” means humiliating military defeat by China or Russia, then the consequences could be severe: indemnities, political crisis, foreign pressure, or even semi-colonial constraints. That would make G7-level development less certain. Also, if Japan were excluded from foreign markets and raw materials, its growth would be harder.

So the careful answer is: yes, a Meiji-modernized but non-expansionist Japan could plausibly have reached G7 economic rank, especially by the late twentieth century, because the fundamentals of its growth lay mostly in domestic modernization and global trade rather than empire. But it would likely have reached that status as a commercial-industrial power, not as the prewar imperial military power Japan actually became; and if its non-expansion resulted from crushing defeats rather than deliberate restraint, the path would be much less secure.

items.model_answer:
If the attack on Pearl Harbor had completely failed, the United States and Japan would still almost certainly have gone to war, but Japan’s strategic position would have been much worse from the start.

The key point is that Pearl Harbor was only one part of Japan’s opening offensive. Japan was also attacking or preparing to attack the Philippines, Guam, Wake Island, Malaya, Hong Kong, and the Dutch East Indies. Even if the Pearl Harbor strike caused little or no damage, the attempted surprise attack plus Japan’s broader offensive against U.S. and Allied territory would likely have led Congress to declare war on Japan anyway.

Militarily, the biggest difference would be that the U.S. Pacific Fleet would have remained intact. That would have deprived Japan of the months of relative freedom it historically gained in the western Pacific. American battleships alone would not have won the war quickly, because aircraft carriers, submarines, logistics, and land-based air power mattered more than old battleships. The U.S. still might not have been able to save the Philippines, because Japan had strong regional air and naval advantages and the Philippines were difficult to reinforce. But Japan’s expansion into Southeast Asia would have been riskier, slower, and more vulnerable to American counteraction.

The outcome would depend on what “completely failed” means. If the Japanese carrier force attacked but escaped unharmed, then the war would probably still follow a broadly similar path, though with the U.S. in a stronger early position. Japan might still seize much of Southeast Asia, but it would face greater naval pressure and perhaps suffer earlier setbacks.

If, however, “completely failed” means the Japanese strike force was discovered and badly damaged or destroyed, then the consequences would be dramatic. Japan’s elite carrier air groups were the core of its offensive power. Losing them in December 1941 would likely prevent or cripple later Japanese operations such as the Indian Ocean raid, Coral Sea, and Midway. The United States might begin major counteroffensives much earlier, and Japan’s perimeter would be far weaker from the beginning.

Politically, a failed Pearl Harbor would still have unified American opinion against Japan. The outrage might be slightly different because the U.S. would not suffer the same shock and losses, but an attempted surprise attack on American territory would still be seen as an act of war. Germany’s response is somewhat less certain: Hitler was not legally required to declare war on the United States because Japan had attacked first, but given his actual choices and the undeclared naval conflict already happening in the Atlantic, he might still have done so.

In the long run, Japan’s chances would become even worse than they were historically. Japan already faced a massive industrial imbalance against the United States. A failed Pearl Harbor would mean Japan had awakened the United States without seriously weakening it. The Pacific War would probably be shorter, Japan’s early conquests less secure, and the United States able to move onto the offensive sooner.

items.original_question: The Highest Patriotism: What if George McGovern became President in 1968 ​ The initial frontrunner for the Democratic nomination in 1968 was President Johnson of course, but an insurgent primary challenge from one Senator Eugene McCarthy set off a spark that would blow open a wide power vacuum in the Democratic party following Johnson's withdrawal from consideration. Johnson had endorsed Hubert Humphrey, his ambitious VP, but he chose not to run in the primaries, instead gaining support through backroom deals with delegates to win at the convention. This led to a bitter primary fight between McCarthy and Robert F. Kennedy, who had jumped into the race shortly before Johnson's withdrawal. As the primaries carried on, this fight would all come to a head with the hotly-contested California primary. Both campaigns put valiant efforts and loads of funding into this contest, but in the end, McCarthy would narrowly prevail, winning 45% to Kennedy's 42% and taking all of California's delegates. Kennedy would immediately announce his withdrawal from the nomination after the loss, but refused to make an endorsement. When it came to the convention, however, most of Kennedy's delegates coalesced around McCarthy, leading to a deadlocked convention between him and Humphrey. Kennedy had only privately backed McCarthy, even though he hated the man. With the convention at an impasse, Kennedy looked for an alternate who could emerge as a compromise candidate, despite his own ego making him hurt that no matter what, it wasn't going to be him. That man was none other than Senator from South Dakota George Stanley McGovern. McGovern was a Kennedy ally who had served as his brother's director for Food for Peace and an ambassador to the Peace Corps his brother founded. However, he was also firmly of the anti-war wing of the party and was more amenable to McCarthy and his delegates than Kennedy, whom McCarthy deeply despised. McCarthy vowed to stay in, but as more and more Kennedy-turned-McCarthy delegates flipped to McGovern, he saw the writing on the wall. After six more ballots, McCarthy would release his delegates, with all but a few holdouts voting for McGovern on the next ballot. However, the race was not over yet. There still was not an agreed upon consensus, and it would take more backroom dealing to put McGovern over the hump. To that, Kennedy looked to the Texas delegation, which was backing Humphrey, led by the old friend of his brother's, Governor John Connally. Kennedy aimed to make a deal with Connally to give his delegates over to McGovern in exchange for major concessions. Initially resistant, and more and more concessions being offered, Connally would finally accept the offer on one singular condition; he would be made VP. With the two coming to an agreement, Texas would announce the switch of its delegates to McGovern, putting him over the line to win the nomination after 10 ballots, and Connally was selected as McGovern's running mate. Republican nominee Richard Nixon had a strong lead in early polls, and it looked as if the McGovern/Connally ticket was heading for a demolishment. Some polls even had McGovern losing Texas despite Connally's presence on the ticket. But slowly McGovern chipped at Nixon. Nixon was seen as a crooked insider and someone who would do anything to win, while McGovern appeared to be more honest in his approach. However, the race still remained in Nixon's favor weeks before the election, despite McGovern's best efforts. Then, a bombshell emerged. Johnson, who had only tacitly supported McGovern, if only for his buddy Connally becoming VP if they won, had leaked to the press that Nixon attempted to sabotage the peace talks occurring in Vietnam. McGovern didn't wish to make the campaign dirty, but he still called the reports "troubling" and placed serious question into his opponent's integrity while not outright placing guilt, which helped his honest image even further, and painted an even greater contrast between the two men . In the end, it was close, but... McGovern/Connally (Democratic) - 279 electoral votes, 42.62% Nixon/Agnew (Republican) - 182 electoral votes, 41.04% Wallace/LeMay (American Independent) - 77 electoral votes, 16.01% ​ ...the last second scandal proved to be just enough for McGovern to win this election by the slimmest of margins. If he had lost any of the states of California, Illinois, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Texas, or Wisconsin, with Texas being decided by just 1.04% for him and only winning 39.74% of the vote there, this election would have been thrown to the House of Representatives, and all of them, decided by only a few points each, had flipped, than Nixon would have won an outright majority himself. George McGovern was never meant to win this election, but through a deadlocked convention, backroom deals, and scandals, it was the honest prairie man that triumphed over them all.

If George McGovern had become president after the 1968 election, the largest immediate difference would almost certainly have been Vietnam. McGovern was not a pacifist in the simple sense—he had been a decorated World War II bomber pilot—but by 1968 he believed the Vietnam War was immoral, strategically mistaken, and corrosive to American democracy. A McGovern presidency beginning in January 1969 would probably have moved quickly toward a declared timetable for withdrawal, a halt to major offensive operations, and a negotiated settlement in Paris.

That would likely have meant no Cambodian invasion, no expansion of the war into Laos on the Nixon scale, no Kent State in the form it occurred, and far fewer American deaths after 1968. The United States still might not have been able to preserve South Vietnam. In fact, South Vietnam may have collapsed earlier than 1975, perhaps around 1970 or 1971, because McGovern would have been less willing than Nixon to use massive bombing and aid to prolong the Saigon government’s survival. Domestically, conservatives would have accused him of “losing Vietnam,” but the antiwar movement would have lost much of its central grievance, and the poisonous escalation of distrust produced by Nixon’s secret bombing, Cambodia, and Watergate would have been avoided.

At home, McGovern would have tried to turn the country toward what he later called “Come Home, America”: reduced military spending, stronger anti-poverty programs, civil rights enforcement, education, health care, and tax reform. But he would not have had a free hand. The Democratic Congress of 1969 still contained many Southern conservatives, and the country was already moving rightward on crime, race, taxes, and cultural politics. McGovern could have expanded parts of the Great Society, but sweeping reforms such as a guaranteed income, national health insurance, or deep defense cuts would have met heavy resistance.

The politics of crime and race would have been especially difficult. Nixon won in 1968 partly by exploiting “law and order” politics and white backlash against urban unrest and civil rights gains. A McGovern victory would not have made those tensions disappear. Riots, rising crime rates, school desegregation battles, and conflicts over busing would still have placed enormous pressure on the White House. McGovern would likely have responded less punitively than Nixon, but that might also have made him politically vulnerable to a Republican Party increasingly shaped by the Sunbelt, suburban backlash, and eventually Ronald Reagan.

The Supreme Court would be one of the biggest long-term changes. Nixon appointed Warren Burger, Harry Blackmun, Lewis Powell, and William Rehnquist. A President McGovern would probably have appointed more liberal justices. That could have altered constitutional law for decades: the death penalty might have remained more restricted, campaign finance law might have developed differently, criminal procedure rights might have stayed stronger, and the Court’s later conservative turn would have been delayed. Roe v. Wade might still have happened, since abortion-law liberalization was already underway, but the decision’s reasoning and subsequent politics could have differed.

In foreign policy, McGovern would likely have pursued arms control with the Soviet Union and a less interventionist Cold War strategy. Détente might still have happened, though perhaps without Nixon and Kissinger’s dramatic style. Opening relations with China is harder to predict. A liberal Democrat might have wanted it, but Nixon’s anti-communist reputation made the China opening politically easier. McGovern might have moved more cautiously or faced fiercer conservative attacks for doing the same thing. In Latin America, a McGovern administration would probably have been less willing to support covert destabilization, making U.S. policy toward Chile, for example, less hostile to Salvador Allende than it was under Nixon.

Economically, McGovern would have inherited serious structural problems: Vietnam inflation, pressure on the dollar, rising deficits, and the early signs of stagflation. Ending the war sooner would have helped, but it would not have prevented all the economic trouble of the 1970s. The collapse of the Bretton Woods monetary system was probably still likely. The 1973 oil shock, if it occurred in the same way, would still have battered the economy. McGovern’s instinct would have been to protect workers and the poor through public spending and regulation, but inflation would have constrained him and made him vulnerable politically.

The 1972 election would probably have been very hard for him. If Vietnam ended with an obvious communist victory, if crime remained high, and if inflation worsened, Republicans would have run a powerful campaign portraying McGovern as weak abroad and too liberal at home. Ronald Reagan, Nelson Rockefeller, or Richard Nixon himself could have been the Republican nominee. Without Watergate, the Republican Party would not have suffered the same mid-1970s collapse. So a plausible outcome is that McGovern serves one term and is defeated in 1972 by a conservative Republican backlash.

The deeper consequence is that America might have been spared some of the worst abuses of the Nixon era—Cambodia, Watergate, the enemies list, and the full-scale imperial presidency—but not the broader crises of the 1970s. Vietnam would likely have ended sooner and with fewer American and Southeast Asian deaths caused by continued U.S. escalation. The Supreme Court would have been more liberal. The federal government might have remained more committed to anti-poverty liberalism. But the conservative reaction to the 1960s would probably still have arrived, perhaps even more sharply, because McGovern’s presidency would have given the right a clear symbol of liberal failure if Vietnam ended badly and the economy deteriorated.

In short: a McGovern presidency in 1969 would probably have meant an earlier end to the Vietnam War, less executive criminality, a more liberal Supreme Court, and a less militarized foreign policy. But it would not have produced a stable progressive era. The same forces that destroyed the New Deal-Great Society consensus—racial backlash, inflation, crime politics, distrust of government, and Cold War anxiety—would still have been powerful, and McGovern may well have become a one-term president remembered as morally prescient on Vietnam but politically overwhelmed by the age he inherited.

If Hubert Humphrey had won the 1968 U.S. presidential election, the most likely immediate effect would have been a less dramatic break with the Johnson administration, but not simply a continuation of it. Humphrey was a liberal Democrat committed to the Great Society, civil rights, labor, and anti-poverty programs, yet he had also been trapped in 1968 by his loyalty to Lyndon Johnson and the Vietnam War. Once president, he likely would have tried to move faster toward a negotiated settlement in Vietnam than Richard Nixon publicly did, but he would still have faced severe military, political, and diplomatic constraints.

The biggest difference would probably have been Vietnam. Humphrey had begun distancing himself from Johnson late in the campaign, calling for a bombing halt and negotiations. As president, he likely would have continued the Paris peace talks and sought de-escalation earlier than Nixon did. There probably would have been no “Vietnamization” in exactly the Nixon form, and perhaps no secret bombing of Cambodia or 1970 Cambodia invasion. That could have reduced some of the radicalization and campus unrest of the early 1970s. However, a quick peace was not guaranteed. North Vietnam and South Vietnam both had reasons to hold out, and Humphrey would have been politically vulnerable to charges that he had “lost” Vietnam. So the war might have ended somewhat earlier and less expansively, but not necessarily cleanly or immediately.

Domestically, Humphrey would likely have tried to preserve and extend the Great Society. He supported federal civil rights enforcement, urban aid, education spending, Medicare, anti-poverty programs, and pro-labor policy. His presidency would probably have been more favorable to unions, cities, and social welfare programs than Nixon’s. He may also have pursued some version of national health insurance or expanded health coverage, though passage would have depended on Congress and the budget pressures caused by Vietnam and inflation.

On race and civil rights, a Humphrey victory would have slowed the Republican “Southern strategy” at the presidential level, at least temporarily. Nixon’s victory helped consolidate a long-term shift in which many white Southern conservatives moved into the Republican Party. That shift was already underway because of civil rights, Goldwater’s 1964 campaign, and social change, so Humphrey could not have stopped it entirely. But without Nixon using “law and order,” anti-busing politics, and appeals to white backlash from the White House, the partisan realignment may have been less rapid or taken a different form.

The Supreme Court could have changed substantially. Nixon appointed Warren Burger, Harry Blackmun, Lewis Powell, and William Rehnquist. A President Humphrey would likely have appointed more liberal justices. That could have affected criminal procedure, school desegregation, abortion, executive power, campaign finance, and economic regulation. Roe v. Wade might still have happened, but its reasoning, vote alignment, or later durability could have been different. The Court would likely have remained closer to the Warren Court tradition for longer.

Economically, Humphrey would have inherited inflationary pressure, Vietnam costs, and Great Society commitments. He may have been more willing than Nixon to use fiscal tools and wage-price guidelines, but the structural problems of the 1970s—global competition, oil shocks, inflation, and productivity slowdown—would still have emerged. The 1973 oil crisis, if it still occurred after the Arab-Israeli war, would have hit any administration hard. Humphrey’s liberal economic instincts might have produced more social spending and stronger labor protections, but also greater vulnerability to accusations of inflationary mismanagement.

Politically, Humphrey’s presidency would have been difficult from the start. The Democratic Party was fractured between labor liberals, civil rights activists, antiwar students, urban machines, and Southern conservatives. George Wallace’s strong 1968 third-party campaign showed the depth of white backlash. Humphrey would have had to govern a divided country without a landslide mandate. If Vietnam dragged on, the antiwar left would have turned on him quickly. If he withdrew too fast, conservatives would have attacked him. His reelection prospects in 1972 would have depended heavily on whether he could end the war and stabilize the economy.

One major consequence is that there would likely have been no Watergate scandal, at least not in the form that occurred under Nixon. That alone could have changed American trust in government. The post-1970s culture of suspicion toward the presidency might have developed more slowly. On the other hand, the country was already deeply polarized by Vietnam, race, crime, generational conflict, and economic stress, so Humphrey would not have restored consensus politics simply by winning.

In foreign policy beyond Vietnam, Humphrey probably would have continued Cold War containment but with a more traditional Democratic internationalist style. Nixon and Kissinger’s opening to China might have been delayed or handled differently, since it depended partly on Nixon’s anti-communist credibility and Kissinger’s secret diplomacy. Détente with the Soviet Union might still have occurred because both superpowers had incentives to reduce tensions, but the timing and style would likely have differed.

Overall, a Humphrey victory in 1968 would probably have meant an earlier or less destructive path out of Vietnam, a more liberal Supreme Court, stronger defense of Great Society liberalism, and a slower conservative Republican ascendancy. But it would not have erased the central crises of the era. The United States would still have faced racial conflict, inflation, urban unrest, cultural polarization, and the breakdown of the New Deal coalition. Humphrey might have softened the transition into the 1970s, but he probably could not have prevented the broader conservative backlash that was already forming.

items.question: What If the PRC had never carried out Reform and Opening Up?
human_answers: I agree with most of what you said but that’s not quite what happened to Hua - he was backed by Ye Jianying, an ‘elder’, and implemented reforms while publicly proclaiming his support of Mao Zedong Thought. It was Hua who saw the reintroduction of "material incentives". However Hua relied on collective leadership and as Ye's health decline Hua was outflanked by Deng, who took a much harsher stance of de-Maoification despite being economically similar to Hua. I’m going to go on a bit of a tangent to explain why I agree with the rest of what you said and think some equivalent to reform and opening was the most likely outcome - Deng spent the 80s balancing the other “elders” and younger officials. As @Georg von Frundsberg said, other elders were more 'conservative' but generally embraced reform - while younger officials like Hu and Zhao were aggressively reformist. Deng himself was a lot closer to the centre than is remembered - on agriculture for example Zhao Shukai had a good article about how Deng was slow to embrace reform and one of his signature reforms, "household production" (allowing households to dictate production instead of communes) was only adopted by central diktat in 1982 after years of discussion. However throughout the tumultuous 80s political instability remained, culminating in 1989, the removal of Zhao Ziyang and the introduction of martial. Deng was ont he defence for three years until 1992, at which point he returned to power by coordinating “reformist” officials through the southern tour. Deng enjoyed is last five years at his relative peak of influence and admiration since he had outlived everyone else. I mention this to show though that Reform and Opening up was somewhat inevitable. There was a large chunk of the elders that were open to reform and an even larger pool of younger officials. Someone sometime was going to remove the Gang of Four and the only real question left was how much reform and when. To return to OP’s question, the only real alternative to reform and opening up was a coup. People were tired of the stagnant economy and the damage done by the cultural revolution was significant - in certain periods it was closer to a civil war, as PLA and militia fought in the streets. If the government tried to stick with central planning it would be removed by the majority of officials, and if not by them then a popular uprising.

Without reform and opening up in 1978 I think the only alternative would be to chug along with five year plans and central planning. This was attempted immediately after Mao's death, but it failed because everyone believed that continuing that way was a dead end, so it's plausible but unlikely that the Communist Party goes down that path. There's reason to believe that the Cultural Revolution was launched in part as a reaction to the bureaucracy and corruption of the Stalinist party-state, as a way to try and find an alternative to it, which was eventually put to bed in 1968 when Mao sent in the PLA. Broadly, you can characterise the initial years of the Cultural Revolution as the 'left-wing' attempt to find an alternative to the Soviet model, and Reform and Opening up as the 'right-wing' attempt to find an alternative in the wake of the GPCR's failure. Maybe they could've made it work, compared to the post-war Soviet communist party, the Chinese communist party was far more afraid of stagnancy and was far more willing to put themselves behind ambitious economic programmes (this is probably the main the reason they carried out Reform and Opening up and the USSR didn't), and maybe that allows them to pull through and create a creating a working planned economy that marches proudly into the 21st century, avoiding concessions to market economics. Most people will probably dismiss this possibility. It is perhaps more likely that the whole thing ossifies and stagnates at some point, prompting the party to do something like reform and opening up at a later date. If the party has reached Soviet levels of complacency and don't do anything, the system will begin to rot, the black market will explode and you'll get something like North Korea. I don't think Chinese citizens would be as poor as North Koreans are though, considering the collapse of North Korea's living standards was largely caused by the disappearance of Soviet economic aid, something China stopped receiving long before then, but I'm not wholly sure on that one. EDIT: I can't believe I forgot to mention this, but people associated with China's New Left movement often look favourably upon Belarus' Market Socialism as an alternative to what happened in China, with all the social chaos it caused. I am not entirely familiar with how Market Socialism works in Belarus, but in a journal article by Chinese economists praising the Belarusian model they take a liking to the dominance of state-owned companies, central planning, strong leadership and stronger social security and welfare than what exists in China and the rest of the ex-USSR. I don't really know much about how things actually work in practice in Belarus and if it's at all feasible China could copy this economic model, but it gives some pointers.
