R \approx \frac{83^2}{9.81} \approx 700\text{ m}.
\]

That implies a loop roughly 1.4 km tall. But the train would also have to climb that height. Its kinetic energy at 300 km/h is only enough to climb about 350 m vertically, ignoring losses, so it could not coast through such a loop at that speed. If the loop were made small enough for the train to complete it by momentum alone, the g-forces at the bottom would become dangerously high, several g’s, far beyond what a conventional passenger train and its passengers are designed to tolerate.

For passenger comfort, the loop would need to be very large so the centripetal acceleration was gentle. But a large loop requires either much higher speed, powerful propulsion through the loop, or special track restraints that can hold the train onto the guideway even when gravity is pulling it away from the rails. At the top, passengers could feel weightless or even be pulled against restraints depending on the speed and radius.

Structurally, the problems are just as serious. A high-speed train is long and heavy, with cars connected by couplers and suspensions designed for nearly horizontal track. A vertical loop would impose huge compression, tension, bending, and wheel-load changes along the train. The track would also have to withstand enormous dynamic loads.

So if an ordinary high-speed train “had to” go through a vertical loop, it would likely derail or fail catastrophically. If a train were specially built for it, the loop would need to be enormous, the vehicle would need locked-on guide wheels or maglev-style capture, passengers would need restraints, and the ride would be closer to a giant roller coaster than to normal rail transport.

items.question: What If a Bowling Ball Were Enlarged to the Size of Earth?
human_answers: A good, professional-quality bowling ball is smoother than the Earth. Phil Plait, of Bad Astronomy, took a look at the claim that the Earth was smoother than a billiard ball.
items.original_question: 有人告诉我，如果地球缩小到保龄球大小，它会比保龄球更光滑。我的问题是，如果保龄球被吹到地球那么大，会是什么样子？
items.model_answer:
If a bowling ball were enlarged to Earth’s size while keeping the same material density, it would not remain a giant usable bowling ball. It would become a low-density planet.

A regulation bowling ball has a density of roughly 1.3–1.5 g/cm³, much less than Earth’s average density of 5.5 g/cm³. So an Earth-sized bowling ball would have only about one quarter of Earth’s mass, roughly \(1.4–1.6 \times 10^{24}\) kg. Its surface gravity would be about 2.4–2.7 m/s², around one quarter of Earth gravity. A person weighing 80 kg on Earth would feel like they weighed about 20 kg there.

It would not become a black hole. Its Schwarzschild radius would be only a few millimeters, while its actual radius would be about 6,371 km.

The distinctive bowling-ball holes would be the big problem. Scaled up, the finger holes would be hundreds to thousands of kilometers wide and deep. The material of a bowling ball—plastic, resin, urethane, reactive resin, etc.—could not support structures that large under planetary gravity. The walls would collapse, the holes would cave in, and the body would slowly reshape itself into a more gravitationally stable sphere.

The interior pressure would be enormous by ordinary material standards, reaching many gigapascals near the center. That is far beyond what bowling-ball material can withstand. The ball would crack, compress, heat, deform, and likely partially melt or chemically break down. Over time it would differentiate somewhat: denser components would sink, lighter material would rise, and the original “bowling ball” structure would be erased.

So the direct answer is: an Earth-sized bowling ball would be a weak-gravity, low-density planet. It would not keep its finger holes, it would not stay rigid, and it would not behave like a scaled-up sports object. Gravity would crush and reshape it into a roughly spherical planetary body.

items.question: What Would an Alien Civilization on the Nearest Habitable Exoplanet See When Looking at Us?
human_answers: Answer: [Image: image] Let’s try a more complete answer. We’ll start with ...
items.original_question: 让我们假设最近的宜居系外行星上有生命，并且他们拥有与我们相当的技术。如果他们现在看着我们的星星，他们会看到什么？
items.model_answer:
An alien civilization on the nearest potentially habitable exoplanet, usually taken to be Proxima Centauri b about 4.24 light-years away, would see us as we were about 4.24 years ago. They would not see present-day Earth in real time.

To their eyes, the Sun would be an ordinary bright star in their sky, around apparent magnitude 0.4, easily visible without instruments. Earth itself would be extremely hard to see: it would appear less than an arcsecond from the Sun at maximum separation and roughly 10 billion times fainter in visible light. With technology comparable to or better than our best planned exoplanet-imaging instruments, they might be able to separate Earth’s faint reflected light from the glare of the Sun.

If they had advanced telescopes, they could potentially infer that Earth is a small rocky planet in the Sun’s habitable zone. By analyzing Earth’s light spectrum, they might detect signs of an atmosphere containing oxygen, water vapor, carbon dioxide, methane, and possibly the “red edge” signature of vegetation. Those would be strong hints that Earth is biologically active.

They would not see cities, people, or continents directly unless they had extraordinarily powerful telescopes far beyond current human capability. They might detect indirect signs of technology, such as artificial radio emissions, atmospheric pollutants, nighttime illumination, or unusual industrial gases, but most of our radio leakage would be very weak by the time it reached them. Powerful directed radar signals would be more detectable, but only if aimed their way or caught by chance.

So the direct answer is: from Proxima Centauri b, Earth would appear as a tiny, faint blue-white point almost lost in the Sun’s glare, showing our planet as it was just over four years ago. With sufficiently advanced instruments, they could recognize it as a living, possibly technological world.

items.question: What If the Sun Suddenly Went Out?
human_answers: This is probably the single most popular question submitted to What If. Part of why I haven’t answered it is that it's been answered already.
items.original_question: 如果太阳突然熄灭，地球会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If the Sun suddenly stopped emitting light and heat but kept its mass, Earth would not notice for about 8 minutes and 20 seconds, because sunlight takes that long to reach us. After that, the sky would go dark except for stars, planets, and artificial lights. Earth would remain in its orbit, because the Sun’s gravity would still be there.

The effects would become catastrophic quickly. Within days, surface temperatures would drop below freezing in many places. Weather systems would collapse because they are powered by solar heating. Photosynthesis would stop almost immediately, so plants and phytoplankton would begin dying; this would eventually destroy most food chains and greatly reduce oxygen production, though the atmosphere already contains enough oxygen to last far longer than humans could survive the cold and ecological collapse.

After about a week, the average surface temperature might fall well below 0°C. After a year, Earth’s average surface temperature could be around −70°C or colder. The oceans would start freezing from the top down, but they would not freeze solid quickly because water stores enormous heat and ice insulates the liquid beneath. Deep ocean water could remain liquid for a very long time, especially near hydrothermal vents.

Most surface life would die. Humans could survive only in artificial habitats powered by stored energy, nuclear power, geothermal energy, or perhaps fusion if available. The best long-term refuges would be underground or underwater, where heat loss is slower and geothermal energy is accessible.

If instead the Sun literally vanished, not just “went out,” Earth would again not notice for 8 minutes and 20 seconds. After that, sunlight would disappear and the Sun’s gravity would cease to affect Earth. Earth would then fly off in a straight-line path tangent to its former orbit, becoming a frozen rogue planet.

So the short answer is: after eight minutes of normality, Earth would become dark, rapidly freeze, and most life would die, though some deep underground or deep-sea life could survive for a very long time if the Sun’s mass remained.

items.question: What Would It Be Like to Row across Lakes of Mercury, Bromine, Gallium, Tungsten, Liquid Nitrogen, or Liquid Helium?
human_answers: Let's take these one at a time. Bromine and mercury are the only known pure elements that are liquid at room temperature.
items.original_question: 驾驶划艇穿过水银湖会是什么感觉？溴呢？液态镓？液态钨？液氮？液氦？
items.model_answer:
Rowing would be governed mostly by density, temperature, vapor/toxicity, and whether your boat and oars survive. In ordinary conditions, only mercury, bromine, and warmed gallium are “rowable” in any recognizable sense. Tungsten, liquid nitrogen, and liquid helium are essentially fatal or mechanically impossible without science-fiction protection.

Mercury would be the strangest but most physically rowable. It is about 13.5 times denser than water, so a boat would float extremely high, with only a shallow part of the hull submerged. The oars would get a very strong bite because each stroke pushes against a very dense fluid. The surface would look mirror-bright and heavy, with rounded beads and high surface tension rather than ordinary splashing. You might be able to move efficiently, but steering would feel odd because the boat has little draft. The real problem is that mercury vapor is toxic, splashes are hazardous, and mercury attacks or amalgamates with some metals, especially aluminum. A wooden, steel, or specially coated boat could float; an aluminum one would be a bad idea.

Bromine would be physically possible but immediately dangerous. Liquid bromine is about three times denser than water, so the boat would float higher than on water, though not as dramatically as on mercury. It is not especially viscous, so rowing would feel more fluid than syrupy. But bromine is volatile, corrosive, and intensely toxic; it gives off red-brown fumes that would damage lungs, eyes, skin, clothing, and many materials. A normal person in a normal boat would not last. With full chemical protection and a resistant boat, it could be rowed, but it would be like rowing across a fuming, corrosive chemical spill.

Gallium would be one of the more plausible ones if kept just above its melting point, around 30 °C. It is about six times denser than water, so a boat would float high and the oars would have a firm bite. It has modest viscosity, so it would not feel like rowing through tar. It is far less volatile than mercury or bromine, so the vapor hazard is much smaller. However, gallium wets surfaces and can embrittle or penetrate some metals, especially aluminum, so the choice of boat and oar material matters. A properly coated or compatible boat could probably be rowed across a lake of liquid gallium. It would look like rowing across a warm, silvery metallic mirror.

Molten tungsten is not realistically rowable. Tungsten melts at about 3422 °C. At that temperature, a human, boat, oars, air, and almost any normal material would burn, melt, vaporize, or be destroyed by radiant heat long before touching the lake. Even if you imagine a magical heat-proof boat and rower, the surrounding environment would be catastrophic. Physically, molten tungsten is extremely dense, so buoyancy would be enormous and the boat would float very high, but the thermal conditions make the scenario essentially impossible.

Liquid nitrogen would be deadly and only marginally boat-like. It is less dense than water, about 0.8 times water’s density, so a boat would float lower than usual. It is also very cold, 77 K, or −196 °C, and would boil violently around warmer objects. The boat, oars, and rower would be covered in boiling nitrogen fog; many materials would become brittle; exposed skin would suffer severe cold injury; and the nitrogen gas would displace oxygen, causing asphyxiation. Because liquid nitrogen is low-viscosity and less dense than water, the oars would feel like they had a weaker bite. With cryogenic equipment and a suitable boat, you might move, but it would be inefficient and surrounded by boiling vapor.

Liquid helium would be the least rowable. It is extremely cold, about 4 K, and very low density, roughly one-eighth that of water. A normal boat would need to displace much more liquid to float, so it would sit very deep or simply be impractical unless built as a very large, very light craft. The oars would have almost no grip because there is so little mass to push against, and at low enough temperatures helium becomes superfluid, meaning it can flow without ordinary viscosity, creep along surfaces, and leak through tiny openings. It would boil furiously around anything warm, embrittle materials, and create an asphyxiating helium atmosphere. Rowing across it in the usual sense would be nearly impossible.

So the rough ranking is: gallium and mercury are physically rowable but hazardous; bromine is rowable but chemically nightmarish; liquid nitrogen is cryogenically lethal and hard to row; liquid helium is almost unrowable; molten tungsten is unsurvivable.

items.question: What If You Dropped 3,000 Super Balls onto a Pedestrian from a Seven-Story Parking Garage?
human_answers: After falling from seven stories, the mass of bouncy balls would be moving at about 20 meters per second. 20 meters per second is about how fast an average person with a good arm could throw a bouncy ball.
items.original_question: 如果将 3,000 个弹力球从七层停车场扔到下面人行道上行走的人身上会怎样？如果这个人活下来，需要多少个弹力球才能杀死他？会发生什么伤害以及相关的犯罪是什么？
items.model_answer:
Assuming “Super Balls” are the classic hard rubber balls about 4–5 cm across and roughly 50 g each, 3,000 of them would have a total mass of about 150 kg. From a seven-story parking garage, roughly 20–25 m high, each ball would hit at about 20 m/s, or around 45 mph, allowing a little for air resistance.

One ball would carry only about 10 joules of energy — painful, like being hit by a hard-thrown small rubber ball, but not usually catastrophic. But 3,000 balls together would carry about 30,000 joules of gravitational energy, comparable to a 150 kg object falling from that height or a person-sized object hitting at highway speed.

Because they are loose balls, the impact would not be exactly like being hit by one solid 150 kg block. The balls would spread out, bounce, ricochet, and many might miss. But if they were dropped directly onto someone in a compact cluster, the person would be struck by hundreds or thousands of hard impacts in a fraction of a second. Super Balls rebound well, so they can transfer a large impulse while bouncing away.

The likely result would be severe injury: the pedestrian could be knocked down, concussed, bruised badly, suffer eye or facial injuries, and possibly suffer skull, neck, or spinal trauma. If most of the 3,000 balls actually hit the person, especially the head and upper body, it could plausibly be fatal.

So the careful answer is: a few Super Balls from that height would hurt; 3,000 dropped together from seven stories onto a pedestrian would be a serious, potentially lethal blunt-impact event, not a harmless prank.

items.question: What If You Drained the Oceans through a 10-Meter Hole at Challenger Deep?
human_answers: I want to get one thing out of the way first: According to my rough calculations, if an aircraft carrier sank and got stuck against the drain, the pressure would easily be enough to fold it up[1]Extrapolated from the maximum pressure tolerable by icebreaker...
items.original_question: 如果在海洋最深点“挑战者深渊”的底部建造一个半径 10 米通向太空的圆形入口，海洋的排水速度有多快？当水被排干时，地球会发生什么变化？

items.question: What If You Dumped Earth's Oceans onto Mars?
human_answers: In the previous What If (http://what-if.xkcd.com/53/), we opened a portal at the bottom of the Mariana Trench and let the oceans drain out. We didn't worry too much about where the oceans were draining to.
items.original_question: 假设你做了“排干海洋”，并将水倒在好奇号火星车顶部，随着水的积累，火星会发生什么变化？
items.model_answer:
If you somehow placed Earth’s oceans gently onto present-day Mars, Mars would not become a warm blue Earth. It would become a mostly flooded planet that then freezes over.

Earth’s oceans contain about \(1.3 \times 10^9\) cubic kilometers of water. Spread over Mars, that is enough for a global layer roughly 9 kilometers deep. Because Mars has large basins and high volcanic provinces, the water would not be uniform: the northern lowlands, Hellas Basin, and other depressions would become extremely deep seas, while only the tallest regions such as Olympus Mons and parts of Tharsis would remain as islands or highlands. Most of Mars would be underwater.

At first, if the water arrived warm and liquid, there would be violent boiling and evaporation at the surface because Mars has a very thin atmosphere. But it would not all boil away; evaporation cools water strongly, and Mars receives much less sunlight than Earth. The surface would quickly chill, form ice, and become covered by a frozen crust. Water vapor would condense as frost and snow, making a cold, cloudy, icy world rather than an Earthlike one.

Over time, the ocean would freeze from the top downward. With Mars’s low average temperature, the upper kilometers would become ice. However, because the water layer would be so deep in many places, pressure plus geothermal heat from Mars’s interior could keep some water liquid beneath the ice, especially in deep basins. The final state might resemble a planet-wide version of Europa or an ice-covered Arctic Ocean: thick surface ice with possible buried salty oceans or lakes below.

The added water would be massive, but not enough to strongly change Mars’s gravity or make it retain a thick Earthlike atmosphere. It would add only about 0.2% to Mars’s mass. It also would not solve Mars’s main habitability problems: weak sunlight, little greenhouse atmosphere, no strong global magnetic field, and long-term atmospheric escape. Over millions to billions of years, exposed surface ice and water vapor would be slowly broken apart by sunlight; hydrogen would escape to space and oxygen would react with the surface or accumulate only under special conditions.

So the short answer is: dumping Earth’s oceans onto Mars would create an enormous global ocean at first, drowning most of the planet, but present-day Mars is too cold and airless to keep it as an open liquid ocean. It would mostly freeze into a thick ice shell, with the best chance for lasting liquid water hidden deep underneath.

items.question: What If You Tried to Hold an Airplane to the Ground with a Rope?
human_answers: Ah, the Just Cause 2 scenario (http://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=just+cause+2+plane+grapple). At takeoff, a 747's four engines can each generate 281.57 kN of thrust.
items.original_question: 如果你想将一架飞机固定在地面上，使其无法起飞，那么绳子必须用什么材料制成？
items.model_answer:
If the rope and anchor were strong enough, the airplane would simply stay on the ground. An airplane does not “want” to rise straight up like a balloon; it needs forward airspeed over its wings to make enough lift. If a rope prevents it from accelerating down the runway, it usually cannot take off.

The rope would mainly have to resist the airplane’s engine thrust, not the airplane’s full weight. For a small propeller plane, that might be a few thousand newtons of force, so a strong tiedown system could hold it. This is basically what happens during engine run-up tests: the plane is held by brakes, chocks, or tiedowns while the engine produces thrust.

For a large jet, the forces are enormous. A modern airliner can produce hundreds of thousands of newtons of thrust, so an ordinary rope would snap almost instantly. A steel cable and a massive concrete anchor might hold it, but the attachment point on the aircraft would also need to be designed for that load. If you tied the rope to the wrong part, it could tear off part of the airplane.

If the rope broke, it would be extremely dangerous. A highly tensioned rope or cable can whip back with enough energy to maim or kill, and the plane could suddenly surge forward.

So the short answer is: yes, you can hold an airplane down with a rope in principle, but the rope, anchor, and attachment point must withstand the aircraft’s thrust. The plane would not take off unless it could still gain enough airspeed or the tether failed.

items.question: What If the Bottom Inch of a Massive Mountain Vanished?
human_answers: The one-inch gap would take about 70 milliseconds to close. Don't stick your hand in.
items.original_question: 如果一座巨大的山峰（比如麦金利山）的底部一英寸消失了怎么办？山体下降1英寸的影响会发生什么？ 1英尺呢？如果山脚升高到山顶现在的高度，然后让整个山落到地上怎么办？
items.model_answer:
If the bottom inch of a massive mountain vanished instantly, the mountain would not hover or neatly remain intact. It would drop about one inch, hit the ground, and violently settle.

The impact speed after falling one inch would only be about:

\[
v=\sqrt{2gh}\approx 0.7\ \text{m/s}
\]

so the mountain would not be “falling fast” in an ordinary sense. But because the mass involved is enormous, the released gravitational energy would be huge. For a large mountain with a mass around \(10^{15}\) to \(10^{16}\) kg, the energy from a one-inch drop would be roughly:

\[
E = mgh \approx 10^{14}\text{–}10^{15}\ \text{J}
\]

That is comparable to tens to hundreds of kilotons of TNT, though most of it would go into crushing rock, friction, heat, landslides, and seismic waves rather than a clean explosion.

In reality, the mountain would not behave like a perfectly rigid block. Mountains are not separate objects sitting on a table; they are part of the crust. If a one-inch layer beneath the whole mountain somehow disappeared, the rock above would begin collapsing into the gap. Stress waves would travel upward through the mountain at a few kilometers per second, so different parts would respond at slightly different times. The base would fracture and grind downward first, then the upper portions would settle.

The likely result would be a sharp earthquake-like event under the mountain, accompanied by cracking, rockfalls, avalanches, dust clouds, and possibly large landslides. Nearby valleys could be badly affected. The mountain’s overall height would decrease by roughly an inch, but its slopes and internal structure could be seriously damaged.

So the short answer is: the mountain would drop, smash into its foundation, and produce a major local seismic and landslide event, but it would not launch upward, explode like a bomb, or disappear wholesale.

items.question: What If a Spacecraft Used Rockets to Slow to a Few Miles per Hour during Reentry?
human_answers: The answers to these questions all hinge on the same idea. It's an idea I've touched on in other articles, but today I want to focus on it specifically: The reason it's hard to get to orbit isn't that space is high up.
items.original_question: 如果航天器使用火星天空起重机等火箭助推器在重返大气层时减速至每小时几英里会怎么样？它会消除对隔热罩的需要吗？
items.model_answer:
If a spacecraft used rockets to slow to only a few miles per hour during reentry, it could in principle come down gently, but it would be extremely inefficient unless done only at the very end.

A spacecraft in low Earth orbit is moving about 17,500 mph, or 7.8 km/s. Reentry normally works by letting the atmosphere remove most of that energy as heat and drag. A heat shield is heavy, but it is far lighter than carrying enough rocket propellant to cancel nearly all orbital speed.

If the spacecraft fired rockets high above the atmosphere and slowed to a few mph, two things would happen:

It would no longer be in orbit, so it would begin falling. Gravity would quickly speed it up again. From around 100 km altitude, even if it started almost stationary, it could reach very high speeds before the lower atmosphere slowed it. To keep descending at only a few mph, it would need to thrust continuously against gravity, essentially hovering downward. That would require an enormous amount of fuel.

The fuel requirement is the main problem. Canceling orbital velocity with chemical rockets takes a huge mass ratio. Depending on engine performance, most of the spacecraft’s mass would need to be propellant just to slow down from orbit, before also paying the extra “gravity losses” of hovering or descending slowly. For a capsule or crew vehicle, that is usually much worse than using a heat shield plus parachutes or a short landing burn.

If rockets were used lower in the atmosphere, after drag had already removed most of the speed, then it becomes much more reasonable. This is basically retropropulsive landing. SpaceX Falcon 9 boosters do this: they use atmospheric drag and controlled entry to shed most energy, then fire engines near the end to land slowly. Some Mars landers also use rockets for final descent because Mars’s atmosphere is too thin for parachutes alone.

So the short answer is: yes, rockets could slow a spacecraft to a few miles per hour during reentry, but doing it from orbital speed or maintaining that speed throughout descent would require impractically large amounts of propellant. It is far more efficient to let the atmosphere do most of the braking, then use parachutes, wings, or a brief rocket burn near landing.

items.question: What If You Tried to Print the Entire English Wikipedia in Real Time?
human_answers: This many: [Image: image] That's surprisingly few printers! But before you try to create a live-updating paper Wikipedia, let's look at what those printers would be doing ...
items.original_question: 如果您有整个（例如英文）维基百科的印刷版本，您需要多少台打印机才能跟上对实时版本所做的更改？
items.model_answer:
Assuming you mean the current article text of English Wikipedia, not every old revision, talk page, image, or media file, printing it would be a huge but not magical job.

English Wikipedia contains on the order of several billion words. At normal book-like density, that is roughly 8–10 million printed pages. Printed single-sided, that would be tens of tonnes of paper and a stack approaching a kilometer high; double-sided, still hundreds of meters of paper stack. A single 30–50 page-per-minute office laser printer running nonstop would take several months to about a year to print one snapshot.

The “real time” part is the killer. Wikipedia changes constantly, roughly on the order of one or two edits per second. By the time your printer had finished page 1, much of what you had already printed would be out of date. If you only printed the edit diffs as they happened, a small printer farm could probably keep up. But if you tried to keep a full physical copy current by replacing changed pages, you would need continuous reprinting, sorting, binding, and refiling, which quickly becomes logistically absurd.

If you meant reprinting the entire encyclopedia every time Wikipedia changed, it becomes completely impossible: with millions of pages per copy and edits arriving every second, you would need tens of millions of fast printers and an enormous supply chain of paper and toner.

So the direct answer is: you can print a snapshot of English Wikipedia with an industrial-scale print job, but you cannot meaningfully print “the entire English Wikipedia in real time” as a current physical encyclopedia. It would be obsolete almost immediately, and keeping it synchronized would be a logistical nightmare.

items.question: What If You Jumped from a Plane with Helium Tanks and a Giant Balloon?
human_answers: As ridiculous as it sounds, this is—sort of—possible. Falling from great heights is dangerous.[citation needed (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Republic_Presidential_Unit_Citation)] A balloon could actually help save you, although a regular helium...
items.original_question: 如果我带着几罐氦气和一个巨大的未充气的气球从飞机上跳下来怎么办？然后，在下降时，我释放氦气并填充气球。我需要下落多长时间才能让气球减慢我的速度以便我能够安全着陆？
items.model_answer:
If you jumped from a plane carrying helium tanks and a giant balloon, it would not work like a cartoon parachute. Unless the system were already engineered and deployed like a real balloon/parachute, you would probably fall, tumble, fail to inflate it safely, and hit the ground too fast.

Helium provides surprisingly little lift. At sea level, one cubic metre of helium lifts only about 1 kilogram after subtracting the helium’s own weight. So to support a 90 kg person, plus harness, balloon fabric, tanks, valves, and other gear, you would need well over 100 cubic metres of helium. That is a balloon roughly 6 metres across just to hover near sea level, and larger if you want a safety margin or are at higher altitude.

The tanks are the big problem. Compressed helium cylinders are heavy. A steel cylinder holding enough helium to lift perhaps 10 kg may itself weigh many times that. If you keep the tanks attached, much of the helium’s lift is wasted lifting the tanks. If you release the tanks after inflation, you now have heavy falling cylinders endangering people below, and you still have to survive the deployment.

Inflating the balloon during freefall is also extremely difficult. From a typical skydiving altitude, you have maybe about a minute before impact. You would need to deploy a huge balloon, keep it from tangling, fill it with a very large volume of gas, and avoid tearing it apart in a high-speed airstream. If the balloon began inflating while you were falling at 50–60 m/s, the drag forces could be violent enough to rip the balloon, snap lines, or injure you.

If the balloon were too small, it would act only as a poor parachute and you might still land lethally fast. If it were large enough and inflated smoothly, it could slow you down; at that point it is essentially a hot-air/helium balloon or a parachute system, not an improvised rescue trick. If it were too large or overfilled, you might stop falling and start rising, then later face bursting, venting, or being carried away by winds.

So the careful answer is: a properly designed, pre-tested balloon system could in principle lower someone safely, because buoyancy and drag are real. But jumping out of a plane with helium tanks and trying to inflate a giant balloon on the way down would be wildly impractical and probably fatal. A parachute is vastly lighter, simpler, faster to deploy, and safer.

items.question: What If All Digital Data Were Stored on Punch Cards?
human_answers: [Image: image] Google almost certainly has more data storage capacity than any other organization on Earth. Google is very secretive about its operations, so it's hard to say for sure.
items.original_question: 如果所有数字数据都存储在打孔卡上，谷歌的数据仓库有多大？
items.model_answer:
If all digital data were stored on punch cards, modern computing would effectively collapse. Punch cards can represent digital bits, but their storage density and access speed are so poor that the world’s data would become physically unmanageable.

A classic IBM punch card stores about 80 bytes. The world’s digital data is on the order of 100 zettabytes or more, meaning roughly \(10^{23}\) bytes. At 80 bytes per card, that would require around \(10^{21}\) punch cards: about a sextillion cards.

Physically, that is absurdly large. One IBM-style card is about 18.7 cm by 8.3 cm and roughly 0.18 mm thick. For 100 zettabytes, the cards would have a total volume of around \(3 \times 10^{15}\) cubic meters. If spread evenly over all land on Earth, they would form a layer tens of meters deep, even before adding boxes, shelves, aisles, buildings, humidity control, fire protection, and indexing systems. Their mass would be on the order of \(10^{18}\) kilograms, comparable to a substantial fraction of Earth’s atmosphere and far beyond plausible paper production.

Access speed would be just as devastating. A fast punch-card reader might read about 1,000 cards per minute, or roughly 80 kilobytes per minute, about 1.3 kilobytes per second. Reading 1 terabyte from punch cards at that speed would take decades. Reading a zettabyte would take longer than the age of the universe on a single reader. Even with huge parallelism, the machinery, labor, and maintenance would be overwhelming.

Random access would almost disappear. Today, a computer can retrieve a file from solid-state storage in microseconds to milliseconds. With punch cards, retrieving data would mean locating physical cards in enormous warehouses, transporting them to readers, reading them sequentially, and possibly re-sorting them afterward. Search engines, streaming video, online banking, cloud computing, machine learning, and ordinary smartphones would be impractical.

Reliability would also be poor at global scale. Punch cards can last a long time in controlled archives, but they are vulnerable to fire, water, mold, insects, bending, mis-sorting, and physical wear. Copying data would require punching more cards, multiplying the already impossible storage burden. Updating data would be clumsy: instead of overwriting bytes, one would replace or append physical cards and maintain elaborate catalogs.

So, in principle, all digital data could be encoded onto punch cards. In practice, it would turn the digital world into a planet-sized paper logistics problem. The internet, modern software, large databases, AI systems, streaming media, and most real-time computing would cease to function as we know them. Punch cards are viable for small historical programs and archives, not for the global digital civilization.

items.question: What If You Began Rising Upward at One Foot per Second?
human_answers: Did you bring a coat? A foot per second isn't that fast—it's substantially slower than a typical elevator.[1]Otis: About Elevators (http://www.otisworldwide.com/pdf/AboutElevators.pdf) It would take you 5-7 seconds to rise out of arms' reach, depending how...
items.original_question: 如果你突然开始以每秒一英尺的速度稳定上升，你到底会怎么死？你会先被冻住还是窒息？或者其他什么？
items.model_answer:
If you merely got an initial upward speed of one foot per second and then nothing kept lifting you, almost nothing would happen: gravity would stop you in about 0.03 seconds, after you rose only about 0.19 inches, and you would fall back down.

If instead some force magically kept you rising at a steady 1 ft/s, you would be ascending slowly in everyday terms—about 0.68 mph—but very fast in altitude-acclimatization terms: 3,600 feet per hour, or about 16 miles per day.

You would reach 10,000 feet in about 2.8 hours. Breathing would become noticeably harder, and an unacclimatized person could develop headache, nausea, confusion, and impaired judgment. Around 18,000 feet, after about 5 hours, air pressure is roughly half sea-level pressure; hypoxia would become serious. By the time you reached Everest altitude, about 29,000 feet after 8 hours, an unprotected person would likely be severely hypoxic, possibly unconscious, and in danger of death. Cold would also be a major threat: the air temperature would generally fall well below freezing within a few hours and could be around −50 °C near airliner cruising altitudes.

At 35,000 feet, reached after about 10 hours, you would need supplemental oxygen to remain conscious. At about 63,000 feet, reached after 17.5 hours, you would pass the Armstrong limit, where water can boil at body temperature; without a pressure suit or pressurized cabin, exposed body fluids such as saliva and tears could boil, and you would rapidly lose consciousness.

If you had a proper pressure suit or capsule with oxygen, temperature control, and radiation protection, you would reach the edge of space—the Kármán line at 100 km—in about 3.8 days. But you would not be “in orbit.” Orbit requires sideways speed of about 7.8 km/s, not just upward motion. If the lifting force stopped at that height, you would fall back to Earth.

So the short answer is: unprotected, you would probably die from hypoxia and cold long before reaching space; protected, you could reach space in about four days, but you would still need enormous horizontal speed to stay there.

items.question: What If the Wind Reached 500 Miles per Hour?
human_answers: Absolutely! [Image: image] Some things don't work like they do in the movies.
items.original_question: 如果风速达到 500 英里/小时，它会卷起人吗？
items.model_answer:
A 500-mile-per-hour wind at ground level would be a civilization-level local disaster in the area it affected. It would be far beyond any hurricane and stronger than even the most violent tornado winds normally measured.

At 500 mph, the air is moving about 223 meters per second, roughly Mach 0.65 at sea level. It is not supersonic, so it would not create a continuous sonic boom, but it would exert enormous force. The dynamic pressure would be about 30,000 pascals, around 0.3 atmospheres, or roughly 600+ pounds per square foot on a flat surface. A wall, roof, window, vehicle, or human body would experience forces of thousands to tens of thousands of pounds depending on size and shape.

For a person outdoors, survival would be extremely unlikely. You would not simply “lean into it”; you would be picked up, tumbled, and slammed into debris or structures. Flying debris would be one of the main killers. Wood, metal, glass, gravel, and pieces of buildings would become high-speed projectiles.

For buildings, ordinary houses would be destroyed. Roofs would be ripped away, walls would fail, windows would shatter instantly, and most above-ground structures not specifically hardened would be severely damaged or obliterated. Cars, trucks, trees, utility poles, signs, and shipping containers could be moved or thrown. Even reinforced structures could suffer major damage from pressure loads and debris impacts.

If such winds occurred over the ocean, they would whip up extreme waves, spray, and storm surge. Near coasts, the flooding and wave damage could be catastrophic. The sea surface would become a mass of foam and airborne water droplets, making visibility almost zero.

A 500 mph wind over a large area would also require an enormous amount of energy. Hurricanes cannot realistically sustain surface winds that high under Earthlike conditions; their strongest winds are usually under 200 mph. Tornadoes can briefly approach or exceed 300 mph in extreme cases, but 500 mph would be extraordinary and likely only possible in a very localized, short-lived, violently rotating flow or in unusual planetary conditions.

So the direct answer is: a 500 mph wind would flatten ordinary structures, loft vehicles and debris, kill exposed people almost instantly, and devastate any landscape in its path. It would be more like being inside an extreme tornado than any normal storm.

items.question: What If You Lived on a Tiny but Ultra-Massive Asteroid?
human_answers: Last week, we looked at at life on a giant world (http://what-if.xkcd.com/67/). This week, let's look at a small one.
items.original_question: 如果一颗小行星很小但质量却很大，你真的能像小王子一样住在上面吗？
items.model_answer:
If you lived on a tiny but ultra-massive asteroid, the experience would be dominated by how much mass is packed into how small a radius. The key quantities are

\[
g=\frac{GM}{R^2}
\]

for surface gravity, and

\[
v_{\rm esc}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}
\]

for escape velocity.

If the asteroid were tiny but only massive enough to give Earthlike gravity, life would be strange but not automatically crushed. For example, a 100-meter-radius object with \(1g\) surface gravity would need a mass of about \(1.5\times10^{15}\) kg, giving it an absurd density hundreds of thousands of times denser than ordinary rock. It would not be a natural asteroid; it would need to be made of exotic or artificially compressed matter.

Standing on it would feel odd. The horizon would be only a few tens of meters away, so the ground would visibly curve. Your head would be noticeably farther from the center than your feet, so gravity at your head would be weaker than at your feet. On a 100-meter-radius body this difference might be a few percent; on a 10-meter-radius body it could be large enough to feel like your body was being stretched.

Even with \(1g\) at the surface, escape velocity could be surprisingly low because the object is so small. On a 100-meter-radius, \(1g\) asteroid, escape velocity would be only about 44 m/s. A fast projectile could leave forever, and on an even smaller one a strong jump or thrown object might escape. It could not hold a normal atmosphere for long, because gas molecules at ordinary temperatures move faster than the escape speed. You would need a sealed habitat.

If “ultra-massive” means something like Earth’s mass squeezed into asteroid size, then you would not live there. The surface gravity would be millions to billions of times Earth gravity, tidal forces would tear you apart, and ordinary matter could not remain as a normal rocky surface. It would behave more like an exotic compact object than an asteroid. If enough mass were packed inside a small enough radius, it would become a black hole; for a radius \(R\), that happens when

\[
R < \frac{2GM}{c^2}.
\]

So the short answer is: a tiny object with carefully chosen mass could give you Earthlike gravity but would be exotic, airless, and weird to live on. A truly ultra-massive tiny asteroid would be lethal or would collapse into something more like a neutron-star-like object or a black hole, not a place you could stand.

items.question: Could You Boil Water by Stirring It?
human_answers: No. The basic idea makes sense.
items.original_question: 我心不在焉地搅拌着一杯热茶，心里想：我这不是给杯子里加了动能吗？我知道搅拌确实有助于冷却茶，但如果我搅拌得更快怎么办？我可以通过搅拌来煮一杯水吗？
items.model_answer:
Yes, in principle you could boil water by stirring it.

Stirring does mechanical work on the water. Because water has viscosity, that mechanical energy is dissipated as heat. If you stir hard enough, long enough, and prevent heat from escaping, the water’s temperature will rise and can eventually reach its boiling point.

For example, heating 1 liter of water from 20°C to 100°C requires about

\[
4.2 \text{ kJ/kg°C} \times 1 \text{ kg} \times 80°C \approx 336 \text{ kJ}
\]

of energy, not counting losses. A 100-watt stirrer, if all its energy became heat in the water, would take roughly

\[
336{,}000 \text{ J} / 100 \text{ W} \approx 3{,}360 \text{ s}
\]

or about 56 minutes just to bring it to 100°C. Actually boiling away significant water would require much more energy because vaporization takes a lot of heat.

In practice, boiling water by ordinary hand-stirring is extremely difficult because heat escapes to the air and container, and a person cannot deliver enough sustained mechanical power efficiently. But with a powerful mechanical stirrer in a well-insulated vessel, yes: stirring alone can heat water to boiling.

One caveat: if the container is sealed, pressure will rise and the boiling point will increase, so the water may get hotter than 100°C without boiling. In an open container at atmospheric pressure, sufficiently vigorous mechanical stirring could, in principle, make it boil.

items.question: What If a Nearby Supernova Hit Earth with Lethal Neutrino Radiation?
human_answers: The phrase "lethal dose of neutrino radiation" is a weird one. I had to turn it over in my head a few times after I heard it.
items.original_question: 距离超新星有多近才能获得致命剂量的中微子辐射？
items.model_answer:
A normal core-collapse supernova could make neutrino radiation lethal at Earth only if it were absurdly close, roughly within a few astronomical units. At ordinary “nearby star” distances, even a few light-years away, the neutrino dose would be essentially harmless because neutrinos interact so weakly.

If Earth did receive a lethal supernova neutrino burst, the immediate effect would be a planet-wide, nearly unshieldable radiation dose lasting about 10 seconds. The neutrinos would pass through the whole Earth, so the night side, deep ocean, caves, and underground bunkers would not help much. A tiny fraction of the neutrinos would interact inside bodies and materials, producing ionizing particles that damage DNA and cells. Humans and many animals would develop acute radiation sickness; at several sieverts many would die over days to weeks, and at higher doses death could occur in hours to days. Microbes, spores, some insects, and radiation-resistant organisms might survive if the dose were only “human-lethal.”

The neutrinos would not blow up, melt, or noticeably heat Earth. Even a fatal biological radiation dose deposits only joules to tens of joules per kilogram, tiny compared with the energy needed to heat rock, boil oceans, or disturb the planet mechanically.

But there is a bigger catch: if a supernova were close enough for its neutrinos alone to be lethal, the rest of the supernova would be catastrophic. The optical, ultraviolet, X-ray, and gamma radiation would arrive shortly after the neutrino burst, followed later by expanding ejecta and cosmic rays. At distances of only a few AU, Earth’s atmosphere and surface environment would likely be devastated or sterilized by these non-neutrino effects. The neutrinos would be the first warning, but not the main destroyer.

So the direct answer is: lethal supernova neutrino radiation would cause an unavoidable, global flash of acute radiation exposure without physically damaging the planet much, but any supernova close enough to do that would also destroy Earth’s biosphere by much more intense radiation and blast effects. In realistic astronomy, no plausible nearby supernova poses a lethal neutrino threat to Earth.

items.question: What If Humans Kept Growing at the Rate of a One-Month-Old Baby?
human_answers: Tall. According to the National Center for Health Statistics, the average newborn's height (length) is approximately 0.5 meters,[1]or 0.56 meters in heels.
items.original_question: 如果我们在整个发育期（即直到十几岁/二十岁出头）都以与第一个月相同的速度生长，人类会达到什么高度？
items.model_answer:
If humans kept growing at the rate of a one-month-old baby, they would become impossibly large very quickly.

A one-month-old typically gains about 3–4 cm in length per month and roughly 0.7–1 kg in mass per month. If that growth continued linearly, a person could be around 8 meters tall by age 18. But if their body kept normal human proportions, their mass would not increase linearly; it would scale roughly with volume. An 8-meter-tall human-shaped body could weigh many tons, not just a few hundred kilograms.

If “rate” means percentage growth rather than absolute growth, the result is even more extreme. Babies grow by a large fraction of their body size each month. Continuing that exponential growth for years would produce absurd sizes—hundreds of meters or more—long before adulthood.

In reality, this could not work biologically. The square-cube law would be the main problem: as height increases, body weight grows faster than bone and muscle strength. Bones scale with cross-sectional area, but mass scales with volume, so the skeleton would fail under the load. The heart would struggle to pump blood, heat removal would become difficult, joints would collapse, and organs would not scale efficiently.

So the short answer is: if humans kept growing like one-month-old babies, they would become gigantic within childhood, but they would not survive. Human growth slows because our bodies are constrained by physics, metabolism, hormones, and skeletal mechanics.

items.question: What If a Tyrannosaurus Rex Were Released in New York City?
human_answers: About half of an adult, or one ten-year old child: [Image: image] Tyrannosaurus rex weighed about as much as an elephant.[1]This always seemed a little off to me; my mental image of elephants is that they're in the same size range as cars or trucks, whereas...
items.original_question: 如果霸王龙被释放到纽约市，它每天需要消耗多少人才能获得所需的卡路里摄入量？
items.model_answer:
If a healthy adult Tyrannosaurus rex were suddenly released in New York City, it would be extremely dangerous, but it would not be an unstoppable “movie monster.”

A full-grown T. rex was roughly 12 meters long, weighed around 6–9 tons, had an enormous bite force, strong senses, and enough strength to smash cars, storefronts, light poles, and barriers. In a crowded area such as Times Square, the immediate danger would be mass panic: people running, traffic collisions, trampling, and the animal attacking or accidentally crushing people. Even if it did not actively “hunt” humans, its movement through dense streets could cause many casualties.

The city would likely respond first with emergency evacuations and road closures. Police would try to create distance rather than confront it directly. Standard firearms might injure it but would be unreliable at stopping it quickly, especially in a crowded urban environment where missed shots would be dangerous. Heavy weapons could kill it, but using them in Manhattan would risk major collateral damage. The preferred response would probably be containment: block off streets with large vehicles, lure or drive it into an open area, and involve wildlife veterinarians, zoo specialists, NYPD emergency units, and possibly the National Guard.

Tranquilizing it would be difficult. A T. rex is far larger than any modern land predator, and the correct drug dose would be uncertain. A dart might not penetrate deeply enough or might take too long to work. If overdosed, the animal could die; if underdosed, it could become more agitated. In practice, responders might need a combination of barriers, vehicles, helicopters or drones for tracking, and chemical immobilization if they wanted to capture it alive.

New York’s environment would also work against the dinosaur. Streets are narrow for an animal of that size, pavement is hard on feet not adapted to it, glass and metal debris could injure it, and bridges, tunnels, and dense buildings would restrict movement. It could not hide for long. Thermal cameras, helicopters, drones, traffic cameras, and social media footage would make tracking it easy. It might damage many vehicles and buildings, but it would eventually be cornered.

Long-term survival would be unlikely. A T. rex would need large quantities of meat, fresh water, and space. It could eat livestock or zoo animals if it reached them, or possibly scavenge, but Manhattan would not provide a sustainable habitat. It would also face stress, unfamiliar noise, pollution, infection risks from injuries, and possible temperature or metabolic issues depending on its biology.

So the realistic outcome is: the first minutes to hours could be catastrophic, especially in a crowded district, but the T. rex would eventually be contained, killed, or immobilized by coordinated emergency forces. It would cause chaos and casualties, but modern surveillance, vehicles, barriers, and organized response would make it very unlikely to roam New York City for long.

items.question: What If You Dumped All the World's Tea into the Great Lakes?
human_answers: Weak, bordering on homeopathic. The standard cup of tea, as described by the International Organization for Standardization in ISO 3103 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=8250), contains two grams of tea per 100 mL of water.[1]Further ISO...
items.original_question: 如果我们把世界上所有的茶叶都倒进五大湖怎么办？与普通的茶相比，湖茶的浓度如何？
items.model_answer:
If by “all the world’s tea” you mean roughly one year of global tea production, the Great Lakes would barely notice.

The world produces about 6–7 million tonnes of dry tea leaves per year. The Great Lakes contain about 22,700 cubic kilometers of water, or about 22,700 trillion liters. If you dumped the dry leaves directly into the lakes and somehow mixed them evenly, the concentration would be only a few tenths of a part per billion by mass. That is far too dilute to make the lakes look, smell, or taste like tea.

If instead you brewed all that tea first, using normal tea strength, you might make on the order of 0.5–1 cubic kilometer of tea. Added to the Great Lakes, that would still be only about 1 part in 20,000–40,000 of their volume. The lake level would rise by only a few millimeters, and even if the tea were hot, the overall temperature of the lakes would increase by only a few thousandths of a degree Celsius.

The main effects would be local, not lake-wide. If the tea or leaves were dumped all in one place, there could be a nasty brown plume, lots of floating or sinking organic matter, oxygen depletion as microbes decomposed it, and possible harm to fish and invertebrates nearby from low oxygen, tannins, caffeine, and other compounds. Harbors, beaches, and water intakes near the dump site could be fouled.

But spread through all five Great Lakes, all the world’s tea would not turn them into tea. It would be an enormous waste of tea and a localized pollution problem, but not a Great-Lakes-scale transformation.

items.question: What If All the World's Viruses Were Gathered in One Place?
human_answers: It would be a huge pile, but human viruses would make up only a tiny fraction of it. HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, has killed tens of millions of people worldwide, and over 30 million people are currently living with HIV.
items.original_question: 如果世界上的所有病毒都集中到一个区域会怎样？它们会占据多少体积以及它们会是什么样子？
items.model_answer:
If all the world’s virus particles were gathered into one place, they would form a surprisingly small but extremely hazardous mass: probably a mountain-sized pile or dense slurry, not something planet-sized.

Earth is estimated to contain roughly \(10^{31}\) virus particles, the overwhelming majority of them bacteriophages—viruses that infect bacteria and archaea, especially in oceans and soils. Since individual viruses are tiny, often tens to hundreds of nanometers across, the total packed volume would likely be on the order of about 1 to 10 cubic kilometers, depending on the assumed average virus size. That is roughly comparable to a small mountain, a large lake’s worth of material, or a cube about 1–2 kilometers on a side. Its total mass might be hundreds of billions to a few trillion kilograms, depending on assumptions.

It would not be a seething “super-organism.” Viruses are not metabolically active on their own; outside host cells, they are basically genetic material in protein or lipid shells. They cannot move, eat, grow, or reproduce without infecting suitable hosts. Most of the pile would not be dangerous to humans because most viruses infect microbes, plants, insects, or other non-human hosts. But it would still contain every human, animal, plant, and bacterial pathogen on Earth, so direct exposure would be extraordinarily dangerous. If aerosolized, washed into water supplies, or spread through ecosystems, it could cause enormous disease outbreaks among many species.

If kept isolated, however, the pile would gradually become less infectious. Ultraviolet light, heat, drying, oxidation, and chemical decay would damage viral genomes and proteins. Some viruses are fragile and would lose infectivity quickly; others, especially hardy non-enveloped viruses, could persist for much longer.

The bigger consequence might actually be ecological. Removing all viruses from the rest of the planet would radically disrupt microbial ecosystems. Viruses kill vast numbers of bacteria and plankton every day, recycle nutrients in the oceans, influence carbon cycling, regulate bacterial populations, and drive microbial evolution. Without them, bacterial and algal communities could boom, crash, or reorganize unpredictably. Marine food webs and biogeochemical cycles would be strongly affected. Many viral diseases would temporarily vanish, but the biosphere would not simply become “healthier”; it would become unstable in ways we cannot fully predict.

So the direct answer is: all the world’s viruses gathered together would make a relatively modest physical heap, perhaps mountain-scale, containing an enormous number of particles. It would be locally extremely biohazardous, but not apocalyptic by mere proximity. The real global danger would come either from dispersing that concentrated collection or from the ecological shock of removing viruses from everywhere else.

items.question: What If You Tried to Catch a Bullet after It Slowed Down?
human_answers: Yes. The "bullet catch" is a common magic trick in which a magician appears to catch a fired bullet in mid-flight—often between their teeth.
items.original_question: 有没有什么方法可以让枪射击后子弹飞到空中，然后可以安全地用手接住？例如射手位于海平面，捕手位于山上，位于枪的最远射程处。
items.model_answer:
If a fired bullet has merely “slowed down” in air, you still should not try to catch it.

A bullet leaves a gun at hundreds of meters per second. Air drag slows it, but by the time it is slow enough for a human to catch safely, it has usually already hit the ground or something else. If it is a bullet fired upward and falling back down, it may reach terminal velocity rather than full muzzle speed, but that can still be around tens to over 100 m/s depending on the bullet. Because the bullet is small and hard, its energy is concentrated on a tiny area, so it can still puncture skin, injure a hand, or in some cases kill.

For example, a 9 mm bullet of about 8 grams moving at 100 m/s has about 40 joules of kinetic energy. That is less than at muzzle speed, but delivered through a small metal point or edge it is still dangerous. Trying to stop it with your hand over a distance of only a few centimeters would produce large forces and likely cause injury.

If the bullet were somehow slowed to the speed of a tossed pebble, then yes, you could catch it, especially with a glove or container. But at that point it is no longer meaningfully “a bullet in flight”; it is just a small piece of metal moving slowly.

So the direct answer is: if it has slowed to ordinary hand-catching speed, yes, but if it is still moving as a ballistic projectile, even a much-slowed bullet is too dangerous to catch.

items.question: What If Astronauts Tried to Reach the Moon by Hitting Golf Balls in Orbit?
human_answers: It depends how good your swing is. That sounds glib, but it's sort of true.
items.original_question: 假设你有一艘绕地球轨道运行的宇宙飞船，你能通过向另一个方向击打高尔夫球来推动你的飞船达到超过逃逸速度的速度吗？如果是这样，需要多少个高尔夫球才能到达月球？
items.model_answer:
If astronauts in low Earth orbit tried to reach the Moon by hitting golf balls, it would not work in any practical sense.

A golf ball in orbit already shares the astronaut’s orbital speed around Earth, about 7.7 km/s for an ISS-like orbit. But to go from low Earth orbit onto a Moon-crossing trajectory, the ball needs an additional forward speed of about 3.2 km/s. That is the trans-lunar injection burn rockets perform.

A very hard golf shot gives the ball only about 50–80 m/s relative to the astronaut, perhaps around 100 m/s in an extreme case. That is roughly 30–60 times too small. Instead of heading for the Moon, the ball would just enter a slightly different Earth orbit. If hit forward, its orbit would become a bit more elliptical, with an apogee only a few hundred kilometers higher. If hit backward, it might lower its orbit and eventually reenter. It would mostly become hazardous space debris.

If the astronauts meant to propel themselves toward the Moon by hitting golf balls away from them, Newton’s third law helps, but only barely. A 45-gram golf ball hit at 70 m/s carries about 3 kg·m/s of momentum. For a suited astronaut of roughly 150 kg, each shot changes the astronaut’s speed by only about 0.02 m/s. Reaching the Moon from low Earth orbit would require thousands of meters per second of velocity change, so one astronaut would need on the order of 100,000–200,000 golf balls, weighing several tonnes, and would still have enormous navigation and life-support problems.

So the key point is: orbit is not “almost at the Moon.” From low Earth orbit, the Moon is still a major orbital-energy jump away. A golf swing can slightly alter an orbit, but it cannot send either the ball or the astronaut to the Moon.

items.question: How Powerful Would Radar Have to Be to Stop a Speeding Car?
human_answers: Radio waves exert force on things. Not a lot of force.
items.original_question: 我偶尔会在限速标志上看到“雷达强制执行”，我不禁要问：无线电波必须有多强才能阻止汽车超速，如果尝试这样做会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If you mean stopping it by radiation pressure from a radar beam, the required power would be enormous: on the order of terawatts, assuming the beam is perfectly aimed and the car intercepts it all.

Electromagnetic radiation carries momentum. If a radar beam is absorbed by the car, the force is

\[
F=\frac{P}{c}
\]

where \(P\) is the power hitting the car and \(c\) is the speed of light. If the car reflects the beam straight back, the force can be at most

\[
F=\frac{2P}{c}
\]

So even under ideal reflection, you need

\[
P=\frac{Fc}{2}
\]

Take a typical car:

\[
m \approx 1500\ \text{kg}
\]

traveling at about 100 mph:

\[
v \approx 45\ \text{m/s}
\]

To stop it over 100 m, the needed deceleration is

\[
a=\frac{v^2}{2d}\approx \frac{45^2}{200}\approx 10\ \text{m/s}^2
\]

so the required force is

\[
F=ma\approx 1500\times 10=15000\ \text{N}
\]

For a perfectly reflecting car, the required radar power hitting the car would be

\[
P=\frac{Fc}{2}\approx \frac{15000\times 3\times 10^8}{2}
\approx 2.3\times 10^{12}\ \text{W}
\]

So the answer is roughly:

\[
\boxed{\text{a few terawatts of radar power hitting the car}}
\]

If the car absorbs rather than reflects the beam, the requirement doubles to around \(4\text{–}5\) terawatts. Realistically it would be worse, because not all the beam would hit the car, not all the momentum would be transferred efficiently, and the beam would likely ionize the air and destroy or vaporize parts of the car long before it “gently” stopped it.

For comparison, a police radar gun emits milliwatts to watts. You would need something like a trillion times more power than an ordinary radar gun. So in practice, radar cannot be used to stop a speeding car by radiation pressure; the required beam would be catastrophically destructive.

items.question: What If All the CO2 in Bottled Soda Were Released into the Atmosphere?
human_answers: For most of the history of civilization, there were about 270 parts per million of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. In the last hundred years, industrial activity has pushed that number up (http://www.skepticalscience.com/print.php?r=45) to 400 parts per m...
items.original_question: 全球瓶装碳酸饮料库存中含有多少 CO 2？需要多少苏打水才能使大气中的CO 2 恢复到工业化前的水平？
items.model_answer:
If all the CO₂ dissolved in bottled soda worldwide were suddenly released into the atmosphere, the global effect would be essentially negligible.

A typical carbonated soft drink contains roughly 5–8 grams of CO₂ per liter. If the world produces on the order of 200 billion liters of carbonated soft drinks per year, that corresponds to about 1–2 million metric tons of CO₂ per year.

For comparison:

The atmosphere contains about 3.3 trillion metric tons of CO₂.

Human activities emit about 37 billion metric tons of CO₂ per year.

One atmospheric ppm of CO₂ equals about 7.8 billion metric tons of CO₂.

So even releasing an entire year’s worth of soda carbonation would raise atmospheric CO₂ by only about 0.0001–0.0003 ppm, far too small to measure against normal atmospheric variation. The climate effect would be effectively zero.

Locally, if huge quantities were released in a confined space, CO₂ could displace oxygen and pose an asphyxiation risk, just as dry ice or fermentation tanks can. But globally, the atmosphere would dilute it immediately.

So the direct answer is: it would fizz a lot, but it would not meaningfully affect Earth’s atmosphere or climate.

items.question: What If I Threw a Tungsten Countertop into the Sun?
human_answers: Not very far. With its high melting point, tungsten is a good[1]Except that the word "good" implies that you have some kind of goal you're working toward, which—given how strange the thing you're doing is—I'm not sure about.
items.original_question: 如果我把钨制台面扔进太阳里，它会下降多远？
items.model_answer:
If you literally threw it by hand from Earth, it would not go into the Sun. Earth is already moving sideways around the Sun at about 30 km/s, and a hand-thrown object keeps almost all of that sideways speed. To make it hit the Sun, you’d need to cancel most of Earth’s orbital velocity—far beyond any “throw.”

If you somehow put a tungsten countertop on a collision course with the Sun, it still would not arrive as a solid slab.

Tungsten is extremely refractory, with a melting point around 3,700 K and a boiling point around 5,800–6,200 K, but the Sun’s visible surface is about 5,800 K and the radiation near it is intense. As the countertop fell inward, sunlight would heat it until it melted into a glowing liquid mass. Closer in, it would rapidly evaporate from the surface. By the time it reached the photosphere or plunged into the upper solar atmosphere, aerodynamic heating, radiation, and impacts with solar plasma would shred, vaporize, and ionize it.

A typical tungsten countertop might weigh one or two tonnes. Falling into the Sun, it would hit at roughly the Sun’s escape speed, about 600 km/s, giving it kinetic energy on the order of 10^14 joules—comparable to a small nuclear weapon. That sounds large, but to the Sun it is nothing: the Sun emits that much energy in about a trillionth of a second.

So the result would be: the countertop melts, vaporizes, becomes ionized tungsten plasma, mixes into the Sun’s outer layers, and has no noticeable effect. No splash, no dent, no visible explosion—just a tiny amount of extra heavy element pollution in an object 10^27 times more massive.

items.question: What If Earth Spun Fast Enough for a Day to Last One Second?
human_answers: If this is going to happen, I hope it doesn't happen late in the afternoon next Friday. The Earth rotates,[citation needed (https://web.archive.org/web/20151210155028/http://www.timecube.com/)] which means its midsection is being flung outward by centrifuga...
items.original_question: 如果地球自转加速到一天只持续一秒钟会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If Earth rotated once every one second, it would not remain a planet in anything like its current form.

A one-second day means Earth’s equator would move at about 40,000 km/s, roughly 13% the speed of light. The required centripetal acceleration at the equator would be about 250 million m/s², or around 25 million g. Earth’s gravity, only about 9.8 m/s² at the surface, would be utterly negligible by comparison.

So at the equator, the “centrifugal” effect would exceed gravity by tens of millions of times. Rock, oceans, atmosphere, buildings, and eventually the planet’s own mass would be flung outward. Earth would tear itself apart almost instantly.

In fact, Earth would start shedding material if its day were shortened to roughly 1.4 hours, not one second. A one-second rotation period is thousands of times faster than the breakup limit.

The rotational energy would also be enormous: around 10³⁹ joules, millions of times greater than Earth’s gravitational binding energy. That is far more than enough to disperse the planet completely. The result would likely be an expanding cloud or disk of superheated rock, metal, vapor, and plasma rather than a recognizable Earth.

If you imagined somehow standing on the surface before it came apart, you would not experience a rapid sunrise and sunset every second. You, the ground, the oceans, and the atmosphere would be launched outward at extreme speed. The planet would fail long before a normal “one-second day” could be experienced.

So the direct answer is: Earth spinning fast enough for a day to last one second would be catastrophically impossible; the planet would disintegrate.

items.question: What If Rain Broke a Windshield before Speed Did?
human_answers: Fast. [Image: image] Raindrops are tiny.
items.original_question: 如果下雨的话，挡风玻璃会被雨打碎，你需要以多快的速度行驶？
items.model_answer:
If a vehicle moved so fast through rain that raindrops broke the windshield before the airflow or “speed” itself destroyed it, the windshield would not shatter because rain had become hard; it would shatter because the relative impact speed had made each drop act like a tiny high-speed projectile.

At normal road speeds, rain cannot break a windshield. A large raindrop has only fractions of a joule of kinetic energy at highway speeds, and because it is liquid it spreads out on impact rather than concentrating force like a stone.

At aircraft-like speeds, the situation changes. Impact energy scales with the square of speed. A large raindrop hitting at several hundred meters per second can deliver a few joules in a very small area and can pit, crack, or erode glass or acrylic. This is a real issue for high-speed aircraft: rain erosion can damage canopies, leading edges, sensors, and coatings.

But there is a catch: the same speed that makes raindrops dangerous also makes the air dangerous. At sea level, the dynamic pressure from air at roughly Mach 1 is already tens of kilopascals over the whole windshield, producing enormous total force. At still higher speeds, heating, vibration, pressure loads, and debris impacts become catastrophic. So for an ordinary car, aerodynamic forces, loss of control, tires, engine limits, and structural failure would matter long before rain alone “shot out” the windshield.

In the counterfactual case where rain did break the windshield first, the immediate result would be violent cracking or spalling, followed by the high-speed airstream forcing water, glass fragments, and pressure into the cabin. Visibility would go to zero almost instantly, and the vehicle would likely become uncontrollable. The practical answer is: rain can damage windshields only at extreme relative speeds, and if you are going that fast in rain, the windshield breaking is only one symptom of a vehicle already far outside survivable operating conditions.

items.question: What If You Drank the Blood of a Drunk Person?
human_answers: You would have to drink a lot of blood. A person contains about 5 liters of blood, or 14 glasses.
items.original_question: 喝醉人的血会醉吗？
items.model_answer:
You probably would not get drunk. The alcohol concentration in a drunk person’s blood is far too low compared with alcoholic drinks.

For example, a legally drunk blood alcohol concentration of 0.08% means about 0.8 grams of ethanol per liter of blood. A standard drink contains about 14 grams of ethanol, so you would need to drink roughly 17 liters of that person’s blood to get the alcohol in one drink—far more blood than a human body contains. Even someone dangerously intoxicated at 0.30% BAC has only about 3 grams of ethanol per liter of blood, meaning you’d still need several liters for a noticeable alcohol dose.

The real problem would not be the alcohol. Drinking human blood can make you nauseated or vomit, and it can transmit serious blood-borne infections such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV if the blood is contaminated. Large amounts could also expose you to excessive iron and other biological material your digestive system is not meant to handle in that quantity.

So the direct answer is: you would not meaningfully become drunk from a small amount of a drunk person’s blood, but you could make yourself sick or expose yourself to dangerous infections.

items.question: How Many Birds Would It Take to Collapse into a Giant Bird Ball?
human_answers: The video shows starlings, birds which ... • gather in giant flocks of sometimes more than a million animals • can talk (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VZYG00_qvE) • sound like R2-D2, though not as much as bobolinks (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ABjBl...
items.original_question: 我在观看这段视频时想知道：需要多少只鸟才能让重力接管并迫使它们变成一个巨大的鸟球？
items.model_answer:
Assuming you mean a self-gravitating “planet” made of birds, the answer is roughly a quintillion birds: about \(10^{18}\) to \(10^{19}\) pigeon-sized birds.

A quick estimate: treat the birds as a loose biological material with bulk density around \(500\)–\(1000\ \text{kg/m}^3\). The central pressure inside a uniform self-gravitating sphere is approximately

\[
P_c \approx \frac{2\pi}{3}G\rho^2R^2 .
\]

To make the pile noticeably collapse and compact under its own gravity, you might require pressures of order atmospheric pressure, \(10^5\ \text{Pa}\), enough to crush voids and deform bird bodies. That gives a radius of a few tens of kilometers, around \(30\)–\(60\) km.

The mass of such a bird sphere would be roughly

\[
M \sim 10^{17}\text{ to }10^{18}\ \text{kg}.
\]

For pigeon-sized birds of mass \(\sim 0.1\ \text{kg}\), that is

\[
N \sim 10^{18}\text{ to }10^{19}\ \text{birds}.
\]

So the direct answer is: about a billion billion birds, give or take an order of magnitude, would be needed for their mutual gravity to crush them into a giant compact bird ball. If you merely ask when birds gravitationally attract each other, any two birds do; if you ask when the effect becomes catastrophic and planet-like, it is around \(10^{18}\) birds.

items.question: What If All the Water on Earth Vanished?
human_answers: As is often the case with these questions, everyone would die. The first people to notice would be swimmers and boaters, for obvious reasons.
items.original_question: 如果地球上所有的水体都神奇地消失了，会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If all the water on Earth suddenly vanished, Earth would become almost instantly uninhabitable.

The oceans, lakes, rivers, glaciers, groundwater, clouds, and water vapor would be gone. The seafloor would be exposed, revealing vast salt flats, deep ocean trenches, and huge underwater mountain ranges. Air would rush into the former ocean basins, but there would be no giant “hole” or vacuum.

Life would collapse very quickly. Humans and most animals would die within days from dehydration, and many would die sooner from heat stress, fires, or ecosystem failure. Plants would wilt and die without water, ending most food chains and oxygen-producing photosynthesis. Microbes, fungi, insects, marine life, forests, crops, and nearly all complex life would be wiped out. A few organisms might survive briefly if they had internal moisture, but if all water inside living cells vanished too, death would be immediate.

The climate would change drastically. Without oceans, clouds, rain, humidity, or the water cycle, there would be no weather as we know it. The oceans currently store and redistribute enormous amounts of heat; without them, temperature swings between day and night and between seasons would become far more extreme. The atmosphere would become much drier, and the strongest greenhouse gas, water vapor, would be gone.

Geologically, the sudden removal of the oceans’ weight would disturb Earth’s crust. Ocean floors would rebound upward over time, likely causing earthquakes and volcanic changes. Plate tectonics would also be affected in the long run because water helps weaken rocks, lubricate faults, and drive melting processes inside Earth.

Earth’s mass would decrease only slightly, because all surface water is tiny compared with the planet’s total mass. Gravity, the Moon’s orbit, and Earth’s orbit around the Sun would change only negligibly.

If water vanished only once, small amounts could eventually be recreated by chemical reactions, volcanic outgassing, and combustion, since burning hydrogen-containing materials produces water. But this would be tiny compared with the lost oceans and would not save the biosphere. If water were magically prevented from ever existing again, Earth would become a permanently dry, largely dead rocky planet.

items.question: How Long Could Humanity Survive on Cannibalism Alone?
human_answers: There are about 500 trillion calories of human in the world. If it could be frozen or otherwise preserved, that would be enough—at least in terms of raw calories—to keep a tiny breeding population (http://www.newscientist.com/article/dn1936-magic-number-for...
items.original_question: 人类仅靠同类相食还能生存多久？
items.model_answer:
Humanity could not survive indefinitely on cannibalism alone. It would be a one-time use of human biomass, not a sustainable food system.

A rough estimate: an average human body contains on the order of 100,000–150,000 usable kilocalories, depending heavily on body size and fat. A person needs about 2,000 kilocalories per day. So one human body could feed one other human for roughly 50–75 days.

If all 8 billion people tried to share the available human biomass evenly, the total “food supply” would last only about two months. After that, there is no new energy entering the system.

If the population were allowed to shrink continuously, with the living eating the dead as efficiently as possible, the decline would be exponential: each remaining person would require about one human body every couple of months. Under very idealized assumptions—perfect preservation, no waste, no disease, no violence losses, and full use of bodies—the last few humans might persist for roughly 4 years. In reality, spoilage, conflict, disease, inedible material, lack of fuel, and nutritional problems would shorten that considerably.

So the direct answer is: cannibalism alone could keep a shrinking human population alive for perhaps a few months on a large scale, and at most a few years for the final survivors under unrealistic ideal conditions. It cannot sustain humanity as a species.

items.question: What If I Fired an Infinitely Powerful Laser into the Sky?
human_answers: A lot of the time, if a question includes the word "infinity," the answer is "an infinite amount"—when there's an answer at all. An infinitely strong laser pointer would deliver an infinite amount of energy to the air in its path, which would in turn radiat...
items.original_question: 如果我向天空中的任意一点发射无限强的激光束，会造成多少伤害？
items.model_answer:
An “infinitely powerful” laser is physically impossible: infinite power for any nonzero time means infinite energy, and physics has no way to supply, contain, or describe that. But if we interpret it as “a laser whose power is increased without limit,” the result is not a clean beam shooting into space. It is a catastrophic explosion starting in the air immediately in front of the laser.

At ordinary intensities, a laser aimed upward can pass through the atmosphere, because air is mostly transparent to many wavelengths. But at extreme intensity, the electric field of the light rips electrons off air molecules. The air becomes plasma. Plasma is not transparent like normal air; it absorbs, scatters, and reflects the beam. So the laser would create a glowing ionized channel, heat it to enormous temperatures, and dump huge amounts of energy into the nearby atmosphere.

As the power rises, that channel becomes a fireball. The heated air expands violently, producing a blast wave, thunder-like shocks, intense ultraviolet and X-ray radiation, electromagnetic pulses, and probably nuclear/particle interactions at sufficiently absurd energies. The beam would not simply “poke a hole in the sky”; the atmosphere in its path would turn into an opaque, exploding plasma.

If the laser were truly infinite, the first bit of matter it encountered—the air near the aperture, dust, the laser optics, even the surrounding electromagnetic field in a more complete theory—would receive infinite energy. That is not a survivable event. In any realistic interpretation, you and the laser are destroyed essentially instantly, followed by increasingly large destruction depending on how much finite energy was actually emitted.

If you somehow placed the source above the atmosphere and fired into empty space, an arbitrarily powerful beam would still not be harmless: its energy density would gravitate.
