At sufficiently high energy concentration, general relativity predicts gravitational collapse; with “infinite” energy, the setup is no longer a laser but a breakdown of the assumptions of physics, likely involving black-hole-like behavior or worse.

So the direct answer is: it would not make a neat pillar of light into space. The atmosphere would ionize, become opaque, and explode around the beam path. With genuinely infinite power, the scenario is unphysical; with merely enormous power, it is a local-to-planetary-scale catastrophe starting right at the laser.

items.question: What If One Person Owned All the Money in the World?
human_answers: So you've somehow found a way to gather all the world's money. We won't worry about how you did it—let's just assume you invented some kind of money-summoning magic spell.
items.original_question: 人们有时会说“如果我拥有世界上所有的钱……”来讨论如果他们没有财务限制他们会做什么。但我很好奇，如果一个人拥有世界上所有的钱，会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If one person owned all the money in the world, the global economy would largely stop functioning almost immediately—unless new money or substitutes for money appeared.

Money is useful because it circulates. People use it to buy food, pay wages, settle debts, invest, and price goods. If everyone except one person had zero money, most ordinary transactions could not happen. Workers could not be paid, businesses could not sell to customers, governments could not collect normal taxes, and debts denominated in money would become unpayable.

The person would not automatically “own everything.” Money is not the same as land, factories, food, machines, or labor. They would own the medium of exchange, not all real resources. But because nobody else had money, they would have enormous bargaining power: they could buy assets or hire people only by giving some money back. The moment they spent any money, however, other people would again have money, so the monopoly would begin to disappear.

If the person refused to spend or lend the money, money would become useless in practice. People would switch to barter, informal credit, IOUs, local currencies, cryptocurrencies, rationing systems, or government-issued replacement money. Governments and central banks would almost certainly declare the old money invalid, issue new currency, tax or confiscate holdings, or otherwise reset the system.

Prices would also become strange. If nobody else has money, ordinary market prices cannot really exist. A loaf of bread might have a “price,” but no one could pay it. The economy would suffer a massive liquidity crisis: goods and labor would still exist, but the payment system would be broken.

So the short answer is: one person owning all the money would not make them practically omnipotent. It would cause a collapse of normal trade, force society to create alternative money or redistribute the existing money, and reveal that real wealth is not money itself but goods, services, productive capacity, institutions, and trust.

items.question: What If Everything except Earth Were Made of Antimatter?
human_answers: This one doesn't end well for us. But—unlike most scenarios involving the word "antimatter"—the end is surprisingly slow and drawn-out.
items.original_question: 如果除了地球之外一切都是反物质怎么办？

items.question: What If You Teleported to the Surface of the Sun for One Nanosecond?
human_answers: Believe it or not, this wouldn't even warm you. The temperature of the surface of the Sun is about 5,800 K,[1]Or °C.
items.original_question: 当我大约 8 岁的时候，在科罗拉多州寒冷的天气里铲雪时，我希望自己能立即被传送到太阳表面，只持续一纳秒，然后立即被传送回来。我想这足以让我暖和起来，但又不足以伤害我。实际上会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
For just one nanosecond, probably almost nothing dramatic would happen to you.

The “surface” of the Sun—the photosphere—is about 5,800 K, but it is also a very thin, low-density plasma, not a solid surface. The Sun’s radiative flux there is enormous, about 63 million watts per square meter. But a nanosecond is so short that the energy delivered is tiny:

\[
63{,}000{,}000\ \text{W/m}^2 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{s}
\approx 0.063\ \text{J/m}^2
\]

Even allowing for radiation and hot particles from multiple directions, the total heat absorbed by your body in one nanosecond would be minuscule. It would not be enough to vaporize you, burn you, or even noticeably warm your skin overall.

Solar gravity is also not a problem on that timescale. The Sun’s surface gravity is about 28 times Earth gravity, but in one nanosecond it would change your velocity by only about:

\[
274\ \text{m/s}^2 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{s}
= 2.7 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m/s}
\]

That is effectively nothing.

So if you were teleported to the photosphere of the Sun and then teleported back after exactly one nanosecond, you would likely survive unharmed. You might receive an extremely tiny amount of surface heating and radiation exposure, but far too little to cause macroscopic damage.

The key is the timescale: the Sun is lethally hot and bright, but one nanosecond is so short that very little energy has time to transfer into your body.

items.question: What If Auto Racing Had Only One Rule: The Driver Must Survive?
human_answers: The best you'll be able to do is about 90 minutes. There are lots of ways you could build your vehicle—an electric car,[1]With wheels designed to dig into the pavement on turns.
items.original_question: 如果你抛开赛车比赛的所有规则，举办一场比赛，只是让一个人以尽可能快的速度绕赛道 200 倍，那么什么策略会获胜呢？假设赛车手必须生存。
items.model_answer:
If auto racing had only one rule—“the driver must survive”—it would stop looking like modern racing and become an extreme engineering arms race, with the human body as the main limiting component.

Assuming the goal is still to finish a course as fast as possible, cars would quickly become enclosed, heavily instrumented, semi-autonomous machines. Open wheels and open cockpits would disappear because they are aerodynamically inefficient and dangerous. The “car” would likely resemble a mix of a Le Mans prototype, fighter jet cockpit, land-speed-record vehicle, and ground-effect fan car: fully enclosed, low-drag, active-aero, active-suspension, all-wheel-drive, with computer-controlled traction, braking, steering assistance, and a crash capsule around the driver.

The biggest limit would not be engine power. With no rulebook, designers could use enormous electric power, turbines, rockets, fan suction, movable aerodynamics, exotic fuels, and active control systems. The real limits would be tire grip, track strength, aerodynamic stability, braking distance, and human tolerance to acceleration. A driver can survive very high g-loads briefly, especially reclined with a g-suit, but sustained cornering or braking at extreme levels causes blackout, organ stress, spinal injury, or loss of control. So the optimal vehicle would not simply be “as fast as possible”; it would be as fast as possible while keeping the driver’s body alive and conscious enough to count as a driver.

On a normal road course, lap times would be limited mostly by cornering and braking. Straight-line speeds could become absurd, but every extra kilometer per hour must be paid back in braking distance and crash risk. On a banked oval or purpose-built track, speeds could climb far higher because the banking would reduce lateral stress on the driver. On a long straight course, vehicles could become jet- or rocket-powered streamliners, potentially approaching aircraft-like speeds, but then “racing” would resemble land-speed record attempts more than circuit racing.

Safety would become paradoxical. The driver would be extremely protected: carbon-composite survival cell, fireproof life-support system, automatic fire suppression, crash energy absorption, perhaps even an ejection or separable capsule system. But everyone else would be in much greater danger unless additional rules existed. A crash at 400–600 km/h releases enormous energy; debris, fire, shock waves, and airborne vehicles would threaten spectators, marshals, and other competitors. The single rule protects only the driver, not the crowd, the track workers, the environment, or even the other drivers unless “the driver” means every driver.

There is also a game-theory problem. If literally no other rules exist, then blocking, ramming, sabotage, smoke screens, oil on the track, or building an armored vehicle to disable rivals might become rational strategies, provided the driver survives. The sport could drift toward a high-speed demolition contest rather than a clean race. If autonomous control is not banned, the “driver” may become mostly a protected passenger while computers do the actual racing, because machines react faster and tolerate instability better than humans.

So the likely outcome is not just “faster Formula 1.” It would be a short-lived, extremely expensive, extremely dangerous technological competition dominated by enclosed capsules, active aerodynamics, automation, huge power, and crash-survival engineering. The human body would be the weak link, and without rules about vehicle design, conduct, tracks, spectators, and fairness, the event would become less a sport and more an experiment in how much speed and violence can be wrapped around a living person without killing them.

items.question: What If Your Income Materialized around You in Cash?
human_answers: First, let's think about coins. The US federal minimum wage in the US is \$7.25/hour, which is about \$15,000/year for a full-time job.
items.original_question: 如果人们的收入以现金的形式实时出现在他们身边会怎样？你需要赚多少钱才会陷入真正的麻烦？
items.model_answer:
If your income literally materialized around you as physical cash, the main effects would be surprisingly mundane for ordinary incomes—unless it appeared in small denominations, coins, or all at once.

Assume U.S. paper money. A bill weighs about 1 gram and has a compact volume of about 1.1 cubic centimeters. So for an annual income \(I\), paid in bills of denomination \(D\):

\[
\text{number of bills}=\frac{I}{D}
\]

\[
\text{mass in kg}\approx \frac{I}{1000D}
\]

For example, if you earn $60,000 per year:

In $100 bills, that is only 600 bills: about 0.6 kg, less than a liter of compact volume, and a stack about 6–7 cm tall. If it appeared continuously, you would get roughly one $100 bill every 14–15 hours. This would be mildly weird, not dangerous.

In $1 bills, it becomes 60,000 bills: about 60 kg of paper, roughly 68 liters if neatly stacked, and a stack about 6.6 meters tall. Spread loosely around you over the year, it would be a persistent mess. If it appeared all at once, it could knock things over or partly bury your feet, but probably would not crush you.

In coins, it could become hazardous. $60,000 in pennies would be 6 million pennies, weighing about 15 metric tons. If that materialized around or above you, it could collapse floors, trap you, or kill you. Even quarters would weigh more than a metric ton.

For very high incomes, even $100 bills become a serious physical object. A $1 million annual income in $100 bills is 10,000 bills, about 10 kg and around 11 liters—basically a heavy shoebox or small backpack. A $1 billion income in $100 bills would be 10 million bills, about 10 metric tons and over 11 cubic meters, comparable to filling part of a room or truck.

The physics also depends on how the cash appears. If bills gently appear at rest around you, they are mostly harmless. If they appear overhead and fall, paper bills are still not very dangerous because they have low terminal velocity. Coins falling from height could injure or kill. If the money appears by displacing air, large volumes could shove air aside and create pressure effects; if it appears inside objects or your body, that would be catastrophic. If it appears as newly created matter, it violates conservation of mass-energy unless the material comes from somewhere.

Economically, if this is just your existing income converted into cash, nothing major changes except convenience, storage, theft risk, and tax/accounting headaches. If it creates new money from nothing, then it is counterfeiting in effect and, at scale, inflationary.

So the short answer is: with normal income in high-denomination bills, it would be strange but manageable; in ones, it would be messy; in coins or at billionaire scale, it could become structurally dangerous or lethal.

items.question: What If You Used Lasers to Evaporate the Rain before It Hit the Ground?
human_answers: Stopping rain with a laser is one of those ideas that sounds totally reasonable, but if you— [Image: image] While the idea of a laser umbrella might be appealing, it— [Image: image] Ok. The idea of stopping rain with a laser is a thing we're currently talki...
items.original_question: 用雨伞或帐篷阻止雨水落在某物上是很无聊的。如果你试图用激光来阻止雨，在每个进入的水滴到达地面十英尺之前瞄准并蒸发它，会怎么样？
items.model_answer:
You could, in principle, evaporate falling rain with lasers, but it would be wildly impractical and dangerous for anything larger than a tiny area.

The main problem is energy. Evaporating water takes about 2.5 megajoules per kilogram. One millimeter of rain over one square meter is one kilogram of water. So even light-to-moderate rain requires enormous continuous power:

A rainfall rate of 1 mm/hour needs about 700 watts per square meter just to evaporate the water. A heavy rain of 10 mm/hour needs about 7 kilowatts per square meter. A severe downpour could require tens of kilowatts per square meter or more. That is before accounting for laser inefficiency, missed droplets, scattering, and energy lost heating the air.

So to protect a person-sized area, you might need several kilowatts to tens of kilowatts of optical laser power. The electrical input would be higher. To protect a street, stadium, or city, the required power would quickly rise to megawatts, gigawatts, or beyond.

There are also practical problems. Raindrops are small and moving quickly, so either you need a broad laser “curtain” with huge power density or a tracking system that targets countless droplets per second. The laser wavelength would need to be strongly absorbed by water, probably infrared, but then the beam would also heat fog, mist, wet surfaces, eyes, skin, clothing, and anything else in its path. It could blind people, burn them, start fires, and create dangerous hot steam or aerosolized droplets.

Even if you succeeded, the water would not disappear. It would become warm water vapor. Near the ground this would make the air extremely humid and probably foggy. If the air were already close to saturation, the vapor could simply recondense into mist or new droplets and fall anyway. You would also be dumping a lot of heat into the local atmosphere, causing turbulence and convection.

So the short answer is: yes, lasers can evaporate raindrops, but using them to “stop” rain would require absurd amounts of power, create hot humid fog or steam, and pose serious safety hazards. For staying dry, an umbrella is vastly more efficient.

items.question: What If Every River in America Froze in Midsummer?
human_answers: This is another question that turns out even worse than I expected. [Image: image] For starters, pretty much every animal in the water would die.
items.original_question: 如果美国所有的河流在仲夏时节立即结冰，会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If every river in America froze in midsummer, it would be a national-scale disaster, not just an odd weather event.

Physically, rivers do not freeze in July unless enormous amounts of heat are removed. So the event would imply either a supernatural one-time freeze or a sudden climate catastrophe with temperatures far below freezing across the continent. If the air stayed cold long enough to freeze flowing rivers, crops, livestock, forests, infrastructure, and people would already be in severe danger.

The most immediate effect would be disruption of water supply. Many cities, farms, power plants, factories, and wastewater systems depend on river intake and discharge. Frozen rivers would block pumps, damage intake structures, reduce available drinking water, and interfere with sewage treatment. Firefighting, sanitation, and industrial cooling would become major problems.

Transportation and commerce would also be hit hard. The Mississippi, Ohio, Missouri, Columbia, and other major river systems carry grain, fuel, chemicals, and bulk goods. Barge traffic would stop. Ports and locks would be damaged or immobilized. Supply chains, especially for agriculture and energy, would be disrupted.

Agriculture would suffer catastrophically. Midsummer is a key growing season. If rivers froze because temperatures plunged, corn, soybeans, fruit, vegetables, and hay crops would be killed or badly damaged by frost. Irrigation systems depending on rivers would fail. Livestock would face cold stress and water shortages. Food prices would rise sharply, and emergency imports or rationing could become necessary.

Electricity production would be affected too. Hydroelectric dams could lose flow or suffer ice damage. Nuclear, coal, gas, and some industrial plants use river water for cooling; frozen intakes could force shutdowns. Grid stress would rise because people would suddenly need winter-level heating in summer while parts of the generating system failed.

Ecologically, the damage would be severe. Many fish and aquatic insects are adapted to seasonal temperature cycles. A sudden freeze would kill warm-water species, disrupt spawning, trap animals, and reduce oxygen in the water. Amphibians, birds, and mammals that depend on rivers would be hit. Riparian plants could be frost-damaged in the middle of their growing season.

When the rivers thawed, a second disaster could follow. Ice jams would cause sudden floods, damaging bridges, levees, dams, roads, and riverside towns. A rapid thaw would release backed-up water, debris, sewage, dead fish, and pollutants all at once. Flooding could be worse than the initial freeze in some places.

So the short answer is: if every American river froze in midsummer, the country would face a combined water, food, energy, transportation, ecological, and public-health emergency. If it were a brief magical freeze, the main consequences would be infrastructure damage and flooding during thaw. If it were caused by actual sustained cold, it would signal a continent-wide climate catastrophe with massive agricultural failure and widespread economic disruption.

items.question: What If You Made a Lava Lamp with Real Lava?
human_answers: This is a surprisingly reasonable idea, by What If standards. I mean, it's not that reasonable.
items.original_question: 如果我用真正的熔岩制作一盏熔岩灯会怎么样？我可以使用什么作为透明介质？我能站在多近的距离观看它？
items.model_answer:
If you tried to make a lava lamp with real lava, it would not work like a normal lava lamp and would be extremely dangerous.

Real lava is molten rock, typically about 700–1,200°C. A regular lava lamp is made of glass and contains wax, water, and other liquids that move because gentle heating changes their density. Real lava is far hotter than the glass, wax, oil, and water could survive. The glass would likely crack, soften, or shatter, while any water or volatile liquid inside would flash into steam and could cause an explosion.

Even if you built the container from high-temperature ceramic or refractory metal, it still would not behave like a decorative lava lamp. Lava is much denser and often much more viscous than lamp wax. It would tend to sit at the bottom, cool against the walls, form a crust, and eventually solidify unless continuously heated to volcanic temperatures. Any “bubbling” would come from trapped gases escaping, not from the smooth rising-and-falling blobs seen in a lava lamp.

To keep it molten, you would need an industrial furnace, not a small bulb. You would also need materials that can withstand high heat, corrosive molten silicate, thermal shock, and possible gas release. The setup would be closer to a laboratory magma experiment or foundry furnace than a lamp.

So the short answer is: a real-lava lava lamp would likely explode, shatter, or solidify. With specialized equipment, you could contain molten rock, but it would be dangerous, power-hungry, and not much like a normal lava lamp.

items.question: What If Every Child's First Laugh Created an Immortal Fairy?
human_answers: "There are always a lot of young ones," explained Wendy, who was now quite an authority, "because you see when a new baby laughs for the first time a new fairy is born, and as there are always new babies there are always new fairies. They live in nests on t...
items.original_question: 如果每个仙女都是从孩子的第一声笑声中诞生并且仙女是不朽的，那么会有多少仙女飞来飞去？
items.model_answer:
If every child’s first laugh created an immortal fairy, the biggest consequence would be that humanity would generate a new permanent intelligent population tied directly to birth rates.

A typical baby first laughs at around 3–4 months old. With roughly 130–140 million births per year today, the world would create about 130 million immortal fairies annually, assuming most children survive long enough and laugh at least once. That is about four fairies every second. If the rule had existed throughout all human history, there could already be on the order of tens of billions to over 100 billion fairies, depending on how far back it applied and how many children reached their first laugh.

Because the fairies are immortal, their population would only increase. Even if human fertility declined, the fairy population would accumulate without a natural upper limit. Over centuries this might be manageable if fairies were tiny, incorporeal, or lived in another realm. But if they had physical bodies, needed space, food, energy, or social infrastructure, the Earth would eventually face severe crowding and ecological pressure. Immortality makes the system fundamentally unstable in the long run: births add fairies, but nothing removes them.

Scientifically, the creation event would violate ordinary conservation of mass and energy unless the fairy’s matter came from somewhere. If a fairy appeared from nothing, that would be direct evidence that known physics is incomplete. If the fairy was formed from ambient matter or energy, the first laugh would become a measurable physical event: a small burst of matter conversion, energy transfer, or dimensional exchange. Hospitals and parents would likely monitor babies’ first laughs carefully.

Socially, every child would be born with the potential to create a lifelong being. A child’s first laugh would become one of the most important ceremonies in human culture. Families might celebrate it like a birth, baptism, naming day, or coming-of-age event. Governments would probably require fairy registration, especially if fairies were intelligent, powerful, or capable of affecting the physical world. Questions of legal personhood would become unavoidable: an immortal, conscious fairy could not ethically be treated as property.

The child-fairy bond would also reshape childhood. If the fairy remained connected to the child, it could become a guardian, companion, witness, or burden. Some children would grow up with an immortal protector; others might feel watched or constrained by a being created by their own joy. If fairies retained memories forever, they would become living archives of human family history, preserving languages, customs, and personal stories across millennia.

There would also be incentives and fears around laughter. Parents might try to trigger a baby’s first laugh early if fairies were beneficial, or delay it if fairies were dangerous, costly, or socially stigmatized. Medical ethics would have to decide whether inducing laughter for fairy creation was acceptable. In extreme cases, societies might regulate infant environments to control when and where fairies appear.

In the best case, immortal fairies would become humanity’s companions: caregivers, historians, ecological stewards, and bridges between generations. In the worst case, they would become an endlessly growing population of powerful, undying beings competing with humans and nature for space and influence.

So the direct answer is: every child’s first laugh creating an immortal fairy would turn laughter into a world-altering reproductive event. It would prove new physics or magic, create a rapidly accumulating immortal species, transform family life and law, and eventually force humanity to solve the problem of infinite population growth in a finite world.

items.question: What If There Were a Lake on the Moon?
human_answers: This would be so cool. In fact, I honestly think it's cool enough that it gives us a pretty good reason to go to the Moon in the first place.
items.original_question: 如果月球上有一个湖会怎样？在里面游泳会是什么感觉？假设它被隐藏在一个规则的大气层中，比如某个巨大的圆顶或其他什么地方。
items.model_answer:
An exposed lake on the Moon would not last as a liquid lake.

The Moon has essentially no atmosphere, so the pressure at the surface is near vacuum. Liquid water is only stable above a minimum pressure, about 0.006 atmospheres at the triple point. On the lunar surface, water would immediately begin to boil, even if it were cold. That boiling would remove heat rapidly, so much of the lake would quickly freeze into ice while some of it became vapor.

After that, the ice would slowly sublimate directly into gas. Sunlight and ultraviolet radiation would break some water molecules apart; hydrogen would tend to escape into space, while oxygen could react with lunar minerals or also be lost. Some water vapor might hop across the lunar surface and eventually freeze in permanently shadowed polar craters, where temperatures are extremely low.

So if you magically placed an open lake on the Moon, it would become a chaotic mixture of boiling water, fog-like vapor, and ice, then gradually disappear or migrate into cold traps. It would not remain a normal lake.

If the lake were inside a sealed, pressurized dome or if the Moon somehow had an atmosphere, then it could exist. In that case, it would look and behave strangely because lunar gravity is only about one-sixth of Earth’s. Waves would move more slowly, splashes would rise higher and travel farther, and floating or swimming would feel different, though buoyancy would still work. The lake would also be an extremely valuable resource: water could support astronauts, grow food, shield against radiation, and be split into hydrogen and oxygen for rocket fuel.

So the short answer is: an open lake on the Moon would rapidly boil, freeze, and evaporate away; a protected lake under pressure could exist and would be one of the most useful things a lunar base could have.

items.question: What If You Dropped a 7-Kilogram Bowling Ball into the Mariana Trench?
human_answers: It is a good thing you mentioned the weight, because of a very surprising fact: Most bowling balls float. It's true.
items.original_question: 您正坐在马里亚纳海沟上方的船上。如果将一个 7 公斤重的保龄球从侧面掉下来，需要多长时间才能落到底部？
items.model_answer:
A 7‑kg bowling ball dropped from a boat over the Mariana Trench would sink, not shoot downward like a rock in air.

A regulation-size bowling ball has a density only somewhat greater than seawater. In water it feels a large buoyant force, so its effective downward force is much smaller than its actual weight. After a short time it would reach a terminal sinking speed of roughly 1–2 meters per second, depending on the exact ball, surface roughness, holes, and water conditions.

The Mariana Trench is about 11,000 meters deep at Challenger Deep, so the ball would take on the order of 2 to 3 hours to reach the bottom.

At the bottom, the pressure is enormous: about 110 megapascals, or more than 1,000 atmospheres. But pressure acts from all directions, so a solid bowling ball would not be “squashed flat” dramatically. It might compress slightly, crack, or have water forced into its finger holes or any internal voids. If there were trapped air inside the holes or pores, that air would be compressed to a tiny fraction of its surface volume.

When it reached the seafloor, it would land gently compared with an object falling through air, probably disturbing some sediment and then sitting in the mud under extreme pressure and near-freezing water.

So the short answer is: it would sink slowly, take a few hours to reach the bottom, experience immense pressure, possibly suffer minor cracking or compression, and then rest on the floor of the Mariana Trench.

items.question: What If There Were Both a Space Elevator and a Stairway to Space?
human_answers: A week or two, if you're a champion stair-climber. Or 12 hours if you're on a motorcycle.
items.original_question: 如果你制造了一部可以进入太空的电梯（就像你提到的十亿层建筑中的电梯）并建造了一个向上的楼梯（假设气压受到调节），那么爬到顶部需要多长时间？
items.model_answer:
If both existed, the space elevator would be the useful one, and the stairway would mostly be a spectacularly impractical curiosity.

A literal “stairway to space” depends on what “space” means. If it only reached the Kármán line, about 100 km up, it would take roughly half a million normal-height steps. A climber would still feel almost full gravity, would need oxygen, pressure protection, heat control, and rest stations, and after reaching the top would not be in orbit; they would simply fall back down unless supported. Getting to “space” is not the same as getting to orbit.

If the stairway reached the height of a real space elevator, near geostationary orbit about 36,000 km above Earth, it would be absurd for humans to climb. It would be around 180 million steps. Even ignoring fatigue, weather, radiation, micrometeorites, and life support, the energy needed for a 70 kg person to climb to geostationary height would be several gigajoules mechanically, corresponding to millions of food calories once human inefficiency is included. It would take years at any realistic climbing pace.

Structurally, the two things are very different. A space elevator is a tension structure: a tether held taut by Earth’s rotation and a counterweight beyond geostationary orbit. A stairway or tower is a compression structure: it has to hold up its own weight from below. A 100 km tower is already far beyond ordinary engineering; a 36,000 km stairway standing from the ground is essentially impossible with known materials. If it “existed” at that scale, it would probably have to be attached to the elevator tether rather than standing on its own.

So in a world with both, people and cargo would ride the elevator. The stairway might be used for stunts, maintenance access over short sections, tourism, or symbolism, but not practical transportation. The elevator solves the main problem—reaching orbital energy gradually—while the stairway just turns space travel into the longest, most dangerous staircase climb imaginable.

items.question: What If Tug-of-War Teams Pulled on an Iron Rod Instead of a Rope?
human_answers: A couple dozen people could pull a half-inch iron rod apart. Tug-of-war, a simple game in which two teams try to pull a rope in opposite directions, has a surprisingly bloody history.
items.original_question: 拔河比赛中的两队是否有可能克服铁棒的极限抗拉强度并将其拉开？团队必须有多大？
items.model_answer:
If tug-of-war teams pulled on an iron rod instead of a rope, the basic physics would be almost the same: the contest would still be decided mostly by which team can push harder against the ground without slipping.

The rod would be in tension, just like a rope. Each team pulls on the rod, and the rod pulls back on them. If the teams pull equally and nobody slips, the rod stays nearly motionless. If one team can generate more horizontal force through better strength, footing, mass, or coordination, the whole rod-and-team system accelerates toward that side and the other team is dragged.

The main differences would come from the rod’s stiffness and strength. An iron rod stretches far less than a rope, so there would be much less “give.” Sudden jerks would be transmitted almost immediately and harshly to the other team, making people more likely to lose grip, stumble, or be injured. A rope stores noticeable elastic energy as it stretches; an iron rod stores much less visible stretch before the forces become very large.

If the rod were thick enough, it would not break and would simply transmit the pulling forces. If it were too thin, the tension could permanently stretch it, neck it, or snap it. If the teams pulled at angles or twisted it, the rod could also bend.

So the short answer is: an iron rod would make tug-of-war stiffer, more abrupt, and more dangerous, but it would not change the fundamental rule. The winning team is still the one that can exert the greater effective force against the ground without losing traction.

items.question: What If the Moon Were Replaced by a Black Hole of the Same Mass?
human_answers: "Not much" and "not much." [Image: image] A black hole the mass of the Moon would have an event horizon about the size of a sand grain. Specifically, according to one of my favorite charts (http://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2003/of03-001/htmldocs/images/chart.pdf), a...
items.original_question: 如果月球被同等质量的黑洞取代会发生什么？如果可能的话，月食会是什么样子？
items.model_answer:
If the Moon were magically replaced by a black hole with exactly the Moon’s mass, in the Moon’s current orbit and velocity, the immediate gravitational effect on Earth would be almost unchanged.

A lunar-mass black hole would have a Schwarzschild radius of only about 0.11 millimeters, so it would be smaller than a grain of sand, but its mass would still be the Moon’s mass. From Earth’s distance, gravity depends mainly on mass and distance, not on whether the mass is rock or a black hole. So Earth would not be “sucked in.” The tides would remain essentially the same, the Earth–Moon barycenter would stay essentially the same, and the object would continue orbiting Earth much like the Moon does now.

The biggest visible change would be that the Moon would disappear from the sky. There would be no moonlight, no familiar lunar phases, and no ordinary solar eclipses, because the black hole’s physical size would be far too tiny to block the Sun. It could cause extremely small gravitational-lensing effects when aligned with background stars or the Sun, but nothing dramatic to the naked eye.

It also would not rapidly consume Earth or nearby matter. Black holes do not pull harder than any other object of the same mass at the same distance. Only matter passing extremely close to the tiny event horizon would be swallowed. Accretion from dust, solar wind, or stray meteoroids would be negligible, so it would not become a bright, dangerous accretion disk. Hawking radiation from a lunar-mass black hole would also be negligible, and its lifetime would be vastly longer than the age of the universe.

Long term, Earth’s axial stability and tidal evolution would remain broadly similar because the same mass would still be orbiting Earth. Coastal tides would continue, but ecosystems and human culture tied to moonlight and lunar phases would be strongly affected.

The major caveat is formation: if the actual Moon somehow collapsed into a black hole, that process would likely be violently energetic and unrealistic. But if it were simply replaced by a same-mass black hole, the result would be surprisingly quiet: the Moon would vanish visually, while its gravity would mostly remain.

items.question: What If You Mounted a High-Power Microwave on a Car to Melt Ice?
human_answers: Believe it or not, your flamethrower idea is actually the more practical of the two. The flamethrower also has the advantage that, unlike the microwave, it won't interfere with wifi (unless you aim it directly at the router).
items.original_question: 我长期以来一直在考虑在汽车前部安装一个火焰喷射器，以便在开车穿过汽车之前融化冰雪。现在我意识到火焰喷射器不切实际，但是高功率微波发射器呢？
items.model_answer:
It would be technically possible to melt a small amount of ice with a microwave source, but mounting one on a car to clear road ice would be impractical, inefficient, and dangerous.

The main problem is power. Melting ice takes a lot of energy: about 334,000 joules per kilogram just to melt ice already at 0°C, and more if the ice is colder. A 1 cm thick sheet of ice across a 3 m lane contains roughly 25–30 kg of ice per meter of road, requiring around 9–10 megajoules per meter to melt, before losses. If the car moved even slowly, the needed microwave power would be enormous. At 10 km/h, clearing a full lane could require tens of megawatts in ideal conditions. Real systems would need even more because much of the microwave energy would reflect, scatter, or heat water unevenly.

A normal car also cannot supply that kind of power. A typical alternator produces maybe 1–3 kW of electrical power. Even a powerful electric vehicle battery could not practically sustain the hundreds of kilowatts or megawatts needed for rapid road deicing without draining itself very quickly and requiring bulky microwave hardware.

Microwaves also do not couple perfectly to ice. Pure ice is relatively transparent to common microwave frequencies compared with liquid water. Wet, salty, or dirty ice absorbs better, but then the heating tends to concentrate in thin wet layers, producing uneven melting, steam, slush, and refreezing. You might create patches of water that freeze again into black ice rather than safely clearing the road.

The safety issues are severe. A high-power microwave emitter mounted on a moving vehicle would expose pedestrians, animals, other drivers, roadside electronics, and possibly the vehicle’s own systems to hazardous radiation. It could cause burns, eye damage, interference with communications and sensors, and arcing near metal objects. A properly shielded microwave oven is safe because the radiation is enclosed; an open road-facing microwave beam would not be.

So the result would not be a practical “ice-melting car.” At low power it would barely do anything useful. At high power it would become an expensive, dangerous, likely illegal microwave emitter that might melt small patches of ice while creating new hazards. Plows, salt/brine, heated pavement, infrared heaters, or mechanical ice removal are far more practical.

items.question: What If a Falling Person Grabbed a Flagpole and Swung Back to the Roof?
human_answers: If you're like me, your first thought on hearing this question was, "That's ridiculous; there's no way that could work." Your first thought is right. But just to be sure, let's take a closer look.
items.original_question: 因此，您从镇上最高的建筑物上方的高处坠落，并且您没有降落伞。但是等等！在那座摩天大楼一侧的中间有一根旗杆伸出来，没有旗帜！你倾斜下降角度并抓住杆子足够长的时间来旋转，这样当你松开杆子时，你现在就会回到天空。当重力减慢你的速度并使你停下来时，你到达摩天大楼的顶部，在那里你伸出手将自己拉到安全的地方。这种情况发生的可能性有多大？
items.model_answer:
In principle, a falling person could grab a strong pole and swing like a pendulum, but swinging back safely onto the roof is extremely unlikely.

If the person falls a height \(h\) before grabbing the flagpole, their speed is roughly

\[
v=\sqrt{2gh}.
\]

After only a 3 m fall, that is about \(7.7\ \text{m/s}\), or 17 mph. When they grab the pole, their arms, shoulders, hands, and the pole must suddenly redirect that motion into a circular swing. The force can easily be several times body weight, with peak forces even higher because the “catch” happens over a short time. For an 80 kg person swinging on a 2 m pole after a 3 m fall, the tension-like load could be around 3,000 N or more, before accounting for the violent impact of the grab. That is enough to tear a grip loose, injure shoulders, break bones, or rip the flagpole from the wall.

There is also an energy problem. To swing back up to the roof, the person must regain nearly all the height they lost. In a perfect frictionless pendulum, if they fell 3 m before grabbing, they could at most rise about 3 m again. But in reality, grabbing the pole wastes energy through impact, muscle deformation, bending of the pole, slipping hands, and air resistance. So they would not swing back to the original roof height unless they had extra speed or an unusually favorable geometry.

So the movie-style maneuver is not strictly forbidden by physics, but it requires an ideal combination of timing, geometry, strength, grip, and pole durability. In real life, the far more likely outcomes are that the person loses their grip, dislocates or injures their arms and shoulders, breaks the flagpole, or swings into the building rather than landing neatly back on the roof.

items.question: What Would Happen to a Human Body Left in Orbit?
human_answers: This isn't really relevant, but I have to ask: Is there a reason you specifically wanted your corpse to be naked? Just making things extra weird for the technicians loading up the capsule and/or throwing you out of the airlock?
items.original_question: 我经常开玩笑说我希望将我的遗体送入轨道。不是“撒我的骨灰”的意思，而是“把我赤裸的尸体扔出气闸”的意思。老实说，我的主要动机是让遥远的未来的某人感到困惑，但这是一个有趣的科学问题：在几年、几十年或几个世纪的过程中，我在轨道上的身体会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
A human body left in orbit would keep orbiting Earth like any other object with the same velocity. It would not immediately “fall down,” and it would not float away unless given a push. What happens next depends mainly on whether the person is alive, whether they are in a spacesuit, and what altitude the orbit is.

If an unprotected living person were exposed to space, they would lose consciousness in about 10–15 seconds because there is no oxygen. They would not instantly explode or instantly freeze. The vacuum would cause gases to expand and water in exposed tissues to boil at body temperature, producing swelling and severe tissue damage. If they tried to hold their breath, lung damage could occur. Death would likely occur within a few minutes from lack of oxygen and pressure-related injuries.

After death, the body would not decay the way it does on Earth. In orbit there is no air, no liquid water supply, and little opportunity for insects or external decomposers. Internal bacteria would continue acting for a while, but the vacuum, dehydration, temperature extremes, and radiation would slow or stop ordinary decomposition. The body would gradually dry out and become mummified or freeze-dried, especially if not protected by a suit.

Temperature would be extreme but not simple. In sunlight, surfaces can heat strongly; in Earth’s shadow, they can become very cold. Because space is a vacuum, heat is lost mostly by radiation, not by air conduction, so the body would not instantly freeze. Over time, repeated heating and cooling, ultraviolet light, charged particles, and cosmic radiation would damage skin, tissues, and materials.

If the body were in a spacesuit, the suit would slow all of this. The body might remain more intact for longer, with decomposition initially occurring inside the sealed environment until oxygen, moisture, and microbial activity changed. Eventually the suit would be degraded by radiation, micrometeoroids, and thermal cycling.

The final fate depends on the orbit. In low Earth orbit, atmospheric drag would eventually slow the body down, causing it to reenter the atmosphere. During reentry it would likely burn, break apart, and be largely destroyed, much like other small biological material or debris. This could happen in months, years, or decades depending on altitude. In a higher orbit, the body could remain there for centuries or longer, slowly desiccating, radiation-damaged, and possibly fragmented by micrometeoroid impacts or collisions with debris.

items.question: What If You Dug Straight Down at One Foot per Second?
human_answers: This question is the reverse of question #64 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/64/), which asked how you'd die if you rose steadily at a foot per second. Digging at the same rate would kill you more quickly.
items.original_question: 如果我以每秒 1 英尺的速度直接向下挖掘会发生什么？什么会先杀死我？
items.model_answer:
At one foot per second, you would be going downward at about 0.305 m/s, or about 26 km per day. If nothing stopped you, you would reach Earth’s center in about 242 days and the opposite side of the planet in about 484 days, roughly 1.3 years.

In reality, you would not get very far.

The first problem is not “falling through the Earth,” but digging and keeping the hole open. Soil and rock above you would collapse unless the shaft were heavily supported. Even a modest human-sized shaft would require removing an enormous amount of material continuously. At one foot per second, you would be excavating far faster than any normal drilling operation.

Then heat becomes fatal. Earth’s temperature rises with depth, on average around 25–30°C per kilometer in the crust. After only a few kilometers, the shaft would be hot enough to be dangerous or unsurvivable without serious cooling. By around 10–12 km depth, temperatures can be hundreds of degrees Celsius; the Kola Superdeep Borehole reached about 12.3 km and encountered unexpectedly high temperatures around 180°C. At your rate, you would reach that depth in about 11 hours.

Pressure is even worse. Rock deep underground is under immense stress. At sufficient depth, tunnels do not stay open; the surrounding rock slowly flows and closes them. The mantle is mostly solid, not a liquid ocean of magma, but it behaves plastically over long times and is far too hot and pressurized for an open tunnel.

If we imagine a magical drill, perfect tunnel supports, cooling, air supply, and waste removal, then you could keep going. Gravity would gradually decrease as you approached the center of Earth. At the exact center, you would be weightless because Earth’s mass would pull equally in all directions. After passing the center, “down” would reverse: gravity would pull you back toward the center, so continuing toward the far side would require climbing or powered digging against gravity.

So the direct answer is: at one foot per second, an impossible ideal dig would take about 8 months to reach Earth’s center and about 16 months to pass through the whole planet. In the real world, heat, pressure, collapse, and excavation limits would stop you within hours to days, long before you got anywhere near the mantle, much less the center.

items.question: What If You Dropped a Submarine into Jupiter?
human_answers: Nope! Jupiter's pressure, density, and temperature curves are different from ours.
items.original_question: 如果将一艘潜艇放入木星大气层会怎样？它最终会达到漂浮的程度吗？可以导航吗？
items.model_answer:
An ordinary submarine dropped into Jupiter would be destroyed long before it reached anything resembling a “deep interior.”

Jupiter has no solid or liquid surface to splash into. Its visible “surface” is just the top of a very deep atmosphere made mostly of hydrogen and helium. If the submarine were simply dropped from space, it would enter that atmosphere at enormous speed, heat up like a spacecraft during reentry, tumble, break apart, and likely burn or fragment high in the clouds.

Even if you somehow lowered it gently into Jupiter, it would still not survive. Near the cloud tops the pressure is roughly comparable to Earth’s sea-level pressure, but gravity is about 2.5 times stronger. As it descended, the pressure and temperature would climb rapidly. A submarine is built to withstand perhaps tens to hundreds of atmospheres of pressure; Jupiter reaches those pressures not very far below the visible cloud layer. The hull would be crushed, likely imploding violently.

Deeper down, the remains would encounter hotter and denser hydrogen-helium gas. At hundreds to thousands of atmospheres and high temperatures, the wreckage would be heated, chemically attacked, melted, and eventually vaporized or dispersed. Farther inside Jupiter, hydrogen becomes a dense supercritical fluid and then metallic hydrogen under millions of atmospheres of pressure, with temperatures of thousands to tens of thousands of kelvin. No normal material or vessel could remain intact there.

If the submarine were magically indestructible and heatproof, it would not fall forever to the center. As Jupiter’s interior becomes denser, the craft would eventually reach a level where the surrounding fluid’s density matched its own, and it would become buoyant or neutrally buoyant. But an actual submarine would be crushed, torn apart, melted, and absorbed into Jupiter’s atmosphere long before that.

items.question: What Would It Be Like to Ride a Submarine into Jupiter?
human_answers: We don't know! We've only flown spacecraft into a gas planet's atmosphere twice (both Jupiter).
items.original_question: 如果你真的乘坐潜艇落入木星大气层，它实际上会是什么样子？在融化或烧毁之前你会看到什么？
items.model_answer:
Riding a submarine into Jupiter would not be like diving into an ocean. Jupiter has no solid or liquid “surface” to splash into; it is mostly hydrogen and helium that get steadily denser, hotter, and higher-pressure as you go down.

Starting near the visible cloud tops, you would enter a cold, turbulent atmosphere of ammonia and water clouds, with gravity about 2.5 times Earth’s. The winds are violent, and entry from space would require a heat shield; a normal submarine would burn up or break apart before it even began “diving.”

If somehow slowed down and sealed, the craft would descend through gas that becomes thicker and darker. Pressure would rise rapidly: at about 10 bars it is already ten times Earth sea-level pressure; at 20–25 bars conditions are hot enough and harsh enough that NASA’s Galileo probe, which entered Jupiter in 1995, stopped transmitting after about an hour. A submarine could withstand some pressure if built like a deep-sea vessel, but Jupiter’s temperature rises along with the pressure. Soon the heat, not just the crushing pressure, would destroy it.

Deeper down, hydrogen stops behaving like an ordinary gas and becomes a supercritical fluid: not a normal liquid ocean with a surface, but a dense, hot fluid. Far deeper still, under millions of atmospheres of pressure and thousands to tens of thousands of degrees, hydrogen becomes metallic. No known submarine material could survive anywhere near those conditions. The craft would be crushed, melted, chemically attacked, and eventually dissolved or mixed into Jupiter’s interior.

So the realistic answer is: you would not ride a submarine into Jupiter for long. You would see clouds and turbulence briefly, then the outside would become dark, hot, and crushing, and the submarine would fail far above anything like Jupiter’s deep interior. With impossible science-fiction materials, the trip would be a descent through increasingly dense glowing hydrogen-helium fluid, not an ocean dive, ending in an opaque, ultra-hot metallic-hydrogen world with no solid bottom to reach.

items.question: What If Earth Were Made Entirely of Protons and the Moon of Electrons?
human_answers: This is, by far, the most destructive What-If scenario to date. You might imagine an electron Moon orbiting a proton Earth, sort of like a gigantic hydrogen atom.
items.original_question: 如果地球完全由质子构成，而月球完全由电子构成怎么办？
items.model_answer:
If Earth were made entirely of protons and the Moon entirely of electrons, they would not become a strange stable planet–moon system. They would almost immediately be destroyed by electromagnetism.

Assume, for scale, that Earth keeps roughly its present mass as protons and the Moon keeps roughly its present mass as electrons. Then Earth would have a net positive charge of about

\[
Q_E \sim +6\times 10^{32}\ \text{C},
\]

and the Moon would have a net negative charge of about

\[
Q_M \sim -10^{34}\ \text{C}.
\]

Those charges are unimaginably enormous. The electric force between them at the current Earth–Moon distance would be around

\[
F \sim 10^{59}\ \text{N},
\]

whereas the real gravitational attraction between Earth and Moon is only about

\[
2\times 10^{20}\ \text{N}.
\]

So the electromagnetic attraction would be roughly \(10^{39}\) times stronger than gravity.

But even before the “proton Earth” and “electron Moon” could fall together, each object would blow itself apart. All the protons in the proton Earth repel one another; all the electrons in the electron Moon repel one another. Gravity is far too weak to hold either body together against that electric repulsion. A proton repels another proton electrically about \(10^{36}\) times more strongly than it attracts it gravitationally.

The electric fields would also be absurdly above the threshold where quantum effects become violent. They would rip pairs of particles out of the vacuum, accelerate particles to near light speed, emit intense radiation, and rapidly try to neutralize charge.

So the result would not be “Earth made of protons orbiting a Moon made of electrons.” It would be a catastrophic explosion and collapse into an intensely energetic plasma. Protons and electrons would rush together, form mostly hydrogen or ionized hydrogen plasma, release enormous radiation, and leave no recognizable Earth or Moon.

items.question: What If All Sunlight Reaching Earth Were Bundled into a 1-Meter Beam?
human_answers: Here's the situation Max is describing: [Image: image] If you were standing in the path of the beam, you would obviously die pretty quickly. You wouldn't really die of anything, in the traditional sense.
items.original_question: 如果太阳输出的所有可见光在到达地球后都被捆绑成直径约为 1m 的类似激光的光束，会怎样？
items.model_answer:
If “all sunlight reaching Earth” means all solar power intercepted by Earth’s disk, the total power is about

\[
P \approx 1361\ \text{W/m}^2 \times \pi R_\oplus^2 \approx 1.7\times 10^{17}\ \text{W}.
\]

That is roughly 174 petawatts, or about 42 megatons of TNT per second.

If that were magically bundled into a 1-meter-diameter beam, its cross-sectional area would be about \(0.785\ \text{m}^2\), so the intensity would be

\[
I \approx 2.2\times 10^{17}\ \text{W/m}^2.
\]

That is absurdly intense: billions of times brighter than the surface of the Sun. The equivalent blackbody temperature associated with that flux is around 1–2 million kelvin.

In practice, such a beam could not be made by ordinary mirrors or lenses. Conservation of optical brightness/étendue prevents passive optics from concentrating sunlight that much. You would need some impossible or active process, like converting all intercepted sunlight into a tightly collimated laser-like beam.

If it did exist and hit Earth, it would not behave like a neat shaft of light reaching the ground. The air in its path would be instantly ionized into plasma. The beam would create a blazing, expanding plasma column, enormous shock waves, and a continuous explosion at the impact region. Rock, water, or metal at the target would be vaporized and ionized. If aimed at the ocean, it could vaporize tens of billions of kilograms of water per second, producing colossal steam explosions and storms.

However, it would not instantly blow Earth apart. The power is enormous locally, but it is still “only” the sunlight Earth already intercepts, concentrated into one spot. For comparison, the energy needed to gravitationally unbind Earth is about \(10^{32}\) joules, so at \(1.7\times10^{17}\) watts it would take tens of millions of years to supply that much energy.

Globally, the rest of Earth would be dark. If the beam’s energy were eventually absorbed and reradiated, Earth’s total energy input could be similar to normal sunlight, but distributed catastrophically: one region becomes a continuous artificial sun/plasma explosion while the rest of the planet loses ordinary daylight. Weather, climate, and the atmosphere would be violently disrupted.

So the short answer is: physically impossible with normal optics; if done by magic, it would be a 174-petawatt, one-meter-wide death beam that turns the atmosphere and target into plasma, causing continuous nuclear-scale devastation at the impact site, but not instantly destroying the whole planet.
